Initially created: 2025-12-06T12:11:21.285+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
edited by imperial command.
Later Táng
Jìn Wáng Lǐ Kèyòng first received the title of Jìn.
Cúnxù succeeded to the title,
and when he ascended to the great position,
he considered himself to have inherited the empire from the Táng,
so the state was named Táng.
The Zīzhì Tōngjiàn refers to it as Hòutáng,
to distinguish it from the Táng of Cháng'ān.
Zhuāngzōng Guāngshèng Shénmǐn Xiào Huángdì (the Elder)
His taboo name was Cúnxù,
the eldest son of Jìn Wáng Kèyòng.
His ancestors were originally named Zhūxié,
descended from a separate branch of the Chùyuè tribe of the Western Tūjué,
residing in the Shātuó sands.
They called themselves Shātuó,
and used Zhūxié as their surname.
It was until Zhíyí submitted to Táng.
Zhíyí's son, Chìxīn, rendered meritorious service to Táng,
and was granted the surname and personal name Lǐ Guóchāng,
and was registered in the imperial clan records.
Kèyòng
was the son of Chìxīn.
The Wǔdài Huìyào states: Zhíyí
was the sixth-generation descendant of Báyěgǔ, the Dūdū of the Shātuó prefecture.
Ōuyáng Shǐ says: Báyěgǔ
was a contemporary of Zhūxié,
not his ancestor.
Tóngguāng first year
(guǐwèi, 923)
In April of this year, he first ascended the throne and changed the reign title.
1 Spring,
the second month,
Jìn Wáng issued an edict to establish officials,
selecting gentry families from the previous dynasty from among the judicial officers of the Four Garrisons,
intending to appoint them as chancellors.
The Four Garrisons were
Hédōng, Wèibó, Yìdìng, and Zhènjì.
Cháo,
read zhí yáo.
Xiàng,
read xī liàng;
same below.
Zhì firmly declined,
Lú Zhì openly cursed the Jìn Wáng's younger brothers,
and was also able to decline the chancellorship in a newly established court,
this must have been prescient.
The King then summoned Gé and Chéng to be appointed as Hànhtái Zuǒ and Yòucéngxiàng.
Kǎoyì states: Xuē Shǐ Táng Jì records
“Lú Chéng.”
Now following Shílù and Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn.
The Lord of Liáng sent Bīngbù Shìláng Cuī Xié and others to enfeoff Wúyuè Wáng Qián Liú as King of Wúyuè.
On dīngmǎo,
Qián Liú first established his state.
His ceremonial guards and titles were mostly in accordance with the system for an emperor.
He called his residence a palace,
his governmental offices a court,
his decrees issued within his territory "zhìchì,"
and all his generals and officials referred to themselves as subjects.
He only did not change the reign title,
and his memorials referred to his state as Wúyuè Guó without mentioning "jūn" (army/military governorship).
Having established a state,
he refused to again refer to himself as the Jiédu Shǐ of Zhènhǎi and Zhèndōng Armies.
He controlled all military and administrative affairs.
He established officials,
including chancellors, imperial secretaries, directors, supernumerary officials, and officials of the guest department.
2 Lǐ Jìtāo, though appointed as Ānyì Liúhòu by Jìn Wáng,
this matter is detailed in the previous volume from the previous year.
His staff officer Wèi Zhuó and牙 General Shēn Méng further instigated him
saying:
“The Jìn court has no capable people,
and will eventually be annexed by Liáng.”
When Jìn Wáng established officials,
in the third month,
he summoned Supervisor Zhāng Jūhàn.
Zhāng Jūhàn,
during the time of Táng Zhāozōng, was Supervisor of Fànyáng.
In the Tiānfù era, when eunuchs were massacred,
Jiédu Shǐ Liú Réngōng hid Jūhàn in the North Stream of Mount Dà'ān to save him.
Later, when Liáng troops attacked Réngōng,
he sent Jūhàn to follow Jìn Wáng in attacking Liáng's Lùzhōu to divert their forces.
Jìn then captured Lùzhōu,
and consequently appointed Jūhàn as Supervisor of Zhāoyì.
Zhuó and Méng again persuaded Jìtāo saying:
“The King urgently summoned these two,
his intentions are clear.”
Jìtāo's younger brother Jìyuǎn also advised Jìtāo to entrust himself to Liáng.
Jìtāo then sent Jìyuǎn to Dàliáng
to request that Zélù be made a vassal of Liáng.
The Lord of Liáng was overjoyed,
and renamed the Ānyì Army Kuāngyì,
appointing Jìtāo as Jiédu Shǐ and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Jìtāo offered his two sons as hostages.
Péi Yuē, an old general of Ānyì, was garrisoned in Zézhōu.
He tearfully addressed his troops saying:
“I have served my late master for over two decades,
‘late master’ refers to Jìtāo's father, Sìzhāo.
Twelve years make one jì.
Shǐ,
read shū lì.
My ambition was to destroy our enemies.
Unfortunately, he passed away,
death is referred to as ‘juān guǎn,’
meaning to abandon one's residence and depart.
Yet the young master suddenly betrays his lord and kin,
abandoning his lord to serve an enemy.
This is not only betraying his lord,
but also betraying the teachings of his kin.”
Bèi,
read pú mèi.
So he held the prefecture and defended himself.
The Lord of Liáng appointed his valiant general Dǒng Zhāng as Zézhōu Cìshǐ,
leading troops to attack him.
Jìtāo dispersed wealth to recruit soldiers.
Guō Wēi, a man from Yáoshān, came to enlist.
Wēi, in a fit of temper, killed someone
and was imprisoned. Jìtāo, valuing his talent and bravery, released him.
This is the beginning of Guō Wēi's story.
The Ōu Shǐ says: Wēi once wandered in the market.
There was a butcher in the market
who dominated the market people with his bravery.
Wēi, drunk, called the butcher to step forward and cut meat.
The cutting was not done properly,
Wēi shouted at him.
The butcher exposed his belly and said:
“You brave man,
can you kill me?”
Wēi immediately stepped forward, took a knife, and stabbed him to death.
The entire market was shocked,
but Wēi remained composed.
He was arrested by officials,
but Jìtāo released him to escape.
3 The Khitans raided Yōuzhōu.
Jìn Wáng asked Guō Chóngtāo for a commander.
Chóngtāo recommended Lí Cúnshěn, Jiédu Shǐ of Hénghǎi.
At that time, Cúnshěn was ill in bed.
On jǐmǎo,
Cúnshěn was transferred to be Jiédu Shǐ of Lúlóng,
and was carried in his illness to the garrison.
Lǐ Sìyuán, Vice Commander-in-chief of Fānhàn Cavalry and Infantry, was appointed to lead as Jiédu Shǐ of Hénghǎi.
At that time, Lǐ Sìyuán was leading troops with Jìn Wáng,
and was made to lead Hénghǎi Command.
4 Jìn Wáng built an altar south of the garrison city of Wèizhōu.
Summer,
fourth month,
on jǐsì,
he ascended the altar,
offered sacrifices to the Emperor on High,
and then ascended the imperial throne.
The word ‘then’ indicates
that he had long harbored the intention of ascending the throne,
and now accomplished it.
He declared a general amnesty
and changed the reign title.
Following the Táng state name,
he changed the Tiānyòu reign title to Tóngguāng.
His legal mother, Qínguó Fūrén Liú Shì, became Empress Dowager.
Gentlemen thus knew that the Emperor would not endure to the end.
Lú Chéng became Zhōngshū Shìláng,
and also Tóng Píngzhāngshì;
Guō Chóngtāo and Zhāng Jūhàn became Shūmì Shǐ.
Xú Wúdǎng said: Shūmì Shǐ,
according to Táng precedents, was held by eunuchs.
Its office was very minor.
It was not until this time that scholars began to participate,
and their power became equal to that of the prime ministers.
I observe that in the late Táng, the two Shūmì and the two Shéncè Zhōngwèi
were known as the Four Nobles.
Their positions were not very minor.
They were just exclusively held by eunuchs.
Xiàng Ānshì said: Táng set up five rooms behind the Zhèngshìtáng,
with the Shūmì Fáng in charge of administrative affairs.
Thus, the importance of Shūmì
was managed by the prime ministers and was never entrusted to others.
Later, as eunuchs gained favor,
the Shūmì position began to be assigned to the court attendants.
Zhāng Xiàn became Gōngbù Shìláng and Zūyōng Shǐ.
Sòng Bái said: The Zūyōng Shǐ position began with Wéi Jiān in Tiānbǎo third year.
Déxiū
was the grandson of Jiàng.
Lǐ Jiàng was a chancellor under Táng Xiànzōng
and was known for his uprightness.
An edict ordered Lú Chéng (盧程) to go to Jìnyáng (晉陽) to enfeoff the Empress Dowager and the Empress.
Originally,
the Empress had no sons,
and her nature was virtuous,
not jealous;
the Empress Dowager had been a concubine of Emperor Wǔ (武皇),
and the Empress often advised Emperor Wǔ to treat her well.
Jìn Wáng (晉王) Kèyòng (克用) posthumously named him Emperor Wǔ.
Because of this, they got along very happily.
When she received the enfeoffment,
the Empress went to the Empress Dowager's palace to congratulate her,
with a joyous expression,
but the Empress Dowager was uneasy and embarrassed.
The Empress said:
"May my son enjoy the kingdom for a long time,
and may we be buried in the earth,
our imperial tombs having masters;
what else is there to speak of!"
Thereupon, they sighed together.
Dòulú Gé (豆盧革) and Lú Chéng (盧程) were both superficial and without other abilities.
The Emperor employed them because they were
from prominent families and were
senior officials in the霸府 (Bàfǔ, Hegemon's Administration).
According to Oū Shǐ (歐史),
the Dòulú (豆盧) family was a renowned clan,
and Gé's father, Zàn (瓚), was the prefect of Shūzhōu (舒州) during the Táng (唐) dynasty.
During the chaos at the end of the Táng dynasty,
Gé fled to Zhōngshān (中山)
and became Wáng Chǔzhí's (王處直) judicial officer.
Lú Chéng's (盧程) family background is unknown.
During the reign of Táng Zhāozōng (唐昭宗), he passed the imperial examination
and became a salt and iron inspector.
At the end of the Táng dynasty, he fled the chaos,
changed his clothes to that of a Daoist priest,
and traveled between Yān (燕) and Zhào (趙).
Dòulú Gé (豆盧革) was the judicial officer of the Yìwǔ (義武) Jìedùshǐ (節度使),
and Lú Rǔbì (盧汝弼) was the deputy commissioner of the Hédōng (河東) Jìedùshǐ.
Both were prominent families from the former Táng dynasty,
and their status was equal to Chéng's.
Thus, they jointly recommended him as the investigative officer of the Hédōng Jìedùshǐ.
The Emperor discussed choosing a chancellor,
but the former prominent families of Táng imperial officials had almost all perished in the chaos.
Lú Rǔbì (盧汝弼) and Sū Xún (蘇循) had already died,
and Lú Zhì (盧質) had declined,
so Gé (革) and Chéng (程) were employed.
For a founding monarch,
to appoint chancellors in this manner,
the state of affairs in the realm can be imagined.
Initially,
Lǐ Shàohóng (李紹宏) was the Chief of the Palace Gate,
with Guō Chóngtāo (郭崇韜) as his deputy.
By this time,
he was recalled from Yōuzhōu (幽州).
In the fifth year of Zhēnmíng (貞明) of the Liáng (梁) dynasty,
Lǐ Shàohóng's (李紹宏) affair in Yōuzhōu is mentioned in the previous volume.
He then recommended Zhāng Jūhàn (張居翰) as Chief of the Bureau of Military Affairs,
making Shàohóng (紹宏) the Commissioner of the Bureau of Meritorious Service.
Shàohóng (紹宏) resented him for this.
According to the Táng system,
the Commissioner of the Bureau of Meritorious Service was below the Chief of the Bureau of Military Affairs,
and his power and authority were far inferior.
Chóngtāo (崇韜) managed all military and state affairs.
Kǒng Qiān (孔謙), the Commissioner of Finance, considered himself talented, diligent, and effective,
and believed he should be the Commissioner of Tribute and Taxation;
public opinion held that Qiān (謙) was of humble origins and low status,
and should not suddenly take on such a heavy responsibility.
Kǒng Qiān (孔謙)
was a clerk from Wèizhōu (魏州).
When Jìn Wáng (晉王) gained Wèizhōu,
he appointed him Commissioner of Finance.
Qiān (謙) was made his deputy,
and Qiān (謙) was also displeased.
Wèizhōu (魏州) was designated Xīngtáng Fǔ (興唐府),
and the Eastern Capital was established;
Xuē Jūzhèng's (薛居正) History of the Five Dynasties states: Upon the enthronement of Jìn Wáng (晉王),
Wèizhōu was elevated to Xīngtáng Fǔ, the Eastern Capital,
Yuánchéng (元城) was renamed Xīngtáng Xiàn (興唐縣),
and Guìxiāng (貴鄉) was renamed Guǎngjìn Xiàn (廣晉縣).
Zhènzhōu (鎮州) was also designated Zhēndìng Fǔ (真定府),
and the Northern Capital was established.
Wáng Zhèngyán (王正言), the judicial officer of the Wèibó (魏博) Jìedùshǐ, was appointed Minister of Rites
and acting governor of Xīngtáng (興唐);
Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥), the Grand Marshal of Cavalry and Infantry in Tàiyuán (太原), was appointed governor of Tàiyuán
and concurrently Deputy Regent of the Western Capital;
Rèn Yuán (任圜), the investigative officer of the Lùzhōu (潞州) Observership, was appointed Minister of Works
and concurrently governor of Zhēndìng (真定),
concurrently Deputy Regent of the Northern Capital;
"京" (jīng),
should be
And concurrently presided over the affairs of the Six Armies and various guards.
According to the Later Táng (後唐), Luòyáng (洛陽) had the Xī Gōng Xīngshèng Gōng (西宮興聖宮).
At this time, Luòyáng had not yet been acquired,
so the Wèizhōu prefectural office was probably designated as Xīngshèng Gōng (興聖宮).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Táng Zhuāngzōng (唐莊宗) was enthroned in Wèizhōu,
and Chancellor Dòulú Gé (豆盧革) then proposed designating it as Xīngshèng Gōng,
with imperial son Jìjí (繼岌) as the Commissioner of Xīngshèng Gōng.

The thirteen Jìedùshǐ were: Tiānxíong (天雄), Chéngdé (成德), Yìwǔ (義武), Hénghǎi (橫海), Lúlóng (盧龍), Dàtóng (大同), Zhènbǔ (振武), Yànmén (鴈門), Hédōng (河東), Hùguó (護國), Jìnjiàng (晉絳), Ānguó (安國), and Zhāoyì (昭義).
Fifty prefectures:

Wèi (魏), Bó (博), Bèi (貝), Chán (澶), Xiāng (相), Yùn (鄆), Míng (洺), Cí (磁), Zhèn (鎮), Jì (冀), Shēn (深), Zhào (趙), Yì (易), Qí (祁), Dìng (定), Cāng (滄), Jǐng (景), Dé (德), Yíng (瀛), Mò (莫), Yōu (幽), Zhuó (涿), Tán (檀), Jì (薊), Shùn (順), Yíng (營), Píng (平), Wèi (蔚), Shuò (朔), Yún (雲), Yìng (應), Xīn (新), Guī (媯), Rú (儒), Wǔ (武), Xīn (忻), Dài (代), Lán (嵐), Shí (石), Xiàn (憲), Lín (麟), Fǔ (府), Bìng (幷), Fén (汾), Cí (慈), Xí (隰), Zé (澤), Lù (潞), Qìn (沁), Liáo (遼),
in total fifty prefectures.
However, Zhāoyì (昭義) governed Zé (澤) and Lù (潞) two prefectures,
which had already submitted to Liáng (梁),
so there were only twelve Jìedùshǐ and forty-eight prefectures remaining.
In the intercalary month,
Emperor Wǔ's great-great-grandfather, Zhíyí (執宜), was posthumously honored as Yìzǔ Zhāoliè Huángdì (懿祖昭烈皇帝);
his grandfather, Guóchāng (國昌), as Xiànzǔ Wénhuángdì (獻祖文皇帝);
and his father, Jìn Wáng (晉王), as Tàizǔ Wǔhuángdì (太祖武皇帝).
An ancestral temple was established in Jìnyáng (晉陽),
with Gāozǔ (高祖), Tàizōng (太宗), Yìzōng (懿宗), Zhāozōng (昭宗), and Yìzǔ (懿祖) and those below him, making seven shrines.
There were four Táng (唐) temples,
and three ancestral temples.
On the Jiǎwǔ (甲午) day of the 5th month,
the Qìdān (契丹) raided Yōuzhōu (幽州),
reached Yìdìng (易定) and then returned.
At that time, the Qìdān (契丹) frequently invaded,
plundering provisions and transport supplies.
Yōuzhōu (幽州) had less than half a year's food supply,
Wèizhōu (衞州) had been taken by Liáng (梁),
and Lùzhōu (潞州) had internally rebelled.
The morale of the people was precarious,
believing that Liáng (梁) could not yet be taken.
The Emperor was troubled by this.
Coincidentally, Lú Shùnmì (盧順密), a general from Yùnzhōu (鄆州), defected.
Previously, Dài Sīyuǎn (戴思遠), the Tiānpíng (天平) Jìedùshǐ of Liáng (梁), was stationed at Yángcūn (楊村).
Dài Sīyuǎn's (戴思遠) stationing at Yángcūn is mentioned in the previous volume, fifth year of Zhēnmíng (貞明) of Liáng (梁).
Formerly,
悉薦翻 (xī jiàn fān).
Shùnmì (順密) said to the Emperor:
"The garrison in Yùnzhōu (鄆州) is less than a thousand men.
Suí Yán (遂嚴) and Yán Yǒng (燕顒) have both lost popular support.
It can be taken by surprise attack."
Guō Chóngtāo (郭崇韜) and others all believed,
"A distant attack by an isolated army,
if it fails,
would be a waste of several thousand men.
Shùnmì (順密) should not be heeded."
The Emperor secretly summoned Lǐ Sìyuán (李嗣源) to his tent and consulted him, saying:
"The Liáng (梁) people's ambition is to swallow Zé (澤) and Lù (潞),
and they are unprepared in the east.
If we take Dōngpíng (東平),
we will shatter their heartland.
Can Dōngpíng (東平) truly be taken?"
Yùnzhōu (鄆州) was originally Dōngpíng Jùn (東平郡).
This matter is found in volume 270, fourth year of Zhēnmíng (貞明) of Liáng (梁).
He replied:
"Warfare has lasted for years,
and the common people are exhausted.
Unless we achieve victory through an unexpected maneuver,
how can great success be accomplished?
I am willing to undertake this campaign alone;
I will surely report success."
The Emperor was pleased.
On the Rén Yín (壬寅) day,
Sìyuán (嗣源) was sent to lead five thousand elite soldiers from his command from Déshèng (德勝) towards Yùnzhōu (鄆州).
By the time they reached Yángliú (楊劉),
it was already dusk,
and the road was dark with rain.
The officers and soldiers were all unwilling to advance.
Gāo Xíngzhōu (高行周) said:
"This is heaven helping us;
they will surely be unprepared."
That night,
they crossed the river and reached the city wall.
The people of Yùn (鄆) were unaware.
This was a shortcut from Yángliú (楊劉) directly to the foot of Yùnzhōu (鄆州) city,
not passing through the seat of Dōng'ē Xiàn (東阿縣).
They killed the guards,
opened the gates to let in the outside troops,
and advanced to attack the inner city (yáchéng).
There was great chaos in the city.
At dawn on the Guǐmǎo (癸卯) day,
Sìyuán's (嗣源) troops all entered,
and then captured the inner city.
Liú Suíyán (劉遂嚴) and Yān Yǒng (燕顒) fled to Dàliáng (大梁).
Sìyuán (嗣源) forbade burning and plundering,
appeased the officials and people,
and apprehended the Prefectural Governor, Jìedùshǐ (節度使) Deputy Cuī Dāng (崔簹), and judicial officer Zhào Fèng (趙鳳), sending them to Xīngtáng (興唐).
The Emperor was greatly pleased, saying:
"The Commander-in-Chief is truly a remarkable talent;
my affairs are accomplished."
He immediately appointed Sìyuán (嗣源) as the Tiānpíng (天平) Jìedùshǐ.
The Lord of Liáng, hearing that Yùnzhōu had fallen,
was greatly alarmed.
He executed Liú Suíyán and Yān Yóng in the marketplace,
dismissed Dài Sīyuǎn as Recruiter-Commissioner,
and demoted him to Acting Military Governor of Xuānhuà.
Ōu Shǐ's *Zhífāng Kǎo* states
that Liáng established the Xuānhuà Army in Dèngzhōu.
He hastened to order them to advance and fight.
Jìng Xiáng knew that the Liáng dynasty was in peril.
He put a rope into his boot,
went to see the Lord of Liáng, and said,
"The late emperor conquered the realm.
He did not consider me unworthy,
and all my plans were adopted.
Now the enemy's power is increasing,
yet Your Majesty disregards my words.
I am useless;
it would be better to die."
He pulled out the rope, intending to hang himself.
The Lord of Liáng stopped him
and asked what he wanted to say.
Xiáng said,
"The situation is urgent!
Unless Wáng Yànzhāng is appointed as the great general,
it cannot be saved."
Jìng Xiáng chose Wáng Yànzhāng merely because of his temporary bravery in combat.
Observing his use of troops, he lacked foresight.
How could he be sufficient to save Liáng from its downfall!
Wáng Yànzhāng was appointed to replace Sīyuǎn as the Northern Recruiter-Commissioner,
with Duàn Níng as his deputy.
The Emperor heard of this,
and personally led the imperial guards to garrison Chánzhōu.
He ordered Zhū Shǒuyīn, the Imperial Commissioner of Cavalry and Infantry of both Fān and Hàn, to defend Déshèng,
cautioning him, saying,
"Wáng Tiěqiāng is brave and decisive.
Driven by his indignant spirit,
he will surely make a sudden assault.
You must be well prepared!"
The *Guǎngyùn* states
that "tángtū"
is written as
" [AS-FEFD] [AS-FBED] tángtū"
or as
"dàngtū."
Táng and dàng have the same meaning.
History says that King Jìn was good at anticipating Wáng Yànzhāng
but not good at employing people to defend Déshèng.
He was a household servant since his youth.
Ōu Shǐ said: Zhū Shǒuyīn served the Emperor as a slave in his youth,
named Huì'ér.
When the Emperor read,
Huì'ér always attended at his side.
The Emperor also sent an envoy to the King of Wú
to inform him that Yùnzhōu had been conquered and
requested that they jointly raise troops to attack Liáng.
In the fifth month,
the envoy arrived in Wú.
Xú Wēn wanted to play both sides,
intending to lead his fleet north along the coast
to assist the victor.
Yán Kěqiú said,
"If the Liáng people invite us to land to provide aid,
how shall we refuse?"
Wēn then stopped.
The Lord of Liáng summoned Wáng Yànzhāng and asked him for the date of defeating the enemy.
Yànzhāng replied,
"Three days."
Everyone around him burst into laughter.
From Dàliáng, an army would take more than three days to reach the Héshàng to resist Jìn,
hence they laughed at his words.
Two days later,
he galloped to Huázhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Dàliáng is 210 *lǐ* north of Huázhōu.
On the *xīnyǒu* day,
he held a grand banquet,
secretly sending people to prepare boats at Yángcūn.
At night,
he ordered six hundred armored soldiers,
all carrying large axes,
loaded with blacksmiths,
equipped with bellows and charcoal,
to sail downstream.
Yángcūn is only eighteen *lǐ* downstream towards Déshèng.
Bellows (*bèi*),
pronounced *púbài*,
are leather bags
used to blow fire.
Yànzhāng pretended to change clothes
and led several thousand elite soldiers along the south bank of the Yellow River towards Déshèng.
It was drizzling slightly,
and Zhū Shǒuyīn was unprepared.
The troops on the boats raised their locks and burned them to break them,
then used large axes to cut the pontoon bridge.
Yànzhāng then led his troops in a swift attack on the South City.
With the pontoon bridge broken,
the South City was quickly captured.
It was exactly three days since he received his orders.
Shǒuyīn used small boats to ferry armored soldiers across the river to reinforce it,
but it was too late.
Yànzhāng advanced to attack Pānzhāng, Májiākǒu, and Jǐngdiàn camps,
all of which he captured.
The two families of Pān and Zhāng lived in the same village,
hence the name.
Diàn is pronounced *dūniàn*.
Cuī Bào's *Gǔjīn Zhù* says: *Diàn* is
where goods are stored and sold.
Someone named Jǐng once set up an inn there,
hence the name.
All of these were vital river crossings,
which the Jìn people had fortified with camps.
The Emperor dispatched the eunuch Jiāo Yànbīn to quickly proceed to Yángliú,
to defend it staunchly with the garrison commander Lǐ Zhōu.
He ordered Shǒuyīn to abandon Déshèng North City,
dismantle houses to make rafts,
load weapons and equipment onto them, and float them downstream,
to assist in the defense of Yángliú.
He moved the fodder, grain, firewood, and charcoal to Chánzhōu,
losing almost half of it.
Wáng Yànzhāng also dismantled the materials from the South City houses and floated them down the river.
Each side traveled along one bank.
Whenever they encountered a bend,
they would engage in combat in the middle of the river,
with arrows raining down like a deluge.
Sometimes entire boats would capsize.
They fought a hundred battles in one day,
with alternating victories and defeats.
By the time they reached Yángliú,
nearly half of the soldiers had been lost.
This refers to the soldiers who floated downstream from Déshèng.
On the *jǐsì* day,
Wáng Yànzhāng and Duàn Níng, with an army of one hundred thousand, attacked Yángliú,
advancing from a hundred directions simultaneously,
ceaselessly day and night.
They linked nine large warships
and stretched them across the river crossing to cut off reinforcements.
The city nearly fell several times,
but Lǐ Zhōu bravely resisted with all his might,
sharing hardships with his soldiers.
Yànzhāng could not conquer it,
so he retreated to encamp south of the city,
forming continuous camps to besiege it.
Yángliú sent an urgent message to the Emperor,
requesting that he travel one hundred *lǐ* a day to reach them.
The Emperor was in Chénzhōu,
nearly two hundred *lǐ* from Yángliú.
He said:
“Lǐ Zhōu is within,
what is there to worry about!”
He traveled sixty *lǐ* a day,
without neglecting hunting.
In the sixth month,
on the *Yǐhài* day,
he arrived at Yángliú.
The Liáng soldiers' trenches and ramparts were complex and numerous,
so formidable that they could not be entered.
The Emperor was troubled by this and
asked Guō Chóngtāo for a plan.
He replied:
“Currently, Yánzhāng holds the crucial ford,
believing he can easily take Dōngpíng.
If the main army does not go south,
then Dōngpíng will not be defensible.
Your servant requests to build a rampart on the east bank of Bózhōu to secure the river ford,
which will not only allow us to respond to and support Dōngpíng,
but also divide the enemy's military strength.
However, I fear that if Yánzhāng learns of it
and directly comes to attack us,
the city cannot be completed.
I wish Your Majesty would recruit soldiers willing to die,
and order them to challenge the enemy daily to hold him in check.
If Yánzhāng does not go east for ten days,
then the city will be complete.”
At this time, Lǐ Sìyuán was defending Yùnzhōu,
and communication from north of the river was cut off.
People's hearts were gradually alienated,
and their safety was not guaranteed even for a morning or evening.
Coincidentally, Kāng Yánxiào, the Commander of the Right Vanguard of Liáng, secretly requested to surrender to Sìyuán.
Yánxiào was
a Hú person from Tàiyuán.
The Ouyáng history states:
Kāng Yánxiào was from Dàiběi,
a soldier in Tàiyuán.
He committed a crime
and fled to Liáng.
Having fled to Liáng,
he was then under the command of Duàn Níng.
Sìyuán sent his *yāyá* Fàn Yánguāng of Línzhāng to deliver Yánxiào's wax-sealed letter to the Emperor.
Yánguāng then spoke to the Emperor, saying:
“Yángliú is now firmly controlled and fortified,
the Liáng people will certainly not be able to take it.
I request to build a rampart at Mǎjiākǒu to open the road to Yùnzhōu.”
The Emperor agreed,
and sent Chóngtāo with ten thousand men to depart at night,
traveling at double speed towards Bózhōu.
They crossed the river at Mǎjiākǒu,
building the city day and night without rest.
Mǎjiākǒu
is what is called the east bank of Bózhōu.
Guō Chóngtāo departed from Yángliú at night,
traveling at double speed,
because he feared the Liáng people would know of it.
He fought bitterly day and night with the Liáng people.
Chóngtāo built the new city in a total of six days.
Wáng Yánzhāng heard of it,
and brought tens of thousands of soldiers, rushing to the site.
On the *Wùzǐ* day,
he fiercely attacked the new city,
linking more than ten large ships in the middle of the river to cut off the path for reinforcements.
At that time, the plank-and-rammed-earth construction was only just finished,
the city walls were still low,
the sand and earth were loose and poor,
and there were no watchtowers or defenses.
Chóngtāo comforted and encouraged the soldiers,
leading them by example.
He resisted the attacks on all sides,
and sent a secret envoy to report the emergency to the Emperor.
The Emperor led his main army from Yángliú to rescue them,
deploying on the west bank of the new city.
Seeing this from inside the city, their morale rose,
and they loudly shouted at the Liáng army.
The Liáng people cut their ropes and gathered their ships.
The Emperor moored his boats, about to cross.
Yánzhāng lifted the siege
and retreated to Zōujiākǒu.
Májiākǒu, Mǎjiākǒu, and Zōujiākǒu
were all river fords.
They were also named after the surnames of the local inhabitants.
Lǐ Sìyuán secretly submitted a memorial requesting to punish Zhū Shǒuyīn for the crime of losing his army;
the Emperor did not comply.
The Emperor did not execute Zhū Shǒuyīn,
which led to the disaster of Jiàngxiāodiàn.
7 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the *Dīngwèi* day,
the Emperor led his troops south along the river.
Yánzhāng and others abandoned Zōujiākǒu
and returned to Yángliú.
On the *Jiǎyín* day,
the scouting general Lǐ Shàoxīng defeated Liáng scouting troops south of Qīngqiūyì.
Duàn Níng believed that the Táng troops had already crossed the river from upstream,
and was startled and changed color,
openly rebuking Yánzhāng,
especially for his deep penetration.
Duàn Níng heard of the defeat at Qīngqiūyì,
and believed that the Táng troops had already crossed the river from upstream and were pressing towards Biàn,
while Yánzhāng and others were still confronting Táng downstream.
He blamed them for penetrating deep into Yùnzhōu territory,
providing no help for the danger in Dàliáng.
Historians say that Duàn Níng relied on internal connections and therefore disrespected the chief commander.
*Shù*
is pronounced as *fān*.
8 On the *Yǐmǎo* day,
Wèi Wáng Zōngkǎn, the Shǔ侍中, died.
9 On the *Wùwǔ* day,
the Emperor sent the cavalry general Lǐ Shàoróng directly to the Liáng camp,
capturing their scouts.
The Liáng people became even more fearful.
He also used fire rafts to burn their linked ships.
Linked ships
refers to those arranged in the river to cut off reinforcements.
On the *Jǐwèi* day,
the siege of Yángliú was lifted.
They fled to defend Yángcūn;
the Táng troops pursued them,
and then garrisoned at Déshèng.
The Liáng troops had previously fiercely attacked various cities.
Nearly ten thousand soldiers suffered from arrows and stones, drowned, or died of heatstroke.
The abandoned supplies, armor, weapons, and tents
amounted to thousands.
By the time the siege of Yángliú was lifted,
the city had been without food for three days.
10 Wáng Yánzhāng resented Zhào and Zhāng for their misrule.
When he became the Commissioner of Campaigns,
he told his confidants:
“When I return successful,
I shall execute all treacherous officials to apologize to the world!”
Zhào and Zhāng heard this,
and privately said to each other:
“We would rather die at the hands of the Shātuó
than be killed by Yánzhāng.”
They collaborated to undermine him.
Duàn Níng had always resented Yánzhāng's ability and flattered Zhào and Zhāng.
In the army, he constantly opposed Yánzhāng,
obstructing him in every possible way,
only fearing that he might succeed.
He secretly watched for Yánzhāng's mistakes to report them to the Liáng ruler.
Whenever a victory report arrived,
Zhào and Zhāng attributed all credit to Níng.
Thus, Yánzhāng's achievements were never realized.
Upon his return to Yángcūn,
the Liáng ruler, believing slanderous reports,
still feared that Yánzhāng might succeed overnight and become uncontrollable,
so he summoned him back to Dàliáng.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The Ouyáng history states:
“The Last Emperor dismissed Yánzhāng and
appointed Duàn Níng as Commissioner of Campaigns.
Yánzhāng rushed to the capital and had an audience.
He drew on the ground with his tablet,
explaining the course of victories and defeats.
Yán and others prompted the officials to impeach Yánzhāng for disrespect,
ordering him to return to his residence.”
We now follow the *Shílù*.
On the *Jiǎzǐ* day,
the Emperor arrived at Yángliú and praised Lǐ Zhōu, saying:
“Without your excellent defense,
my affairs would have failed.”
11 Lú Chéng, the Vice Director of the Chancellery and concurrently Grand Councilor, interfered in a private matter concerning Xīngtáng Fǔ.
When the prefectural official could not comply,
he whipped the official's back.
Rèn Tuán, the Grand Master of Ceremonies and concurrently Deputy Prefect of Xīngtáng,
who was Yuán's younger brother
and the Emperor's cousin's husband,
went to Chéng to complain about it.
Chéng cursed him, saying:
“What kind of insect are you,
trying to rely on your wife's influence?!”
Tuán complained to the Emperor.
The Emperor angrily said:
“I mistakenly appointed this idiot,
and he dares to insult my Nine Ministers!”
He wanted to bestow self-execution upon him.
Lú Zhì strenuously interceded for him,
so he was demoted to Right Household Administrator.
18 The emperor was at Cháochéng.
Liáng’s Duàn Níng advanced to the south of Línhé.
This was to the south of Línhé County, Wèizhōu.
According to the Suí Zhì,
Línhé County was established in the sixth year of Kāihuáng.
According to the Xīn Tángshū Dìlǐ Zhì,
in the seventeenth year of Zhēnguān, Chánshuǐ County was abolished and merged into it.
Chánshuǐ was Chányuān,
but to avoid the personal name of Gāozǔ,
the character
“yuān”
was changed
to “shuǐ.”
Línhé
and Chányuān,
their locations were probably close.
Sòng Bái said: Línhé County was originally Dōnglí County.
During the Xiàochāng reign of the Wèi, Jǐjùn Commandery was divided to establish Líyángjùn Commandery,
which administered Líyáng, Dōnglí, and Dùnqiū three counties.
This was Dōnglí.
Suí established Línhé County in the fifth year of Kāihuáng.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Línhé County is sixty lǐ west of Chánzhōu.
There were daily raids.
West of Chánzhōu
is south of Xiāngzhōu.
Millions of bundles of forage and grain were lost.
The Deputy Commissioner of Rent and Taxation, Kǒng Qiān, levied excessive taxes to supply the army,
causing many common people to flee.
Rent and taxes became even scarcer,
and the accumulated stores in the granaries could not last for half a year.
Zélù had not yet been subdued.
Lú Wénjìn and Wáng Yù led Khitans to repeatedly pass south of Yíng and Zhuó.
This refers to the Khitan invasion of Zhèn and Dìng territories in the second year of Liáng Lóngdé.
They penetrated deeply to raid.
Furthermore, it was heard that the Liáng people intended to launch a large-scale multi-pronged invasion.
This was Kāng Yánxiào’s statement.
He summoned all the generals for a meeting.
The Commissioner of Xuanhui, Lǐ Shàohóng, and others all believed that everything outside the city gates of Yùnzhōu was enemy territory,
and it was isolated and difficult to defend.
It was better to not have it than to have it.
They requested to exchange it for Wèizhōu and Líyáng with Liáng.
Liáng took Wèizhōu;
see the previous volume, previous year.
In the second year of Zhēnmíng, Jìn took all of Héběi,
but Líyáng alone was held by Liáng.
They proposed to use the river as a border,
cease military operations, and allow the people to rest,
wait for financial resources to accumulate slightly,
and then plan for a future campaign.
The emperor was displeased
and said:
“If this is the case, I will have no burial ground.”
He then dismissed the generals
and summoned Guō Chóngtāo alone to consult him.
Guō replied:
“Your Majesty has not combed your hair or bathed,
nor taken off your armor,
for over fifteen years.
In the second year of Liáng Tàizǔ’s Kāipíng reign,
the emperor succeeded to the title of Prince of Jìn and began fighting at Jiāzhài.
By this year, he had been in military service for seventeen years.
‘Jie’ (櫛)
is pronounced cè sè fān.
Now you have formally assumed the imperial title,
and the gentry and common people of Héběi daily look forward to peace and prosperity.
Having just gained even an inch of land like Yùnzhōu,
if you cannot defend it and abandon it,
how can you hope to completely possess the Central Plains?
Your servant fears that the officers and soldiers will become disheartened.
In the future, when provisions run out and the masses disperse,
even if you draw the river as a boundary,
who will defend it for Your Majesty?
Your servant once thoroughly inquired Kāng Yánxiào about the affairs of Hénán.
Weighing our own situation against theirs,
and pondering day and night,
the key to success or failure will be decided this year.
Liáng has now given all its elite troops to Duàn Níng,
who occupies our southern border.
They have also dammed the river to secure themselves.
Duàn Níng dammed the river from Suānzǎo to flow into Yùnzhōu to restrict Táng forces,
calling it the ‘Escort Water.’
Relying on this, they no longer make preparations.
They send Wáng Yànzhāng to invade and press Yùnzhōu,
hoping that disloyal individuals might cause unrest
and a change would arise from within.
Duàn Níng is fundamentally not a general's material;
he cannot make decisions based on immediate circumstances,
and is nothing to fear.
All the defectors say that Dàliáng has no troops,
its foundation is empty internally,
and it is being spied upon by the enemy.
This is what is called ‘emphasizing offense and lightly guarding,’
and there has never been anyone who did not perish by it.
‘Jiàng’ (降)
is pronounced hù jiāng fān;
the same below.
Firmly defend Yángliú,
then take your elite troops and join forces with Yùnzhōu,
driving straight into Biàn.
With their city already empty,
they will surely collapse at the mere sight of our approach.
If the false ruler is captured,
then the generals will surrender on their own.
Otherwise,
this autumn's grain harvest is poor,
and army provisions will soon run out.
If Your Majesty does not make a decisive move,
how can this great achievement be accomplished?
The proverb says: ‘Building a house in the middle of the road,
it will not be completed in three years.’
Emperors respond to destiny
and must have Heaven’s mandate.
It is merely for Your Majesty not to doubt.”
The emperor said:
“This perfectly matches my will.
A man who succeeds becomes a king;
one who fails becomes a captive.
I have made my decision!”
The Sītiān reported:
“This year, the celestial path is unfavorable for deep incursions;
there will certainly be no success.”
The emperor did not listen.
Wáng Yànzhāng led his troops across the Wènshuǐ,
intending to attack Yùnzhōu.
The Wènshuǐ flows south of Yùnchéng.
This is what the Chūnqiū refers to when it says Yùn, Huān, and Guīyīn were the fields of Wènyáng.
Wèn (汶)
is pronounced wèn.
They defeated his vanguard at Dìfáng Zhèn,
capturing three hundred officers and soldiers,
and beheading two hundred.
Yànzhāng retreated to defend Zhōngdū.
The Jiù Tángshū Dìlǐ Zhì states: Zhōngdū County of Yùnzhōu
was Hàn Pínglù County.
Its old seat was Yīnmì Chéng,
thirty-nine lǐ west of the present seat.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo,
it was renamed Zhōngdū County
and moved to its present seat.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Zhōngdū County is sixty lǐ southeast of Yùnzhōu.
In recent times, Zhōngdū was changed to Wènshàng County.
“Yīnmì Chéng”
is written as “Zhìmì Chéng” in Sòng Bái’s Xù Tōngdiǎn.
On Wùchén,
the news of victory reached Cháochéng.
The emperor was greatly pleased
and said to Guō Chóngtāo:
“The victory at Yùnzhōu
is enough to boost our morale.”
On Jǐsì,
he ordered the officers and soldiers to send all their family members back to Xīngtáng.
They were sent back from the traveling camp at Cháochéng to Wèizhōu.
19 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on Xīnwèi, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
20 The emperor sent Lady of Wèiguó Liú Shì and his imperial son Jìjí back to Xīngtáng,
bidding them farewell with these words:
“The success or failure of this endeavor
rests on this one decision.
If it does not succeed,
I shall gather my family in the Wèi palace and set it on fire!”
Historians say that the emperor’s action at this time lacked a strategy for sure victory.
The emperor designated Wèizhōu as Dōngjīng Xīngtáng Fǔ.
On the day of Rénshēn,
the Emperor led a large army across the Hé River from Yángliú.
On Guǐyǒu,
they arrived at Yùnzhōu.
In the middle of the night,
they advanced, crossing the Wèn River.
Lǐ Sìyuán was made the vanguard.
At dawn on Jiǎxū,
they encountered the Liáng troops,
defeated them in one battle,
pursued them to Zhōngdū,
and surrounded its city.
The city had no defenses.
After a short while,
After a short while,
refers to a very brief period of time.
They pursued the attack
and breached it.
Wáng Yànzhāng fled with dozens of cavalrymen.
The Longwǔ Grand General Lǐ Shàoqí pursued him alone on horseback.
Recognizing his voice,
he said:
"It is Wáng Tiěqiāng!"
According to Xuē Shǐ,
Xià Lǔqí had previously served Liáng Zǔ
and was always on good terms with Yànzhāng,
hence he recognized his voice.
Qí,
read as Jì.
Yànzhāng was heavily wounded,
his horse stumbled,
and he was captured.
Also captured were the Supervisor Dūjiān Zhāng Hànjié,
the Cāozhōu Prefect Lǐ Zhījié, the Deputy Generals Zhào Tíngyǐn and Liú Sìbīn, and over two hundred others.
Several thousand heads were severed.
Tíngyǐn was
from Kāifēng;
Sìbīn was
a relative of Zhījùn.
Liú Zhījùn surrendered to Liáng from Xú,
then to Qí from Liáng,
then to Shǔ from Qí,
and was killed by Shǔ.
Yànzhāng once said to people:
"Lǐ Yàzǐ is just a cock-fighting brat,
what is there to fear!"
Now,
the Emperor said to Yànzhāng:
"You always called me a brat.
Are you convinced today?"
He also asked:
"You are known as a good general,
why did you not defend Yǎnzhōu?
Zhōngdū has no ramparts,
how could it defend itself?"
Yànzhāng replied:
"Heaven's mandate is gone,
there is nothing more to say."
The Emperor admired Yànzhāng's talent
and wished to employ him.
He bestowed medicine to treat his wounds
and repeatedly sent people to persuade him.
Yànzhāng said:
"I was originally a common man.
Under the grace of Liáng,
I rose to the position of a supreme general
and fought against the Emperor for fifteen years.
Now my army is defeated and my strength exhausted,
death is my due.
Even if the Emperor pities me and spares my life,
how can I face the people of the world?
How can one be a Liáng general in the morning
and a Táng subject in the evening?
This is something I will not do."
The Emperor again sent Lǐ Sìyuán to persuade him in person.
Yànzhāng, lying down, said to Sìyuán:
"Aren't you Miǎojíliè?"
Yànzhāng always looked down on Sìyuán,
hence he called him by his childhood name.
Thereupon, the generals offered their congratulations.
The Emperor raised his cup and toasted Sìyuán, saying:
"Today's achievement
is thanks to your and Chóngtāo's efforts.
Had I followed the advice of Shàohóng and his like,
the great cause would have been lost."
The Emperor also said to his generals:
"Previously, my only concern was Wáng Yànzhāng.
Now that he has been captured,
this is Heaven's will to destroy Liáng.
Duàn Níng is still by the river.
Regarding the plan for advance or retreat,
which direction should we take?"
The generals believed:
"Although reports say Dàliáng is undefended,
we do not know the truth.
Currently, all the troops from the eastern prefectures are under Duàn Níng's command.
What remains are empty cities.
With His Majesty's heavenly might approaching,
none will fail to submit.
If we first expand our territory
eastward to the sea,
and then observe the opportune moment to act,
we can ensure complete victory."
Kāng Yánxiào firmly pleaded to quickly take Dàliáng.
Lǐ Sìyuán said:
"Speed is paramount in warfare.
Now that Yànzhāng has been captured,
Duàn Níng must not know it yet.
Even if someone runs to inform him,
it will take at least three days for him to ascertain the truth.
If he were to know our direction
and immediately dispatch reinforcements,
the direct route would be blocked by the breached river,
referring to the Hùjiàshuǐ (Guard's Water) breached by Duàn Níng.
For tens of thousands of troops,
boats and rafts would also be difficult to procure quickly.
This place is very close to Dàliáng.
There are no mountains or treacherous terrain ahead.
We can march in formation
day and night,
and reach it in two nights.
If Duàn Níng has not left the river,
Yǒuzhēn will already be captured by us.
Yánxiào's words are correct.
I ask Your Majesty to advance slowly with the main army,
and I am willing to lead a thousand cavalry as vanguard."
The Emperor agreed.
When the order was issued,
all the armies eagerly wished to go.
That evening,
Sìyuán led the vanguard to Dàliáng, doubling their pace.
On Yǐhài,
the Emperor departed from Zhōngdū,
carrying Wáng Yànzhāng with him.
He sent an imperial envoy to ask Yànzhāng:
"Will I succeed on this expedition?"
He replied:
"Duàn Níng has 60,000 elite troops.
Although the commander is not talented,
he will not turn his back so quickly.
It will probably be difficult to succeed."
The Emperor knew he would ultimately not be used,
so he executed him.
Today, there is a tomb and shrine for Wáng Yànzhāng in Wènshàng County.
On Dīngchǒu,
they arrived at Cāozhōu.
Jiǔyù Zhì: From the southwest of Cāozhōu to Dàliáng is over 240 lǐ.
Some of Wáng Yànzhāng's defeated soldiers were the first to reach Dàliáng,
informing the Lord of Liáng
that “Yànzhāng has been captured,
and the Táng army is advancing swiftly and will soon arrive.”
Thereupon,
the Lord of Liáng gathered his family and wept, saying:
“Our dynasty's fortune is exhausted!”
He summoned his close ministers to ask for a plan,
but none could respond.
The Lord of Liáng said to Jìng Xiáng:
“I have often disregarded your words,
which has led to this.
Now the situation is urgent,
so please do not bear a grudge.
What shall we do?”
Xiáng wept and said:
“Your servant received great kindness from the late emperor
for nearly three cycles of twelve years (three decades).
When Liáng Tàizǔ garrisoned Xuānwǔ,
Jìng Xiáng immediately became a staff member,
eventually becoming a chancellor,
until the fall of Liáng.
Hence, he himself said he had received kindness for nearly three decades.
From this perspective,

Shòuzhōu is a few *lǐ* from the Huái River,
with no fewer than five thousand infantry and cavalry.
If I had other ambitions,
how could Wáng Rěn, with a single horseman, replace me?
My loyalty prevents me from betraying the state.
Even if I were demoted to a county magistrate, I would accept it,
let alone a prefect!
Why should I defend myself and expose the court's fault?"
Xú Zhīgào wanted to enforce the law among the generals,
and requested Tàizhāng be arrested and punished.
Xú Wēn said:
"Were it not for Tàizhāng,
I would have died at the hands of Zhāng Hào."
The event is mentioned in Volume 266, Liáng Taìzǔ's Kaīpíng Second Year.
"How can I betray him?"
He ordered Zhīgào to marry his daughter to his son Jǐngtōng to resolve the matter.
24 A comet appeared in Yúguǐ,
over a *zhàng* long.
Yúguǐ consists of five stars,
and is the divisional star of Qín and Yōngzhōu.
*Huì*
is pronounced *xiáng suì* (祥歲),
and also *xú zuì* (徐醉).
*Jiàn*
is pronounced *xián biàn* (賢遍).
*Cháng*
is pronounced *zhí liàng* (直亮).
The ruler of Shǔ ordered a Daoist ritual (道場) to be established at Yùjúhuà.
Yùjúhuà is in Chéngdū.
Péng Chéng's record states: In the first year of Yǒngshòu of the Later Hàn,
Lǐ Laǒjūn and Zhāng Daòlíng arrived here,
and a jade couch with shaped legs emerged from the ground.
Laǒjūn ascended and sat,
explaining the North and South Dipper Sūtras to Daòlíng.
After he left, the seat disappeared,
and a cave formed in the ground.
Hence, it was named
"Yùjú."
Daoist scriptures state that the twenty-four transformations correspond to the twenty-four solar terms.
Yùjú is one of them,
and the common people believed and venerated it.
They thought:
"The people's grievances have reached up to Heaven,
hence the comet appeared.
This is a sign of national demise,
and cannot be averted by prayers or sacrifices."
The ruler of Shǔ was enraged
and exiled Yún to Lízhōu,
where he died on the way.
25 Guō Chóngtāo submitted a memorial saying:
"The military governors and prefects of Hénán who submitted memorials merely stated their names,
as new officials have not yet been appointed.
They may be burdened with worry and doubt."
In the eleventh month,
an imperial edict was finally issued appointing them to new offices.
26 Lǐ Shàoqīn, the Rearguard of Huázhōu, by giving bribes to the inner court through the jester Jǐng Jìn,
was appointed Military Governor of Tàiníng.
The Emperor was skilled in music from a young age,
so many jesters were favored
and often attended him.
The Emperor sometimes powdered his face himself
and played with the jesters in the courtyard
to please Lady Liú.
The jester's stage name was
"Lǐ Tiānxià" (Li the World).
Once, while acting as a jester,
he called out to himself:
"Lǐ Tiānxià!
Lǐ Tiānxià!"
The jester Jìng Xīnmó immediately stepped forward and slapped his cheek.
The Emperor blanched,
and all the jesters were astonished.
Xīnmó slowly said:
"There is only one person who governs the world;
who else should you call?"
The Emperor was pleased
and generously rewarded him.
The Emperor once hunted in Zhōngmóu,
trampling the people's crops.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Zhōngmóu County is seventy *lǐ* west of Dàliáng.
*Jiàn*
is pronounced *cí yǎn* (慈演).
[Jìng Xīnmó said:] "Your Majesty is the father and mother of the people.
How can you destroy their food,
causing them to die in ditches?"
The Emperor was angry,
scolded him away,
and was about to kill him.
Jìng Xīnmó chased and seized him before the horse,
and rebuked him saying:
"You are a county magistrate,
do you not know that our Son of Heaven loves to hunt?
How dare you allow the people to cultivate crops,
thus hindering our Son of Heaven's galloping?
Your crime deserves death!"
He then asked to carry out the execution.
The Emperor laughed and released him.
The court performers entered and exited the imperial palace,
insulting and toying with the gentry.
Loyal ministers were angry and resentful,
but dared not voice their displeasure.
The Sū tells: "To insult a gentleman
is to prevent him from fully expressing his mind."
How much more so when performers are allowed to insult and toy with them!
The regional governors from all directions vied to bribe them.
How many countless people without talent sought profit and position through them!
Jǐng Jìn was their leader.
Jìn liked to gather petty, vulgar affairs from the common people and report them to the emperor.
The emperor also wished to know about external matters,
so he entrusted Jìn with acting as his eyes and ears.
Whenever Jìn presented a matter,
the emperor would often dismiss his attendants to question him,
thereby allowing Jìn to spread his slanders and evil deeds,
and interfere in government affairs.
From the marshals and chancellors down to the great ministers, all feared him.
Kǒng Yán always treated him like an elder brother.
"Kǒng Yán"
should be
"Kǒng Qiān."
On the 27th, Rén Yín day,
Qí Wáng sent an envoy with a letter
to congratulate the emperor on destroying the Liáng dynasty,
referring to himself as a "junior uncle,"
with extremely arrogant language and禮.
Qí Wáng Lǐ Mào-zhēn regarded himself and Jìn Wáng Lǐ Kè-yòng as having been co-equal regional governors in the Táng dynasty,
and both had been granted surnames for their meritorious service and were registered as members of the Táng imperial clan.
Their relationship was therefore like brothers,
which is why he referred to himself as the emperor's "junior uncle."
On the 28th, Guǐ Mǎo day,
Zhū Yǒu-qiān, the Military Commissioner of Hézhōng, came to court.
The emperor held a banquet for him
and bestowed countless favors and gifts upon him.
On the 29th, Zhāng Quán-yì requested the emperor to move the capital to Luòyáng;

The *Kǎo Yì* states: The *Shílù* says:
"On Jiǎ Chén day,
it was debated whether to repair the Grand Ancestral Temple in Luòyáng."
According to the text, the Liáng dynasty designated Biànzhōu as the Eastern Capital,
and Luòjīng as the Western Capital.
Zhuāngzōng designated Wèizhōu as the Eastern Capital,
Tàiyuán as the Western Capital,
and Zhēndìng as the Northern Capital.
After destroying the Liáng dynasty,
the Eastern Capital was abolished and reverted to Biànzhōu,
Yǒngpíng Jūn was made the Western Capital,
but it is not stated what Luòyáng was designated as.
If it were designated as the Eastern Capital,
then it would be no different from Wèizhōu.
All other texts simply refer to it as Luòjīng,
and there has never been an imperial edict changing the Liáng dynasty's Western Capital to Luòjīng.
It was not until the third year of Tóngguāng that an edict was issued to revert Luòjīng to the Eastern Capital.
Could it be that when Yǒngpíng was made the Western Capital, the Liáng dynasty's Western Capital was immediately changed to Luòjīng, but the historical record omitted this?
Since there is nothing to verify this now,
it is simply referred to as Luòyáng.
On the 30th, Yǐ Sì day,
Zhū Yǒu-qiān was granted the name Lǐ Jì-lín,
and Jì-jí was ordered to treat him as an elder brother.
On the 31st, Kāng Yán-xiào was appointed Defense Commissioner of Zhèngzhōu
and granted the name Lǐ Shào-chēn.
On the 32nd, the Northern Capital was abolished
and reverted to Chéngdé Jūn.
In April of this year,
the Northern Capital was established in Zhènzhōu.
On the 33rd, Yuán Xiàng-xiān, the Military Commissioner of Xuānwǔ, was granted the name Lǐ Shào-ān.
Wēn Tāo, the Military Commissioner of Kuāngguó, came to court

Shào-chōng brought much gold and silk to bribe Lady Liú and powerful officials and eunuchs.
Within ten days,
he was sent back to his commandery.
Guō Chóng-tāo said:
"The state has avenged the Táng dynasty,
yet Wēn Tāo almost entirely excavated the Táng imperial tombs,

How can he be allowed to remain a regional governor?
What will the righteous gentlemen of the realm say about us!"
The emperor said:
"At the beginning of our entry into Biàn,
his crimes were already pardoned."
So he was sent back.
On the 34th, Wù Shēn day,
the Central Secretariat memorialized, stating:
"The national expenditure is not yet sufficient.
We request that a limited number of officials in the Three Departments, Nine Courts, and Five Directorates be retained,
and all others be dismissed.
Those currently in office will be replaced in turn after serving twenty-five months.
'Currently in office'
means those currently holding official positions.
*Xiàn*,
read as *xián biàn*.
The Bureau of Military Affairs shall comply with this."
In the order of court assemblies,
military officials were arranged on the west,
hence they were called the Western Ranks.
People generally complained and grumbled.
At first,
Emperor Jūn of Liáng was about to perform the Southern Suburban Sacrifice in Luòyáng,
but stopped upon hearing that Yángliú had fallen,
as seen in Volume 270, third year of Zhēnmíng.
Zhāng Quán-yì requested the emperor to quickly proceed to Luòyáng
to complete the visit to the temple.
The Táng Eastern Capital also had a Grand Ancestral Temple;

hence Zhāng Quán-yì requested the emperor to repair and visit it.
This was granted.
On the 36th, Bǐng Chén day,
Kāifēng Fǔ, the Liáng dynasty's Eastern Capital, was reinstated as Xuānwǔ Jūn Biànzhōu.
The Liáng dynasty designated Sòngzhōu as Xuānwǔ Jūn,
and an edict changed its name to Guīdé Jūn.
When the Liáng capital was Biàn,
the title of Xuānwǔ Jūn was moved to Sòngzhōu.
*Gēng*,
read as *gōng héng*.
On the 37th, an edict ordered civil and military officials to first proceed to Luòyáng.
On the 38th, some argued that Guō Chóng-tāo, a meritorious minister, being a chancellor

Some recommended Xuē Tíng-guī, Minister of Rites,

Both were venerable and learned,

Chóng-tāo memorialized that Tíng-guī was superficial and lacked the qualities for chancellorship,
and Qí was treacherous and lacked the demeanor of a scholar.
Zhào Guāng-yìn, Left Administrator of the Department of State Affairs, was honest and upright.
Even before the fall of the Liáng dynasty,
northerners all praised him as having the makings of a chancellor.
All three of them had served the Liáng dynasty.
Tíng-guī and Qí, as Tàizǔ's ceremonial envoys,
must have, during the Táng dynasty, received imperial orders to invest the King of Jìn.
On Dīng Sì day,
Guāng-yìn was appointed Central Secretariat Attendant,
and, along with Yuè, made Acting Chancellor (Tóng Píngzhāng Shì).
Guāng-yìn was
the younger brother of Guāng-féng;
Zhào Guāng-féng is mentioned in Volume 266, first year of Kāipíng of Liáng Tàizǔ.
He was the son of Xiù;
Tíng-guī was
the son of Féng.
Xuē Féng
had a literary reputation during the Huìchāng era of the Táng dynasty.
He was prone to self-importance;
Yuè was merely cautious and conventional.
After Zhào Guāng-féng was dismissed from chancellorship in the Liáng court,
in the first year of Zhēnmíng of Liáng Jūn Wáng, Zhào Guāng-féng was dismissed from chancellorship.
Guāng-yìn visited him then,
and they discussed political affairs.
Another day,
Guāng-féng posted a sign at his door saying:
"Please do not discuss Central Secretariat matters."
Kǒng Qiān, the Deputy Commissioner of Tribute and Taxation, feared Zhāng Xiàn's uprightness
and wished to monopolize the commission's affairs.
He wished to monopolize the affairs of the Tribute and Taxation Commission.
*Shǐ*,
read as *shū lì*.
He said, "The Eastern Capital is a crucial place
and requires a great minister to govern it;
no one but Minister Zhāng will do."
Chóng-tāo immediately memorialized to appoint Xiàn as Deputy Resident of the Eastern Capital,
overseeing the duties of the Resident.
Zhāng Xiàn was sent out to govern Wèizhōu.
On Wù Wǔ day,
Dòu-lú Gé was appointed acting Commissioner of Tribute and Taxation,
concurrently Commissioner of Salt, Iron, and Transport for all circuits.
Qiān was greatly disappointed.
On the 40th, Jǐ Wèi day,
Zhāng Quán-yì was additionally appointed Protectorate Grand Master of the Secretariat,
and Gāo Jì-xīng Protectorate Grand Master of the Chancellery.
At that time, Jì-xīng came to court,
and the emperor treated him very kindly.
Casually, he asked:
"I wish to wage war against Wú and Shǔ.
Which of the two kingdoms should be attacked first?"
Jì-xīng, considering the difficulty of taking the Shǔ region due to its perilous terrain,
replied:
"The land of Wú is barren and its people poor;

It is better to attack Shǔ first.
The land of Shǔ is rich and fertile,
and its ruler is tyrannical while its people are resentful.
Attacking it will surely lead to victory.
After conquering Shǔ,
following the river downstream,
taking Wú will be as easy as turning one's hand."
The emperor said:
"Excellent!"
On the 41st, Xīn Yǒu day,
Yǒngpíng Jūn Dà'ān Fǔ was reinstated as Xījīng Jìngzhào Fǔ.
The Liáng dynasty changed Cháng'ān to Yǒngpíng Jūn,
as seen in Volume 267, third year of Kāipíng of Tàizǔ;
and changed Jìngzhào Fǔ to Dà'ān Fǔ, as seen in Volume 266, first year of Kāipíng.
In the 42nd *jiǎzǐ* year,
Emperor (Míngzōng) Fā arrived at Dàliáng;
In the twelfth month,
on the *gēngwǔ* day,
he arrived at Luòyáng.
In the 43rd year, Wúyuè Wáng Qián Liú appointed Dù Jiànhuī, the acting commander of the army, as Left Chancellor.
On the 44th *rénshēn* day,
an edict declared the palace and gardens in Biànzhōu an imperial traveling palace.
In the 45th year, Yàozhōu was renamed Shùnyì Jūn,
Yánzhōu was renamed Zhāngwǔ Jūn,
Dèngzhōu was renamed Wēishèng Jūn,
Jìnzhōu was renamed Jiànxióng Jūn,
and Ānzhōu was renamed Ānyuǎn Jūn;
The Emperor, having overthrown Liáng,
specifically changed the names of the armies established by Liáng,
but did not change those of other regional commanders.
Liáng had renamed Yàozhōu to Chóngzhōu,
and had renamed Yìshèng Jūn to Jìngshèng Jūn,
which was established by Qí.
Yánzhōu
was Táng's Bǎosài Jūn,
and Qí had made it Zhōngyì Jūn.
Dèngzhōu
was Liáng's Xuānhuà Jūn.
Jìnzhōu
was initially Liáng's Dìngchāng Jūn,
later renamed Jiànníng Jūn.
Ānzhōu
was Liáng's Xuānwēi Jūn.
All were restored to their old Táng names.
On the 46th *gēngchén* day,
the Censorate reported:
"Zhū Wēn usurped the throne,
and deleted and altered the laws, ordinances, and formats of our dynasty.
The matter of Liáng altering laws, ordinances, and formats can be found in volume 267, Kāipíng 4th year.
'Our dynasty'
refers to the former Táng dynasty.
Now, the laws used by the Censorate, Ministry of Justice, and Grand Court of Justice are all those of the false court.
We have heard that only the imperial library in Dìngzhōu has a complete set of the laws, ordinances, and formats of our dynasty.
We request an order for that circuit to transcribe and submit them."
This was approved.
In the 47th year, Lǐ Jìtāo, hearing that the Emperor had overthrown Liáng,
was worried and fearful,
not knowing what to do.
He wished to flee north to Qìdān,
but then an imperial edict summoned him to the court;
As Jìtāo was about to leave,
his younger brother Jìyuǎn said:
"Brother, with a reputation for rebellion,
where can you hide yourself?
Going or not going is the same.
It would be better to dig deep moats and build high ramparts,
living off accumulated grain,
which might still prolong your years;
If you go to court,
you will die immediately."
Someone else said to Jìtāo:
"Your late Duke had great merits for the state."
"Late Duke"
refers to Jìtāo's father, Sìzhāo;
Sìzhāo held the office of Minister of the Secretariat,
hence the稱.
"He is your uncle."
Lǐ Sìzhāo, as the adopted son of the Jìn King,
was the Emperor's elder brother,
so the Emperor was Jìtāo's uncle.
Jìtāo's mother, Lady Yáng,
was skilled at accumulating wealth;
her family assets amounted to a million.
So, she went with Lady Yáng,
bringing 400,000 *liǎng* of silver,
and other goods in equivalent amounts,
generously distributing bribes and gifts.
Entertainers and eunuchs competed to speak on his behalf, saying:
"Jìtāo initially had no evil intentions;
he was merely misled by wicked men.
Sìzhāo was a virtuous relative,
and should not be without an heir."
Lady Yáng also entered the palace to see the Emperor,
weeping and pleading for his life,
citing his ancestors.
She also sought compassion from Lady Liú,
and Lady Liú also spoke on his behalf.
When Jìtāo arrived to face his punishment,
the Emperor pardoned him,
keeping him for over a month,
often taking him on hunting excursions,
treating him with the same favor as before.
The Imperial younger brother, Cúnwò, the Military Commissioner of Yìchéng and Joint Administrator of Affairs, strongly criticized him.
The matter of Jìtāo and his brothers wanting to kill Cúnwò can be found in the previous volume, Liáng Jūn Wáng Lóngdé 2nd year.
Liáng had changed Huázhōu's Yìchéng Jūn to Xuānyì Jūn;
the Emperor restored the old Táng name.
Jìtāo again bribed those around him to seek return to his commandery,
but the Emperor did not permit it.
Jìtāo secretly sent someone to deliver a letter to Jìyuǎn,
instructing the soldiers to set fires,
hoping that the Son of Heaven would send him back to pacify them.
The matter was exposed,
and on the *xīnsì* day,
he was demoted to Administrator of Dēngzhōu,
and soon after was beheaded south of Tiānjīn Qiáo,
along with his two sons.
An envoy was sent to execute Lǐ Jìyuǎn in Shàngdǎng,
and Lǐ Jìdá was appointed Military City Inspector.
Lǐ Jìchóu, the acting administrator of the military prefecture, was summoned to the court.
Jìchóu had taken over Jìtāo's residence,
sorting through his concubines and maids,
and searching for his wealth,
not leaving promptly.
*Jí*
means "to go."
"Four members of our family, brothers and father and sons, were executed at the same time."
Jìtāo, his two sons,
and Jìyuǎn make four people.
Jìtāo had seven brothers;
Jìchóu was the eldest,
hence he was called "big brother."
"I am truly ashamed of this,
I have no face to look at people,
living is worse than dying!"
On the 48th *jiǎshēn* day,
Jìdá, in mourning attire,
led a hundred cavalry under his command to the Gate of Halberds and shouted:
Shǐ Zhào says: "Halberds were arranged at the gate,
hence it was called the Gate of Halberds."
*Shuài*
is read as *lǜ*.
*Shuāi*
is pronounced *cāng huí fān*.
*Hū*
is pronounced *huǒ gù fān*.
"Who will rebel with me?"
He then attacked the *yázhái*.
*Yázhái*
refers to the official residence.
Lǐ Jìkē, the Deputy Military Commissioner, heard the commotion
and recruited over a thousand market people
to attack the inner city.
Jìdá knew the situation was hopeless,
opened the east gate,
and returned to his private residence.
The east gate
was the east gate of Lùzhōu's administrative city.
He planned to flee to Qìdān,
but a few *lǐ* outside the city,
all his accompanying cavalry scattered,

On the 49th *jiǎshēn* day,
Wú Wáng again sent Lú Pín of Luòyáng, a Minister of Agriculture, as an envoy.

When he arrived,
everything was as Kěqiú had predicted.

he reported that the Táng ruler was extravagant in his hunting expeditions,

causing resentment both inside and outside the court.
Gāo Jìxīng (高季興) was in Luòyáng (洛陽).
The emperor’s attendant court entertainers
and eunuchs were insatiably greedy for bribes.
The term 'líng guān' (伶官)
and 'huàn' (宦)
refers to court entertainers and eunuchs respectively.
'Yàn' (厭)
is pronounced 'yú yán' (於鹽).
Jìxīng (季興) was furious about this.
The emperor wanted to detain Jìxīng (季興),

Jìxīng (季興) hastened away,

he said, "This journey has two mistakes: my coming to court was one mistake,

This means both sides made mistakes.
The Jìedùshǐ (節度使), Kǒng Qíng (孔勍), detained him for a banquet.
In the middle of the night,
Jìxīng (季興) broke through the gate and left.

he arrived in Jiānglíng (江陵),

Liáng Zhèn's (梁震) words are mentioned above.
'Jǐ' (幾)
is pronounced 'jū yī' (居依).
"The new dynasty fought a hundred battles to finally gain Hénán (河南).

'Cháo' (朝)
is pronounced 'zhí yáo'.

such boastfulness,

I have nothing to worry about."
Thereupon, he repaired the city walls, accumulated grain,
and recruited former Liáng (梁) soldiers,
making preparations for defense and warfare.

and was being watched by neighboring enemies and treacherous heroes.

1. Spring,
first month,
on the day of Jiǎchén (甲辰),

is pronounced 'gōng héng' (工衡).

Zhèngyán was dull and weak;

The Grand Empress Dowager said:

Upon the Emperor's ascension,

Guóchāng was honored with the temple name Xiànzǔ,
and his mausoleum was named Chángníng.
Kèyòng was honored with the temple name Tàizǔ,
and his mausoleum was named Jiànjí.
All three mausoleums were in Yànmén County, Dàizhōu,

The Grand Empress Dowager's refusal to come

her heart certainly had other considerations,
and her words and reasoning were very sound.
(This sets the stage for both the Empress Dowager and Grand Empress Dowager falling ill from sorrow and worry.)
On *gēngshēn*,
the Emperor went out to welcome them at Héyáng;
on *xīnyǒu*,

11 In the second month,
on *jǐsì*, the first day of the month,
the Emperor performed sacrifices at the southern suburbs,

Kǒng Qiān desired to amass wealth to curry favor,

Qiān collected taxes again.
From then on, whenever imperial edicts were issued,
people no longer believed them,
and the common folk were filled with sorrow and resentment.
Guō Chóngtāo, upon first arriving in Biàn and Luò,
frequently accepted gifts from the regional governors.
Some of his intimates remonstrated with him,
to which Chóngtāo said:
"My position combines both general and prime minister.
(Guō Chóngtāo was Commissioner of Military Affairs,
conferred with the title of Shìzhōng,
and concurrently held the Jiedushi of Chéngdé.
As Commissioner of Military Affairs,
nothing in the empire was unrelated to him.
Shìzhōng was the chief official of the three departments,
and he also held a jiedushi,
hence the statement that his position combined general and prime minister.)
How could I need external resources?
It's just that during the late period of the false Liáng,
bribery became common.
Now, the regional governors in Hénán are all former officials of Liáng,
enemies of His Majesty.
If I refuse their gifts,
will they not be apprehensive?
I merely store these for the state in my private residence."
When it was time for the sacrifice at the southern suburbs,
Chóngtāo was the first to present 100,000 *mín* of money for the army.
Earlier,
the eunuchs had advised the Emperor to divide the empire's financial resources and tribute into inner and outer treasuries.
What was submitted by prefectures and counties went into the outer treasury
to cover general expenses,
while contributions from regional commands went into the inner treasury
for banquets, entertainment, and rewards for those around the Emperor.
Consequently, the outer treasury was constantly empty and depleted, while the inner treasury accumulated vast sums.
When the responsible officials prepared for the suburban sacrifice,
they lacked funds for the army.
Chóngtāo spoke to the Emperor, saying:
"Your subject has already exhausted all his household possessions to assist with this great ceremony;
I wish Your Majesty would also contribute funds from the inner treasury to assist the officials."
The Emperor remained silent for a long time,
then said:
"I have my own reserves stored in Jìnyáng;
I can order the Rent and Tax Commissioner to transport them to help."
Thereupon, several hundred thousand in gold and silks from Lǐ Jìtāo's private residence were taken to supplement the funds.
(Lǐ Jìtāo's father, Sīzhāo, followed Jìn Wáng Kèyòng when he rose up in Jìnyáng,
hence his private residence was there.
Jìtāo was executed for rebellion,
and his family's assets were confiscated.)
From this, resentment and disloyalty began to emerge.
(This sets the stage for the later mutiny and defection of various armies.)

Chóngtāo's position combined general and prime minister,
and he also held the authority of a Jiedushi.
He took the empire's affairs as his personal responsibility,
his power equaled that of the sovereign,
and carriages and horses filled his gate day and night.
His nature was resolute and quick-tempered;
he would act whenever an issue arose,
suppressing many requests from favorites and opportunists.
The eunuchs resented him,
and daily disparaged him to the Emperor;
Chóngtāo wrung his hands,
unable to restrain them.
Dòulú Gé and Wéi Yuè once asked him:

"During the turmoil and collapse,
I lost my genealogy.
I once heard my ancestors say
that I am four generations removed from Fényáng."
Gé said:
"Then you are indeed a distant cousin."
Chóngtāo, from then on, regarded himself as a noble,
often distinguishing between social classes,
promoting the showy and superficial,
and disdaining the meritorious old guard.
When someone sought office,
Chóngtāo would say:
"I deeply recognize your abilities,
but your family background is humble;
I dare not employ you,
for fear of being ridiculed by the eminent."
Thus, the favorites resented him internally,
and the meritorious old guard resented him externally.
Chóngtāo repeatedly requested to yield the post of Commissioner of Military Affairs to Lǐ Shàohóng,

Chóngtāo was depressed and discontented,

His confidant said:
"That cannot be.
If a dragon loses its water,

Previously,

The Emperor agreed.
Guō Chóngtāo (郭崇韜) remonstrated:

the Emperor believed he had kept his word.
Can this be for governance?)
"You

Everyone was filled with indignation and sighs.

Furthermore,
unnecessary construction projects [tǔmù] (土木)

In the 35th year, *wùshēn* (924 CE),
the Lord of Shǔ sent Lǐ Yán back.

"Returned" (還),

*wùwǔ*,

Why did he stay for so long?

*jǐhài*,

Now, we follow the dates in the *Shǔshū*.
The Emperor, because of Yán's entry into Shǔ,
ordered him to use horses to trade for precious artifacts in the palace,
but Shǔ law prohibited fine silks, brocades, and rare treasures from entering Zhōngguó,
only allowing coarser, inferior items to enter Zhōngguó,
which were called
"grass-entry goods."
When Yán returned,

the Emperor angrily said:
"How can Wáng Yǎn escape becoming a 'grass-entry person'!"
Yán then spoke to the Emperor, saying:
"Yǎn is childish and foolish, indulgent and dissolute,

distancing old veterans,
and befriending petty individuals.

are sycophantic and autocratic,
insatiably greedy for bribes.
The worthy and the foolish have exchanged places,
rewards and punishments are in disorder.

once a large army arrives,

This laid the groundwork for the campaign against Shǔ.
In the 36th year, because Lùzhōu rebelled,
*gēngxū*,
an edict was issued to all prefectures and garrisons in the realm, prohibiting them from repairing city walls or digging moats,

The destruction of defensive city equipment

*jiǎyín*,
Lǐ Shàobīn, the *Hénghǎi Jiédùshǐ*, was appointed *Dōngběimiàn Xíngyíng Zhāotǎoshǐ*,

From the thirteenth year of *Xiántōng* to this year, fifty-four years have passed,

"间" (*jiān*),
