and how can the people live!
I wish to be granted death first."
The Emperor comforted him and sent him away.
This was one instance of remonstrance against hunting.
The Prefect of Zhōngmóu almost faced death,
but the Prefect of Luòyáng received comfort and was sent away.
It must be that a court performer interceded for him.
Upon examining Hé Zé's conduct throughout his life,
he was truly not an honest and upright scholar.
He was from Guǎngzhōu.
Xuē Shǐ says: Hé Zé,
from Guǎngzhōu.
During Liáng Zhēnmíng's reign, Liú Zhì, the Military Commissioner of Qīnghǎi, recommended his talent,
and he passed the imperial examination as a *jìnshì*.
53 The Qìdān attacked Bóhǎi,
and returned without success.
54 Wáng Zōngchóu, the former Military Commissioner of Shānnán and concurrently Grand Counselor, seeing the Shǔ ruler's loss of virtue,
plotted with Wáng Zōngbì to depose and establish a new ruler.
Zōngbì hesitated and had not yet decided.
On Gēngxū,
Zōngchóu died from worry and indignation.
Zōngbì said to Sòng Guāngsì and Jǐng Rùnchéng, the Commissioners of Military Affairs,
"Zōngchóu taught me to kill you all.
Today there is no longer this worry."
Guāngsì and the others prostrated themselves, weeping in gratitude.
Zōngbì's son Chéngbān heard of this,
and said to others,
"It will be difficult for our family to escape disaster."
55 On Yǐmǎo,
the Shǔ ruler appointed Zhāng Wǔ, the former Military Commissioner of Zhènjiāng Army, as the Commissioner for Relief and Suppression of the Gorge Road.
Shǔ established the Zhènjiāng Army in Kuízhōu.
56 On Dīngsì,
Yōuzhōu reported a Qìdān invasion.
57 In winter,
the tenth month,
on Xīnwèi,
Lǐ Cúnbà, the Military Commissioner of Tiānpíng, and Fú Xí, the Military Commissioner of Pínglú, stated:
"Many subordinate departments claim to directly receive orders from the Rent and Tax Commissioner's office for public affairs.
The Commissioner's office is completely unaware,
which disrupts regulations."
"Commissioner's office" here refers to the Military Commissioner's office.
"Wèn,"
pronounced wèn.
The recent practice was all "direct issuance."
At that time, the Rent and Tax Commissioner's decrees were issued directly to the various departments for requisitioning,
without involving the Military Commissioner or the Surveillance Commissioner,
which was called "direct issuance."
"Xià,"
pronounced hùjià.
"According to court precedents,
imperial edicts do not go down to subordinate departments.
A military prefecture is the main administrative seat,
and its dependent departments are subordinate departments."
"The reports from these two circuits now present
the old regulations of our dynasty.
What the Rent and Tax Office presents
are recent practices of the false court."
At that time, Liáng was referred to as the "false court" to denounce it.
"All matters must be reported via memorial by the respective circuit,
and the Rent and Tax office's collections must also be notified to the Surveillance Commissioner."
The Táng system stipulated:
the Military Commissioner managed military affairs,
and the Surveillance Commissioner managed civil affairs.
Therefore, edicts for Rent and Tax collections were only to be sent to the Surveillance Commissioner's office.
Ultimately, this was not implemented.
Historical records state that the collections were severe and urgent,
only aiming to complete them quickly,
and thus they proceeded without obeying the edict.
58 Yìdìng reported a Qìdān invasion.
59 Wáng Chéngxiū, the Commissioner of the Northern Bureau of the Shǔ Xuānhuī Academy, requested to select twelve thousand valiant men from all armies,
to establish forty Left and Right Longwǔ infantry and cavalry armies under the Emperor's command.
Their weapons, equipment, and rewards were all superior to other armies.
Chéngxiū was appointed Commander-in-chief of the Longwǔ Army's Infantry and Cavalry,
with his subordinate general Ān Zhòngbà as his deputy.
No old general was not resentful and ashamed.
Zhòngbà,
a native of Yúnzhōu,
served Chéngxiū with cunning flattery and bribery,
hence Chéngxiū was pleased with him.
This sets the stage for Ān Zhòngbà's betrayal of Wáng Chéngxiū and surrender to Táng.
60 Qián Liú, the King of Wúyuè, again resumed the tribute system of the present dynasty.
Qián Liú was originally a Táng subject;
after the fall of Táng, he served Liáng;
after the fall of Liáng, he again served Táng,
hence it says "again resumed the tribute system of the present dynasty."
On Rénwǔ,
the Emperor bestowed titles upon him according to his Liáng official ranks.
Liú offered generous tributes,
and also bribed influential officials,
seeking a golden seal, jade tablet, an edict granting him the privilege of not being called by his personal name, and the title of king.
The officials stated:
"According to precedents, only the Son of Heaven uses jade tablets;
kings and dukes all use bamboo tablets.
Bamboo tablets are made of woven bamboo,
to preserve ancient customs.
There is no practice of enfeoffing kings of states."
"There is no precedent for enfeoffing a king as a 'king of a state'."
The Emperor accommodated all of Liú's wishes.
61 Wú Wáng (吳王) visited Báishā (白沙) to observe the warships,
and renamed Báishā (白沙) to Yíngluán Zhèn (迎鑾鎮).
Lù Zhèn's (路振) Jiǔguó Zhì (九國志) states: Yáng Pǔ (楊溥) toured Báishā (白沙),
and Tàixué Bóshì (太學博士) Wáng Gǔ (王穀) submitted a memorial requesting to rename Báishā (白沙) to Yíngluán (迎鑾),
which briefly stated:
"Where the sun and moon pass,
all stars become the Yellow Path;
where the imperial carriage stops,
all cities become the Red District."
Báishā (白沙)
was in Yángzǐ Xiàn (楊子縣).
At the end of the Five Dynasties, Yángzǐ (楊子) was changed to Yǒngzhēn Xiàn (永貞縣).
In the second year of Qiándé (乾德) in the Sòng (宋) dynasty, Yíngluán Zhèn (迎鑾鎮) in Yǒngzhēn Xiàn (永貞縣) of Yángzhōu (揚州) was established as Jiàn'ān Jūn (建安軍).
In the sixth year of Dàzhōng Xiángfú (大中祥符), it was promoted to Zhēnzhōu (真州).
Before this, Yǒngzhēn Xiàn (永貞縣) had been restored to Yángzǐ (楊子).
The area was sixty lǐ (里) east to Yángzhōu (揚州),
and bordered the Great River (大江) to the south.
Crossing the river south to Jīnlíng (金陵) was also sixty lǐ (里).
更 (Gēng),
read gōng héng fān (工衡翻).
Wēn (溫) appointed his trusted subordinate Zhái Qián (翟虔) as Gémén (閤門), Gōngchéng (宮城), Wǔbèi (武備) and other commissioners,
to observe the king's daily life.
Qián (虔) restricted the king very strictly.
Sending Zhōng Tàizhāng (鍾泰章) to kill Zhāng Hào (張顥) and close the Yáchéng Mén (牙城門) to attack Zhū Jǐn (朱瑾)
were all Zhái Qián's (翟虔) doings,
thus Xú Wēn (徐溫) deeply trusted him.
翟 (Zhái),
read zhí gé fān (直格翻).
The king, when speaking to Wēn (溫), referred to "rain" as "water,"
and Wēn (溫) asked for the reason.
The king said:
"It is Zhái Qián's (翟虔) father's given name.
I have become thoroughly accustomed to avoiding it."
He then said to Wēn (溫):
"Your loyalty and sincerity,
I know well.
However, Zhái Qián (翟虔) is disrespectful,
and many things needed in the palace and by the imperial clan are not obtained."
須 (Xū) means
what one desires,
what one seeks.
He requested to have him executed,
but the king said:
"Execution would be too much;
distant exile would be acceptable."
So he was exiled to Fǔzhōu (撫州).
62 In the eleventh month,
the Shǔ Zhǔ (蜀主) sent his Hànlín Xuéshì (翰林學士) Ōuyáng Bīn (歐陽彬) to establish friendly relations.
Kǎoyì (考異) says: Shílù (實錄):
"In the seventh month,
on the day of Wùwǔ (戊午),
the Shǔ Zhǔ (蜀主) sent Hùbù Shìláng (戶部侍郎) Ōuyáng Bīn (歐陽彬) as an envoy,
sending a letter with the rites of an equal state."
Shǔ Shū Hòuzhǔ Jì (蜀書後主紀):
"In the eleventh month,
on the day of Yǐwèi (乙未),
Hànlín Xuéshì (翰林學士) and Bīngbù Shìláng (兵部侍郎) Ōuyáng Bīn (歐陽彬) was appointed as the envoy for good relations with the Táng (唐) state."
We follow this now.
He was a native of Héngshān (衡山).
He also sent Lǐ Yánchóu (李彥稠) to return east.
Lǐ Yánchóu (李彥稠) saw the emperor in Shǔ (蜀) in the ninth month.
還 (Huán),
read cóng xuān fān (從宣翻),
also as is.
63 On the day of Guǐmǎo (癸卯),
the emperor led his imperial guard on a hunt at Yīquè (伊闕).
Yīquè Xiàn (伊闕縣) was over two hundred lǐ (里) south of Luòyáng (洛陽),
with Yīquè Shān (伊闕山),
which Dà Yǔ (大禹) had carved.
The Sòng (宋) dynasty reduced Yīquè Xiàn (伊闕縣) to a town,
incorporating it into Yīyáng Xiàn (伊陽縣).
帥 (Shuài),
read shuài (率).
He traversed mountains and dangerous terrain,
continuing for days without stopping,
sometimes forming an encirclement at night;
many soldiers died or were injured from falling off cliffs and into valleys.
History states that the emperor was addicted to hunting and did not care for his soldiers.
折 (Zhē),
read ér shè fān (而設翻).
On the day of Bǐngwǔ (丙午),
he returned to the palace.
64 Shǔ (蜀), having established friendly relations with Táng (唐),
disbanded the garrison at Wēiwǔ Chéng (威武城),
and recalled Guān Hóngyè (關宏業) and twenty-four armies to Chéngdū (成都).
On the day of Wùshēn (戊申),
he also disbanded the thirty-seven armies of Wǔdìng (武定) and Wǔxīng (武興) Zhāotǎo (招討) Liú Qián (劉潛) and others.
65 On the day of Dīngsì (丁巳),
Hùguó Jiédùshǐ (護國節度使) Lǐ Jìlín (李繼麟) was granted an iron charter.
His sons, Lìngdé (令德) and Lìngxī (令錫), were both made Jiédùshǐ (節度使),
and all his sons old enough to wear clothes were immediately appointed officials,
his favor surpassing all other vassal princes.
Zhū Yǒuqīan's (朱友謙) favor
was precisely what hastened his misfortune.
His repeated changes were many;
how could it not affect him?
冠 (Guān),
read gōng huàn fān (工喚翻).
66 On the day of Gēngshēn (庚申),
Wèizhōu (蔚州) reported that the Qìdān (契丹) had invaded.
67 On the day of Xīnyǒu (辛酉),
the Shǔ Zhǔ (蜀主) disbanded the Tiānxíong Jūn (天雄軍) Zhāotǎo (招討),
and ordered Wáng Chéngqiān (王承騫) and twenty-nine armies to return to Chéngdū (成都).
68 In the twelfth month,
on the first day, Yǐchǒu (乙丑),
the Shǔ Zhǔ (蜀主) appointed Yòupúshè (右僕射) Zhāng Gé (張格) concurrently as Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事).
Initially,
Gé's (格) offense is detailed in volume 270, Liáng Jūnwáng Zhēnmíng (梁均王貞明) fourth year.
When he again served as prime minister and wielded power,
he beat him to death with a staff.
Xǔ Jì (許寂) said to people:
"Master Zhāng (張) has high talent but shallow insight.
After executing Lǔ Ròu (魯柔),
who else would dare to feel secure!
This is the beginning of bringing disaster upon oneself."
Zhāng Gé (張格) was indeed mistaken,
but Xǔ Jì (許寂), also holding the position of prime minister,
did not realize that Shǔ (蜀) was on the verge of collapse,
only knowing that Zhāng Gé (張格) was bringing disaster upon himself.
When Shǔ (蜀) falls,
can those who served as prime ministers avoid calamity?
69 The Shǔ Zhǔ (蜀主) disbanded the Jīnzhōu (金州) garrison,
and ordered Wáng Chéngxūn (王承勳) and seven armies to return to Chéngdū (成都).
The Shǔ Zhǔ (蜀主) relied on peace with Táng (唐) and withdrew border defenses,
which was like taming tigers and leopards without strictly setting up cages.
70 On the day of Jǐsì (己巳),
Xuānwǔ Jiédùshǐ (宣武節度使) Lǐ Sìyuán (李嗣源) was ordered to lead thirty-seven thousand imperial guard soldiers to Biànzhōu (汴州),
and then proceed to Yōuzhōu (幽州) to defend against the Qìdān (契丹).
Lǐ Sìyuán (李嗣源) was ordered to lead troops to the garrison,
and then proceed north to guard the border.
71 On the day of Gēngwǔ (庚午),
the emperor and empress visited Zhāng Quányì's (張全義) residence.
Quányì (全義) presented numerous tributes;
during the drinking,
the empress reported:
"I lost my parents when I was young,
and whenever I see an elder, I think of them.
I request to serve Quányì (全義) as my father."
The emperor consented.
Quányì (全義) was alarmed and firmly declined,
but after repeated urgings,
he finally accepted the empress's bow,
and again presented tributes to express gratitude.
The next day,
the empress ordered Hànlín Xuéshì (翰lín Xuéshì) Zhào Fèng (趙鳳) to draft a letter of thanks to Quányì (全義).
Fèng (鳳) secretly memorialized:
"Since ancient times, there has been no mother of All Under Heaven who bowed to a subject as father."
The emperor praised his honesty,
but nevertheless carried it out.
From then on, the empress and Quányì (全義) sent envoys back and forth daily to exchange greetings and gifts without interruption.
72 Initially,
during the reigns of Táng (唐) Xī (僖) and Zhāo (昭),
although eunuchs were powerful,
none had ever been granted military governorships.
Shǔ (蜀) Ān Zhòngbà (安重霸) persuaded Wáng Chéngxīu (王承休) to seek the Qínzhōu (秦州) Jiédùshǐ (節度使) post.
Chéngxīu (承休) told the Shǔ Zhǔ (蜀主):
"Qínzhōu (秦州) has many beautiful women.
Please allow me to select and present them to Your Majesty."
The Shǔ Zhǔ (蜀主) agreed.
On the day of Gēngwǔ (庚午),
Chéngxīu (承休) was appointed Tiānxíong Jiédùshǐ (天雄節度使),
and enfeoffed as Lǔguó Gōng (魯國公);
history states that the disorder of Shǔ (蜀) politics included things unseen even at the end of Táng (唐).
In the tenth month of this year,
Shǔ (蜀) first established the Lóngwǔ Jūn (龍武軍).
73 On the day of Yǐhài (乙亥),
the Shǔ Zhǔ (蜀主) appointed former Wǔdé Jiédùshǐ (武德節度使) and concurrent Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令) Xú Yánqióng (徐延瓊) as Jīngchéng Nèiwài Mǎbù Dūzhīhuīshǐ (京城內外馬步都指揮使).
Shǔ (蜀) referred to the city of Chéngdū (成都) as the Jīngchéng (京城).
Everyone was displeased.
The Shǔ Zhǔ's (蜀主) mother and concubine
were both of the Xú (徐) clan.
The Shǔ Zhǔ (蜀主) established a deathbed edict not to let the Xú (徐) clan brothers command troops,
but although Wáng Yǎn (王衍) was foolish and dissolute,
none of Shǔ's (蜀) officials spoke to Yǎn (衍) about the deathbed edict.
Wáng Zōngbì (王宗弼) was also not reliable enough!
The reason everyone was displeased with Xú Yánqióng (徐延瓊)
was simply because of his irregular promotion.
74 On the day of Rénwǔ (壬午),
Běijīng (北京) reported that the Qìdān (契丹) had invaded Lánzhōu (嵐州).
At the beginning of Tóngguāng (同光),
Zhènzhōu (鎮州) was made Běidū (北都),
and Tàiyuán (太原) was made Xījīng (西京);
soon Běidū (北都) was abolished and restored to Zhènzhōu (鎮州),
and Tàiyuán (太原) was made Běijīng (北京).
嵐 (Lán),
read lú hán fān (盧含翻).
75 On the day of Xīnmǎo (辛卯),
the Shǔ Zhǔ (蜀主) changed the next year's era name to Xiánkāng (咸康).
76 Lúlóng Jiédùshǐ (盧龍節度使) Lǐ Cúnxián (李存賢) died.
77 In this year,
the Shǔ Zhǔ (蜀主) transferred Pǔ Wáng (普王) Zōngrén (宗仁) to Wèi Wáng (衞王),
Yǎ Wáng (雅王) Zōnglù (宗輅) to Bīnwáng (豳王),
Bāo Wáng (褒王) Zōngjì (宗紀) to Zhào Wáng (趙王),
Róng Wáng (榮王) Zōngzhì (宗智) to Hán Wáng (韓王),
Xīng Wáng (興王) Zōngzé (宗澤) to Sòng Wáng (宋王),
Péng Wáng (彭王) Zōngdǐng (宗鼎) to Lǔ Wáng (魯王),
Zhōng Wáng (忠王) Zōngpíng (宗平) to Xuē Wáng (薛王),
Zī Wáng (資王) Zōngtè (宗特) to Jǔ Wáng (莒王);
Zōnglù (宗輅), Zōngzhì (宗智), and Zōngpíng (宗平) were all relieved of military duties.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the jiǎwǔ day,
Shǔ granted a general amnesty.
2 On the bǐngshēn day,
an imperial decree ordered the officials to rebury Zhāozōng and the Young Emperor,
because their burials were very incomplete due to Zhū Wēn's assassination of them.
Shào,
pronounced like the characters "shī zhào" when read quickly.
The Later Táng dynasty considered itself the successor of Táng,
yet in the end could not rebury Zhāozōng and the Young Emperor;
the Later Hàn dynasty considered itself to have continued the Hàn legacy,
yet Chánglíng and Yuánlíng did not receive a single offering throughout the Qiányòu era.
Historians record this to show their reproach.
3 The Qìdān invaded Yōuzhōu.
4 On the gēngzǐ day,
the Emperor departed Luòyáng;
on the gēngxū day,
he arrived at Xīngtáng.
At that time, Wèizhōu was called Xīngtáng Fǔ.
5 An imperial edict ordered Fú Xí, the Jìedùshǐ of Pínglú, to construct a remote dike at Suānzǎo to defend against the overflowing river.
A remote dike
is one built far from the plain to hold back water.
Zhì,
pronounced like the character "zhí" when read quickly.
6 Initially,
when Lǐ Sìyuán went on the northern expedition—
this refers to the time last year when he defended against the Qìdān in the north—
there were fine imperial armors in the eastern capital's treasury.
Sìyuán, in a dispatch to Deputy Resident Magistrate Zhāng Xiàn, requested five hundred sets.
Xiàn, due to the urgency of the military campaign,
did not have time to report it but supplied them;
the Emperor angrily said:
“Xiàn did not obey an imperial edict,
and presumptuously gave my armors to Sìyuán,
what did he mean by that!”
Xiàn was fined one month's salary,
and ordered to personally go to the army to retrieve them.
He was to go to Sìyuán's army to retrieve the fine armors.
The Emperor, knowing that Wáng Dū, the Jìedùshǐ of Yìwǔ, was about to come to court,
wanted to open a polo field.
Xiàn said:
“The interim palace courtyard has been used as a polo field.
The year before last, Your Majesty was enthroned here,
and that altar cannot be destroyed.
Please open a polo field west of the palace.”
Several days passed,
and it was not yet completed.
The Emperor ordered the destruction of the enthronement altar.
Xiàn said to Guō Chóngtāo:
“This altar
is where the sovereign offered rites to the High God and first received the mandate;
how can it be destroyed!”
Chóngtāo discreetly spoke to the Emperor,
who immediately ordered two Yúhòu to destroy it.
The two Yúhòu were the Horse Army Yúhòu and the Foot Army Yúhòu;
another saying is: the Left and Right Yúhòu.
“Forgetting Heaven and betraying one's origins,
there is no greater misfortune.”
7 In the second month,
on the jiǎxū day,
Lǐ Shàobīn, the Jìedùshǐ of Hénghǎi, was made Jìedùshǐ of Lúlóng.
Lǐ Shàobīn reverted to his surname Zhào during Míngzōng's time,
and was bestowed the name Déjūn.
Déjūn's defense of Yōuzhōu was not without merit;
later, he took advantage of the crisis to pressure the sovereign,
and externally traded with the Qìdān,
resulting not only in his father and son becoming captives,
but Yōuzhōu also falling into Qìdān hands.
8 On the bǐngzǐ day,
Lǐ Sìyuán reported defeating the Qìdān at Zhuōzhōu.
9 The Emperor was worried about the Qìdān,
and discussed with Guō Chóngtāo.
Because veteran generals of great prestige had mostly fallen,
and Lǐ Shàobīn's standing was always low,
he wished to move Lǐ Sìyuán to Zhenzhēng,
to support Shàobīn.
Chóngtāo found this deeply convenient.
At that time, Chóngtāo was in charge of Zhenzhēng.
The Emperor wished to move Chóngtāo to Biànzhōu,
intending to have the two exchange their military governorships.
“Your servant manages the inner pivot,
and participates in major external policies.
My wealth and honor are at their peak;
why must I again lead a frontier region?
Moreover, some of your servants have followed Your Majesty for many years,
and have been through a hundred battles,
yet what they gained is merely a single prefecture.
Your servant has not had the toil of a sweating horse,
but merely by attending on Your Majesty's side,
occasionally assisting in your sagely plans,
I have reached this position,
and I am constantly uneasy.
Now, by entrusting responsibilities to worthy officials,
if your servant could be relieved of the imperial staff,
that would be my greatest wish.
Furthermore, Biànzhōu is a crucial point east of the pass.
Biànzhōu is east of Céngāo Guān,
south to Huái and Sì,
north to Huá and Wèi,
a vital strategic location.
If your servant does not go to the administrative seat,
but merely lets others assume the position,
how is that different from an empty city?
This is not how to secure the foundation of the state.”
The Emperor said:
“I deeply understand your loyalty and devotion.
However, you devised strategies for me,
to seize Wènyáng,
and secure the Héjīn;
then from this route you directly
marched to Dàliáng,
accomplishing my imperial enterprise.
How can the merits of a hundred battles compare to that!
Now that I am honored as the Son of Heaven,
how can I let you be without even an inch of territory!”
Chóngtāo repeatedly declined,
and the Emperor then agreed.
On the gēngchén day,
Lǐ Sìyuán was transferred to be the Jìedùshǐ of Chéngdé.
10The Hàn ruler heard that the Emperor had destroyed Liáng and was afraid.
He sent the Palace Garden Commissioner Hé Cí to offer tribute,
and also to observe the strengths and weaknesses of the Central Plains.
On the jiǎshēn day,
Cí arrived in Wèi.
At that time, the Emperor was in the capital of Wèi.
He reported that the Emperor was arrogant, indulgent, and without good governance,
and not to be feared.
The Hàn ruler was greatly pleased,
and from then on ceased communication with the Central Plains.
11The Emperor was inherently strong-willed and fond of victory,
not wishing power to reside with his subordinates.
After entering Luò,
he believed the slander of jesters and eunuchs,
and rather alienated and mistrusted veteran generals.
Lǐ Sìyuán's family was in Tàiyuán.
In the third month,
on the dīngyǒu day,
he memorialized to appoint Lǐ Cóngkē, the Cìshǐ of Wèizhōu, as the Northern Capital's Imperial Cavalry and Infantry Commander-in-Chief to facilitate his family.
The Emperor angrily said:
“Sìyuán holds military power and occupies a major command.
Military administration is mine;
how can he request on behalf of his son!”
So he demoted Cóngkē to Tūqí Commander,
leading a few hundred men to garrison Shímén Zhèn.
Shímén Zhèn was the Táng dynasty's Héngshuǐ Zhà.
Shuài,
pronounced as "shuài".
He submitted a memorial to clarify the matter,
and after a long time, it was resolved.
On the xīncǒu day,
Sìyuán requested to go to the eastern capital for an audience,
but was not permitted.
Guō Chóngtāo, seeing Sìyuán's high merits and heavy position,
also feared him.
He privately told people:
“Commander-in-Chief Lìnggōng will not long remain a subordinate.”
Lǐ Sìyuán was the Zhōngshū Lìng and Commander-in-Chief of all Chinese and Barbarian Cavalry and Infantry,
hence he was referred to as such.
He secretly urged the Emperor to summon him to the imperial guard,
to strip him of his military power,
and also advised the Emperor to eliminate him,
but the Emperor did not follow any of these suggestions.
This laid the groundwork for Lǐ Sìyuán's suspicion and fear.
Did Guō Chóngtāo also know that he was feared by the jesters and eunuchs?
12On the jǐyǒu day,
the Emperor departed Xīngtáng,
crossed the river at Déshèng,
and passed through Yángcūn and Qīchéng,
observing the old battle sites,
pointing them out to his officials for his amusement.
This is the old habit of the Emperor
who said, “I gained the empire with my ten fingers.”
Lè,
pronounced "luò".
13 The palaces in Luòyáng were grand and deep.
The eunuchs, wishing to expand the number of consorts and concubines,
falsely claimed that ghosts were seen in the palace at night.
The Emperor wished to have exorcists dispel them.
Talismans, holy water, and incantations were used,
performed by shamans and sorcerers who used their arts to deceive the world.
*Ráng* [to dispel],
means to ward off.
"Your servant once served the Son of Heaven during the Xiántōng and Gānfú eras.
*Dài* [to serve],
means to reach.
Xiántōng [咸通] was
the reign title of Táng Yìzōng [唐懿宗];
Gānfú [乾符] was
the reign title of Xīzōng [僖宗].
The noble and humble of the six palaces were no less than ten thousand.
Now, the women's quarters are more than half empty,
hence the ghosts wander there."
The Emperor then ordered the eunuch Wáng Yǔnpíng [王允平] and the actor Jǐng Jìn [景進] to select women from among the populace,
reaching as far as Tàiyuán [太原], Yōu [幽], and Zhèn [鎮],
to fill the imperial harem.
There were no fewer than three thousand of them,
without regard to their origins.
When the Emperor returned from Xīngtáng [興唐],
they were transported by ox-carts,
strung out in long lines filling the road.
Zhāng Xiàn [張憲] reported:
"More than a thousand women have escaped from the various camps.
It is feared that the accompanying armies have harbored them."
In reality, they had all entered the palace.
"Various camps" [諸營]
refers to the various camps in Wèizhōu [魏州].
Historians say that the Emperor's animosity towards the Wèi [魏] soldiers was not due to a single incident.
*Cóng* [從],
read as *cái yòng*.
On *Gēngchén* [庚辰],
the Emperor arrived in Luòyáng [洛陽];
on *Xīnyǒu* [辛酉],
an edict was issued to re-establish Luòyáng as the Eastern Capital,
and Xīngtáng [興唐] Prefecture as the Yè Capital.
During the flourishing period of Táng,
Luòyáng [洛陽] was made the Eastern Capital.
In the early days of Tóngguāng [同光],
Jìnyáng [晉陽] was made the Western Capital,
Wèizhōu [魏州] the Eastern Capital.
Soon thereafter, Luòyáng was made the Luò [洛] Capital.
Now, reverting to the old Táng [唐] system, Luòyáng is the Eastern Capital,
which also means Cháng'ān [長安] is restored as the Western Capital.
Jìnyáng's [晉陽] Western Capital had previously been changed to the Northern Capital,
and with Luòyáng [洛陽] restored to its former status as the Eastern Capital,
Wèizhōu's [魏州] Eastern Capital was changed to the Yè [鄴] Capital.
However, Xiāngzhōu [相州] was the ancient site of Yè,
while Wèizhōu's [魏州] administrative seat was Yuánchéng [元城],
which was not Yè.
Yè [鄴],
was a Wèi [魏] city during the Warring States period.
In the Hàn [漢] dynasty, it was Yè County,
and the administrative seat of Wèi Commandery was there.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, Cáo Cāo [曹操] was made King of Wèi [魏],
and resided in Yè.
Mùróng Wěi [慕容暐] of Former Yàn [燕] made Yè his capital,
and established Guìxiāng [貴鄉] County,
which belonged to Chānglè [昌樂] Commandery.
This is what is meant by the "Guìxiāng at Shāqiū [沙丘] Weir" in the *Shuǐjīng Zhù* [水經註].
In the third year of Kāihuáng [開皇] of the Suí [隋] dynasty, Chānglè [昌樂] Commandery was abolished,
and Guìxiāng County belonged to Wèizhōu [魏州],
thus becoming the administrative seat of the prefecture.
At this time, it was located within the city walls alongside Xīngtáng [興唐] County.
Xīngtáng was originally Yuánchéng.
Zhuāngzōng [莊宗] designated Wèizhōu [魏州] as the Yè Capital [鄴都],
specifically naming it so because the Hàn-Wèi [漢魏] Commandery of Yè [鄴] was governed there, and Cáo Cāo [曹操] made Yè his capital as King of Wèi.
However, Xiāngzhōu [相州] had governed Ānyáng [安陽] since the Suí [隋] dynasty,
and Yè [鄴] was a subordinate county.
The administrative seats of Wèizhōu [魏州] and Xiāngzhōu [相州] were not ancient Yè.
14 In summer,
the fourth month,
on *Guǐhài* [癸亥] *shuò* [朔] (the first day),
there was a solar eclipse.
15 Initially,
Chénghuì [誠惠], a monk from Wǔtái [五臺] Mountain, misled people with his deceitful magic.
He claimed he could subdue heavenly dragons,
summon wind and rain.
The Emperor revered and trusted him,
personally leading the Empress, imperial brother, and imperial sons to bow before him.
Chénghuì remained seated, not rising,
and none of the officials dared not to bow.
At that time, there was a great drought.
The Emperor personally welcomed Chénghuì from the Yè Capital [鄴都] to Luòyáng [洛陽],
asking him to pray for rain.
Officials and common people looked up to him day and night,
but it did not rain for several weeks.
Someone said to Chénghuì:
"Someone said" [謂者],
means to inform or tell.
"The official [the Emperor] finds the Master's rain prayers ineffective,
and will likely burn him."
"Official" [官]
refers to Zhuāngzōng [莊宗];
"Master" [師]
refers to Chénghuì.
Ashamed and afraid, he died.
Historians state that heterodox teachings are often deceptive and not to be trusted.
16 On *Gēngyín* [庚寅],
Zhào Guāngyìn [趙光胤], the Vice Director of the Central Secretariat and concurrently Grand Councilor, died.
17 The Empress Dowager had been separated from Tàizǔ [太祖] for a long time.
In the first month of the second year,
the Empress Dowager left Jìnyáng [晉陽].
Although pleasures filled her surroundings, she never smiled.
After Tàizǔ separated from the Empress Dowager,
he also became depressed and fell ill.
The Empress Dowager sent imperial envoys with medicine one after another on the road.
Hearing that his illness worsened, she would cease eating.
She also said to the Emperor:
"My bond with Tàizǔ is like that of brothers.
I wish to go visit him myself."
The Emperor, citing the summer heat and long journey,
earnestly advised against it,
and after a long while, she stopped,
only sending imperial brother Cúnwò [存渥] and others to go welcome and attend to him.
In the fifth month,
on *Dīngyǒu* [丁酉],
the Northern Capital reported that Tàizǔ had passed away.
The Empress Dowager grieved and did not eat for several days.
The Emperor consoled her and remained by her side.
From then on, the Empress Dowager fell ill.
She again wished to personally attend Tàizǔ's funeral.
The Emperor strongly advised against it, and she stopped.
18 Mǐn [閩] King Shěnzhī [審知] was gravely ill.
He ordered his son, the Deputy Military Commissioner Yánhàn [延翰], to temporarily oversee the military government affairs.
19 Since the great drought in spring and summer,
in the sixth month,
on *Rénshēn* [壬申],
it finally rained.
20 The Emperor suffered from the humid heat.
He searched for a cool place within the forbidden palace,
but none met his satisfaction.
The eunuchs then said:
"Your servants saw Cháng'ān [長安] at its peak,
with hundreds of towers and pavilions in the Dàmíng [大明] and Xīngqìng [興慶] Palaces.
Táng [唐] capital was Cháng'ān;
Dàmíng Palace was the Eastern Inner Palace,
Xīngqìng Palace was the Southern Inner Palace.
*Guàn* [觀],
read as *gōng huàn*."
"The grandeur of the palaces was not even comparable to the residences of high-ranking officials at that time."
The Emperor then ordered the Palace and Park Commissioner Wáng Yǔnpíng [王允平] to build a separate tower for cooling.
The eunuchs said:
"Guō Chóngtāo [郭崇韜] always had a worried look,
criticized by Kǒng Qiān [孔謙] for insufficient expenditures.
We fear that even if Your Majesty wishes to build,
it will ultimately be impossible."
The Emperor said:
"I will use money from my inner treasury;
it is unrelated to public funds."
"Public funds" [經費],
refers to the regular national allocations,
whose expenses were derived from the rent and corvée commissioner.
He sent an imperial envoy to tell him:
"This year's intense heat is extraordinary.
When I was on the river [battlefront] in the past,
confronting the Liáng [梁] people,
the mobile camp was low and damp.
Wearing armor and riding a horse,
personally facing arrows and stones,
I still did not experience such heat.
Now I am in the deep palace, and the heat is unbearable.
What can be done?"
Guō Chóngtāo replied:
"When Your Majesty was on the river [battlefront] in the past,
the formidable enemy was not yet eliminated.
Deeply mindful of revenge and shame,
even with intense heat,
it did not bother Your sacred heart.
Now external threats have been removed,
and the realm submits.
Therefore, even in precious towers and secluded halls, you feel the oppressive heat.
If Your Majesty would not forget the time of hardship,
the heat would naturally dissipate."
Guō Chóngtāo's words,
clearly indicating how comfort changes people,
can be said to be gentle and incisive.
But what could be done if the Emperor did not listen?
The eunuchs said:
"Chóngtāo's residence [郭崇韜],
is no different from the imperial residence;
it's fitting that he doesn't know the Supreme One's heat."
The Emperor ultimately ordered Yǔnpíng [允平] to build the tower,
employing ten thousand people daily,
spending colossal sums.
Chóngtāo [崇韜] remonstrated:
"Now the two rivers [regions] suffer from drought and flood,
and military provisions are insufficient.
I wish that construction would cease for a while,
to await a year of abundance."
The Emperor did not listen.
21 The Emperor was about to attack Shǔ,
on the xīn-mǎo day,
an edict was issued ordering the whole realm to requisition warhorses.
22 Chén Yànqiān, the Military Inspector of Zhenhǎi Circuit and Militant Commander of Chǔzhōu, fell ill.
Chén Yànqiān
was a trusted confidant of Xú Wēn.
Xú Wēn sent him medicine, gold, and silk,
which arrived continuously along the road.
As Yànqiān was dying,
he secretly left a letter for Xú Wēn,
requesting that his biological son be appointed as his heir.
He moved Xú Wēn with the deep affection of a father and son, born of the same blood.
23 The Empress Dowager was gravely ill.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the jiǎ-wǔ day,
Lǐ Sìyuán, the Military Governor of Chéngdé Circuit, stating that border affairs had somewhat subsided,
submitted a memorial requesting permission to enter the court to visit the Empress Dowager.
The Emperor did not permit it.
On the rén-yín day,
the Empress Dowager passed away.
The Emperor was excessively grief-stricken and emaciated,
only eating after five days.
24 In the eighth month,
on the guǐ-wèi day,
Luó Guàn, the Magistrate of Hénán, was beaten to death.
Previously,
Guàn served as the Junior Secretary of the Board of Rites.
His nature was strong and upright,
and he was recognized by Guō Chóngtāo,
who appointed him Magistrate of Hénán.
In governing, he did not shy away from powerful magnates.
The requests for favors from entertainers and eunuchs,
piled up on his desk,
but he did not respond to any of them.
He showed all of them to Chóngtāo,
who reported them to the Emperor,
which made the entertainers and eunuchs gnash their teeth.
Zhāng Quányì, the Prefect of Hénán, also disliked Guàn for his haughtiness
and sent a maid to complain to the Empress.
Empress Liú treated Zhāng Quányì like a father,
which allowed his maid to enter and exit the palace.
The Emperor harbored his anger but did not yet express it.
It happened that the Emperor personally went to Shòu'ān to inspect the workers at Kūnlíng.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* says: Shòu'ān County is seventy *lǐ* southwest of Luòyáng.
The *Wǔdài Huìyào* says: The Emperor desired to inter the Empress Dowager in the ancestral mausoleum of Emperor Tàizǔ in Dàizhōu.
The Chancellery and Department of State Affairs deliberated and memorialized:
"A ruler takes the four seas as his home;
there should be no distinction between north and south.
Luòyáng is the residence of emperors and kings.
For four seasons of worship,
it is reasonable that it should be conveniently nearby.
One cannot travel far to Dàizhōu.
All the mausoleums of the Hàn dynasty were near Qín and Yōng;
the imperial tombs of our state are spread across the capital region.
After Emperor Wén of the Later Wèi moved the capital from Dài to Luò,
all imperial mausoleums were in Hénán,
and an edict was also issued prohibiting meritorious ministers from being buried in the north.
Now, the various mausoleums of the Wèi clan are still in the capital region.
Interring her in Dàizhōu
would not be reasonable or appropriate."
Thus, Kūnlíng was constructed.
Many bridges were in disrepair.
The Emperor asked who was in charge,
and a eunuch replied that it was under Hénán's jurisdiction.
The Emperor was enraged
and ordered Guàn imprisoned.
The jailers beat and flogged him
until his body was covered in wounds.
The next day,
an edict was proclaimed to execute him.
Chóngtāo remonstrated, saying:
"Guàn is accused of bridge and road disrepair.
The law does not prescribe death for this."
The Emperor angrily said:
"The Empress Dowager's funeral carriage is about to depart,
and the Son of Heaven travels back and forth morning and night.
The bridges and roads are in disrepair,
and you say he is innocent?
This is partisanship!"
Chóngtāo replied:
"Your Majesty, with the dignity of ten thousand chariots,
is angry at a mere county magistrate.
This will make the world say that Your Majesty's application of the law is unfair.
This is my fault."
The Emperor said:
"Since he is your beloved,
you may decide his fate."
He flicked his sleeves and entered the palace.
Chóngtāo followed him,
remonstrating ceaselessly;
the Emperor personally closed the palace gate,
and Chóngtāo could not enter.
Guàn ultimately died,
his body exposed at the prefectural gate.
People near and far felt he was wronged.
Luó Guàn's death
showed that Chóngtāo could have left but could not,
leading to his own annihilation.
How lamentable!
25 On the dīng-hài day,
the Emperor sent Lǐ Déxiū, the Minister of Personnel, and others to bestow upon the King of Wúyuè a jade tablet, a gold seal,
and a red imperial robe.
26 In the ninth month,
the Ruler of Shǔ, with the Empress Dowager and the Empress, traveled to Qīngchéng Shān,
visiting Zhàngrén Guān and Shàngqīng Gōng.
Qīngchéng Shān is thirty-three *lǐ* north of Qīngchéng County in Shǔzhōu.
Dù Guāngtíng said: The Mín Shān mountain range extends for a thousand *lǐ* without interruption,
and Qīngchéng Shān is its first peak.
Zhàngrén Guān is twenty *lǐ* north of Qīngchéng.
Shàngqīng Gōng is beside the Zhàngrén temple on Gāotái Shān.
Gāotái Shān is on Mín Shān,
with a Heavenly Pond.
The Jìn dynasty established a Heavenly Palace there,
named Shàngqīng Gōng.
Forty *lǐ* north of Méngyáng County in Péngzhōu is Géxiān Shān,
the fifth of the twenty-four transformations.
27 On the yǐ-wèi day,
the Imperial Prince Jìjí was enfeoffed as King of Wèi.
28 On the dīng-yǒu day,
the Emperor discussed attacking Shǔ with the chancellors.
Lǐ Shàoqīn, the Military Governor of Wēishèng Circuit, had always fawned upon Lǐ Shàohóng, the Commissioner of Xuanhui.
Shàohóng recommended him,
saying: "Shàojīn possesses extraordinary talent that surpasses the age,
even Sūn and Wú are not his equal;
he can be entrusted with a great responsibility."
Guō Chóngtāo said:
"Duàn Níng is a general who led his state to ruin,
his deceit and flattery are unparalleled;
he cannot be trusted."
Dèngzhōu Xuānhuà Army was renamed Wēishèng Army.
Duàn Níng surrendered
and was granted the name Lǐ Shàojīn.
These matters are all seen in the first year of the previous volume.
Chóngtāo said:
"The Khitan are currently flourishing.
The Commander-in-Chief must not leave Héshuò.
The King of Wèi is destined to be the heir apparent,
but he has not yet established extraordinary merit.
I request that, following precedent,
he be made the Commander-in-Chief for the attack on Shǔ."
During Ān Lùshān's rebellion,
Emperor Xuánzōng appointed his sons as various circuit commanders;
this is a Tang precedent.
The Emperor said:
"The child is young.
How can he go alone?
We must find a deputy for him."
Afterwards, he said:
"No one can replace you."
On the gēng-zǐ day,
King Wèi Jìjí was appointed Grand Commander of the Western Sichuan Four-Front Field Army,
and Chóngtāo was appointed Grand Pacification and Deployment Commissioner of the Northeastern Front Field Army,
with all military affairs entrusted to him.
Furthermore, Gāo Jìxīng, the Military Governor of Jīngnán Circuit, was appointed Grand Pacification Commissioner of the Southeastern Front Field Army;
Lǐ Jìyǎn, the Military Governor of Fèngxiáng Circuit, was appointed Grand Commissioner for Army Supply, Transport, and Reception;
Lǐ Lìngdé, the Military Governor of Tóngzhōu Circuit, was appointed Deputy Pacification Commissioner of the Field Army;

Lǐ Shàochēn, the Military Governor of Shǎnzhōu Circuit, was appointed Grand Commander for Arranging and Chopping the Fān and Hàn Cavalry and Infantry, concurrently serving as Grand Commander of Cavalry and Infantry.
Lǐ Lìngdé
was the son of Zhū Yǒuqīan;
Lǐ Shàochēn
was Kāng Yánxiào;
both surrendered to Tang and were granted new names.
Chén
is read as zhèn.
Máo Zhāng, the Military Governor of Huázhōu Circuit, was appointed Grand Quartermaster of the Left Wing Cavalry and Infantry;
Dǒng Zhāng, the Military Governor of Bīnzhōu Circuit, was appointed Grand Quartermaster of the Right Wing Cavalry and Infantry;
Lǐ Yán, the Commissioner of Guest Affairs, was appointed Pacification Commissioner within the Western Sichuan Administrative Region,
leading an army of sixty thousand to attack Shǔ.
An edict also commanded Jìxīng to seize Kuí, Zhōng, and Wàn prefectures for his own jurisdiction.
During the Tang dynasty, Kuí, Zhōng, and Wàn prefectures originally belonged to the Jīngnán Circuit.
During the chaos at the end of the Tang,
Wáng Jiàn seized Shǔ
and incorporated these prefectures.
Lǐ Cóngxí, a Court Official for Imperial Services, was appointed Grand Commander and Supervisor of the Central Army Cavalry and Infantry;
Gāo Tíng'ān and Lǚ Zhīróu, high-ranking officials, were appointed Calligraphy Masters of the King of Wèi's Residence.
Lǐ Cóngxí and others were all eunuchs.
On the xīn-chǒu day,
Rèn Yuán, the Minister of Public Works, and Lǐ Yú, a Hanlin Academician, were both appointed to participate in the military affairs of the Commander-in-Chief.
29 From the jiǎ-wǔ day of the sixth month,
there was continuous rain,
and the sun and stars were rarely seen.
The Jiāng, Hé, and all rivers overflowed,
and it did not clear for seventy-five days.

30 Guō Chóngtāo, recalling his old favor of recommending and promoting Mèng Zhīxiáng, the Defense Commissioner of the Northern Capital (this matter is found in Volume 270, the fifth year of Zhēnmíng of Liáng Jūnwáng),
spoke to the Emperor, saying:
"Mèng Zhīxiáng is trustworthy, prudent, and resourceful.
If Western Sichuan is conquered and a commander is sought,
no one surpasses this man."
He also recommended Zhāng Xiàn, the Deputy Defense Commissioner of Yèdū, as cautious and discerning,
suitable to be a chancellor.
On the wù-shēn day,
the main army marched west.
Lǐ Shàochēn and others passed through Chángjǔ.
Chángjǔ
was the land of Han's Jū Xiàn.
During the Western Wèi, Pántóu Jùn was established.
During the Suí, Chángjǔ Xiàn was established.
During the Táng, it belonged to Xīngzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: "It is 100 lǐ west of the prefecture."
They first requested to repair the bridges and棧 (plank roads) to await the Táng army,
thus the army's march had no fear of dangers or obstacles.
On the Xīnsì day,
Wáng Chéngjiàn, the Cìshǐ of Xīngzhōu, abandoned the city and fled.
Shàochēn and others captured Xīngzhōu.
The Kǎoyì says: The Shílù states:
"On the Jiǎshēn day,
King Wèi arrived at Gùzhèn,
and Kāng Yánxiào took Xīngzhōu."
The Shíguó Jìnián states:
"On the Xīnsì day,
Chéngjiàn fled.
On the Jiǎshēn day,
Jìjí and Guō Chóngtāo arrived at Wēiwǔ Chéng."
We follow this account.
On the Yǐyǒu day,
Wáng Chéngpǔ, the Cìshǐ of Chéngzhōu, abandoned the city and fled.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: "From Xīngzhōu west to Chéngzhōu is 215 lǐ."
Sānquán Xiàn
belonged to Xīngyuán Fǔ during the Táng.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: "From Xīngzhōu southeast to Sānquán is 145 lǐ,
with the dangers of Bǎiláo Guān and Jīnniú Dào."
Five thousand heads were severed,
and the remaining troops scattered and fled.
Also, 150,000 hú of grain were obtained at Sānquán,
thus the army's provisions were ample.
Yōu
means abundant.
On the Wùzǐ day,
the Empress Dowager Zhēnjiǎn was buried at Kūnlíng.
The Shǔ Lord heard that Wáng Zōngxūn and others had been defeated,
and from Lìzhōu, he doubled back westward,
cutting the floating bridge at Júbǎi Jīn.
He ordered Wáng Zōngbì, the Zhōngshū Lìng and Pàn Liùjūn Zhūwèi Shì, to lead a large army to defend Lìzhōu,
and also commanded the execution of Wáng Zōngxūn and the other three Zhāotǎo envoys.
This was due to the defeat at Sānquán.
Lǐ Shàochēn marched day and night towards Lìzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: "From Sānquán west to Lìzhōu is 189 lǐ."
Qù
is pronounced as Qī Yù.
"Please do not let the Táng troops enter our territory;
we will surrender our prefectures and counties.
If you do not keep your promise,
we will fight a decisive battle outside the city to repay our court."
Chóngtāo replied with a conciliatory letter.
On the Yǐ
chǒu day,
King Wèi Jìjí arrived at Xīngzhōu.
Guāng Bǎo surrendered the five prefectures of Zǐ, Mián, Jiàn, Lóng, and Pǔ.
Wáng Chéngzhào, the Wǔdìng Jiédùshǐ, surrendered the three prefectures of Yáng, Péng, and Bì.
Wáng Zōngwēi, the Shānnán Jiédùshǐ,
surrendered the five prefectures of Liáng, Kāi, Tōng, Qú, and Lín.
Qúzhōu's Línshān Xiàn:
in the first year of Táng Wǔdé, Línzhōu was established;
in the eighth year, the prefecture was abolished,
and Línshān Xiàn was made to belong to Qúzhōu;
it must be that Shǔ re-established Línzhōu.
"Lín"
should be
"Lín,"
pronounced Lì Zhēn.
Also, during the Táng Zhēnguān era, Línzhōu was established to settle the Qīng people who had submitted,
belonging to Sōngzhōu Dūdūfǔ.
After Táng Zhìdé, it had been lost for a long time.
It should be the Lín of Qú and Lín.
All surrendered.
Chéngzhào
was the son of Zōngkǎn.
All other cities and towns submitted at the mere mention of their approach.
Wáng Chéngxiū, the Tiānxiong Jiédùshǐ, and his deputy, Ān Chóngbà, plotted to ambush the Táng army,
intending to attack the Táng army from Qínzhōu from behind.
"If we attack and do not win,
then the great cause is lost.
Shǔ has 100,000 elite soldiers and impregnable defenses.
Even if the Táng army is brave,
how can they directly cross Jiànmén?
However, since you have received national grace,
when you hear of trouble, you cannot fail to respond.
I wish to go west with you."
He meant going west from Qínzhōu to Chéngdū.
He thought it was true.
Chóngbà requested to bribe the Qiāng people to buy passage through Wén and Fúzhōu to return.
Chéngxiū agreed,
and sent Chóngbà to lead the Lóngwǔ army and 12,000 recruited soldiers to follow.
When they were about to depart,
the local people saw them off outside the city.
As Chéngxiū set out on the road,
Chóngbà bowed before his horse and said:
"The state exerted all its strength to obtain Qín and Lǒng.
Shǔ obtained Qín and Lǒng.
See Volume 269, Liáng Jūn Wáng Zhēnmíng First Year.
Who will guard them?
Kāifǔ, go!
Chóngbà requests to stay behind to guard for you."
Shǔ had probably bestowed upon Wáng Chéngxiū the title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
hence the address.
Wéi
is pronounced Yú Wěi;
the next Wéi is the same.
Shǒu
is pronounced Shì Yòu.
There was nothing to be done,
so he went south with Wáng Zōngruì, the Zhāotǎo Fùshǐ, via Fú and Wén.
That land was barren,
and the Qiāng people raided them.
Fighting and marching,
the soldiers froze and starved.
By the time they reached Màozhōu,
only two thousand of their troops remained.
This path from Qínzhōu through Wén and Fú,
following the mountains to Màozhōu.
This laid the groundwork for Wáng Chéngxiū and Zōngruì to be executed by King Wèi Jìjí.
Bǐ
is pronounced Bì Lì.
Gāo Jìxìng had always wanted to take the Three Gorges,
but feared the reputation of Zhāng Wǔ, the Shǔ Xiálù Zhāotǎo Shǐ,
and dared not advance.
At this time,
taking advantage of the Táng army's power,
he sent his son Gāo Cónghuì, the Xíngjūn Sīmǎ, to temporarily handle military affairs,
and personally led a naval force up the gorges to capture Shīzhōu.
Zhāng Wǔ used an iron chain to block the river.
Jìxìng sent brave warriors in boats to cut it.
A strong wind suddenly arose,
and the boats got entangled in the chain,
unable to advance or retreat.
Arrows and stones rained down,
destroying their warships,
and Jìxìng fled in a light boat.
If all of Shǔ's border commanders were like Zhāng Wǔ,
how could Sànguān have been so easily entered?
This laid the groundwork for Mèng Zhīxiáng to reuse Zhāng Wǔ later.
He sent envoys from Kuí, Zhōng, and Wàn prefectures to King Wèi to surrender.
Guō Chóngtāo sent a letter to Wáng Zōngbì and others,
explaining the advantages and disadvantages.
Before Lǐ Shàochēn arrived at Lìzhōu,
Zōngbì abandoned the city and led his troops back west.
Wáng Zōngxūn and the other three Zhāotǎo envoys caught up with Zōngbì at Báidiáo.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states:
"Jīnshuǐ Xiàn in Jiǎnzhōu has Báidiáo Zhèn."
Diáo
is pronounced Dū Liáo.
"Sòng Guāngsì ordered me to kill you all."
They then held each other and wept,
and subsequently conspired to submit to Táng.
