(Yǐyǒu, 925)
First month of November,
on the Bǐngshēn day,
the Shǔ Lord arrived at Chéngdū.
All officials and the imperial harem welcomed him at Qīlǐ Tíng.
The pavilion was seven lǐ from Chéngdū city,
hence its name.
He imitated the Huíhú in his procession into the palace.
On the Dīngyǒu day,
he appeared before his ministers at Wénmíng Diàn.
According to the Wǔdài Huìyào,
in the first year of Liáng Kāimíng, Luòyáng Palace's Zhēnguān Diàn was renamed Wénmíng Diàn.
Zhēnguān Diàn
was the front hall of Luòyáng Palace,
renamed after Táng Zhāozōng moved to Luò.
Now Shǔ also has a Wénmíng Diàn.
The Shǔ palace imitated the Táng palace system.
It is implied that Wénmíng
was a palace name at the end of Táng.
Lord and ministers looked at each other,
yet not a single word was uttered to save the nation from calamity.
On the Wùxū day,
Lǐ Shàochēn arrived at Lìzhōu
and repaired the Júbǎi floating bridge.
The Júbǎi floating bridge had been cut by Shǔ,
so it was repaired for crossing.
Shǔ had established the Zhāowǔ Jiédù at Lìzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: "From Lìzhōu southeast to Làngzhōu is 235 lǐ."
On the Jiǎchén day,
King Wèi Jìjí arrived at Jiànzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: "From Jiànzhōu northeast to Lìzhōu is 190 lǐ."
Shǔ had established the Wǔxìn army at Suízhōu.
Wáng Zōngbì 王宗弼 arrived at Chéngdū 成都.
He ascended the Dàxuán Mén 大玄門
and took self-protective measures with his soldiers.
The Shǔ Zhǔ 蜀主 (Ruler of Shǔ) and the Grand Empress Dowager personally went to comfort him,
but Zōngbì 宗弼 was arrogant and disrespectful, no longer observing the rites of a subject.
On the *yǐsì* 乙巳 day,
he forcibly moved the Shǔ Zhǔ 蜀主, the Grand Empress Dowager, and all the princes of the imperial harem to the Western Palace.
He seized their seals and tallies,
and ordered his trusted officers to intercept and take the gold and silk from the inner treasury at Yìxīng Mén 義興門,
all of which he brought to his own home.
His son, Chéngjuān 承涓, entered the palace with a sword,
taking several of the Shǔ Zhǔ’s 蜀主 favorite concubines with him.
On the *bǐngwǔ* 丙午 day,
Zōngbì 宗bì declared himself Acting Commander of the West Chuan Army and Provisional Governor (Quán Xīchuān Bīngmǎ Liúhòu 權西川兵馬留後).
Lǐ Shàochēn 李紹琛 advanced to Miánzhōu 綿州.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* 九域志 states: "From Jiànzhōu 劍州 west to Miánzhōu 綿州 is two hundred eighty *lǐ*."
He then cut the pontoon bridge over the Miánjiāng 綿江.
The water was deep,
and there were no boats or rafts to cross.
Shàochēn 紹琛 said to Lǐ Yán 李嚴:
"Our army is deep within enemy territory.
It is advantageous to fight quickly.
Seizing the moment when the people of Shǔ 蜀 are demoralized,
if we can get just a hundred cavalry past the Lùtóu Guān 鹿頭關,
they will surrender without delay.
If we wait to repair the bridge,
we will certainly be delayed for several days,
which might allow Wáng Yǎn 王衍 to reinforce the nearby pass,
blunting our military might."
The nearby pass
refers to Lùtóu Guān 鹿頭關.
*Zhé* 折 (blunt),
pronunciation *zhī shé fān*.
"Then the outcome of victory or defeat will be unknown."
He meant that an army that has advanced deep into enemy territory benefits from swift and decisive attacks,
and cannot sustain a prolonged campaign.
Barely a thousand soldiers managed to cross,
while over a thousand more drowned.
They then entered Lùtóu Guān 鹿頭關.
On the *dīngwèi* 丁未 day,
they advanced to occupy Hànzhōu 漢州.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* 九域志 states: "From Miánzhōu 綿州 southwest to Hànzhōu 漢州 is one hundred eighty-nine *lǐ*."
The rear army finally arrived.
Zōngbì 宗弼 sent an envoy with silks, horses, oxen, and wine to reward the army,
and also sent a letter from the Shǔ Zhǔ 蜀主 to Lǐ Yán 李嚴,
which said:
"If you come, I will surrender immediately."
Someone said to Yán 嚴:
"Someone said to Yán 嚴" means
"someone spoke to Yán 嚴."
"You were the first to propose the campaign against Shǔ 蜀."
The matter is recorded in the previous volume, previous year.
"You cannot go."
Yán 嚴 did not listen,
but gladly hastened into Chéngdū 成都.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* 九域志 states: "From Hànzhōu 漢州 south to Chéngdū 成都 is ninety-five *lǐ*."
He announced that the main army would soon arrive.
The ruler, officials, and imperial harem of Shǔ 蜀 all wept bitterly.
The Shǔ Zhǔ 蜀主 introduced Yán 嚴 to the Grand Empress Dowager,
entrusting his mother and wife to him.
Zōngbì 宗bì was still preparing defenses on the city walls,
but Yán 嚴 ordered all the watchtowers and battlements removed.
*Chéng* 乘 (ascend),
means "to ascend."
*Qù* 去 (remove),
pronunciation *qiāng lǚ fān*.
On the *jǐyǒu* 己酉 day,
Wèi Wáng Jìjí 魏王繼岌 arrived at Miánzhōu 綿州.
The Shǔ Zhǔ 蜀主 ordered Hanlin Academician Lǐ Hào 李昊 to draft the instrument of surrender,
and also ordered Censor-in-chief, Minister of Personnel, and Co-administrator of Affairs Wáng Kǎi 王鍇 to draft a letter of surrender.
The instrument of surrender was for the Emperor,
and the letter of surrender was for the army at the front.
*Kǎi* 鍇,
pronunciation *kǒu hài fān*.
Wáng Zōngbì 王宗弼 claimed that the ruler and officials of Shǔ 蜀 had long wished to surrender,
but that the Inner Privy Councilors Sòng Guāngsì 宋光嗣 and Jǐng Rùnchéng 景潤澄, and the Commissioners of the Xuanhui Bureau Lǐ Zhōulù 李周輅 and Ōuyáng Huàng 歐陽晃 had misled the Shǔ Zhǔ 蜀主.
He had them all executed,
and sent their heads in boxes to Jìjí 繼岌.

He also accused Wénsīdiàn Dàxuéshì 文思殿大學士 (Grand Academician of the Wensi Hall), Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū 禮部尚書), and Intendant of Chéngdū (Chéngdū Yǐn 成都尹) Hán Zhāo 韓昭 of being a flattering sycophant,
and had him publicly beheaded at the gate of the Jīnmǎ Fāng 金馬坊.
The Jīnmǎ Fāng 金馬坊 was within the city of Chéngdū 成都,
named for the shrine of the Golden Horse and Green Chicken.
Hence the name of the ward.
There was also the Bìjī Fāng 碧雞坊.
He emptied his household of gold, silk, courtesans, and concubines to bribe Zōngbì 宗弼,
and barely escaped death.
Zōngbì 宗Bì killed anyone
with whom he had a previous disagreement.
On the *xīnhài* 辛亥 day,
Jìjí 繼岌 arrived at Déyáng 德陽.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* 九域志 states: "Déyáng Xiàn 德陽縣 is eighty-five *lǐ* northeast of Hànzhōu 漢州."
He claimed to have moved the Shǔ Zhǔ 蜀主 to the Western Residence (Xī Dì 西第),
and to have already presented a memorial of surrender to Táng 唐.
He did not dare to say "Western Palace" (Xī Gōng 西宮),
hence he said "Western Residence" (Xī Dì 西第).
He awaited the imperial army.
He also sent his son Chéngbān 承班 with the Shǔ Zhǔ’s 蜀主 imperial harem and treasures to bribe Jìjí 繼岌 and Guō Chóngtāo 郭崇韜,
seeking the position of Jìedùshǐ 節度使 (Military Governor) of Xīchuān 西川.
Jìjí 繼岌 said:
"These are all our family's possessions;
why present them as offerings?"
He kept the items and sent Chéngbān 承班 away.
Zōngbì’s 宗弼 offerings,
and Jìjí’s 繼岌 retention—
the difference between the worthy and the unworthy
was immeasurable.
Lǐ Shàochēn 李紹琛 stayed in Hànzhōu 漢州 for eight days awaiting the Commander-in-chief.
The Commander-in-chief
was Jìjí 繼岌.
On the *jiǎyín* 甲寅 day,
Jìjí 繼岌 arrived at Hànzhōu 漢州,
and Wáng Zōngbì 王宗弼 welcomed and paid homage to him.
On the *yǐmǎo* 乙卯 day,
he arrived at Chéngdū 成都.
On the *bǐngchén* 丙辰 day,
Lǐ Yán 李嚴 led the Shǔ Zhǔ 蜀主 and his officials, with imperial escort, to surrender at Shēngqiān Qiáo 升遷橋.
According to Xuē Shǐ 薛史,
Shēngqiān Qiáo 升遷橋 was five *lǐ* north of Chéngdū 成都.
With their heads bound with grass ropes,
the officials wore mourning clothes, were barefoot, and carried coffins in carts,
weeping and awaiting their fate.
Jìjí 繼岌 accepted the jade,
Chóngtāo 崇韜 untied their bonds,
burned the coffins,
and, acting under imperial authority, absolved them of their crimes.
The ruler and his officials bowed in gratitude facing northeast.
Wáng Jiàn 王建 seized Shǔ 蜀 in the second year of Dàshùn 大順 of Táng Zhāozōng 唐昭宗 (891 CE),
and it perished with Yǎn 衍.
On the *dīngsì* 丁巳 day,
the main army entered Chéngdū 成都.
Chóngtāo 崇韜 forbade soldiers from plundering,
and markets remained open as usual.
From the departure of the expeditionary force to the conquest of Shǔ 蜀,
it took seventy days in total.
The *Kǎoyì* 考異 states: The *Shílù* 實錄 says:
"From the army's departure from Luòchéng 洛城 to the capture of Shǔ 蜀 city,
it took seventy-five days."
The *Xuē Shǐ* 薛史 follows this.
However, the Táng 唐 army left Luòchéng 洛城 on the *wùshēn* 戊申 day of the ninth month
and entered Chéngdū 成都 on the *dīngsì* 丁巳 day of the eleventh month,
which is only seventy days.
The *Shílù* 實錄 and *Xuē Shǐ* 薛史 are mistaken.
There were ten military governorships (jiédù 節度) in total: Wǔdé 武德, Wǔxìn 武信, Yǒngpíng 永平, Wǔtài 武泰, Zhènjiāng 鎮江, Shānnán 山南, Wǔdìng 武定, Tiānxíong 天雄, Wǔxīng 武興, and Zhāowǔ 昭武.
Xīchuān 西川 was the capital of Shǔ 蜀,
and was not included.

The *Ōu Shǐ Zhífāng Kǎo* 歐史職方考 states: The Former Shǔ 蜀 possessed only fifty-three prefectures (zhōu 州): Yì 益, Hàn 漢, Péng 彭, Shǔ 蜀, Mián 綿, Méi 眉, Jiā 嘉, Jiàn 劍, Zǐ 梓, Suì 遂, Guǒ 果, Làng 閬, Pǔ 普, Líng 陵, Zī 資, Róng 榮, Jiǎn 簡, Qióng 邛, Lí 黎, Yǎ 雅, Wéi 維, Mào 茂, Wén 文, Lóng 龍, Qián 黔, Shī 施, Kuí 夔, Zhōng 忠, Wàn 萬, Guī 歸, Xiá 峽, Xīng 興, Lì 利, Kāi 開, Tōng 通, Fú 涪, Yú 渝, Lú 瀘, Hé 合, Chāng 昌, Bā 巴, Péng 蓬, Jí 集, Bì 璧, Qú 渠, Róng 戎, Liáng 梁, Yáng 洋, Jīn 金, Qín 秦, Fèng 鳳, Jiē 階, and Chéng 成.
The army numbered thirty thousand,
and their armor, weapons, money, provisions, gold, silver, silks, and brocades amounted to tens of millions.
When Gāo Jìxīng 高季興 heard that Shǔ 蜀 had fallen,
he was eating,
and dropped his knife and chopsticks,
saying:
"This is my fault."
Gāo Jìxīng’s 高季興 advice to attack Shǔ 蜀 is found in Volume 272, first year.
"There's no need to worry.
The Táng Zhǔ 唐主 (Ruler of Táng) will become even more arrogant now that he has Shǔ 蜀,
and his downfall is not far off."
Liáng Zhèn’s 梁震 assessment of Zhuāngzōng 莊宗 was as clear as looking at a candle and counting.
"I know it will not be a blessing for us!"
(I know it will not be a blessing for us!)
No blessing for Jīngnán 荊南 has ever been heard of.
With only three prefectures, situated between powerful states,
trembling and barely able to preserve itself,
what blessing could there be?
Chǔ Wáng Yīn 楚王殷 heard that Shǔ 蜀 had fallen,
and submitted a memorial stating:
"Your subject has already prepared a 'rabbit fur' retreat in the Hènglù 衡麓 area."
Hènglù 衡麓
means the foot of Héngshān 衡山.
The foot of a mountain is called *lù* 麓.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* 左傳 states: Rǔ Yǐngōng 魯隱公 ordered the construction of Tùqiú 菟裘,
saying, "I will grow old there."
Mǎ Yīn 馬殷 meant he would retire from service and grow old at Hènglù 衡麓;
he was afraid upon hearing of Shǔ’s 蜀 fall.
*Tù* 菟,
pronunciation *tóng dōu fān*.
*Líng* 齡
means "year."
The *Jì Wén Wáng Shìzǐ* 記文王世子 states: "In ancient times, *niánlíng* 年齡 was used,
and *chǐ* 齒 (teeth) also meant *líng* 齡."
*Shàng* 上 (present),
pronunciation *shí zhǎng fān*.
2 The achievement of pacifying Shǔ,
Lǐ Shàochēn's was the greatest,
his rank being above Dǒng Zhāng;
but Zhāng had always been on good terms with Guō Chóngtāo,
and Chóngtāo frequently summoned Zhāng to discuss military matters.
Shàochēn was resentful in his heart,
and said to Zhāng:
"I achieved the pacification of Shǔ,
while you and others merely followed along like logs,
yet you whisper at Grand Duke Guō's door,
plotting to harm each other.
I am the commander-in-chief."
The Emperor appointed Lǐ Shàochēn as the Commander of the Campaigning Infantry and Cavalry,
and Dǒng Zhāng as the Left Wing Usher,
hence the remark.
Zhāng complained to Chóngtāo.
In the twelfth month,
Chóngtāo memorialized to appoint Zhāng as the Jìedùshǐ of Dōngchuān.
The *Kǎoyì* says: *Zhuāngzōng Shílù*:
"On the *bǐngyín* day of the twelfth month,
Dǒng Zhāng, Jìngnán Jìedùshǐ, was appointed as the Deputy Grand Envoy of Dōngchuān Jìedù. "
Furthermore, Kāng Yánxiào's biography states:
"Guō Chóngtāo appointed Dǒng Zhāng as Dōngchuān Jìedùshǐ.
Yánxiào and the Huázhōu Jìedùshǐ Máo Zhāng met Chóngtāo,
requesting that Rèn Shàngshū of the Ministry of Works be appointed as the commander of Dōngchuān.
Chóngtāo angrily said: 'Is Shàochēn rebellious,
daring to defy my command!'
In less than two *xún* (twenty days),
Chóngtāo was killed by Jìjì. "
According to records, the main army entered Xīchuān on the *dīngsì* day of the eleventh month, the twenty-eighth day;
Dǒng Zhāng was appointed to Dōngchuān on the *bǐngyín* day of the twelfth month, the eighth day;
a total of ten days.
Chóngtāo was killed on the eighth day of the first month of the following year,
a total of sixty days from the entry into Xīchuān.
Yet it says
"Chóngtāo was killed in less than two *xún*,"
which does not match the dates at all.
It is likely that the *bǐngyín* day of the twelfth month was when Chóngtāo first memorialized for Zhāng to govern Dōngchuān,
not the day the imperial edict was issued.
The statement
"in less than two *xún*"
is also probably incorrect.
By relieving Dǒng Zhāng of his military post,
Lǐ Shàochēn could not enforce military law upon him.
This was how Chóngtāo protected Dǒng Zhāng.
He said:
"I braved white blades,
traversed perilous obstacles,
and pacified the two Chuāns.
Can Zhāng merely sit and take possession of them!"
He then met Chóngtāo and said:
"Dōngchuān is an important place.
Rèn Shàngshū has both literary and martial talent,
and should be memorialized as its commander."
Rèn Huán was at that time the Shàngshū of the Ministry of Works and participated in military affairs.
帥 (*shuài*),
pronounced as *suǒ lèi*.
"Is Shàochēn rebellious?
How dare you defy my command!"
Shàochēn, afraid, withdrew.
In the beginning,
the Emperor sent the eunuch Lǐ Cóngxí and others to accompany Wèi Wáng Jìjì in the expedition against Shǔ;
although Jìjì was the Dūtǒng,
all military arrangements and appointments were decided by Guō Chóngtāo.
Chóngtāo spent the entire day making decisions,
with generals, officials, and guests bustling in and out of his courtyard.
In the Dūtǒng's mansion, however, apart from the chief general's morning audience,
the gate was desolate,
which Cóngxí and others found deeply shameful.
When Shǔ was defeated,
Shǔ's noble officials and generals competed to present treasures, musicians, and dancers to Chóngtāo and his son Tínghuì,
while Wèi Wáng received nothing more than a horse, a bundle of silk, a spittoon, and a fly whisk,
which further displeased Cóngxí and others.
When Wáng Zōngbì had appointed himself as the Liúhòu of Xīchuān,
he bribed Chóngtāo to seek the position of Jìedùshǐ.
Chóngtāo pretended to agree to it.
The *Kǎoyì* states: Both *Shílù* and Xuē's *Shǐ* say that Chóngtāo promised him the command of Shǔ.
However, Chóngtāo possessed foresight and strategy,
how could he lead a great army to conquer Xīchuān
only to hand it over to Zōngbì?
This is something even an ordinary person would not do.
It is likely that at that time Zōngbì still occupied Chéngdū,
and Chóngtāo feared that he might change his mind and resist,
so he merely pretended to agree to appease him.
Then, leading the people of Shǔ, he presented a petition to Jìjì,
requesting to retain Chóngtāo to govern Shǔ.
Cóngxí and others then said to Jìjì:
"Duke Guō and his son are arrogant and overbearing.
Now they even have the people of Shǔ request him to be the commander.
Their ambition is unfathomable;
Your Highness must guard against them."
Jìjì said to Chóngtāo:
"The Sovereign relies on the Shìzhōng as on mountains.
He cannot be separated from the imperial court."
Guō Chóngtāo held the office of Shìzhōng,
hence Jìjì referred to him as such.
pronounced as *lì zhì fān*.
"Moreover, this is not something I dare to know.
I ask these people to go to the court and express themselves."
From then on, Jìjì and Chóngtāo began to suspect each other.
This section, from "The achievement of pacifying Shǔ" onwards,
lays the groundwork for Lǐ Shàochēn's rebellion;
from "In the beginning, the Emperor sent Lǐ Cóngxí to accompany Jìjì" onwards,
it lays the groundwork for the killing of Guō Chóngtāo.
At that time, Sòng Guāngbǎo came from Zǐzhōu,
complaining that Wáng Zōngbì had falsely accused and killed Sòng Guāngsì and others;
furthermore,
Chóngtāo demanded tens of thousands of *mín* in military funds from Zōngbì,
but Zōngbì was stingy,
causing the soldiers to be resentful and angry.
At night,
they set fires and made a commotion.
Chóngtāo wanted to execute Zōngbì to clear his own name.
On the *jǐsì* day,
he informed Jìjì to arrest Zōngbì, Wáng Zōngxūn, and Wáng Zōngwò.
He enumerated their disloyalty,
executed them and their families,
and confiscated their property.
The people of Shǔ competed to eat Zōngbì's flesh.
3 On the *xīnwèi* day, Mǐn Zhōngyì Wáng Shěnzhī died
at the age of sixty-four.
Yánhàn, courtesy name Zǐyì,
was Shěnzhī's eldest son.
Yánhàn sent the Right Army Supervisor Liǔ Yōng and others with twenty thousand soldiers to attack them.
4 On the *guǐyǒu* day, Wáng Chéngxiū and Wáng Zōngruì arrived in Chéngdū.
They had departed from Qínzhōu in the tenth month,
so this was their first arrival in Chéngdū.
"You held a large command,
and commanded a strong army,
why did you not resist?"
He replied:
"I feared the Divine Might of the Great King."
He said:
"If so, why did you not surrender?"
He replied:
"The King's army had not entered the border."
He said:
"How many people accompanied you into Qiāng territory?"
He replied:
"Twelve thousand men."
He said:
"How many have returned now?"
He replied:
"Two thousand men."
He said:
"That is enough to compensate for the deaths of ten thousand men."
He had them all beheaded,
including their sons.
5 On the *bǐngzǐ* day, Mèng Zhīxiáng, who was serving as the Manager of the Northern Capital's Liúshǒu Affairs, was appointed as Xīchuān Jìedùshǐ and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
He was urgently summoned to Luòyáng.
He was summoned to Luòyáng and then proceeded to his post.
This laid the groundwork for Mèng Zhīxiáng to control Shǔ.
The Pīmì Chéngzhǐ Duàn Huái and others disliked Zhāng Xiàn, the Liúshǒu of Yèdū,
and did not want him at court.
Duàn Huái must have been a eunuch.
"The Northern Capital cannot do without Zhāng Xiàn.
Although Xiàn possesses the caliber of a prime minister,"
Guō Chóngtāo had recommended Zhāng Xiàn as prime minister,
and the Emperor wanted to employ him,
hence Duàn Huái and others said this.
"A prime minister is before the Son of Heaven.
If there are successes or failures in affairs,
they can be rectified.
Compared to the Northern Capital, which alone holds the security of a region,
it is not as important."
So Xiàn was transferred to be the Tàiyuán Yǐn,
and managed the Liúshǒu Affairs of the Northern Capital.
As the Yǐn managing Liúshǒu Affairs,
he was not formally the Liúshǒu.
He managed the Liúshǒu Affairs of Yèdū.
Zhèng Yán was confused and senile,
so the Emperor appointed Shǐ Yànqióng, a Wǔdé Envoy, as the Supervisor of Yèdū's military.
The Hòutáng Wǔdé Envoy was originally in charge of palace affairs.
During Míngzōng's time, there was once a drought,
followed by snow.
He sat exposed in the courtyard,
and an edict instructed the Wǔdé Department not to sweep the snow in the palace,
which is evidence of this.
He was originally an entertainer,
favored by the Emperor.
All military and financial affairs of Wèi, Bó, and the other six prefectures were decided by Yànqióng,
who wielded power and authority wantonly,
and treated generals and assistants with contempt.
From Zhèng Yán downwards, all flattered him.
This laid the groundwork for Wáng Zhèngyán and Shǐ Yànqióng's inability to defend Yèdū.
6 Initially,
the Emperor had obtained nearly eight thousand men of the Yínqiāng Xiàojié Dū (Silver Spears and Loyalty Corps) from Wèizhōu.
He made them his personal army.
(See volume 269, Liáng Jūn Wáng Zhēnmíng First Year.)
Jìn (近),
is the Jìn (靳) of Jìn Fān.
In the Battle of Jiāhé,
he indeed relied on their effectiveness,
and they repeatedly achieved extraordinary merits.
He often promised them great rewards once the Liáng were destroyed.
When Hénán was pacified,
(the Liáng were destroyed and Hénán was pacified),
the soldiers, relying on their accomplishments,
became arrogant and insatiable,
and further developed resentment.
This year, there was a great famine,
many people became displaced,
taxes and levies were insufficient,
roads were muddy and impassable,
and transportation by water and land was difficult.
Cáo (漕)
means water transport;
niǎn (輦)
means land transport.
Sè (澀),
is the Sèlì (色立) pronunciation.
There was nothing to provide for the soldiers.
Kǒng Qiān, the Supervisor of Rent and Imposts, daily at the outside of the Shàngdōng Mén,
(The three eastern gates of Luòchéng: the central one was called Jiànchūn,
the left one Shàngdōng,
and the right one Yǒngtōng.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Luòyáng's Shàngdōng Mén and Jiànchūn Mén were both military posts,
belonging to Hénán Xiàn.
This was likely due to the chaos and ruin,
no longer like the prosperity of the former Táng dynasty.)
dispensed provisions to those who arrived.
Soldiers lacked food;
some hired out their wives and sold their children.
The old and weak gathered wild vegetables in the fields,
in groups of dozens,
often dying of starvation.
Rumors and complaints spread,
but the Emperor continued his hunting excursions without cease.
On Jǐmǎo,
he hunted at Báishā,
accompanied by the Empress, the imperial princes, and the entire imperial harem.
On Gēngchén,
he lodged at Yīquè;
on Xīnsì,
he lodged at Tánbó;
on Rénwǔ,
he lodged at Kānjiàn;
on Guǐwèi,
he returned to the palace.
From Báishā to Kānjiàn,
all these places were east of Luòyáng.
According to Xuē Shǐ, Lǐ Yú took refuge in Luò
and presented a memorial regarding his villa at Báishā.
Kānjiàn is near Yīquè.
Cóng (從),
is the cáiyòng (才用) pronunciation.
Kān (龕),
is the kǔhán (苦含) pronunciation.
Officials and soldiers collapsed on the roads.
The famine was particularly severe in the Yī and Rǔ river regions.
Wherever the imperial guards passed,
they demanded provisions.
If they did not get them,
they destroyed household utensils,
and dismantled houses for firewood,
acting worse than bandits.
All county officials fled and hid in the mountains and valleys.
7 A white dragon was seen at the Hàn Palace;
the Hàn Lord changed his reign title to Báilóng,
and his name to Gōng.
8 Zhǎnghé Piàoxìn Zhèng Mín dispatched his bùxiè Zhèng Zhāochún to seek marriage with Hàn.
The Hàn Lord married his daughter, Princess Zēngchéng, to him.
Zhǎnghé was the Nánzhāo of the Táng dynasty.
Towards the end of the Táng,
Nánzhāo changed its name to Dàlǐ;
now it changed again to Zhǎnghé.
The Wǔdài Huìyào states: After Guō Chóngtāo pacified Shǔ,
he obtained dozens of barbarian captives that Wáng Yǎn had taken.
He sent envoys with imperial commands into their territory,
but they were stopped at the border.
Only barbarian captives with official credentials were allowed to pass.
Later, a dispatch was forwarded,
stating: "Dūshuǎng, Grand Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Dà Zhǎnghé, and the Bùxiè, etc., respectfully present a memorial to the Great Táng Emperor, our maternal uncle."
It was sent by messenger to Lízhōu.
The paper was thick and hard like leather,
the brushwork was vigorous and strong,
with an imperial style.
It was signed by Dūshuǎng Tuóchóu, Rěnshuǎng Wángbǎo, Dūshuǎng Mílè, Rěnshuǎng Dǒng Déyì, Dūshuǎng Zhǎngyuán Wěi, Rěnshuǎng Yáng Xīxiè, etc.
There was also a scroll of colored stationery,
and a rhyming poem of one chapter.
The chapter had three rhymes,
ten couplets in total,
somewhat like a jīzhú cí,
and quite presumptuous in its implication of a marital relationship with the current dynasty.
Its language was also not humble.
9 Lǐ Sìyuán, the Jiédùshǐ of Chéngdé, came to court.
10 In the intercalary month,
on Jǐchǒu, the first day of the month,
Mèng Zhīxiáng arrived in Luòyáng.
The Emperor treated him with exceptional favor.
11 The Emperor, noting the insufficiency of military provisions,
consulted his courtiers.
Dòulú Gé and others below him had no ideas.
Lǐ Qí, the Minister of Personnel, submitted a memorial,
stating:
"In ancient times, expenditures were determined by income,
and troops were raised based on the agricultural situation.
Therefore, even with floods and droughts, there was no concern about scarcity.
In recent times, farmers are taxed to support soldiers,
but it has never been the case that farmers are wealthy and well-supplied while soldiers are lacking,
or that farmers are impoverished and emaciated while soldiers are well-fed.
Even if we cannot currently remit and reduce taxes,
if we simply abolish the methods of 'collapsing payment' and 'forced distribution'—
Collapsing payment (zhénà 折納)
means coercing the people to sell at a discounted price and pay what they don't have;
Forced distribution (niǔpèi 紐配)
means calculating a sum and forcibly distributing it.
The Emperor then ordered the relevant authorities to act as Lǐ Qí had suggested,
but ultimately, it could not be implemented.
12 On Dīngyǒu,
an edict was issued, decreeing that officials appointed by the Shǔ court of the fourth rank and above would be demoted by varying degrees;
those of the fifth rank and below who lacked merit or ability would all be released to return to their hometowns.
Those who had previously surrendered or had performed meritorious service
were entrusted to Chóngtāo to be commended and employed according to the circumstances.
An edict was also bestowed upon Wáng Yǎn,
which roughly stated:
"I shall certainly grant you territory and enfeoff you,
and I will never abandon a person in danger.
The three luminaries are above,
and my word is trustworthy."
He swore by the three luminaries, yet ultimately killed him;
this was not trustworthiness.
13 On Gēngzǐ,
Gāo Wànxīng, the Jiédùshǐ of Zhāngwǔ and Bǎodà, and concurrent Grand Councilor, died.
In the fourth year of Liáng Zhēnmíng,
Gāo Wànxīng concurrently garrisoned Fūyán.
Táng established the Bǎosāi Army at Yánzhōu.
Qí was changed to Zhōngyì Army,
and Later Táng changed it to Zhāngwǔ Army.
Fū (鄜)
was the Bǎodà Army.
14 The Emperor, finding military provisions insufficient,
wished to move to Biànzhōu.
Censors submitted a memorial, stating:
"It is better to be frugal and make do with what we have.
Since ancient times, there has been no Son of Heaven who moved to where the food was.
Now, the Yáng family is not yet destroyed,
so it is not appropriate to show our weaknesses."
(This meant that since Wú was close by in Huáinán,
it was inappropriate to let them know the weaknesses of the Central Plains.)
Shàng (上),
is the shípái (時掌) pronunciation.
15 On Xīnhài,
the Emperor's younger brothers were enfeoffed: Cúnměi as Prince Yōng,
Cúnbà as Prince Yǒng,
Cúnlǐ as Prince Xuē,
Cúnwò as Prince Shēn,
Cúnyì as Prince Mù,
Cúnquè as Prince Tōng,
and Cúnjì as Prince Yǎ.
16 Guō Chóngtāo had always disliked eunuchs.
He once secretly told Wèi Wáng Jìjí:
"When Your Highness obtains the empire in the future,
even a gelding horse should not be ridden,
let alone employing eunuchs!
You should completely remove them
and exclusively employ scholars."
Lǚ Zhīróu overheard this.
(Lǚ Zhīróu was then Dūtǒng Yá Tōngyè.)
At that time, although Chéngdū had fallen,
brigands and thieves arose throughout Shǔ,
covering the mountains and forests.
Guō Chóngtāo feared that once the main army departed,
they would become a future menace.
He ordered Rèn Yuán and Zhāng Jūn to proceed along separate routes to suppress them,
which is why he delayed his return.
The Emperor sent the eunuch Xiàng Yánzì to urge him on.
Guō Chóngtāo did not come out to the suburbs to welcome him,
and when they met,
his manners were arrogant.
Eunuchs were indeed detestable,
but the Son of Heaven sent them to convey his commands.
To respect them was to respect the sovereign;
how could one meet them with arrogance!
That Emperor Zhuāngzōng of Táng sent a penal official to convey commands to a high minister was wrong;
that Guō Chóngtāo met him with arrogance was also wrong.
Alas!
Penal officials conveying commands,
this has been the case ever since the Kāiyuán era of Táng.
Lǐ Cóngxí said to Yánzì:
"The Prince of Wèi
is the Crown Prince;
His Majesty is well,
yet Duke Guō wields power like this.
Guō Tínghuì leads his followers in and out,
daily carousing with the military generals and Shǔ's local magnates,
swearing oaths and making grand gestures.
Recently, I heard he informed his father, asking to be appointed as the military commissioner of Shǔ;
he also said,
'Shǔ is rich and fertile;
the Elder ought to make good plans for himself.'
Now all the generals and officers of the armies are partisans of the Guō clan.
The Prince has placed himself in the jaws of tigers and wolves.
If a change occurs one morning,
we will not know where our bones will rest."
They then faced each other and wept.
Yánzì returned,
and recounted everything to Empress Liú.
The Empress wept and pleaded with the Emperor,
asking him to quickly save Lǐ Jìjí from death.
Earlier, when the Emperor heard that the people of Shǔ requested Guō Chóngtāo to be their military commissioner,
he was already displeased.
Now, hearing Yánzì's words,
he could not but feel suspicious.
The Emperor examined the records of Shǔ's treasuries,
and said:
"People say there are countless treasures in Shǔ.
Why is what is here so meager?"
Yánzì replied:
"Your servant heard that when Shǔ fell,
all its treasures went to Guō Chóngtāo and his son.
Guō Chóngtāo has ten thousand taels of gold,
four hundred thousand taels of silver,
a million strings of cash,
a thousand famous horses,
and other items to match.
What Tínghuì took
is in addition to that.
Thus, what the imperial government received was not much."
The Emperor then showed his anger on his face.
When Mèng Zhīxiáng was about to depart,
the Emperor said to him:
"I hear Guō Chóngtāo has rebellious intentions.
When you arrive,
execute him for me."
Zhīxiáng said:
"Guō Chóngtāo is a meritorious elder of the state;
he should not have such intentions.
I will wait until I reach Shǔ to observe him.
If he has no other intentions, then I will send him back."
The Emperor agreed.
On the day Rénzǐ,
Zhīxiáng departed from Luòyáng.
The Emperor soon after sent the Imperial Robe and Armor Store Keeper, Mǎ Yànkuī,
to rush to Chéngdū to observe Guō Chóngtāo's actions.
If he obeyed the edict and led the army back, that would be it.
If he showed signs of delay or defiance,
then Mǎ Yànkuī was to conspire with Lǐ Jìjí.
This is how Emperor Zhuāngzōng ordered Mèng Zhīxiáng and Mǎ Yànkuī.
Even if Lǐ Cóngxí and others had not acted according to Empress Liú's instruction,
and Guō Chóngtāo had returned east,
he still would not have been able to keep himself safe.
He said:
"Your servant sees that Xiàng Yánzì says the situation in Shǔ is critical and could change at any moment.
Now, the Emperor, when he should make a decisive cut, does not."
This means the Emperor's edict was ambivalent,
without a resolute order to kill Guō Chóngtāo.
"If it is cut,
a rebellion will instantly erupt.
There is no room for error;
how can we wait for instructions from three thousand *lǐ* away in an emergency!"
Chéngdū to Luòyáng is three thousand two hundred and sixteen *lǐ*,
as seen in the Old Book of Táng's Geography Treatise.
The Emperor said:
"These are mere rumors;
their veracity is unknown.
How can one make such a hasty and decisive judgment!"
The Empress failed in her plea,
retired,
and personally wrote an instruction to Lǐ Jìjí,
ordering him to kill Guō Chóngtāo.
When Zhīxiáng traveled to Shíháo,
Shíháo Village is east of Shǎn Prefecture, west of Xīn'ān County,
the place of Dù Shàolíng's poem
"I sought shelter at Shíháo Village at dusk."
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: Shǎn Prefecture, Shǎn County has Shíháo Town.
urging Zhīxiáng to hasten to the town,
Zhīxiáng secretly sighed, saying:
"Trouble is about to begin!"
Thereupon, he traveled day and night.
Mèng Zhīxiáng doubled his pace
not to save Guō Chóngtāo from death,
but for fear that Guō Chóngtāo's death would lead to other troubles.
17 Initially,
King Yīn of Chǔ, having obtained Húnán,
did not levy taxes on merchants and travelers.
Consequently, merchants and travelers from all directions converged.
Húnán was rich in lead and iron.
Mǎ Yīn, following the strategy of his Military Governor's Recorder Gāo Yù,
The Military Governor's Recorder
refers to the Recorder for All Armies.
Gāo Yù was in Mǎ Yīn's administration,
his position was above that of the Military Commissioner.
merchants, upon leaving the territory, had no use for these items,
and exchanged them for other goods before departing.
Thus, he was able to exchange the surplus goods within his territory for all kinds of goods under heaven,
and the state became rich and prosperous.
The people of Húnán did not engage in sericulture.
Gāo Yù ordered the people to pay their taxes in silk instead of money.
Before long,
looms became very prevalent among the populace.
18 Wúyuè King Qián Liú sent an envoy, Shěn Táo, with a letter,
informing Wú that he had received the jade scroll and been enfeoffed as King of Wúyuè.
The people of Wú objected because their state name was the same as his,
disliking that he resided in Yuè but also held the name of the state of Wú.
They sent Shěn Táo back,
and furthermore forbade their border garrisons from allowing Wúyuè envoys and merchants to pass.
Míngzōng Shèngdé Héwǔ Qīnxiào Huángdì Shàngzhīshàng
whose taboo name was Sìyuán,
was from Yīng Prefecture.
His ancestors were originally barbarians
and had no surname.
His father, Diàn,
was the commander of Yànmén.
The Emperor's childhood name was Máo Jíliè.
Tàizǔ adopted him as a son,
so he took the surname Lǐ and the given name Sìyuán.
After ascending the throne, he changed his name to Dǎn.
Tiānchéng first year
(Bǐngxū, 926)
This year, the reign title was changed in the fourth month,
see next volume.
1 In spring,
first month,
on the day Gēngshēn,
Prince Jìjí of Wèi sent Lǐ Jìyǎn and Lǐ Yán to escort Wáng Yǎn and his clan members, as well as several thousand officials, to Luòyáng.
2 Lǐ Jìlín (李繼麟), Military Governor of Hézhōng (河中) and Grand Preceptor, relied on his old friendship with the Emperor.
Moreover, he had rendered meritorious service.
In the second year of Qiānhuà (乾化) of the Liáng (梁) dynasty [912 CE],
Zhū Yǒuqiān (朱友謙) had brought Hézhōng (河中) to join the Jìn (晉),
hence he relied on their old friendship.
After joining the Jìn (晉),
the King of Jìn (晉) fought the Liáng (梁) people on the river,
and Fén (汾) and Jìn (晉) had no worries about their rear.
This was considered his meritorious service.
He also relied on this.
So he refused to comply.
When the great army was on its expedition to Shǔ (蜀),
Jìlín (繼麟) reviewed his troops,
and sent his son, Lìngdé (令德), to lead them as a follower.
Jǐng Jìn (景進) and the eunuchs slandered him, saying:
"Jìlín (繼lín) heard that the great army had set out,
and thought it was coming to attack him,
so he was alarmed and afraid,
and reviewed his troops to defend himself."
They also said:
"The reason Chóngtāo (崇韜) dared to be obstinate in Shǔ (蜀) was
because he conspired with Hézhōng (河中),
and they responded to each other internally and externally."
Jìlín (繼lín), hearing this, was frightened,
and wanted to go to court in person to clear himself.
His intimates restrained him.
Jìlín (繼lín) said:
"Grand Councillor Guō's (郭) merit is greater than mine.
Now circumstances are becoming perilous.
If I can see His Majesty,
and personally present my utmost sincerity,
then the slanderers will be punished."
Grand Councillor Guō (郭),
refers to Chóngtāo (崇韜).
"Merit is greater"
because he had the merit of destroying Liáng (梁) and Shǔ (蜀),
which he (Jìlín) could not match.
"Slanderers"
refers to the entertainers and eunuchs.
On the day of Guǐhài (癸亥),
Jìlín (繼lín) came to court.
This set the stage for Jìlín's (繼lín) misfortune.
3 Wèi Wáng Jìjí (魏王繼岌) was about to depart Chéngdū (成都).
He ordered Rèn Yuán (任圜) to take temporary charge of remaining affairs,
awaiting Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥).
The deployment of all armies was already settled.
The deployment for those going and those staying was already settled.
Mǎ Yànkuī (馬彥珪) arrived,
and showed the Empress's decree to Jìjí (繼岌).
Jìjí (繼岌) said:
"The great army is about to depart.
"Chuífā (垂發)"
means "about to depart."
How can I do such a perfidious thing?
You gentlemen, do not speak of it again.
Moreover, His Majesty has no edict;
is it permissible to kill the Commander of the Expedition solely by the Empress's decree?"
Lǐ Cóngxí (李從襲) and others wept and said:
"Since this trace exists,
if Chóngtāo (崇韜) hears of it,
and changes course midway,
it will be even more irredeemable."
They cleverly explained the advantages and disadvantages together,
and Jìjí (繼岌) had no choice but to follow.
On the morning of Jiǎzǐ (甲子),
Cóngxí (從襲), by Jìjí's (繼岌) order, summoned Chóngtāo (崇韜) to discuss matters.
Jìjí (繼岌) ascended a tower to avoid him.
As Chóngtāo (崇tāo) was ascending the steps,
Jìjí's (繼岌) attendant Lǐ Huán (李環) smashed his head,
and also killed his sons Tínghuì (廷誨) and Tíngxìn (廷信).
Outsiders still did not know this.
Fúyáng (滏陽) Lǐ Sōng (李崧), the judicial officer for the Supreme Commander,
said to Jìjí (繼岌):
"Now, having marched three thousand li away,
and with no imperial edict in the first place,
to suddenly kill a great general—
Your Highness, why do you perform such a dangerous act?
Could you not have endured until Luòyáng (洛陽)?"
Jìjí (繼岌) said:
"What you say is true;
it is too late to regret."
Sōng (崧) then summoned several scribes,
ascended the tower, removed the ladder,
forged an imperial edict,
and proclaimed it with a wax seal.
He molded a wax impression to make the seal of the Central Secretariat,
and used it to seal the edict and proclaim it.
All of Chóngtāo's (崇韜) attendants fled and hid.
Only Fúyáng (滏陽) Zhāng Lì (張礪), his chief secretary, went to the Wèi Wáng Fǔ (魏王府) and wept bitterly for a long time.
Zhāng Lì (張礪) was Chóngtāo's (崇韜) chief secretary.
The historian states that he served his master faithfully from beginning to end.
4 Wèi Wáng Tōngyè (魏王通謁) presented over two hundred musicians from Shǔ (蜀) to Lǐ Tíng'ān (李廷安).
Among them was Yán Xù (嚴旭),
whom Wáng Yǎn (王衍) had appointed Prefect of Péngzhōu (蓬州).
The Emperor asked:
"How did you obtain the post of Prefect?"
He replied:
"By singing."
The Emperor made him sing and praised him,
promising to reinstate him to his former post.
Everyone said that the Emperor conquered Shǔ (蜀) but did not investigate the reasons for Shǔ's (蜀) demise,
and therefore failed soon after;
they did not realize this was merely the Emperor's natural habit,
which could be seen from the affairs of Lǐ Cúnxián (李存賢) and Zhōu Zā (周匝).
5 On the day of Wùchén (戊辰),
Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥) arrived in Chéngdū (成都).
At that time, Guō Chóngtāo (郭崇韜) had just been killed,
and the people were still uneasy.
Zhīxiáng (知祥) comforted and pacified the officials and populace,
rewarded the generals and soldiers,
and those who remained or departed were all settled.
The historian speaks of Mèng Zhīxiáng's (孟知祥) talent,
which enabled him to possess Shǔ (蜀).
"Kào (犒)",
read as kǔ dào.
6 The Mǐn (閩) people defeated Chén Běn (陳本)
and beheaded him.
Chén Běn (陳本) besieged Tíngzhōu (汀州),
see the twelfth month of the previous year.
7 The Qìdān (契丹) ruler attacked the Nǚzhēn (女真) and Bóhǎi (勃海).
The Nǚzhēn (女真) first appear here.
Their country was originally the Sùshèn (肅慎) clan.
During the Eastern Hàn (漢) it was called Yìlóu (挹婁),
during the Yuán Wèi (元魏) it was called Wùjí (勿吉),
during the Suí (隋) and Táng (唐) it was called Mòhé (靺鞨),
and during the Five Dynasties it began to be called Nǚzhēn (女真).
There were several types of Nǚzhēn (女真).
Those living south of the Húntóng Jiāng (混同江) were called Shú Nǚzhēn (熟女真) (civilized Nǚzhēn),
and those north of the river were called Shēng Nǚzhēn (生女真) (wild Nǚzhēn).
Húntóng Jiāng (混同江) is the Yālù Shuǐ (鴨淥水).
On the day of Wùyín (戊寅),
they sent Méilǎo Xié Lǐ (梅老鞋里) to foster good relations.
8 Mǎ Yànkuī (馬彥珪) returned to Luòyáng (洛陽),
and then an edict was issued exposing the crimes of Guō Chóngtāo (郭崇韜),
and also killing his sons Tíngyuè (廷說), Tíngràng (廷讓), and Tíngyì (廷議).
These were Guō Chóngtāo's (郭崇韜) sons who were in Luòyáng (洛陽).
"Shuō (說)",
read as yuè.
Opinions were diverse and numerous,
and the Emperor sent eunuchs to secretly investigate.
Mù Wáng Cúnyì (睦王存乂), Military Governor of Bǎodà (保大),
was Chóngtāo's (崇韜) son-in-law.
The eunuchs, wishing to eliminate all of Chóngtāo's (崇韜) faction,
said,
"Cúnyì (存乂) rolled up his sleeves before the generals and wept,
crying out injustice for Chóngtāo (崇韜),
and his words were resentful and disgruntled."
On the day of Gēngchén (庚辰),
Cúnyì (存乂) was confined to his residence,
and soon after, he was killed.
Jǐng Jìn (景進) said:
"Someone from Hézhōng (河中) has reported treason,
saying that Lǐ Jìlín (李繼麟) conspired with Guō Chóngtāo (郭崇韜) to rebel;
after Chóngtāo (崇韜) died,
he again conspired with Cúnyì (存乂)."
The eunuchs then jointly urged the Emperor to quickly eliminate him.
The Emperor then transferred Jìlín (繼麟) to be Military Governor of Yìchéng (義成).
That night,
he sent Zhū Shǒuyīn (朱守殷), Commander of the Fān (蕃) and Hàn (漢) cavalry and infantry, with troops to surround his residence.
Ōu Shǐ (歐史) writes
"surrounded his lodge,"
presumably meaning that Zhū Yǒuqiān (朱友謙) had no private residence in Luòyáng (洛陽).
His original name Zhū Yǒuqiān (朱友謙) was restored.
When Táng Zhāozōng (唐昭宗) moved to Luòyáng (洛陽),
the imperial carriage entered the palace through the Huī'ān Mén (徽安門).
According to the Táng Liù Diǎn (唐六典): the two northern gates of the Eastern Capital were:
the eastern one called Yánxǐ (延喜),
and the western one Huī'ān (徽安).
Zhū Yǒuqiān (朱友謙) being granted a new name is mentioned in Volume 272, first year.
Lìngdé (令德) was made Military Governor of Wǔxìn (武信),
Lìngxī (令錫) was made Military Governor of Zhōngwǔ (忠武).
An edict ordered Wèi Wáng Jìjí (魏王繼岌) to execute Lìngdé (令德) in Suìzhōu (遂州),
and Zhèngzhōu (鄭州) Prefect Wáng Sītóng (王思同) to execute Lìngxī (令錫) in Xǔzhōu (許州).
The Táng (唐) dynasty established the Zhōngwǔ (忠武) army in Xǔzhōu (許州) and the Kuāngguó (匡國) army in Tóngzhōu (同州).
By the time of the Liáng (梁) dynasty, both army titles were changed.
After the Later Táng (後唐) destroyed the Liáng (梁),
both were restored to their former names.
Shàoqí (紹奇) arrived at his house.
Yǒuqiān's (友謙) wife, Lady Zhāng (張), led over two hundred family members to see Shàoqí (紹奇)
and said:
"The Zhū (朱) clan deserves death,
but I wish that common people not be implicated."
Then she separated out a hundred of their maids and servants,
and had a hundred members of their clan go to their execution.
Lady Zhāng (張) also took out an iron certificate and showed it to Shàoqí (紹奇), saying:
"This was granted by the Emperor last year.
I am a woman,
and cannot read,
so I do not know what it says."
Shàoqí (紹奇) also felt ashamed because of this.
Yǒuqiān's (友謙) former generals, such as Shǐ Wǔ (史武) and seven others, who were then Prefects, were all punished by clan extermination.
At that time, the various armies in Luòzhōng were hungry and distressed.
They spread rumors recklessly.
Court entertainers gathered these rumors and reported them to the Emperor.
Thus, Zhū Yǒuqīan and Guō Chóngtāo both fell victim to misfortune.
Lǐ Sìyuán, the Jìedùshǐ of Chéngdé and concurrently Zhōngshūlìng, was also implicated by rumors.
The Emperor sent Zhū Shǒuyīn to investigate him.
Shǒuyīn privately said to Sìyuán:
"Your Excellency's achievements and reputation shake the lord.
You should plan your return to your fief to avoid disaster."
"Zhèn" (振),
should be written as
"Zhèn" (震).
"Yuǎn" (遠),
read as yù yuàn.
"My heart does not betray Heaven and Earth.
When misfortune or fortune comes,
there is nothing to avoid;
I entrust everything to fate."
Lǐ Sìyuán's response to Zhū Shǒuyīn's words
shows his composure in the face of life and death, fortune and misfortune.
A hero's caliber is indeed beyond reach.
Old meritorious officials could not protect themselves.
Sìyuán was in peril four times,
but relied on the help of the Xuānhuīshǐ Lǐ Shàohóng, who protected him on all sides,
and thus he survived.

9 Wèi Wáng Jìjí left the Commander of Horse and Foot Troops Lǐ Rénhǎn from Chénliú, the Commander of Horse Troops Pān Rénsì from Dōngguāng, the Commander of the Left Flank Zhào Tíngyǐn, the Commander of the Right Flank Zhāng Yè from Jùnyí, the Commander of the Yá Nèi Guard Wǔ Zhāng from Wénshuǐ, and the Commander of the Xiāoruì Guard Lǐ Yánhòu from Píng'ēn, to garrison Chéngdū.
This laid the groundwork for these generals in Shǔ to later pledge their loyalty to Méng Zhīxiáng.
On Jiǎshēn
Jìjí departed Chéngdū,
ordering Lǐ Shàochēn to lead twelve thousand men as the rearguard,
their movement always one shè behind the main army.
Thirty lǐ constitutes one shè.
Meaning, the rearguard was thirty lǐ behind the main army.
"Shuài" (帥),
read as "lǜ" (率).
10 In the second month,
on the first day of the month, Jǐchǒu,
Lǐ Shàohóng, the Xuānhuī Nányuàn Shǐ, was appointed Pímìshǐ.
Replacing Guō Chóngtāo.
11 Yáng Rénhuì, the Wèibó Commander,
led his troops to garrison Wǎqiáo.
After a year, they were due to return.
When they reached Bèizhōu,
fearing that the capital Yèdū was empty
and that their arrival might lead to unrest,
an imperial edict ordered them to remain stationed in Bèizhōu.
At that time, no one in the empire knew Guō Chóngtāo's crime.
A popular rumor circulated, saying:
"Chóngtāo killed Jìjí
and crowned himself king in Shǔ,
which is why his family was exterminated."
Zhū Yǒuqīan's son, Zhū Jiànhuī, was the Cìshǐ of Chánzhōu.
The Emperor secretly ordered Shǐ Yànqióng, the Jiānjūn of Yèdū, to kill him.
Chánzhōu
was under the jurisdiction of Wèibó.
Hence, a secret edict was sent to the Wèibó Jiānjūn to kill Zhū Jiànhuī.
"Chán" (澶),
read as shí lián.
"Shǐ Wǔdé rode his horse out of the city at midnight,
without saying where he was going."
Shǐ Yànqióng served as Jiānjūn by virtue of his Wǔdé post,
thus referring to his inner court title.
"The Empress blamed the Emperor for Jìjí's death
and had already assassinated the Emperor,
which is why Yànqióng was urgently summoned for consultation."
People's fear intensified.
As rumors spread,
and Shǐ Yànqióng's actions were suspicious and alarming,
the rumors grew even more rampant,
and chaos followed.
Huángfǔ Huī, a soldier in Yáng Rénhuì's unit, along with his followers, gambled at night and lost.
Taking advantage of the widespread public unease,
they revolted,
seizing Rénhuì and saying:
"The reason His Majesty holds the empire
is because of the strength of our Wèi army.
Meaning, they relied on the Wèibó army's strength to defeat Liáng.
Our horses have not had their saddles removed for over ten years.
Now that the empire is settled,
the Son of Heaven does not remember our past toils,
but instead grows more suspicious.
We were garrisoned far away for over a year,
and were just happy to be relieved and return.
Though we are so close to home,
we are not allowed to see our families."
This refers to being ordered to remain stationed in Bèizhōu,
not allowed to return to Wèizhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Bèizhōu is two hundred and twenty-five lǐ south of Wèizhōu.
"The capital is already in chaos.
The generals and soldiers wish to return with you,
and still report to the imperial court.
If the Son of Heaven is safe and sound,
and raises an army to suppress us,
the strength of our Wèibó army is sufficient to resist them."
Huángfǔ Huī
was a soldier of the Yínqiāng Xiàojié corps.
He fought alongside Zhuāngzōng on the Yellow River,
accustomed to seeing Zhuāngzōng's military tactics
and the courage or cowardice of the various armies,
hence he dared to utter these words.
Rénhuì refused to comply,
so Huī killed him.
He then seized a junior officer;
when the officer refused,
he killed him too.
Zhào Zàilǐ, the Xiàojié Commander, heard of the uprising,
fled over a wall without even tying his belt.
Huī pursued and caught him,
dragging him down by his foot,
and showed him two heads.
He showed him the heads of Yáng Rénhuì and the junior officer.
The rebellious soldiers then acclaimed him as their leader,
and burned and plundered Bèizhōu.
Huī
was from Wèizhōu;
Zàilǐ
was from Zhuōzhōu.
At dawn,
Huī and his followers escorted Zàilǐ south towards Línqīng, Yǒngjì, and Guǎntáo,
plundering as they went.
read as qī yù.
"Piāo" (剽),
read as pǐ miào.
On the evening of Rénchén,
someone arrived from Bèizhōu reporting that a military rebellion was about to attack Yèdū.
Sūn Duó, the Dōuxúnjiǎnshǐ, and others immediately went to Shǐ Yànqióng,
requesting permission to arm themselves and man the city walls in preparation.
Yànqióng suspected Duó and the others of having ulterior motives,
and said:
"The informant said the rebels reached Línqīng today.
Calculating the distance, they won't arrive until the evening of the sixth day."
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Línqīng County is one hundred and fifty lǐ south of Wèizhōu City.
Huángfǔ Huī and others reached Línqīng on Rénchén.
Shǐ Yànqióng estimated they would arrive at Wèizhōu on the evening of the sixth day
because he assumed an army would travel fifty lǐ a day,
thus calculating that it would take them three days to arrive.
Rénchén was the fourth day of the second month;
the sixth day
refers to the sixth day of the second month,
which was Jiǎwǔ.
Sūn Duó said:
"Since the rebels have started an uprising,
marching day and night at double speed.
How could they travel according to a fixed schedule!
I request that your Excellency lead the troops to man the city walls."
Shǐ Yànqióng had likely been promoted to Púyè,
which is why Sūn Duó addressed him as such.
"Shuài" (帥),
read as "lǜ" (率).
"Once the rebels' momentum is thwarted,
they will surely disperse,
and then we can suppress them.
If we must wait until they reach the city walls,
and by chance there are traitors providing inside support,
then the situation will be dire."
Yànqióng said:
"Just strictly guard the city walls;
why must we fight them proactively!"
That night,
the rebel vanguard attacked the North Gate,
arrows and crossbow bolts flying in confusion.
At that time, Yànqióng was leading his troops to lodge in the North Gate tower.
Hearing the rebels' shouts,
he immediately panicked and fled.
Yànqióng rode alone to Luòyáng.
On Guǐsì,
the rebels entered Yèdū.
Sūn Duó and others resisted but were defeated
and fled.
Zhào Zàilǐ occupied the palace city.
The Emperor had been enthroned in Wèizhōu,
taking the Yáchéng as his palace city.
The soldiers were allowed to plunder extensively.
Jìn
was from Dìngzhōu.
Wáng Zhèngyán was just leaning on his desk, summoning clerks to draft a memorial,
but none arrived.
Zhèngyán grew angry.
His family members said,
"The bandits have already entered the city,
looting and killing in the marketplace.
All the officials have fled and dispersed.
Who are you still calling for, My Lord!"
Zhèngyán exclaimed in surprise,
"I didn't know that until now!"
He then sought a horse,
but could not obtain one.
So, he led his subordinates on foot out of the prefectural office to see Zàilǐ,
bowing twice to beg for punishment.
Zàilǐ also bowed,
saying,
"The soldiers merely wish to return home.
Shàngshū is of great virtue;
do not humble yourself!"
He consoled and dismissed him.
Wáng Zhèngyán, as Hùbù Shàngshū, was sent out to govern as Liúshǒu,
which is why Zhào Zàilǐ addressed him so.
The crowd then acclaimed Zàilǐ as Wèibó Liúhòu,
and fully reported his situation in a memorial.
The family of Běijīng Liúshǒu Zhāng Xiàn was in Yèdū.
Last year, Zhāng Xiàn was transferred from Yèdū Liúshǒu to Běijīng,
so his family remained in Yèdū.
They sent an envoy with a letter to entice Xiàn.
Xiàn did not open the seal,
but executed the envoy and reported it.
On the 12th day, jiǎwǔ,
Jǐng Jìn was appointed Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū, Jiǎnjiào Yòu Sànqí Chángshì concurrently Yùshǐ Dàfū, Shàng Zhùguó.
On the 13th day, bǐngshēn,
Shǐ Yànqióng arrived in Luòyáng.
He had fled from Yèdū to Luòyáng.
Shàohóng again requested the use of Lǐ Shàoqīn.
During the campaign to conquer Shǔ,
Lǐ Shàohóng had already recommended Lǐ Shàoqīn, but he was not employed,
hence the mention of "again."
An order was issued to draw up a strategy.
The subordinate generals Shàoqīn requested
were all old generals of Liáng,
those he was close to.
The Emperor suspected him and stopped the plan.
The Empress said,
"This is a minor matter,
not enough to trouble a great general.
Shàoróng can handle it."
Shàoróng
was Yuán Xíngqīn.
Troops from all circuits were also summoned
to prepare for their disobedience.
When Guō Chóngtāo died,
Lǐ Shàochēn said to Dǒng Zhāng,
"Are you going to go whispering at whose door again?"
Zhāng was afraid and apologized.
Wèi Wáng Jìjí's army returned to Wǔlián
and met an imperial envoy
who conveyed that Zhū Yǒuqīan had already been executed,
and ordered Dǒng Zhāng to lead troops to Suìzhōu to execute Zhū Língdé.
At that time, Shàochēn was leading the rear guard in Wèichéng.
The Western Wèi established Wèichéng Xiàn in Bāxī,
which belonged to Miánzhōu during the Táng.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: 65 lǐ east of the prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: Wèichéng was originally the land of Hàn Fúxiàn.
The Western Wèi established Tóngzhōu in Fúxiàn,
and carved out this area to establish Wèichéng Xiàn.
Lǐ Yīng's Jìyún states: 50 lǐ east of Sìxī, there are east and west wells.
The area west of the wells was the boundary of Fúxiàn,
and the area east of the wells was the boundary of Wèichéng.
As the Emperor did not entrust him with killing Língdé but entrusted Zhāng,
he was greatly alarmed.
Soon after, Zhāng passed Shàochēn's army
without paying respects.
Shàochēn was enraged,
and while drinking, said to his generals,
"The state's conquest of Dàliáng to the south
and pacification of Bā and Shǔ to the west
were all due to Duke Guō's planning and my military achievements.
As for removing the rebellious and showing allegiance,
and forming a pincer movement with the state to defeat Liáng,
that was Duke Zhū.
Now, Duke Zhū and Duke Guō, both innocent, have had their families exterminated.
After returning to court,
it will be our turn.
How unjust!
Oh Heaven!
What can be done!"
Most of the troops Shàochēn commanded were from Hézhōng.
Hézhōng generals Jiāo Wǔ and others cried loudly at the camp gate, saying,
"What crime did Xīpíng Wáng commit to have his entire family slaughtered like butchers?"
If we return, we will be executed along with Shǐ Wǔ and others.
It means that since Shǐ Wǔ and others, as Hézhōng generals, were executed,
if they return east, they will also share the same crime and be executed.
On that day,
Wèi Wáng Jìjí reached Níxī.
Shàochēn, upon reaching Jiànzhōu, sent someone to inform Jìjí, saying,
"The Hézhōng generals and soldiers are crying incessantly
and are on the verge of mutiny."
On the day dìngyǒu,
Shàochēn, leading his troops from Jiànzhōu, turned back west.
He declared himself Xīchuān Jiédù and Sānchuān Zhìzhì, etc., commander,
and issued a proclamation to Chéngdū,
stating that he was acting on an imperial edict to replace Mèng Zhīxiáng in pacifying the people of Shǔ.
Within three days, his forces reached 50,000.
On the 15th day, wùxū,
Lǐ Jìyǎn arrived in Fèngxiáng.
The Supervising Army Commissioner Chái Chónghòu did not hand over the tally and seal to him,
but urged him to proceed to the imperial court.
In the third year of Guāngqǐ of Táng Xīzōng (887 CE),
Lǐ Màozhēn occupied Fèngxiáng,
and it was replaced at this time.
Later, Míngzōng again ordered Lǐ Jìyǎn to garrison Fèngxiáng.
On the 16th day, jǐhài,
Wèi Wáng Jìjí arrived in Lìzhōu.
Lǐ Shàochēn sent men to cut off the Jíbá Jīn crossing.
Jìjí, hearing of this,
appointed Rèn Yuán as Deputy Commander of the Punitive Expedition,
leading 7,000 infantry and cavalry,
and, with Commander-in-Chief Liáng Hàn'yǒng
and Supervising Army Lǐ Yán'ān, pursued and attacked him.
The Kǎoyì states: Zhuāngzōng Shílù:
"On the day jǐhài,
Jìjí memorialized that Kāng Yánxiào had rebelled,
and sent Rèn Yuán to pursue and attack him."
However, Yánxiào rebelled on the day dìngyǒu in Jiànzhōu,
how could the report have already reached Luòyáng by jǐhài!
The Kuǎngběn states:
"On the day jǐhài,
Wèi Wáng arrived in Lìzhōu.
The Jíbá Jīn envoy came at night to inform Jìjí,
saying that Lǐ Shàochēn had ordered the cutting of the pontoon bridge.
Jìjí appointed Rèn Yuán as Deputy Commander of the Punitive Expedition,
ordering him to lead 7,000 infantry and cavalry,
and, with Commander-in-Chief Liáng Hàn'yǒng and Supervising Army Lǐ Yán'ān, to attack him."
We follow this account now.
On the 17th day, gēngzǐ,
400 soldiers of the Xíngzhōu Zuǒ Yòu Bùzhí troops, including Zhào Tài,
bùzhí troops
refers to infantry who are on long-term duty.
An imperial edict ordered the Northeast Pacification Deputy Commander Lǐ Shàozhēn to attack them.
Lǐ Shàozhēn was Huò Yànwēi.
On the 18th day, xīchǒu,
Rèn Yuán first ordered a separate general, Hé Jiànchóng, to attack Jiànmén Pass,
and they captured it.
It was feared that Lǐ Shàochēn would defend Jiànmén Pass,
so it was attacked and captured first.
Where would Shàochēn go then!
On the 19th day, Lǐ Shàoróng arrived in Yèdū
and attacked its south gate.
He sent someone with an imperial edict to pacify them.
Zhào Zàilǐ treated the army with sheep and wine,
and bowed from atop the city wall, saying,
"The generals and soldiers miss their homes and wish to return.
If xiànggōng would truly make a good report on our behalf,
and we could be spared from death,
how would we dare not to reform ourselves!"
Thereupon, he proclaimed the imperial edict throughout the army.
Shǐ Yànqióng pointed his halberd and cursed loudly, saying,
"You utterly despicable bandits!
When the city falls, you'll be torn into ten thousand pieces!"
Huángfǔ Huī said to his troops,
"Judging from what Shǐ Wǔdé said,
the Emperor will not pardon us."
Thereupon, they gathered and rioted,
snatching the imperial edict
and destroying it by hand.
Luè
means to seize.
Huài
is pronounced guài.
Shàoróng's attack was unsuccessful,
and he reported the situation.
The Emperor was furious and said,
"On the day the city is captured,
leave no living thing!"
He massively dispatched various armies to attack them.
On the day rén'yín,
Shàoróng retreated to station in Chánzhōu.
On the 20th day of the *jiǎchén* night,
Wáng Wēn and five other soldiers from the Cóngmǎzhí killed the army commander,
plotting to rebel.
They were captured and executed.
Guō Cóngqiān, the commander of the Cóngmǎzhí,
was originally an actor.
His stage name was Guō Méngāo.
When the Emperor and the Liáng forces were in a standoff at Déshèng,
Déshèng is also Dèshèng.
Guō Cóngqiān answered the call,
captured and executed enemies, and returned,
thus gaining even more favor.
The Emperor selected the bravest and most skilled from all armies to be his personal guard,
dividing them into four commands,
known as the Cóngmǎzhí.
Guō Cóngqiān accumulated merits from army commander to commander.
When Guō Chóngtāo was in power,
Guō Cóngqiān treated him as an uncle,
and Mù Wáng Cún Yì adopted Guō Cóngqiān as his foster son.
When Chóngtāo and Cún Yì fell into disfavor,
Guō Cóngqiān frequently entertained the various officers of the Cóngmǎzhí with his private wealth,
weeping before them,
speaking of Chóngtāo's injustice.
When Wáng Wēn rebelled,
the Emperor jokingly said to him:
"You have betrayed me by siding with Chóngtāo and Cún Yì,
and now you incite Wáng Wēn to rebel.
What do you intend to do?"
Guō Cóngqiān became even more fearful.
After he withdrew,
he secretly said to his officers:
"Because of Wáng Wēn, the Emperor
intends to bury all of you alive
once Yèdū is pacified.
Ruò
is equivalent to 'you'.
Do not plan for the long term."
Thus, all the personal guards felt insecure.
This laid the groundwork for Zhāng Pòbài's rebellion and Guō Cóngqiān's regicide.
Guō Chóngtāo was a meritorious veteran,
but his entire clan was exterminated without cause.
The rebellion of Kāng Yánxiào,
the rebellion of Huángfǔ Huī,
and the rebellion of Zhāng Pòbài,
ultimately led to Guō Cóngqiān's regicide,
all because of Chóngtāo's death which made the hearts of the generals and officers feel insecure.
On the 21st day, *yǐsì*,
Wáng Yǎn arrived at Cháng'ān,
and an imperial edict ordered him to stop.
To prevent him from reaching Luòyáng.
Previously,
although the Emperor's younger brothers held the title of Jìedùshǐ,
they all remained in the capital,
merely receiving their stipends.
On the *wùshēn* day,
for the first time, Yǒng Wáng Cún Bà, the Hùguó Jìedùshǐ, was ordered to go to Hézhōng.
Having killed Zhū Yǒuqīan,
Cún Bà was then ordered to proceed to his post to replace him.
On the 23rd day, *dīngwèi*,
Lǐ Shàoróng, with troops from various circuits, again attacked Yèdū.
On the *gēngxū* day,
the deputy general Yáng Chóngbà led several hundred men to scale the city wall,
but with no follow-up,
