According to Xuē Shǐ,
Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne in Wèizhōu
and appointed his son Jìjī as the acting prefect of the Northern Capital and administrator of the Xīngshèng Palace.
After pacifying Hénán,
he was appointed acting prefect of the Eastern Capital and administrator of the Xīngshèng Palace.
Thus, both the Eastern Capital and the Northern Capital had a Xīngshèng Palace.
The record by Sòng Bái is seen earlier.
This showed the gradual process of his true ascension.
The character "見" (jiàn)
is pronounced "xián biàn" (both "xián" and "biàn" tones).
The hundred officials addressed him as "Your Highness."
There were still over a thousand surviving concubines of Zhuāngzōng.
The Xuānhuī envoy selected several hundred beautiful young ones and presented them to the supervisor of the state.
The supervisor of the state said:
"What use are these!"
He replied:
"The duties in the palace cannot be lacking."
The supervisor of the state said:
"Those in charge of palace duties should be familiar with old customs; how would these people know!"
So he reinstated all the old and experienced personnel,
and those who were young were all sent back to their relatives.
Those without relatives were allowed to go wherever they pleased.
The palace women sent from Shǔ also followed this arrangement.
On the day of Yǐwèi,
he appointed the Zhōngmén envoy Ān Chónghuǐ as the Púmì envoy.
Ān Chónghuǐ was originally the Zhōngmén envoy of the Chéngdé Army
and was a trusted confidant of the supervisor of the state.
Yánlǎng
was from Kāifēng.
He served the Liáng dynasty as a tax official.
According to Ōu Shǐ,
Zhāng Yánlǎng served Liáng,
rising from a tax official to the provisions commissioner of Yùnzhōu.
Míngzōng captured Yùnzhōu and obtained him,
again appointing him as provisions commissioner.
Later, he was transferred to the garrisons of Xuānwǔ and Chéngdé,
serving as the Yuáncóng Kǒumù official,
which is probably why he was chosen as the Bìejià of Zhènzhōu.
He was good at serving powerful officials,
and married his daughter to Chónghuǐ's son,
which is why Chónghuǐ promoted him.
The supervisor of the state ordered that all the princes be sought out.
Tōng Wáng Cúnquè and Yǎ Wáng Cúnjì were hiding among the populace.
Someone secretly informed Ān Chónghuǐ,
who plotted with Lǐ Shàozhēn, saying:
"Now that Your Highness is supervising the state and handling the mourning,
the princes should be dealt with early
to unite the people's hearts.
Your Highness is merciful by nature;
this matter should not reach his ears."
So he secretly sent men to their rural residence to kill them.
More than a month later,
the supervisor of the state heard of it
and severely reprimanded Chónghuǐ,
grieving and regretting it for a long time.
Empress Liú and Shēn Wáng Cúnwò fled to Jìnyáng.
On the way, she had a private affair with Cúnwò.
When Cúnwò arrived at Jìnyáng,
Lǐ Yānchāo refused to admit him.
He fled to Fēnggǔ.
"Fēnggǔ"
should probably be
"Lángǔ."
In the third year of Cháng'ān of the Táng dynasty, Lángǔ County was established from Yífāng County,
subordinate to Lánzhōu.
The next day,
Yǒng Wáng Cúnbà also arrived at Jìnyáng.
All his accompanying soldiers had scattered and fled.
Cúnbà shaved his head and, in monastic robes, visited Lǐ Yānchāo, saying,
"I wish to become a mountain monk.
I hope for your protection."
The soldiers clamored to kill him.
Yānchāo said:
"When the Sixth Duke arrives,
we should memorialize and await instructions."
Cúnbà was the sixth.
They killed him beneath the stele at the government office gate.
Empress Liú became a nun in Jìnyáng.
The supervisor of the state sent someone to kill her there.
Xuē Wáng Cúnlǐ and Zhuāngzōng's young sons Jìsōng, Jìtóng, Jìchán, and Jìshān Yáo,
Yáo
is pronounced "ní me."
Only Yōng Wáng Cúnměi was spared due to hemiplegia from a stroke,
and resided in Jìnyáng.
The Shatuo, strong since the late Táng,
had come to this.
Perhaps some descendants of the Chìxīn branch still survived;
the bloodline of the successive Jìn princes
was extinguished.
Furthermore, Míngzōng,
an adopted son of the Jìn prince,
after gaining the state,
watched passively as his adopted father's surviving children were treated as fish and meat.
How could he bear it!
How could he then expect offerings of wheat gruel to be sprinkled on his tomb!
6 Xú Wēn and Gāo Jìxīng, hearing of Zhuāngzōng's assassination,
respected Yán Kěqiú and Liáng Zhèn even more.
Yán Kěqiú had predicted internal strife in Táng (see volume 272, first year of Tóngguāng under Zhuāngzōng);
Liáng Zhèn had predicted Zhuāngzōng's downfall (see volume 274, third year).
Liáng Zhèn (梁震) recommended Sūn Guāngxiàn (孫光xiàn), former Assistant Officer of Língzhōu (陵州) from Guìpíng (貴平), to Jìxìng (季興),
who made him his chief secretary.
Guìpíng County (貴平縣)
was in the southeastern border of Hàn (漢)'s Guǎngdū County (廣都縣).
The Later Wèi (後魏) established Hérén Commandery (和仁郡),
and also established the three counties of Píngjǐng (平井), Guìpíng (貴平), and Kětán (可曇).
The Táng (唐) abolished Píngjǐng (平井) and Kětán (可曇),
and made Guìpíng County (貴平縣) govern Hérén City (和仁城).
In the 14th year of Kāiyuán (開元) (726 CE), its seat was moved to Lùchuān (祿川),
subordinate to Língzhōu (陵州).
The Sòng (宋) abolished Guìpíng (貴平) and merged it into Guǎngdū County (廣都縣).
When Jìxìng (季興) wanted to attack Chǔ (楚),
Sūn Guāngxiàn (孫光xiàn) remonstrated, saying:
"After the chaos and displacement in Jīngnán (荊南),
it is thanks to your Excellency that the soldiers and people have been able to rest,
and life is just beginning to revive.
If we again make an enemy of the Chǔ (楚) state,
other countries will take advantage of our weakness,
which is truly cause for worry."
Jìxìng (季興) then ceased his plans.
7 On the day of Wùxū (戊戌),
Lǐ Shàoróng (李紹róng) arrived in Luòyáng (洛陽).
He had been shackled and sent from Shǎnzhoū (陝州) to Luòyáng (洛陽).
"How have I wronged you,
that you should kill my son?"
This referred to Shàoróng (紹róng) killing Cóngshěn (從審).
See the third month of this year in the previous volume.
"How did the late Emperor wrong you?"
Then he was beheaded.
Though Yuán Xíngqīn (元行欽) died,
how could the Supervisor of the State (Jiānguó 監國) not feel ashamed of his words!
The conferral of Lǐ Shàoróng (李紹róng)'s given name is recorded in Volume 269, the first year of Liáng Jūnwáng Zhēnmíng (梁均王貞明).
8 The Supervisor of the State (Jiānguó 監國) feared that the expeditionary army returning from Shǔ (蜀) might cause trouble,
so he appointed Shí Jìngtáng (石敬táng) as Acting Military Commissioner of Shǎnzhoū (陝州);
on the day of Jǐhài (己亥),
he appointed Lǐ Cóngkē (李從kē) as Acting Military Commissioner of Hézhōng (河中).
Shǎnzhoū (陝州) was to guard against their direct advance to Luòyáng (洛陽),
and Hézhōng (河中) to guard against their return north to Jìnyáng (晉陽).
Shǎn (陝),
pronounced "shī rǎn".
9 Zhāng Jūhàn (張居翰), Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ 樞密使), requested to retire to his hometown,
which was granted.
Lǐ Shàozhēn (李紹zhēn) repeatedly recommended Kǒng Xún (孔循)'s talent,
so on the day of Gēngzǐ (庚子),
Kǒng Xún (孔循) was appointed Deputy Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Fùshǐ 樞密副使).
Lǐ Shàohóng (李紹hóng) requested to revert to his original surname, Mǎ (馬).
The conferral of Lǐ Shàohóng (李紹hóng)'s given name is recorded in Volume 270, the fifth year of Liáng Jūnwáng Zhēnmíng (梁均王貞明).
The Supervisor of the State (Jiānguó 監國) issued an edict,

enumerating the crimes of the Rent and Tribute Commissioner Kǒng Qiān (孔謙) for being treacherous, sycophantic, oppressive, and exploiting the impoverished military and civilians, and then had him executed.
All the harsh collection laws established by Kǒng Qiān (孔謙)
were abolished.
Consequently, the offices of Rent and Tribute Commissioner (Zūyōngshǐ 租庸使) and Inner Affairs Directorate (Nèigōu Sī 內勾司) were abolished.
The Rent and Tribute Commissioner (Zūyōngshǐ 租庸使)
was established in the late Táng (唐) and the Liáng (梁) dynasties.
The Inner Affairs Directorate (Nèigōu Sī 內勾司)
was established in the second year of Tóngguāng (同光) (924 CE) by Zhuāngzōng (莊宗).
One Chancellor (Zǎixiàng 宰相) was entrusted to handle these affairs exclusively.

According to the Táng (唐) system: the affairs of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù 戶部) and the Ministry of Finance (Dùzhī 度支) were managed by their respective Directors (Lángzhōng 郎中) and Vice Ministers (Shìláng 侍郎),
and a Salt and Iron Transport Commissioner (Yántiě Zhuǎnyùnshǐ 鹽鐵轉運使) was also established.
Later, during military campaigns,
the national finances became paramount,
so Chancellors (Zǎixiàng 宰相) were put in charge of these duties.
After Qiánfú (乾符) (874 CE),
the empire fell into chaos,
and national expenditure became increasingly empty,
so the Rent and Tribute Commissioner (Zūyōngshǐ 租庸使) was first established.
Military campaigns were unpredictable,
and levies were imposed as needed,
ceasing when the war ended.
When the Liáng (梁) rose,
they established the Rent and Tribute Commissioner (Zūyōngshǐ 租庸使)
to manage all money and grain of the empire,
abolishing the officials of Salt and Iron (Yántiě 鹽鐵), Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù 戶部), and Ministry of Finance (Dùzhī 度支).
When Zhuāngzōng (莊zōng) destroyed the Liáng (梁),
he kept this system unchanged.
When Míngzōng (明zōng) ascended the throne,
he executed the Rent and Tribute Commissioner Kǒng Qiān (孔謙) and abolished his office,
appointing one Grand Minister (Dàchén 大臣) to oversee the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù 戶部), Ministry of Finance (Dùzhī 度支), and Salt and Iron (Yántiě 鹽鐵),
known as the Commissioner of the Three Departments (Pàn Sānsī 判三司).
By the first year of Chángxìng (長興) (930 CE),
Zhāng Yánlǎng (張延lǎng) then requested the establishment of the Commissioner of the Three Departments (Sānsīshǐ 三司使),
and the matter was submitted to the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū 中書).
The Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū 中書) followed the old Táng (唐) precedent,
appointing Yánlǎng (延lǎng) as a Senior Minister (Tèjìn 特進) and Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū 工部尚書),
serving concurrently as Commissioner of Salt and Iron Transport (Yántiě Zhuǎnyùnshǐ 鹽鐵轉運使) for all circuits,
and concurrently managing the affairs of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù 戶部) and Ministry of Finance (Dùzhī 度支);
an imperial edict appointed Yánlǎng (延lǎng) as Commissioner of the Three Departments (Sānsīshǐ 三司使),
his rank being below that of the Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Xuānhuīshǐ 宣徽使).
The establishment of the Commissioner (Shǐ 使) for the Three Departments (Sānsī 三司)
thus began with the Liáng (梁).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: In the second year of Tóngguāng (同光) (924 CE),
Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū (左諫議大夫) Dòu Zhuān (竇專) memorialized requesting the abolition of the title Rent and Tribute Commissioner (Zūyōngshǐ 租庸使) and its return to the Three Departments (Sānsī 三司),
stating briefly: "I have observed that all kinds of money and grain across the empire
were formerly under the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù 戶部),
which established the offices of Ministry of Finance (Dùzhī 度支), Ministry of Treasury (Jīnbù 金部), and Ministry of Granaries (Cāngbù 倉部),
each with its Director (Lángzhōng 郎zhōng) and Assistant Director (Yuánwài Yuánwài),
to manage the land tax, mountain and sea salt and iron, distinguishing between expenditure, calculation, collection, and transport.
Later, due to the excessive number of rents and taxes,
the office of Commissioner of the Three Departments (Sānsīshǐ 三司使) was added
to jointly contribute to national power
and achieve abundant wealth.
During the An (安)-Shǐ (史) Rebellion,
households fled,
rent collection was untimely,
and expenses were often lacking.
Only the prefectures and counties of Jiāng (江), Huái (淮), and Lǐngbiǎo (嶺biǎo) remained intact,
so all the goods and wealth of the Three Departments (Sānsī 三司)
were sent through one envoy to collect taxes,
investigating and auditing everywhere,
named Rent and Tribute (Zūyōng 租庸).
After the recovery of the capital city,
this office was soon abolished.
In the Guǎngmíng (廣明) period (880-881 CE),
Huáng Cháo (黃巢) rebelled,
and Xīzōng (僖zōng) fled.
As before, taxes were levied in Jiāng (江) and Huái (淮), and a Rent and Tribute Commissioner (Zūyōngshǐ 租庸使) was established.
Upon returning to the capital,
it was also soon abolished.
The false Liáng (梁) used the four frontier governors to control collection and transport,
establishing the title of Palace Commissioner (Gōngshǐ 宮使);
later, the Palace Commissioner (Gōngshǐ 宮使) was abolished,
and the Rent and Tribute Commissioner (Zūyōngshǐ 租庸使) was re-established.
Because Zhuāngzōng (莊zōng) lost the country due to eunuchs,
an order was issued to all circuits to kill them all.
10Wèi Wáng Jìjí (魏王繼岌) retreated from Xīngpíng (興平) to Wǔgōng (武功).
The eunuch Lǐ Cóngxí (李從xí) said:
"Calamity and fortune are unpredictable;
retreat is not as good as advance.
I urge Your Highness to proceed east quickly to relieve the internal crisis."
Jìjí (繼岌) followed his advice.
Returning,
he reached the Wèishuǐ (渭水) River,
where the acting Western Capital Military Commissioner Zhāng Jiān (張籛) had already cut off the pontoon bridge.
They floated across the river.
On that day, they arrived at Wèinán (渭南),
but his trusted aides Lǚ Zhīróu (呂知柔) and others had all fled.
Cóngxí (從xí) said to Jìjí (繼岌):
"The time has passed.
Your Highness should plan for yourself."
Jìjí (繼岌) hesitated, shedding tears,
then lay down on the bed,
and ordered his servant Lǐ Huán (李環) to strangle him.
Jìjí (繼岌) had killed Guō Chóngtāo (郭崇韜) because of Lǐ Cóngxí (李從xí) and Lǚ Zhīróu (呂知柔),
and yet the one who killed Jìjí (繼岌) was not another person!
Lǐ Huán (李環) was indeed the one who had bludgeoned Chóngtāo (崇韜) to death.
The "Kǎoyì" (考異) (Textual Research) states: Zhuāngzōng Shílù (莊zōng實錄) (Veritable Records of Zhuāngzōng) records that
"Lǐ Cóngxí (李從xí) was initially the Surveillance Commissioner for the expedition to Shǔ (蜀),
and later advised Jìjí (繼岌) to kill Guō Chóngtāo (郭崇韜)."
Míngzōng Shílù (明zōng實錄) (Veritable Records of Míngzōng) states
"The eunuch Surveillance Commissioner Lǐ Jìxí (李繼xí) advised Jìjí (繼岌) to return east,"
and ordered him to commit suicide.
It also states
"Rèn Yuán (任圜)'s army supervisor Lǐ Tíngxí (李廷xí) wanted to spare Kāng Yánxiào (康延孝),"
and that when he reached Huázhōu (華州) and was killed by Lǐ Chōng (李沖),
it again states
"Lǐ Cóngxí (李從xí)."
Presumably,
"Cóngxí (從xí)"
was mistakenly written as
"Jìxí (繼xí)"
and
"Tíngxí (廷xí)."
Now, we follow Zhuāngzōng Shílù (莊zōng實錄).
The Supervisor of the State (Jiānguó 監國) ordered Shí Jìngtáng (石敬táng) to appease them,
and all the soldiers expressed no dissent.
History says that the Western Army's loyalty turned to the new lord.
Earlier,
the Supervisor of the State (Jiānguó 監國) had ordered his trusted associate Lǐ Chōng (李沖) to be the Surveillance Commissioner of Huázhōu (華州),
to receive the Western Army.
Lǐ Chōng (李沖) forcibly compelled the Huázhōu (華州) Military Commissioner Shǐ Yánróng (史彥róng) to go to court;
when Tóngzhōu (同州) Military Commissioner Lǐ Cúnjìng (李存jìng) passed through Huázhōu (華州),
Lǐ Chōng (李沖) killed him
and slaughtered his family;
he also killed the Western Sichuan Expeditionary Army Surveillance Commissioner Lǐ Cóngxí (李從xí).
Lǐ Cóngxí (李從xí) deserved death for his numerous crimes,
but the Supervisor of the State (Jiānguó 監國) had not yet executed him publicly,
so Lǐ Chōng (李沖)'s killing him was an error in justice.
Zhònghuǐ (重誨) sent Yánróng (彥róng) back to his post
and summoned Lǐ Chōng (李沖) back to court.
Since the Supervisor of the State (Jiānguó 監國) entered Luòyáng (洛陽),
all internal and external affairs were decided by Lǐ Shàozhēn (李紹zhēn).
Lǐ Shàozhēn (李紹zhēn) forcibly arrested Wēishèng (威勝) Military Commissioner Lǐ Shàoqīn (李紹qīn) and Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince Lǐ Shàochōng (李紹chōng) and imprisoned them,
intending to kill them.
Ān Zhònghuǐ (安重誨) said to Lǐ Shàozhēn (李紹zhēn):
"Wēn Tāo (溫韜) and Duàn Níng (段凝)'s crimes were all committed during the Liáng (梁) dynasty.
Now that Your Highness has just suppressed the internal rebellion,
you hope to bring peace to all nations;
how can you be solely seeking revenge for yourself!"
Lǐ Shàozhēn (李紹zhēn) was somewhat discouraged by this.
On the day of Xīnchǒu (辛丑),
the Supervisor of the State (Jiānguó 監國) decreed
that Lǐ Shàochōng (李紹chōng) and Lǐ Shàoqīn (李紹qīn) revert to their original names Wēn Tāo (溫韜) and Duàn Níng (段凝).
The conferral of given names for Wēn Tāo (溫韜) and Duàn Níng (段凝) is recorded in Volume 272, the first year of Zhuāngzōng Tóngguāng (莊zōng同光).
11On the day of Rén'yín (壬寅),
Kǒng Xún (孔循) was appointed Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ 樞密使).
12 The officials in charge discussed the enthronement ceremony.
Lǐ Shàozhēn and Kǒng Xún believed that the destiny of Táng had ended,
and that a new dynastic title should be established.
The Regent asked his左右 (attendants):
"What is a dynastic title?"
They replied:
"The late emperor bestowed the surname Lǐ upon (us) for Táng,
to avenge Táng."
"Bestowed the surname Lǐ upon (us) for Táng"
means that Xiànzǔ was first granted the surname Lǐ for his achievement in pacifying Páng Xūn.
"To avenge Táng"
means Zhuāngzōng's destruction of Liáng.
為 (wèi),
reads as yú wěi.
Therefore, it is called Táng.
This implies that the first year of Tóngguāng continued the twentieth year of Tiānyòu.
Huò Yānwēi and Kǒng Xún had both served Liáng.
It is not certain that all those around the Regent at the time were scholars;
judging by the wording of their replies,
their arguments regarding the legitimacy of the dynasty were very strict,
which even scholars could not easily refute.
"When I was thirteen, I served Xiànzǔ.
Xiànzǔ regarded me as a kinsman,
and treated me as his son.
When Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne,
he honored his ancestor Guóchāng as Xiànzǔ."
The Regent was also of Shātuó stock,
hence "kinsman."
"Zhuāngzōng posthumously honored his father, Jìn Wáng Kèyòng, as Tàizǔ Wǔhuángdì.
In managing state affairs and in battle,
I was never absent;
Wǔhuáng's foundation is my foundation,
and the late emperor's realm is my realm.
How can there be one family and different states?"
He ordered the executive officials to discuss again.
The Minister of Personnel, Lǐ Qí, said:
"If the dynastic title is changed,
then the late emperor would become a stranger.
Where would the funerary cart be placed?"
"Not only would Your Highness forget three generations of former rulers,"
refers to the Regent having served Xiànzǔ, Tàizǔ, and Zhuāngzōng over three generations.
"Many previous dynasties had collateral branches succeed to the throne.
The ceremony of a嗣子 (heir) ascending the throne before the coffin should be adopted."
The Classics state: "A corpse in a bed is called shī (尸),
a corpse in a coffin is called jiù (柩)."
Zhèng Shì's commentary says: "Shī (尸)
means 'laid out,'
signifying the physical form is present;
jiù (柩) means 'to thoroughly investigate,'
and Bái Hǔ Tōng says
'long-lasting'."
Jiù (柩),
pronounced like 'xīn jiù zhī jiù' (new and old).
On the day of bǐngwǔ,
the Regent proceeded from Xīngshèng Palace to Xī Palace,
donned sackcloth mourning attire (zhǎncui),
and ascended the
throne before the coffin.
Zhǎncui
means the lower hem is not finished. A son wears it for his father.
衰 (cuī),
reads as cāng huí.
From the day of jǐchǒu when he entered Luòyáng
until this day, twenty days had passed.
The reason he had not dared to ascend the throne earlier was
that Wèi Wáng Jìjí was still alive;
now that Jìjí was dead,
he decided to do so.
Afterwards, he wore the imperial robe and crown to receive the imperial decree.
Xú Wúdǎng said: "Since the ceremony for an heir has been adopted,
to immediately shed the mourning attire and wear the imperial crown
shows his deceitful intentions."
13 On the day of wùshēn,
an imperial edict was issued to officials both inside and outside the court
that they were not allowed to present hawks, hounds, rare curiosities, or similar items.
14 The officials in charge impeached and reported Zhāng Xiàn, the Administrator of Tàiyuán, for the crime of abandoning the city;
on the day of gēngxū,
Xiàn was granted death.
Zhāng Xiàn was a high official of the former court,
so he was punished with death.
15 Rèn Yuán led twenty-six thousand Sichuan expeditionary troops to Luòyáng.
At the beginning of the Sichuan campaign,
sixty thousand troops were dispatched. Excluding those garrisoned in Sichuan and those who rebelled, died, or deserted with Kāng Yánxiào,
only twenty-six thousand returned to Luòyáng.
He ordered each to return to their camps.
According to the historical writing style of the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn,
the two characters "Míngzōng"
should have been written as
This is because it was a pre-existing text from a former historian,
accidentally overlooked and not corrected.
16 On the day of jiǎyín,
a general amnesty was declared,
and the reign era was changed.
The reign era was first changed to Tiānchéng.
Three hundred eunuchs,
one hundred musicians from the music bureau,
twenty falconers,
and fifty imperial chefs were dismissed;
the rest were allowed to go wherever they wished.
All officials whose titles were nominal and without substance were abolished.
Troops were distributed to feed in the nearby capital region
to save on transportation costs.
The surtax on summer and autumn taxes was abolished.
According to old regulations,
a surtax had previously been levied on the summer and autumn taxes,
one shēng per dòu.
From now on, only the principal tax amount was to be collected,
without the surtax.
Contributions were allowed on the four festivals of Zhèngyuán (New Year's Day), Zhì (Winter Solstice), Duānwǔ (Dragon Boat Festival), and Jiàngdàn (Emperor's Birthday).
Yuánzhèng (New Year's Day), Dōngzhì (Winter Solstice), Duānwǔ, and Jiàngdàn festival make four.
According to the Wǔdài Huìyào,
Emperor Dài Zōng was born on the ninth day of the ninth month in the eighth year of Xiántōng of Táng
in Jīnfèng City, Dàiběi.
That day was designated Yìngshèng Festival.
Governors and lower-ranking officials were not allowed to make contributions.
Candidates whose documents had been defaced (túhuǐ wénshū)
(túhuǐ xuǎnrén gàoshēn)
can be seen in volume 273, the second year of Tóngguāng of Zhuāngzōng.
The rest reverted to old regulations.
The Táng Liùdiǎn states: the duties of the Minister and Vice Ministers of Personnel
were to manage all officials in the empire,
dividing their selection into three bureaus (sānquán):
the first was the Shàngshū Quán,
the second was the Zhōng Quán,
and the third was the Dōng Quán.
Or it is said that the Ministry of Personnel's Dōng Quán, Xī Quán, and Líuwài Quán constituted the Sān Quán.
Sòng Bái said: In the seventh month of the fourth year of Tàihé,
the Ministry of Personnel reported:
"In the Xī Quán Vice Minister's office of our department,
it was formerly the Zhōng Quán after the Shàngshū Quán,
and then the Dōng Quán.
During the Qiányuán era,
Vice Minister Cuī Qì proposed changing the Zhōng Quán to Xī Quán,
placing the senior Vice Minister on the left and
the newly appointed Vice Minister on the right.
This was a reversal of tradition,
which critics disapproved of.
We request that from now on, the senior Vice Minister reside in the Xī Quán,
and the newly appointed Vice Minister reside in the Dōng Quán."
An imperial edict approved this.
It also said: The Minister of War was the Zhōng Quán,
and with the Dōng Quán and Xī Quán, they formed the Sān Quán.
17 In the fifth month,
on the first day, bǐngchén,
Zhèng Yù, the太子賓客 (Grand Master of the Crown Prince's Household),
and Rèn Yuán, the Minister of Works, were both appointed Vice Ministers of the Central Secretariat and Grand Counselors (Tóng Píngzhāngshì);
Yuán also held the concurrent post of Commissioner of the Three Bureaus (Pàn Sānsī).
Yuán was as concerned with public affairs as with his own family,
selecting capable and outstanding individuals,
putting an end to corruption.
Within a year,
the treasuries were full,
the army and people were prosperous,
and the court administration was largely established.
History states that Rèn Yuán had achievements as a prime minister.
粗 (cū),
reads as zuò wǔ.
Because of this, Ān Zhònghuì became jealous of him.
This sets the stage for Ān Zhònghuì's slander and murder of Rèn Yuán.

18 Lǐ Shàozhēn, Military Governor of Wǔníng; Lǐ Shàojióng, Military Governor of Zhōngwǔ; Lǐ Shàoyīng, Prefect of Bèizhōu; Lǐ Shàoqián, Defense Commissioner of Qízhōu; Lǐ Shàoqí, Military Governor of Héyáng; and Lǐ Shàonéng, Prefect of Míngzhōu,
each requested to revert to their original names: Huò Yānwēi, Cháng Cóngjiǎn, Fáng Zhīwēn, Wáng Yànqiú, Xià Lǔqí, and Mǐ Jūnlì.
This was granted.
Lǐ Shàozhēn and Shàoqián were granted surnames when they surrendered as Liáng generals.
Lǐ Shàojióng, Shàoyīng, Shàoqí, and Shàonéng were granted surnames for their meritorious service in battle to Zhuāngzōng.
The Zīzhì Tōngjiàn does not fully record the reasons for their bestowed surnames,
it omits them.
He was from Chénzhōu.
Yànqiú was originally a son of the Wáng clan,
raised by the Dù clan,
so he requested to revert to the surname Wáng.
19 On the day of dīngsì,
it was first ordered that outside of regular court sessions (zhèngyá chángcháo),
all officials should attend the inner palace for greetings every five days.
At that time, zhèngyá chángcháo was held at Wénmíng Palace,
attended on the first and fifteenth of the lunar month.
Nèidiàn (Inner Palace)
refers to Zhōngxīng Palace.
朝 (cháo),
reads as zhí yáo.
20 Several hundred eunuchs hid in mountains and forests,
or shaved their heads to become monks.
Over seventy of them reached Jìnyáng,
and an imperial edict ordered Lǐ Cóngwēn, the Commander of the Northern Capital, to execute them all.
Cóngwēn was
the Emperor's nephew.
21 The Emperor, considering the former Prefect of Xiàngzhōu, Ān Jīnquán, had rendered meritorious service at Jìnyáng
(the details are found in volume 269, the second year of Zhēnmíng of Liáng Jūn Wáng),
Xiàng (相),
reads as xī liàng.
On the day of rénxū,
Jīnquán was appointed Military Governor of Zhènwǔ and Grand Counselor (Tóng Píngzhāngshì).
On the 22nd day of the *bǐngyín* month,
Zhào Zàilǐ requested the Emperor to visit Yèdū.
On the *wùchén* day,
Zhào Zàilǐ was appointed Jìchéng Jiédùshǐ;
he declined, citing that the military situation had not yet been settled,
and did not proceed to his post.
Zhào Zàilǐ was in fact coerced and controlled by the Wèi troops,
and not allowed to go to Huázhōu.
On the 23rd, Lǐ Yànchāo entered the court.
The Emperor said:
"Hédōng is free from trouble,
this is your achievement."
The Hédōng military administration was in Jìnyáng.
Lǐ Cúnzhǎo died,
Zhāng Xiàn fled,
the stability of the army was all due to Lǐ Yànchāo's efforts.
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
he was appointed Jiànxíong Liúhòu.
He was sent to govern Jìnzhōu but was not yet granted the formal insignia of a jiédùshǐ,
merely serving as a liúhòu.
On the 24th day of the *jiǎxū* month,
Wáng Yánhàn was additionally granted the title of Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Wáng Yánhàn inherited his ancestors' enterprise,
and held the Mǐn region.
The Emperor was illiterate,
so all memorials from the four directions were read to him by Ān Chónghuǐ.
Chónghuǐ also could not fully comprehend everything,
so he memorialized, saying:
"Your servant, with a loyal and sincere heart, serves Your Majesty,
and has been able to manage the pivot of governance.
Now, current affairs I can roughly understand,
but as for ancient matters,
they are beyond my reach.
I wish to emulate the previous dynasty's shìjiǎng and shìdú, and more recently, the zhíchóngzhèng and pìmìyuàn,
to select literati to work with me,
to be prepared for responses."
Thereupon, the Duānmíng Diàn Xuéshì position was established.
Chūnmíng Tuìcháo Lù states: The Duānmíng Diàn
was the main audience hall in Xījīng.
It was likely that the Wénmíng Diàn was renamed Duānmíng Diàn.
Wǔdài Huìyào states: In the first month of the second year of Táng Tóngguāng (924 CE), the Jiěxiè Diàn was renamed Duānmíng Diàn.
According to this, the Duānmíng Diàn was a place for informal receptions of imperial scholars,
certainly not the main audience hall.
The Wǔdài Huìyào should be taken as the basis.
The Duānmíng Diàn Xuéshì began at this point.
Sòng Bái said: In the fourth year of Chángxīng (933 CE),
Liú Xù became prime minister,
and expressed his gratitude.
On that day, there was a great sacrificial ceremony,
and Míngzōng did not preside in the Zhōngxīng Diàn but sat in the Duānmíng Diàn.
When Xù arrived at the Zhōngxīng Diàn gate,
the imperial envoy said:
"According to old rites,
prime ministers offering thanks must be summoned in the main hall.
Today, due to the great sacrificial ceremony, His Majesty is not in the main hall.
Please wait until tomorrow."
Zhào Yánshòu said:
"The decree appointing the prime minister was issued three days ago,
so the expression of gratitude should not be delayed."
He immediately reported this.
Although Xù expressed gratitude in the Duānmíng Diàn,
having been appointed prime minister from a Duānmíng Xuéshì,
he again expressed gratitude in his former hall,
which the literati considered an honor.
On the *yǐhài* day,
Hànlín Xuéshì Féng Dào and Zhào Fèng were appointed to this position.
On the 26th day of the *bǐngzǐ* month,
Guō Chóngtāo was permitted to be buried,
and Zhū Yǒuqiān's offices and titles were restored;
these two had died due to slander, as seen in the first month of this year in the previous volume.
All properties previously confiscated were returned to them.
On the 27th day of the *wùyín* month,
Ān Chónghuǐ was appointed to lead the Shānnán Dōngdào Jiédùshǐ.
Chónghuǐ, considering Xiāngyáng an important strategic location—
Xiāngyáng controlled Shǔ and guarded Jīng,
hence it was called a strategic location—
deemed it unsuitable to hold concurrently.
He firmly declined;
it was granted.
On the 28th, an edict was issued to dispatch Zhāng Jiàn and 3,000 men from the Biànzhōu Kònghè Zhīhuīshǐ to garrison Wǎqiáo.
In the sixth month,
on the *dīngyǒu* day,
they left the city,
then returned,
and rebelled.
The Kònghè,
the imperial guard of the Liáng dynasty,
had grown arrogant and were reluctant to be garrisoned far away,
hence they rebelled.
Indeed, at that time, all troops in the empire were arrogant.
The character "復" (fù)
is pronounced *fúyòu* in this context.
They killed the acting Prefect, Gāo Tì.
They forced the Mǎbù Dūzhīhuīshǐ and Cáozhōu Cìshǐ, Lǐ Yànráo, to be their commander.
Yànráo said:
"If you want me to be your commander,
you must obey my command
to forbid burning and looting."
The multitude followed him.
At dawn on the *jǐhài* day,
Yànráo ambushed them with armed men in his chamber.
When the generals entered to congratulate him,
Yànráo said:
"The instigators of the rebellion the other day were only a few individuals."
Thereupon, he seized Zhāng Jiàn and four others,
and executed them.
Their faction, led by Zhāng Shěnqióng, raised a great clamor at the Jiànguó Mén.
Yànráo led his troops to attack them,
exterminating all 400 of their men.
The army and prefecture were then pacified.
On the same day,
he handed over the military and prefectural affairs to Wéi Yǎn, the jiédù tuīguān, to temporarily manage,
and fully reported the situation.
Fú Yànráo was influenced in Biàn and caused chaos in Huá.
Was it that the generals and soldiers of that time were arrogant and perverse,
a habit that became custom,
and Yànráo, over time, was transformed along with them?
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
an edict was issued appointing Pìmìshǐ Kǒng Xún to administer Biànzhōu,
to round up the 3,000 households involved in the rebellion,
and execute them all.
Yànráo was
Yànchāo's younger brother.
On the 29th, the officials of Shǔ arrived in Luòyáng.
Mǎ Quán, Yongpíng Jiédùshǐ and concurrently Shìzhōng, said:
"The country has fallen to this point;
living is worse than dying!"
He refused to eat and died.
The official title of Mǎ Quán is recorded here;
he was an official of Shǔ.
Shǔ had established the Yǒngpíng Army in Yázhōu.
As for the cìshǐ, shàoyǐn, pànguān, and sīmǎ of various prefectures,
some also returned to Shǔ.
On the 30th day of the *xīnchǒu* month,
Yú Kěhóng and others, the Dūzhīhuīshǐ of Huázhōu, started a rebellion by arson,
attacking the three commands of the Wèibó garrison soldiers,
and driving them out.
On the 31st day of the *yǐsì* month,
an imperial edict stated:
"My two personal names,
as long as they are not used together,
do not need to be avoided at all."
Not avoiding individual characters of a two-character personal name,
was an ancient practice.
On the 32nd day of the *wùshēn* month,
Mèng Zhīxiáng, Xīchuān Jiédùshǐ, was additionally granted the concurrent title of Shìzhōng.
On the 33rd, Lǐ Jìyǎn arrived in Huázhōu.
Hearing of the chaos in Luòzhōng,
he returned to Fèngxiáng;
the Emperor, for his sake, executed Chái Chónghòu.
34 Gāo Jìxīng submitted a memorial requesting Kuízhōu, Zhōngzhōu, and Wànzhōu as subordinate prefectures.
An imperial edict granted this.
When Zhuāngzōng campaigned against Shǔ,
he decreed Gāo Jìxīng to take Kuízhōu, Zhōngzhōu, and Wànzhōu as his directly administered prefectures.
Jìxīng was unable to take them.
After Wáng Yǎn was defeated,
the three prefectures returned to Táng.
Jìxīng then requested them as directly administered prefectures,
but this was not granted.
This served as a pretext for Jìxīng's disobedience to the imperial command and his subsequent military campaign.
The *Kǎoyì* says: Zhuāngzōng’s *Shílù* states:
"Wáng Jiàn established the Zhènjiāng Jūn Jiédù in Kuízhōu,
with Kuízhōu, Zhōngzhōu, Wànzhōu, and Shīzhōu as its subordinate prefectures.
The Yún’ān Salt Monopoly, benefiting from salt revenues,
was elevated by Jiàn to Ānzhōu.
When the emperor led his army to pacify Shǔ,
he decreed Jìxīng to reclaim his formerly administered subordinate prefectures.
Before the Jīngnán army advanced,
the commander of Kuízhōu surrendered the prefecture to Jìjí."
The *Shíguó Jìnián Jīngnán Shǐ* states:
"In the second month of Tiānchéng first year (926),
Wáng submitted a memorial requesting that Kuízhōu, Zhōngzhōu, Wànzhōu, and the Yún’ān Salt Monopoly be attached to his circuit.
Zhuāngzōng granted this.
Before the imperial edict was issued,
Zhuāngzōng was assassinated.
In the sixth month,
Wáng again requested the three prefectures.
Míngzōng granted this."
Liú Shù remarks:
Zhuāngzōng’s *Shílù* and Xuē Shǐ’s *Dìjì* both state,
"In the *gēngxū* day of the eleventh month of Tóngguāng third year (925),
Gāo Jìxīng of Jīngnán reported the recovery of Kuízhōu, Zhōngzhōu, and other prefectures."
Zēng Yán’s *Bóhǎi Xíngnián Jì* states
"obtained Kuízhōu, Zhōngzhōu, Wànzhōu, and other prefectures."
Míngzōng’s *Shílù* and Xuē Shǐ’s biography of Wéi Shuō both state:
"When attacking Xīshǔ,
Jìxīng requested to attack the area within the gorges.
The former court granted this,
stipulating that if he could obtain the three prefectures,
they would be made his subordinate prefectures.
After Sānchuān was pacified,
Jìxīng had no achievement, not even an inch."
Zhuāngzōng’s *Shílù*:
"In the *bǐngyín* day of the third month of Tóngguāng fourth year (926),
Gāo Jìxīng requested that Kuízhōu, Zhōngzhōu, Wànzhōu, and other prefectures within the gorges be assigned to his circuit."
Míngzōng’s *Shílù*:
"In the *jiǎyín* day of the sixth month of Tiānchéng first year (926),
Gāo Jìxīng reported: 'Last winter, the former court decreed me to attack and take the subordinate prefectures within the gorges.
Soon, officials from Shīzhōu learned of my ascent into the gorges
and were the first to surrender.
Kuízhōu, Zhōngzhōu, and Wànzhōu were expected to be recovered morning or evening.
However, Guō Chóngtāo specifically sent a document ordering me to return.
Just as I was about to make my case,
the change (of emperor) occurred.' "
This account is quite close to the truth,
therefore it is followed.
For in the tenth month of the third year (Tóngguāng 3),
Kuízhōu, Zhōngzhōu, and Wànzhōu surrendered to Jìjí.
In the *gēngxū* day of the eleventh month,
Jìxīng submitted a memorial requesting the three prefectures as subordinate prefectures.
The old history mistakenly states he reported their recovery.
The *Xíngnián Jì* contains the most errors
and cannot be relied upon.
Perhaps although Kuízhōu surrendered directly to Jìjí,
Jìxīng’s memorial stated he "recovered" the three prefectures,
claiming it as his own achievement,
which is not surprising.
We now follow Míngzōng’s *Shílù*.
35 Ān Chónghuì, relying on imperial favor, became arrogant and overbearing.
The Palace Attendant Mǎ Yán mistakenly obstructed his escort.
The Left and Right Class Palace Attendants
were imperial attendants.
Before Xīníng (1068-1077) in the Sòng dynasty, they were considered minor officials of the western ranks holding sinecure posts.
The *Zhíguān Fēnjì* says: Palace Attendant,
in the Five Dynasties was originally called Diànqián Chéngzhǐ.
In the fifth year of Tiānfú (940) of the Jìn dynasty, an edict stipulated that, except for Hànlín Chéngzhǐ,
Diànqián Chéngzhǐ should be renamed Diànzhí.
However, in Tiānchéng first year (926), Ān Chónghuì executed the Palace Attendant Mǎ Yán.
In Qīngtài first year (934) of Lù Wáng, the Palace Attendant Chéngzhǐ Dūzhī Zhào Chǔyuàn and others were ordered to wear the *lánkuò* robe.
This indicates that the official title Diànzhí existed before Tiānfú of Jìn.
The *Zhíguān Fēnjì* is mistaken.
During the Guǎngshùn period (951-953) of the Later Zhōu, Palace Attendants Chǔ Yánzuò and Wáng Luán also appear in history.
The Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Qí reported this.
Lǐ Qí was apprehensive of Ān Chónghuì's power
and dared not impeach him.
He merely reported the matter.
In the seventh month,
Chónghuì, through the emperor, issued an edict
stating that Yán mistakenly collided with a high minister,
and warned officials inside and outside the court.
This single incident
was sufficient for Ān Chónghuì to bring about his own death.
36 Yú Kěhóng and the garrison commander of Wèibó mutually accused each other of rebellion.
The emperor sent an envoy to investigate and found the truth.
On the *xīnyǒu* day,
Kěhóng was executed in the marketplace.
His chief instigator, the entire camp of Zuǒ Chóngyá of Huázhōu, was exterminated.
Those who aided the rebellion, the two commanders of Yòu Chóngyá and one hundred officers and soldiers of Jiànpíng, were also exterminated.
37 On the *rénshēn* day,
it was first decreed that all officials should attend court every five days
and present memorials in turn.
At that time, following the system of the prosperous Táng,
all officials would present memorials in turn concerning the public affairs of their respective departments.
38 The Khitan ruler attacked Bóhǎi,
capturing its Fúyúchéng.
This was the Fúyúchéng of Gāolì during the Táng dynasty.
At that time, Wáng Jiàn, the King of Gāolì, ruled the kingdom,
guarding it with the Húntóng Jiāng as a boundary.
The area west of Húntóng Jiāng could not be held by him;
thus Fúyúchéng belonged to the Bóhǎi Kingdom.
Húntóng Jiāng is the Yālù Shuǐ.
*Fū* (夫) is pronounced *fú*.
He commanded his eldest son, Tūyù, to guard Dōngdān,
styling him Rén Huáng Wáng.
His second son, Déguāng, was to guard Xīlóu,
styling him Yuánshuài Tàizǐ.
This served as a pretext for Tūyù’s later defection.
Sòng Bái said: Yēlǜ Déguāng's original name was Yàoqūzhī.
He admired Chinese characters
and changed it.
The emperor sent the Attendant Official Yáo Kūn to convey condolences to the Khitan.
The *Kǎoyì* says: Hàn Gāozǔ’s *Shílù* records it as
"Miáo Shēn,"
but we now follow Zhuāngzōng’s biographies.
He wept bitterly, saying:
"My court's Dìng'er (Zhuāngzōng) is dead.
I wanted to save him,
but as Bóhǎi had not yet fallen,
I could not go,
causing my son to meet this end."
He wept ceaselessly.
The barbarian word
"cháodìng"
is like the Chinese word for friend.
He also asked Kūn:
"The current Son of Heaven heard that Luòyáng was in distress;
why did he not save him?"
Kūn replied:
"The distance was too great to reach."
He asked:
"Why did he establish himself?"
Kūn explained the reasons for the emperor's ascension.
The Khitan ruler said:
"Chinese people like to embellish their stories;
do not speak much!"
Tūyù, attending by his side,
said:
"Is it permissible to lead an ox into another's field and then take away his ox?"
He cited Shēn Shú’s words from the *Zuǒzhuàn*.
Historians say that the Khitan admired China
and emulated Chinese people in their speech and writing.
"China was without a ruler,
and the Táng Son of Heaven had no choice but to establish himself.
This is just like when the Heavenly King first founded his state;
did he seize it by force?"
This refers to Ābǎojī’s refusal to yield and his destruction of the seven tribes.
*Qiáng* (強) is read as *qiáng*.
"It is naturally so."
Hearing Yáo Kūn's words,
he had to admit it.
"I heard my son was solely fond of music, women, and hunting.
It is fitting that he met this end.
Since I heard of it,
my entire family has not drunk alcohol,
I have dismissed all entertainers,
and released my eagles and hounds.
If you also imitate my son's behavior,
you will soon perish yourself."
The Khitan ruler's wisdom was such,
and indeed it was fitting that he could establish a state and pass it down through generations.
"Although my son and I were old acquaintances,
we frequently engaged in warfare.
With the current Son of Heaven, however, there is no grievance,
which is sufficient for cultivating good relations.
If you grant me the land north of the Yellow River,
I will not invade south again."
Kūn replied:
"This is not something an envoy has the authority to decide."
The Khitan ruler became angry
and imprisoned him.
After more than ten days,
he summoned him again,
saying:
"The area north of the Yellow River may be difficult to obtain.
Obtaining Zhènzhōu, Dìngzhōu, and Yōuzhōu would also be acceptable."
He provided paper and brush and urged him to draft a petition.
Kūn refused,
and he wanted to kill him.
Hán Yánhuī remonstrated,
so he was imprisoned again.
Imprisoning him repeatedly
was to pressure Yáo Kūn to draft the petition.
Even if Yáo Kūn were to draft the petition,
would China agree to cede territory to him?
This was merely employing the old trick of deceiving and misleading.
On the 39th day, *bǐngzǐ*,
Emperor Guāngshèng Shénmǐn Xiào was interred at Yōnglíng,
Yōnglíng being in Xīn'ān County, Hénán.
*Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* states:
"On the *yǐhài* day,
the imperial coffin was sent off,
and on that day, it was moved to Yōnglíng."
According to the eulogy for Emperor Zhuāngzōng's *Shílù*, it was *bǐngzǐ*.
We follow this now.
On the 40th day, *dīngchǒu*,
Wáng Jiànlì, the Acting Military Governor of Zhènzhōu, reported that Liú Yīnzhào, the Prefect of Zhuōzhōu, refused to be replaced
and was plotting rebellion;
he had already been apprehended and subdued.
Of the regional commands of Táng,
Zhuōzhōu
was a dependency of the Yōuzhōu Military Governor,
not under the Zhènzhōu Military Governor.
That Wáng Jiànlì was able to subdue him
indicates that when Emperor Míngzōng first gained the empire,
many regional commands and prefectures were still wavering.
Wáng Jiànlì was a close confidant of Emperor Míngzōng.
Crossing into another territory to apprehend and subdue Liú Yīnzhào,
he reported that Liú Yīnzhào had refused to be replaced,
and the court also permitted it.
On the 41st day, *jǐmǎo*,
the Zhāngguó Army was established in Yìngzhōu.
The geographical treatises of the Old and New Books of Táng did not yet list Yìngzhōu.
Ōu's *Shǐ Zhífāng Kǎo* was the first to mention Yìngzhōu,
hence it belonged to the Dàtóng Military Command but its initial establishment was not recorded.
It is likely that King Jìn Kèyòng divided Yúnzhōu to establish Yìngzhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Yìngzhōu was a frontier prefecture,
governing Jīnchéng and Hùnyuán Counties.
I secretly believe that Jīnchéng County was established using Jīnfèngchéng, the birthplace of Emperor Míngzōng;
now the Zhāngguó Army military command is established there,
also because it is the Emperor's hometown.
The Xiongnu must know: Yìngzhōu is eight hundred and fifty *lǐ* east of Yōuzhōu.
Furthermore, Xuē's *Shǐ Zhōumì Zhuàn* states that
Shénwǔchuān belonged to Yìngzhōu.
It was when Zhūyé Zhíyí moved to Hédōng
that he first settled at Huánghuāduī in Shénwǔchuān.
The Shatuo thus established their hegemony,
hence Yìngzhōu was established in that area.
Dòulú Gé and Wéi Shuō, Attendants at the Department of the Palace Affairs and Simultaneously Grand Councillors, reported to the Emperor;
sometimes their demeanor was not entirely respectful.
All officials' salaries were commuted to goods,
but Gé's father and son alone received actual money.
All officials received their salaries from May,
but Gé's father and son received theirs from January.
Because of this, public opinion was沸騰.
Shuō adopted his grandson as a son
and recommended him for office.
He accepted a bribe from the candidate Wáng Cān
and appointed him to a local office.
Local office refers to
officials in prefectures and counties near the capital.
Gé and Shuō were reported again.
Xīfǔ resented them
and submitted a memorial stating
"Gé and Shuō were disloyal to the previous court,
flattering to curry favor";
then he falsely accused them:
"Gé forcibly seized commoners' land
and allowed his tenants to commit murder;
Shuō seized a neighbor's well
and took hidden treasures."
Hidden treasures refers to
items buried by former inhabitants that had not yet been unearthed.
This likely refers to items hidden in the well.
Shuō was Prefect of Xùzhōu.
On the *gēngchén* day,
Xīfǔ was bestowed with gold and silk
and promoted to Sanqí Chángshì.
*Sǎn*
is read as *xī dǎn*.
*Qí*
is read as *qí jì*.
On the 43rd day, *xīnsì*,
Abǎojī, the Khitan ruler, died in Fúyú City.
Empress Shùlǜ summoned the wives of the generals and tribal chiefs who were difficult to control
and said to them:
"I am now a widow;
you must not fail to follow my example."
She then gathered their husbands and tearfully asked:
"Do you miss the late Emperor?"
They replied:
"Having received the late Emperor's kindness,
how can we not miss him!"
She said:
"If you truly miss him,
you should go see him."
She then killed them.
This sets the stage for Empress Shùlǜ imprisoning herself in Abǎojī's tomb.
On the 44th day, *guǐwèi*,
Dòulú Gé was again demoted to Household Administrator of Fèizhōu,
and Wéi Shuō to Household Administrator of Yízhōu.
On the *jiǎshēn* day,
Gé was exiled to Língzhōu,
and Shuō was exiled to Hézhōu.
Since the late Táng,
those exiled were usually granted death.
Did Gé and Shuō even reach their places of exile?
Méng Zhīxiáng secretly harbored ambitions to control Shǔ.
He inspected the armory
and found two hundred thousand sets of armor,
establishing sixteen camps of Left and Right Yá and other troops,
totaling sixteen thousand men,
encamped inside and outside the imperial city.
In the eighth month,
on the first day, *yǐyǒu*,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the 47th day, *dīnghài*,
Empress Shùlǜ of Khitan sent her youngest son, Ānduān Shàojūn, to guard Dōngdān,
and with her eldest son, Tūyù, carried the Khitan ruler's coffin,
leading their forces from Fúyú City.
Initially,
Guō Chóngtāo had divided the Shǔ cavalry into six camps, such as the Left and Right Xiāowèi,
totaling three thousand men;
and the infantry into twenty camps, such as the Left and Right Níngyuǎn,
totaling twenty-four thousand men.
On the *gēngyín* day,
Méng Zhīxiáng added six camps, such as the Left and Right Chōngshān,
totaling six thousand men,
encamped inside and outside the outer city wall;
he also established twenty camps, such as the Yìníng,
totaling sixteen thousand men,
stationed in various prefectures and counties within his jurisdiction for sustenance;
thus they were stationed and fed in the prefectures and counties where they were garrisoned.
A total of four thousand men
were stationed within the territory of Chéngdū.
Wáng Gōngyǎn had already killed Yáng Xīwàng;
the details are in the third month of this year in the previous volume.
He publicly stated that Fú Xí's governance was strict and urgent,
and that the military and populace were unwilling for him to return.
When Xí returned,
arriving at Qízhōu,
Gōngyǎn resisted him,
and Xí dared not advance.
Qízhōu is over three hundred forty *lǐ* east of Qīngzhōu,
with Zīzhōu still in between.
Fú Xí, hearing that Wáng Gōngyǎn was blocking him with troops,
immediately dared not advance.
To expect him to quell the rebellion
would be difficult.
An imperial edict appointed him Prefect of Dēngzhōu.
Gōngyǎn did not proceed to his post in time,
claiming that military sentiment detained him.
The Emperor then transferred Huò Yànwēi, Military Governor of Tiānpíng, to be Military Governor of Pínglú,
gathering troops in Zīzhōu
to plan an attack.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Zīzhōu is one hundred twenty *lǐ* northeast of Qīngzhōu.
On the *yǐwèi* day,
he first took office.
On the *dīngyǒu* day,
Yànwēi arrived at Qīngzhōu,
pursued and captured him,
and executed his entire clan and party,
including the Aide Hán Shūsì of Běihǎi.
His son, Xīzài, was about to flee to Wú;
he secretly informed his friend, the *jìnshì* Lǐ Gǔ of Rǔyīn.
Gǔ escorted him to Zhèngyáng.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Yǐngshàng County in Yǐngzhōu has Zhèngyáng Town,
west of Huáijīn.
The eastern ford of the Huái is called Dōngzhèngyáng,
which is the territory of Wú.
Xīzài said to Gǔ:
"If Wú employs me as Chancellor,
I will advance directly to pacify the Central Plains."
Gǔ laughed and said:
"If the Central Plains employs me as Chancellor,
taking Wú would be like taking something from a bag."
Later, Emperor Shìzōng of Zhōu appointed Lǐ Gǔ as Chancellor
and used his strategy to take Huáinán;
but Hán Xīzài also served as Chancellor for Southern Táng,
but ultimately could not accomplish anything.
*Xiàng*
is read as *xī liàng*.
On the 50th day, *gēngzǐ*,
Yōuzhōu reported that the Khitan were invading the border,
and Ān Shěntōng, the Defense Commissioner of Qízhōu, was ordered to lead troops to repel them.
In the ninth month,
on the *rénxū* day,
Méng Zhīxiáng established six camps of Left and Right Fēizhào troops,
totaling six thousand men,
stationed in various prefectures along the river,
practicing naval warfare to guard against Kuí and Xiá.
On the 52nd day, *guǐyǒu*,
Lǐ Shàobīn, Military Governor of Lúlóng, requested to revert to his original surname Zhào.
Ōu's *Shǐ* states: Zhào Déjūn was from Yōuzhōu.
He served Liú Shǒuwén and Shǒuguāng as a military commander.
Emperor Zhuāngzōng captured him during the campaign against Yàn
and bestowed upon him the surname and given name Lǐ Shàobīn.
He was then bestowed the name Déjūn.
Déjūn's adopted son, Yánshòu, married Princess Xīngpíng, the Emperor's daughter,
hence Déjūn enjoyed particular favor.
Yánshòu was originally the son of Liú Áng, the Magistrate of Tiáoxiāo.
53 King Chǔ Yīn was additionally appointed Grand Preceptor.
Sùlǜ Hòu, the Khitan empress, loved her second son, Dégūang.
She wished to enthrone him.
Arriving at Xīlóu,
Xīlóu
was the Khitan Upper Capital.
Earlier,
the Khitan ruler had ordered Dégūang to stay and guard.
He told the various chieftains:
"I love both my sons.
I don't know which one to enthrone.
You choose the one who is worthy of being enthroned and hold his reins."
The chieftains understood his intention.
They vied to hold Dégūang's reins, cheering and saying:
"We wish to serve Grand Marshal Tàizǐ."
The empress said:
"How dare I go against
the will of the multitude?"
So, she enthroned him as Tiānhuáng Wáng.
Tūyù was indignant.
Leading several hundred cavalry, he intended to flee to Táng,
but was intercepted by scouts.
Sùlǜ Hòu did not punish him,
but sent him back to Dōngdān.
Tiānhuáng Wáng honored Sùlǜ Hòu as Tàihòu,
and all state affairs were decided by her.
Tàihòu again took her niece as Tiānhuáng Wáng Hòu.
Tiānhuáng Wáng was by nature filial and diligent.
If his mother was ill and did not eat, he would also not eat.
Attending before his mother, if his responses did not please her,
and she raised her eyebrows to look at him,
he would immediately be frightened and retreat,
not daring to appear again unless recalled.
He appointed Hán Yánhuī as Zhèngshì Lìng.
ōushǐ says: The Khitan made Hán Yánhuī their prime minister,
calling him Zhèngshì Lìng.
The incident of Ābǎojī imprisoning Yáo Kūn is mentioned above.
Kǎoyì says: The Hàn Gāozǔ Shílù states
"Mò Gūnèi,"
but we follow Míngzōng Shílù and Huìyào here.
55 On a Rénwǔ day,
Lǐ Jìyǎn was granted the name Cóngyǎn.
He was treated as a son.
56 In winter,
tenth month,
on a Jiǎshēn day, the first day of the month,
spring and winter clothing was first bestowed upon civil and military officials.
Wǔdài Huìyào: In the third year of Tóngguāng,
the Zūyōng Yuàn presented a memorial on the newly established salaries for vice envoys, judicial officers, and below in the four capitals and various circuits,
which included silk for spring clothing and silk for winter clothing.
This was probably for already-made clothing bestowed upon civil and military officials in the capital.
57 Wáng Yánhàn, the Zhaowǔ Jiédùshǐ and Tóngpíngzhāngshì.
"Zhaowǔ"
should be
"Wēiwǔ."
On a Jǐchǒu day,
he declared himself King of the Great Mǐn Kingdom.
He built palaces,
established a hundred officials,
and all his regalia and cultural artifacts imitated the system of the Son of Heaven.
Those below him addressed him as Diànxià.
He granted an amnesty within his territory,
and posthumously honored his father Shěnzhī as Zhaowǔ Wáng.
This sets the stage for Wáng Yánhàn's eventual downfall.
58 Máo Zhāng, the Jìngnán Jiédùshǐ,
was arrogant, presumptuous, and unlawful.
He trained troops and maintained weapons,
harboring ambitions of rebellion.
For someone like Máo Zhāng,
what could his rebellion achieve?
Nothing more than wanting to hold Bīnzhōu.
On a Rénchén day,
Zhāng was transferred to be Zhaoyì Jiédùshǐ.
Zhuāngzōng had changed Lùzhōu Zhaoyì Army to Ānyì Army,
then later restored its original name.
Chéngyuē and the Guānchá Pànguān, Biān Wèi of Cháng'ān, quietly persuaded him.
After a long time,
he finally agreed to be replaced.
59 On a Gēngzǐ day,
Yōuzhōu reported that Lú Wénjìn, the Khitan Lúlóng Jiédùshǐ, had come to defect.
Lú Wénjìn entered Khitan in the second year of Liáng Jūnwáng Qiànhuà, which is mentioned in the 270th scroll.
Wénjìn guarded Píngzhōu for the Khitan.
When the emperor ascended the throne,
he sent a secret envoy to persuade him,
stating that after the change of dynasties,
there would be no more old grudges.
Zhuāngzōng resented Lú Wénjìn for killing his younger brother and fleeing to Khitan,
and for then leading Khitan to harass the border.
Now that Zhuāngzōng had died and Míngzōng had ascended,
there were no longer any old grudges.
Wishing to return,
he killed the Khitan garrison in Píngzhōu,
and leading his host of over 100,000 men and 8,000 carts of tents, came to defect.
This sets the stage for Lú Wénjìn's later defection to Huáinán.
Shuài [帥],
is read as lǜ [率].
60 Initially,
Wèi Wáng Jìjí and Guō Chóngtāo ordered the wealthy households of Shǔ to contribute five million strings of money for rewards.
They allowed payment in gold, silver, and silk.
They pressed for collection day and night,
leading to some suicides.
After supplying the army,
there were still two million strings remaining.
By this time,
Rèn Yuán was in charge of the Three Bureaus,
and knew Chéngdū was rich and prosperous.
At the end of Tóngguāng,
Rèn Yuán joined the army to conquer Shǔ,
thus knowing its wealth.
When the emperor ascended the throne,
he promoted Mèng Zhīxiáng to Shìzhōng,
so he sent Zhào Jìliáng with official dispatches and national credentials to Shǔ,
and also to establish transfer and transport operations.
On a Jiǎchén day,
Jìliáng arrived in Chéngdū.
The people of Shǔ wished to give nothing,
but Zhīxiáng said:
"The treasury's stores were accumulated by others;
it is acceptable to surrender them.
As for the taxes from the prefectures and counties,
they are for supporting the 100,000 garrison troops;
they absolutely cannot be taken."
Looking at Mèng Zhīxiáng's words,
his ambition to independently control the land of Shǔ was already evident.
He dared not speak again of the duties of establishing transfer and transport operations.
Ān Chónghuǐ believed that Zhīxiáng and Dǒng Zhāng, the Dōngchuān Jiédùshǐ, both occupied strategic locations
and commanded strong armies.
He feared they would become difficult to control over time.
Moreover, Zhīxiáng was a close relative of Zhuāngzōng by marriage.
Mèng Zhīxiáng's wife
was Zhuāngzōng's paternal cousin.
Lǐ Yán, the Kèshěngshǐ and Sìzhōu Fángyùshǐ.
Zhíguān Fēnjì says: Liáng had Kèshěngshǐ,
which Sòng inherited,

in charge of tributes from all directions, foreign nations' tributary missions, visits of regional governors, bestowing wine, food, and provisions, as well as gifts for prime ministers, close retainers, commanders of the imperial army, and return edicts for gifts from various prefectures' tribute envoys.
Lǐ Yán merely held the title of Sìzhōu Fángyùshǐ,
and Sìzhōu at the time belonged to Wú.
He would surely be able to control Zhīxiáng.
On a Jǐyǒu day,
Yán was appointed Xīchuān Dūjiān,
and Zhū Hóngzhāo of Tàiyuán, the Wénsīshǐ, was appointed Dōngchuān Fùshǐ.
Wénsīshǐ
managed the Wénsī Yuàn,
which Sòng used as a rank for officials of the western bureau,
to place military officers.
He said to Yán:
"Your earlier plan to destroy Shǔ
is recorded in the 273rd scroll, Zhuāngzōng Tóngguāng second year.
You must repay the people of Shǔ with your life."
This sets the stage for Lǐ Yán's death at the hands of Mèng Zhīxiáng.
61 According to the old system,
the Lìbù (Ministry of Personnel) would issue 'gàoshēn' (official appointments),
but first demanded that the recipient pay for the vermilion glue, silk, and scroll axis.
Sòng Bái said: Traditionally,
for those such as enfeoffed princes, imperial consorts, prime ministers, Hanlin academicians, Zhongshu sherén, and Jìedù, Guānchá, Tuánliàn, and Fángyù envoys of various circuits,
later, the Zhōngshū Shě (Central Secretariat)
would affix an official announcement onto a plain silk scroll axis,
send it down to the responsible department for writing,
and after stamping and signing,
it would be submitted for imperial bestowal.
For civil and military officials of both ranks, officials of various circuits, and recommended generals and officers,
after an imperial edict was issued,
they all had to pay for the vermilion glue, silk, and paper at their respective circuit's Jìnzòuyuàn (Memorial Submission Office) or personally at the responsible department,
to request the issuance.
Lù Yóu said: Jiāng Línjǐ's Jiāyòu Zázhì states that in the Táng dynasty, 'gàoshēn' were initially made of paper,
during Emperor Sùzōng's reign, silk was used,
and after Zhēnyuán, only绫 (damask silk) was used.
While I was in Chéngdū, I saw Zhōu Shìzōng's appointment of Liú Rénshàn as Shìzhōng, which was made of paper.
It was with the son of Jīn Yànhēng, the Shàngshū.
The poor would only receive 'chìdié' (imperial diplomas),
often not taking the 'gàoshēn'.
Receiving 'chìdié' was for verification of their service,
merely to secure temporary emoluments and benefits.
As for 'gàoshēn',
without the money, they could not obtain it.
In the Jiǎxū year,
Lìbù Shìláng Liú Yuè submitted a memorial, saying:
"The 'gàoshēn' contains words of commendation, censure, and admonition;
these are the phrases issued by the Zhōngshū Shě.
The edict designated 'bān chéng, láng, gěi, jiàn' (classified as Assistant, Director, Grand Councilor, and Remonstrator).
'Chéng' and 'láng'
refer to the Zǔoyòu Chéng of the Shàngshū Shě and the Directors of the twenty-four bureaus.
'Gěi' refers to the Gěishìzhōng.
'Jiàn' refers to the Jiànyì Dàfū.
They should be granted 'gàoshēn'."
Afterwards, the presiding officials deliberated,
believing that the vermilion glue, silk, and scroll axis
incurred little expense,
and since the court granted official salaries,
why begrudge such a small cost!
"Shòu" (receive)
should be
"shòu" (bestow).
Ōu Shǐ said: Traditionally,
'gàoshēn' for Lìbù officials were issued only after payment for the vermilion glue, silk, and scroll axis,
though those of high rank were granted them.
The poor, unable to pay,
often received only 'chìdié' without 'gàoshēn'.
During the chaos of the Five Dynasties,
this became common practice,
and lower-ranking officials were no longer issued 'gàoshēn'.
The Zhōngshū Shě merely recorded the official pronouncements and compiled them into 'chìjiǎ' (imperial edict registers).
Liú Yuè proposed,
stating that
"the official pronouncements either acknowledge one's talent,
or commend one's accomplishments,
or impart training and admonition;
yet those who receive appointments, not being issued 'gàoshēn',
remain unaware of the reasons for their appointment,
which is contrary to the intent of the imperial pronouncements and edicts.
I request that all be granted them."
From this, all officials were granted 'gàoshēn',
starting with Yuè.
"All who were appointed to office no longer had to pay,
and were all granted 'gàoshēn'."
At that time,
besides the regularly appointed officials,
other probationary titles and assigned ranks were merely to encourage and inspire generals and officers in the army.
"Probationary title"
means "probationary (such and such) official of (such and such) rank,"
all of which were included in the titles.
"Assigned rank"
means assigning titles such as generals and commanders of various ranks.
The number of appointments gradually increased,
extending even to soldiers in the army,
and clerks of state and garrison administrations,
all of whom received the silver-blue rank and censorate titles.
The 'gàoshēn' issued annually numbered in the tens of thousands.
The historian, due to the 'gàoshēn' text,
commented on the excessive appointments at the time.
62 Mǐn King Yán Hàn scorned and abandoned his brothers.
Scarcely a month after inheriting the throne, he dispatched his brother Yán Jūn to be Prefect of Quánzhōu.
Yán Hàn took many women from the populace to fill his harem,
and the selection never ceased.
Yán Jūn submitted a strongly worded remonstrance,
which angered Yán Hàn,
leading to a rift between them.
His adoptive father Shěn Zhī's adopted son, Yán Bǐng, was Prefect of Jiànzhōu.
Yán Bǐng was originally a son of the Zhōu family,
adopted by Wáng Shěnzhī as his son.
Yán Bǐng's reply was disrespectful,
also creating a rift.
In the twelfth month,
Yán Bǐng and Yán Jūn combined their forces to attack Fúzhōu.
Yán Bǐng, traveling downstream, arrived first.
From Jiànxī, he traveled downstream eastward to Fúzhōu.
The water route, winding for several hundred li,
had swift currents,
allowing a light boat to depart in the morning and arrive in the evening.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Jiànzhōu is 520 li southeast of Fúzhōu,
presumably referring to the land route.
The army was defeated,
and Táo committed suicide.
That night,
Yán Bǐng led over a hundred brave men to the west gate,
scaled the city wall,
seized the gatekeepers,
and broke into the armory to take weapons.
Upon reaching the sleeping chambers,
Yán Hàn was alarmed and hid in another room.
On the morning of Xīnmǎo,
Yán Bǐng seized him,
exposed his crimes,
and also accused Yán Hàn and his wife Cuī Shì of jointly murdering the late king,
slandering him with the crime of regicide and parricide.
He was beheaded outside Zǐchén Mén.
The Táng capital, Cháng'ān,
had Zǐchén Diàn and Zǐchén Mén within the palace.
The Mǐn people merely usurped these names.
When Yán Jūn reached the south of the city,
Yán Bǐng opened the gate to admit him,
and supported Yán Jūn as the Wēiwǔ Liúhòu.
Wáng Yánjūn
was Shěnzhī's second son.
63 On Guǐsì,
Lú Wénjìn was appointed Yìchéng Jìedùshǐ and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
64 On Gēngzǐ,
the imperial prince Cóngróng was appointed Tiānxíong Jìedùshǐ and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
65 Zhào Jìliáng and others transported ten 'yì' of gold and silk from Shǔ to Luòyáng.
Poem: Wàn, yì, and zǐ.
Explanation: Ten thousand 'yì' is called 'zhào'.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: The statement "ten thousand 'yì' is called 'zhào'"
depends on the method of calculation.
The number 'yì' has two methods, small and large.
The small method uses ten as the increment: ten 'wàn' is 'yì',
and ten 'yì' is 'zhào'.
The large method uses 'wàn' as the increment: counting 'wàn' to 'wàn' makes 'yì',
so 'wàn wàn' is 'yì',
and then counting 'yì' to 'wàn yì' makes 'zhào'.
Therefore, the commentary on the 'Shī Sòng' by the Máo family says
that counting 'wàn' to 'wàn' is 'yì',
and counting 'yì' to 'yì' is 'zǐ'.
'Zhào' is between 'yì' and 'zǐ',
this is the large number method.
The 'Wèi Fēng' criticized the corrupt officials in power:
"How can you take three hundred 'yì' of grain!"
The state of Wèi was small,
so the amount should not have been excessive,
thus it is stated using the small number method,
hence "ten 'wàn' is 'yì'."
Now, Zhào Jìliáng transported ten 'yì' of gold and silk.
If calculated by the small 'yì', it would only be one million.
How could that relieve the court's shortage?
If calculated by the large 'yì',
then it would be one billion.
It is unknown which is correct.
They relied on this to alleviate the situation.
66 In this year,
Wúyuè King Qián Liú, seeing the chaos in the central plains
and the disruption of imperial commands,
changed his era name to Bǎozhèng.
Later, when communication with the central plains resumed,
he concealed this and did not mention it.
1 In spring,
first month,
on Guǐchǒu (the first day of the month),
the Emperor changed his name to Dǎn.
2 Mèng Zhīxiáng, hearing that Lǐ Yán was coming to supervise his army,
disliked it.
Someone suggested submitting a memorial to stop him,
but Zhīxiáng said:
"Why must it be so?"
(meaning, why must it be like this?)
He sent officials to Mián and Jiàn to welcome him.
Mián and Jiàn are names of two prefectures.
Zhīxiáng stated that he had previously received a secret imperial edict granting him discretion to act as he saw fit.
(Mèng Zhīxiáng said he had previously received a secret imperial edict from Emperor Zhuāngzōng).
On Rénxū,
Lǐ Jìngzhōu, the Deputy Jìedùshǐ of Xīchuān and Commander-in-Chief of the Inner and Outer Infantry and Cavalry, was appointed Liúhòu of Suìzhōu,
replacing Lǐ Shàowén.
This was then reported to the court.
Yán first sent an envoy to Chéngdū.
Zhīxiáng considered that he had old favors with Yán.
(Mèng Zhīxiáng saved Lǐ Yán's life, as seen in volume 268, Liáng Jūnwáng Gānhuà second year).
So he grandly displayed his armor and weapons to him,
but Yán paid no attention.
3 Ān Zhònghuǐ, because Kǒng Xún had served in the palace for a short time,
believed he was familiar with precedents and practices,
and knew the abilities of court officials,
so he often listened to his advice.
Kǒng Xún had served in Liáng Tàizǔ's tent for a short time,
and at the end of the Táng dynasty, he successively held positions in the Xuānhuī and Shūmì Yuan.
Therefore, Ān Zhònghuǐ believed he was familiar with precedents and knew people.
少 (shào),
read as 'shī zhào' (詩照).
諳 (ān),
read as 'wū hán' (烏含).
行 (xíng),
read as 'xià mèng' (下孟).
See last year.
Xún did not want to employ people from Héběi.
Kǒng Xún had grown up in Hénán from a young age,
hence he did not want to employ people from Héběi.
Zhèng Yù
also recommended Cén Yù, the Grand Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
Rèn Yuán wanted to employ Lǐ Qí, the Censor-in-Chief.
Zhèng Yù had always disliked Lǐ Qí,
so Xún strongly tried to dissuade him,
saying to Zhònghuǐ:
"Lǐ Qí is not without literary talent,
but he is not incorruptible.
If a Chancellor is merely upright and possesses a dignified bearing,
that is sufficient to serve as a model for many scholars."
Another day, the matter was discussed before the Emperor.
The Emperor asked who could be Chancellor.
Zhònghuǐ replied with Xié.

Wáng Yánjūn, the Retained Commissioner of Wēiwǔ, was appointed Jìedùshǐ of that circuit,
and King of Lángyé.
26 Kǒng Xún reached Jiānglíng.
Unable to conquer it,
he sent someone into the city to persuade Gāo Jìxīng;
Jìxīng was disrespectful.
On the day Bǐngyín,
an envoy was sent to bestow ten thousand sets of summer clothing upon the Húnán Mobile Army.
On the day Dīngmǎo,
another envoy was sent to bestow a saddled horse and a jade belt upon Chǔ Wáng Yīn,
urging him to supply provisions to the mobile army,
but ultimately, nothing was obtained.
Húnán and Jīngnán were interdependent like the lips and teeth.
Although Chǔ people were heavily rewarded to urge them to supply the army,
they ultimately did not obey the imperial edict.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
an edict ordered Liú Xùn and others to withdraw their troops.
27 Chǔ Wáng Yīn sent his Central Army Commissioner (zhōngjūnshǐ) Shǐ Guāngxiàn to present tribute.
The Emperor bestowed ten fine horses
and two beautiful women upon him.
Passing through Jiānglíng,
Gāo Jìxīng seized Guāngxiàn and took the gifts,
and furthermore requested to attach his entire domain to Wú.
Xú Wēn said:
"Those who govern a nation should focus on practical results and discard empty titles.
The Gāo clan has served Táng for a long time.
Since Táng destroyed Liáng,
the Gāo clan immediately served Táng.
According to the Old Book of Tang's Geography section: Luòyáng to Jiānglíng is 1,315 lǐ.
It is very difficult for us to use a naval fleet to sail upstream and rescue them.
If one's vassal cannot be rescued,
causing them to be in danger and perish,
how can one not feel ashamed!"
So he accepted their tribute items,
declined their offer to become a vassal,
and allowed them to attach themselves to Táng.
Historians say Xú Wēn was capable of preserving his own state
and did not pursue distant strategies.
28 Rèn Yuán was of a rigid and upright character,
and also relied on his old acquaintance with the Emperor.
Rèn Yuán and the Emperor had served Zhuāngzōng together,
and he had also brought back all the Shǔ expeditionary forces to the Emperor.
Many powerful favorites resented him.
According to the old system,
travel permits were issued by the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù).
According to the old Táng system, envoys traveling to the four directions
were all given permits by the Hùbù.
He requested that they be issued from the palace,
so that the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmìyuàn) could exclusively handle the matter.
They went back and forth several times, with increasingly harsh tones.
When the Emperor retired from court,
a palace maid asked the Emperor:
"Who was that arguing with Zhònghuǐ just now?"
Chángyǔ,
jìnfāng wéishì.
"The prime minister."
The palace maid said:
"I was in the palace in Cháng'ān,"
This was a Táng palace maid,
experienced in matters.
"He must have disrespected Your Majesty."
The Emperor became even more displeased.
Táng Míngzōng, having risen from the ranks to become Emperor,
often suspected prime ministers of slighting him.
The deaths of Dòulú Gé and Wéi Yuè,
he still said they brought it upon themselves.
However, to dismiss Rèn Yuán on this account,
and ultimately put him to death,
was a great mistake.
Yuán then requested to be relieved of his duties as Commissioner of Three Departments (Sānsī).
This was Ān Zhònghuǐ's prelude to slandering and killing Rèn Yuán.
During the Five Dynasties, the Commissioner and Deputy Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmìyuàn Dūchéngzhǐ, Fùchéngzhǐ) were established,
filled by generals of various guards.
Quánpàn refers to
the acting Commissioner of Three Departments.
He was from Wèizhōu.
29 Sixth month,
on the day Gēngchén,
the Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (tàizǐ jiànshì) Wēn Niǎn requested the establishment of a Crown Prince.
30 On the day Bǐngxū,
Rèn Yuán, Menxià Shìláng and Tóngpíngzhāngshì,
was dismissed and appointed Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince (tàizǐ shǎobǎo).
31 On the day Jǐchǒu,
Zhāng Yánlǎng, the Commissioner of the Northern Bureau of Privy Affairs (Xuānhuī Běiyuànshǐ), was appointed acting Commissioner of Three Departments (Sānsī).
On the *rénchén* day,
Liú Xùn was demoted to the Inspector of Tánzhōu.
This was because he had achieved no merit in the campaign against Jīngnán.
Tánzhōu belonged to Mìyún Commandery,
and was named after the ancient county of Bái Tán.
On the *bǐngshēn* day,
Mǎ Yīn, Prince of Chǔ, was enfeoffed as King of the State of Chǔ.
Xīfāng Yè defeated the Jīngnán navy in the gorges,
and recaptured the three prefectures of Kuí, Zhōng, and Wàn.
Punctuation by Dèng Guǎngmíng, collated by Niè Chóngqí
Sīmǎ Guāng
Compiled by Imperial Edict
Later Táng
Tiānchéng second year
(year of *dīnghài*, 927)
1. In autumn,
seventh month,
Wáng Yànqiú, Jiedushi of Guīdé, was appointed Deputy Commander of the Northern Front.
As Wū Zhèn had died,
Wáng Yànqiú replaced him.
According to Xuē Shǐ,
on the *jiǎchén* day of the seventh month of this year, an edict stated:
"In this dynasty, imperial princes remotely holding regional governorships
have had deputy commanders managing the affairs of the Jiedushi,
long unchanged.
Henceforth, for Xīchuān and Dōngchuān, the title of deputy commander shall be dropped,
and only the title of Jiedushi shall be used."
Subsequently, all regional governors were formally appointed as Jiedushi.
2. On the *bǐngyín* day,
Kuízhōu was elevated to Níngjiāng Army,
and Xīfāng Yè was made its Jiedushi.
This was a reward for defeating Gāo Jìxīng's army
and recapturing Kuí, Zhōng, and Wàn.
Shǔ had called Kuízhōu Zhènjiāng Army;
it was now changed to Níngjiāng Army.
3. On the *guǐsì* day,
Dòulú Gé and Wéi Shuō were blamed for ceding the three prefectures of Kuí, Zhōng, and Wàn to Gāo Jìxīng.
In the first year, these three prefectures were given to Jìxīng,
and Gé and Shuō were still chancellors,
so they were now charged with this crime.
4. Duàn Níng was exiled to Liáozhōu,
Wēn Tāo to Dézhōu,
and Liú Xùn to Púzhōu.
Since the late Táng,
those exiled or demoted rarely reached their designated locations.
Liáo, Dé, and Pú were all within Táng territory,
and these three individuals were all made to reach their places of exile.
5. Rèn Yuán requested to retire and reside in Cízhōu;
this was granted.
6. In the eighth month,
on the first day, *jǐmǎo*,
there was a solar eclipse.
7. When the envoy for the enfeoffment ceremony arrived in Chángshā,
Mǎ Yīn, Prince of Chǔ, established his state.
Mǎ Yīn, Prince of Chǔ, was enfeoffed as King of the state in the sixth month of this year, as mentioned in the previous volume.
He appointed various officials,
all like those of the Son of Heaven,
or with slight modifications to their names:
to show he dared not emulate the imperial court.
*Gēng* (更) is pronounced *gōngxíng* (工行) fan.
The *Zhī Zhìgào* (知制誥) was called *Zhī Cízhì* (知辭制),
the Privy Council was called *Zuǒyòu Jīyàosī* (左右機要司),
inferiors addressed him as *Diànxià* (殿下),
and decrees were called *jiào* (教).
Yáo Yànzhāng was appointed Left Chancellor,
Xǔ Déxūn as Right Chancellor,
Lǐ Duó as Situ,
Cuī Yǐng as Sikong,
Tuòbá Héng as Púyè,
and Zhāng Yányáo and Zhāng Yíng as heads of the Jīyàosī.
The one Mǎ Yīn relied upon to establish his state was Gāo Yù,
but when the state was founded and officials appointed,
Yù was not included.
Why?
Could it be that Mǎ Yīn's sons already harbored jealousy towards Yù?
Only the Jiedushi of Láng and Guì were appointed first and then sought orders.
Láng was Wǔpíng Army,
Guì was Jìngjiāng Army,
both belonging to Chǔ at the time.
They were renamed to avoid Mǎ Yīn's father's tabooed name.
8. In the ninth month,
the Emperor said to Ān Chónghuì:
"Zhòngróng's entourage falsely transmits my edicts,
ordering people not to associate with scholars,
fearing it might weaken their resolve.
I consider Zhòngróng young to oversee a great region;
in the third month of this year, Zhòngróng was stationed in Yèdū,
as seen in the previous volume.
*Shào* (少) is pronounced *shīzhào* (詩照) fan.
Now, the words of these treacherous people are like this!"
He wanted to execute them;
Chónghuì requested only a strict warning.
Ān Chónghuì was not a scholar,
so he treated the crime of the speakers leniently.
Did he not consider that falsely transmitting imperial edicts
is a crime with established national penalties?
9. Lǐ Yànchāo, Commissioner of Běidū, requested to restore his original surname, Fú;
this was granted.
Yànchāo was
Lǐ Cúnshěn's son;
Cúnshěn's original surname was Fú.
10. On the *bǐngyín* day,
Kǒng Xún, Privy Council commissioner, was concurrently appointed Eastern Capital Commissioner.
The Emperor intended to make an eastern tour
and sent Kǒng Xún to stay in Luòyáng.
In the third year of Zhuāngzōng's Tóngguāng reign,
Luòyáng was again made the Eastern Capital.
11. On the *rénshēn* day,
the Qìdān came to request renewed friendly relations,
and an envoy was dispatched in response.
12. In winter,
tenth month,
on the *yǐyǒu* day,
the Emperor departed Luòyáng,
heading for Biànzhōu;
on the *dīnghài* day,
he reached Xíngyáng.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Xíngyáng County is sixty *lǐ* west of Zhèngzhōu,
and one hundred forty *lǐ* east to Dàliáng.
Folk rumors circulated that the Emperor intended to personally attack Wú,
and also that he wanted to control the eastern vassals.
Zhū Shǒuyīn, Jiedushi of Xuānwǔ and acting Grand Imperial Secretary, became suspicious and fearful.
His aide, Sūn Shèng from Gāomì, advised Shǒuyīn to rebel.
Gāomì was
an ancient county in the Hàn dynasty,
abolished during the Suí unrest,
and re-established in the third year of Táng Wǔdé in Yìchéngbǎo.
In the sixth year, it was moved to the former Yí'ān city,
which was the ancient county of Gāomì,
belonging to Mìzhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: It is one hundred twenty *lǐ* northeast of the prefecture.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Jiāngnán Lù* writes
"Sūn Jì."
We follow Wáng Pǔ's *Zhōu Shìzōng Shílù*.
*Shèng* (晟) is pronounced *chéngzhèng* (承正) fan.
The Emperor sent Fàn Yánguāng, Director of the Privy Council, to convey his message.
Yánguāng said:
"If we do not attack early,
Biànchéng will be fortified;
I request five hundred cavalry to accompany me."
The Emperor agreed.
Yánguāng departed at dusk,
traveled two hundred *lǐ* before dawn,
reached the foot of Dàliáng city,
and engaged the people of Biàn,
who were greatly astonished.
On the *wùzǐ* day,
the Emperor arrived at Jīngshuǐ.
Jīngshuǐ is east of Xíngyáng
and west of Suǒshuǐ.
Since the Liáng dynasty,
there had been the Imperial Guard Infantry, Imperial Guard Cavalry, and Imperial Guard Foot Army.
Someone said to Ān Chónghuì:
"Those who have lost their positions and are outside,
while the rebels are not yet defeated,
might cause trouble.
It is better to eliminate them."
Chónghuì agreed,
and memorialized to send an envoy to grant Rèn Yuán death.
Rèn Yuán had been dismissed as chancellor in the sixth month of this year, as seen in the previous volume.
"Rèn Yuán is a man of integrity;
how could he rebel!
For you to inflict punishment so indiscriminately,
how can you assist the state!"
When the envoy arrived in Cízhōu,
Yuán gathered his family for a banquet,
and then died,
his spirit undaunted.
13. On the *jǐchǒu* day,
the Emperor arrived at Dàliáng,
attacking from four sides.
Many officials and common people lowered themselves from the city walls and surrendered.
Shǒuyīn knew the situation was hopeless,
killed all his family,
stretched out his neck, and ordered his attendants to behead him.
Those on the city walls, seeing the imperial carriage,
led each other in opening the gates to surrender.
Sūn Shèng fled to Wú,
and Xú Zhīgào treated him as a guest.
This laid the groundwork for Sūn Shèng's loyal service in Jiāngnán.
14. On the *wùxū* day,
an edict pardoned outstanding debts of nearly two million *mín* managed by the Three Departments.
15. On the *xīnchǒu* day,

Xú Wēn, Grand Chancellor of Wú, Supreme Commander of all armies domestic and foreign, Grand Commander of all circuits, Jiedushi of Zhènhǎi and Níngguó, and concurrently Grand Secretariat of the Eastern Sea King, died.
Initially,

Wēn Zǐ's xíngjūn sīmǎ (Acting Army Commander), Zhōngyì Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of Zhōngyì), and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (Chancellor with the same authority as a Pingzhangshi) Zhīxún believed that his elder brother Zhīgào was not the son of the Xú clan.
Xú Wēn adopted Zhīgào as his son.
See volume 260, Emperor Zhāozōng of Táng, Qiánníng 2nd year.
Wēn said:
