"None of you are as good."
Yán Kěqiú and Xíngjūn Fùshǐ (Acting Deputy Army Commander) Xú Jiè repeatedly urged Wēn to replace Zhīgào with Zhīxún.
Xú Zhīgào, concerning Yán Kěqiú,
bound him through marriage,
but Kěqiú's heart was not changed by it.
At Xú Wēn's gate,
those loyal to their duties
were only Yán Kěqiú and Chén Yànqiān.
He could not bear to do it.
Lady Chén said:
"Zhīgào was raised by our family when we were poor and humble."
Lady Chén
was Xú Wēn's wife,
and she treated Zhīgào as her own son.
Kěqiú and others spoke ceaselessly.
Wēn wanted to lead the various fānzhèn (military governorships) to the imperial court,
and urged the King of Wú to declare himself emperor.
Just as he was about to depart,
he fell ill,
and so he dispatched Zhīxún to present a memorial urging accession to the throne,
and consequently kept him to replace Zhīgào in governing.
Zhīgào drafted a memorial requesting the Jiédùshǐ of Hóngzhōu,
intending to submit it at dawn.
That evening,
news of Wēn's death arrived,
so he stopped.
History states that Xú Zhīgào's acquisition of the Wú state's government
also had fate at play;
the undertaking of usurping Wú began from this point.
This laid the groundwork for the incompatibility between Zhīgào and Zhīxún.
His posthumous title was Zhōngwǔ.
16 Zhāng Jūn, the Jiédùshǐ of Shānnán Xīdào, had been ill for a long time.
His generals and aides requested an audience,
but he refused.
The Fùshǐ (Deputy Commander) Fú Yànlín and others suspected he was already dead,
fearing treason from those around him.
They requested to temporarily exchange the tally and seal.
Jūn became angry,
arrested Yànlín and the Pànguān (Judge) Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ (Commander-in-Chief), and imprisoned them,
falsely accusing them of rebellion.
An imperial edict ordered Yànlín and the others to be brought to the capital.
An investigation found no evidence,
so they were released.
Observing the affairs of Kěhóng and Zhāng Jūn,
the emperor's temple name of Míng
was not without reason.
In Tóngguāng 3rd year of Zhuāngzōng,
Cháng'ān was again designated the Western Capital.
17 Guǐmǎo,
Shí Jìngtáng, the Jiédùshǐ of Bǎoyì, was appointed Jiédùshǐ of Xuānwǔ.
Zhū Shǒuyīn rebelled and died,
and Shí Jìngtáng was appointed to replace him.
18 In the 11th month,
Gēngxū,
the King of Wú ascended the imperial throne,
posthumously honoring King Xiàowǔ as Emperor Wǔ,
King Jǐng as Emperor Jǐng,
and King Xuān as Emperor Xuān.
King Xiàowǔ
was Hángmì, King Zhōngwǔ;
King Jǐng
was Wò, King Wēi;
and King Xuān
was Lóngyǎn.
19 Ān Chónghuǐ discussed attacking Wú.
Ān Chónghuǐ wanted to take advantage of Xú Wēn's death to attack Wú,
and also question its crime of claiming the imperial title.
Attacking another country when one's own foundation is unstable is a lesson to be learned from Zhuāngzōng's overturned chariot;
therefore, he was not permitted.
20 Jiǎzǐ,
Wú granted a great amnesty,
and changed its era name to Qiánzhēn.
Bǐngzǐ,
the Wú ruler honored the Grand Lady Wáng as Empress Dowager,
and appointed Xú Zhīxún as Zhū Dào Fù Dūtǒng (Deputy Commander-in-Chief of All Circuits), Zhènhǎi Níngguó Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of Zhènhǎi and Níngguó) concurrently Shìzhōng (Grand Councillor),
as if to make him succeed Xú Wēn's offices and titles.
In reality, all great power within and outside the Wú state reverted to Xú Zhīgào.
21 In the 12th month,
Wùyín shuò (first day of the month),
Mèng Zhīxiáng mobilized 200,000 commoners for labor to repair the city of Chéngdū.
22 The Wú ruler enfeoffed his elder brother Lújiāng Gōng Méng as King of Chángshān,
his younger brother Póyáng Gōng Chè as King of Píngyuán,
and his nephew Nánchāng Gōng Gǒng as King of Jiàn'ān.
23 Initially,
the physiognomist Zhōu Xuánbào from Jìnyáng
once said that the emperor's nobility was beyond words.
When the emperor ascended the throne,
he wanted to summon him to the court.
Zhào Fèng said:
"Xuánbào said Your Majesty would become the Son of Heaven,
and this has now come true.
There is no need for further inquiry.
If he is kept in the capital,
then frivolous, reckless, and dangerous people will surely flock to his door,
scrambling to ask about good and ill fortune.
Since ancient times, many soothsayers' false predictions have led to the extermination of people's clans.
This is not the way to pacify the state."
History states that Zhào Fèng showed discernment.
He was merely given generous gifts of gold and silk.
24 Mǎ Gǎo, a Zhōngshū Shèrén (Secretary of the Imperial Secretariat),
requested to follow the precedent of Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn,
establishing separate ancestral temples for the imperial ancestors outside the Seven Temples.
See volume 41, Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn, Jiànwǔ 3rd year.
Called 'Huáng' (August) but not 'Dì' (Emperor).
Xiàodé Huáng seen in volume 50, Emperor Ān of Hàn, Jiànguāng 1st year;
Xiàorén Huáng seen in volume 56, Emperor Líng, Jiànníng 1st year.
All officials then cited the examples of Démíng, Xuányuán, and Xīngshèng Huángdì,
all of whom had temples established in the capital.
Táng honored Gāoyáo as Démíng Huángdì,
Lǎozǐ as Xuányuán Huángdì,
and the Martial-Enlightened King of Liáng as Xīngshèng Huángdì.
Lì (example),
at that time pronounced shì.
From his great-great-grandparents downwards, all were posthumously honored as Huángdì and Huánghòu,
and their tombs were called líng.
Wǔdài Huìyào states: The emperor posthumously honored his great-great-grandfather Yù as Xiàogōng Huángdì,
with the temple name Huìzǔ,
and his陵 (mausoleum) as Shùnlíng;
his great-great-grandmother Lady Cuī as Zhāo Huánghòu.
His great-grandfather Jiào as Xiàozhì Huángdì,
with the temple name Yìzǔ,
and his líng as Yǎnlíng;
his great-grandmother Lady Zhāng as Shùn Huánghòu.
His grandfather Yǎn as Xiàojìng Huángdì,
with the temple name Lièzǔ,
and his líng as Yìlíng;
his grandmother Lady Hé as Mù Huánghòu.
His father Ní as Xiàochéng Huángdì,
with the temple name Dézǔ,
and his líng as Qìnglíng.
Ōu Shǐ states: His great-great-grandmother Lady Liú;
his great-grandfather's taboo name was Áo;
his father Xiàochéng;
his mother Lady Liú was posthumously titled Yì Huánghòu.
All four mausoleums are in Jīnchéng County, Yìngzhōu.
According to this, the emperor's ancestors were originally barbarians,
having no surnames,
and their names must have been fabricated by the officials of that time.
25 The Hàn ruler went to Kāngzhōu.
Jiǔyù Zhì: From Guǎngzhōu south to Kāngzhōu is 190 lǐ.
26 That year,
a dǒu of grain along the border of Yù and Dài cost no more than ten cash.
1 Spring,
1st month,
Dīngsì,
the Wú ruler enfeoffed his son Lián as King of Jiāngdū,
Lín as King of Jiāngxià,
Qiú as King of Yíchūn,
and Xuāndì's son Lújiāng Gōng Bīn as King of Nányáng.
2 Máo Zhāng, the Jiédùshǐ of Zhāoyì, was arrogant and presumptuous.
He often wore a reddish-brown robe.
A reddish-brown robe
was worn by the Son of Heaven.
Zhě,
pronunciation zhě.
When his attendants advised him against it,
he would cut open their hearts to see.
The emperor heard of this,
and summoned him to be Yòu Jīnwú Wèi Shàngjiāngjūn (General-in-Chief of the Right Armored Guard).
Máo Zhāng was summoned from Bīnzhōu for arrogance and presumption,
and behaved similarly again when in Lùzhōu,
so calling him rebellious is appropriate.
However, one imperial edict was enough to summon him, and he readily entered the guard,
indicating that he was obstinate, arrogant, and tyrannical,
but fundamentally had no ulterior motives,
not knowing that presuming on imperial prerogatives was wrong.
Nevertheless, it also shows that Míngzōng was able to tolerate him.
3 Qìdān captured Píngzhōu.
In the winter of the 1st year, Lú Wénjìn defected,
and Táng acquired Píngzhōu,
but it was again captured by Qìdān at this time.
4 2nd month,
Dīngchǒu shuò,
there was a solar eclipse.
5 The emperor was about to go to Yèdū.
At that time, the families of the imperial guard armies had just moved to Dàliáng,
and upon hearing that they were going to Yèdū again,
they were all displeased,
and murmurs of rumors spread.
The emperor heard of this,
and did not proceed with the journey.
6 Since Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng,
envoys from Wú had been coming and going continuously.
Gēngchén,
an envoy from Wú arrived.
Ān Chónghuǐ believed that Yáng Pǔ dared to treat the imperial court as an equal,
both being established as emperors,
which was treating them as equals.
He refused to accept, and from then on, relations with Wú were severed.
7. Zhāng Jūn arrived at Cháng'ān.
Last year, Zhāng Jūn was transferred to stay and guard Xīdū.
This was the Emperor's intention.
He was appointed as the Left Commander-in-Chief of the Guards.
8. On the day of Rénchén,
Níngjiāng Jiédùshǐ Xīfāng Yè attacked and captured Guīzhōu;
not long after,
Jīngnán recaptured it.
Guīzhōu
was under the jurisdiction of Gāo Jìxīng.
Jiǔyù Zhì: From Kuízhōu east to Guīzhōu is three hundred and thirty *lǐ*.
*Jǐ*,
read *jū qǐ*.
*Fù*,
read *fú yòu*;
the following "復" (fù) should be read the same.
9. The Privy Councilor (*Shūmìshǐ*) and Grand Councilor (*Tóng Píngzhāngshì*) Kǒng Xún
was cunning and sycophantic,
and Ān Zhònghuì greatly trusted him.
The Emperor wanted to marry Ān Zhònghuì's daughter to a prince,
but Kǒng Xún said to Ān Zhònghuì:
"Your position is close and confidential,
it is not appropriate to again marry a prince."
Ān Zhònghuì declined.
After a long time,
someone said to Ān Zhònghuì:
"Kǒng Xún is good at alienating people;
he should not be kept in a confidential position."
Kǒng Xún learned of this
and secretly sent someone to associate with Wáng Dé,
asking to take his daughter as a concubine;
Wáng Dé requested to marry Kǒng Xún's daughter to Cónghòu,
and the Emperor permitted it.
Wáng Dé was favored by the Emperor,
and his words were always heeded.
Later, he was promoted to *Shū*.
On the day of Yǐwèi,
Kǒng Xún was appointed Grand Councilor (*Tóng Píngzhāngshì*)
and concurrently Chōngwǔ Jiédùshǐ and Resident Commissioner of the Eastern Capital (*Dōngdū Liúshǒu*).
This removed him from his close and confidential posts.
Ān Zhònghuì was strong-willed and stubborn.
Huá Wēnqí, the Qínzhōu Jiédùshǐ, came to court
and requested to remain at the capital.
The Emperor praised him,
as at that time all the military governors were happy to be in their provincial commands and act as they pleased.
Only Huá Wēnqí came to court and requested to stay,
hence the praise.
*Huá*,
read *hù huà*.
He was granted extra money and grain monthly.
Additional money and grain were bestowed beyond his regular salary.
The Emperor said to Ān Zhònghuì:
"Wēnqí is an old acquaintance;
he should be given a significant military command."
Huá Wēnqí had already served as a military governor during the Liáng dynasty,
hence the comment.
*Chǔ*,
read *chāng lǚ*.
Later,
the Emperor repeatedly mentioned it,
and Ān Zhònghuì angrily said:
"I have repeatedly submitted memorials without fault;
only the Privy Councilor can replace me."
The Emperor said:
"That is also acceptable."
Ān Zhònghuì had nothing to say.
Huá Wēnqí's talent was indeed insufficient for a significant command.
Given the harmony between ruler and minister,
Ān Zhònghuì's detailed and clear presentations
should have ensured Míngzōng's full compliance;
but now, the communication between superiors and subordinates could not convey their intentions,
only inciting each other.
This was due to a lack of learning.
He did not go out for several months.
Ān Zhònghuì disliked Wáng Jiànlì, the Chéngdé Jiédùshǐ and Grand Councilor (*Tóng Píngzhāngshì*),
and memorialized that Wáng Jiànlì was colluding with Wáng Dū
and harbored rebellious intentions.
Wáng Jiànlì also memorialized that Ān Zhònghuì wielded excessive power
and requested to come to court to personally explain the situation.
The Emperor summoned him;
upon his arrival,
he stated that Ān Zhònghuì had married into the family of Zhāng Yánlǎng, the Xuānhuī Envoy and Administrator of the Three Bureaus (*Pàn Sānsī*),
forming a powerful faction
and abusing authority.
In the third month,
on the day of Xīnhài,
the Emperor met Ān Zhònghuì,
his expression showing great anger,
and said:
"Today I will give you a commandery to rest in,
and Wáng Jiànlì will replace you.
Zhāng Yánlǎng will also be dismissed to an outer post."
Ān Zhònghuì said:
"I have served Your Majesty for several decades, clearing obstacles;
when Your Majesty ascended the throne,
I filled the vacancy in the privy council.
To "fill the vacancy" (*chéngfá*)
means to take another's place due to their absence.
It means that at that time there was a lack of people,
so I was able to take up the confidential post.
Now, to suddenly cast me out to an outer commandery,
I wish to hear my crime!"
The Emperor rose, displeased.
This section, from Kǒng Xún onwards, speaks of the conflict between Ān Zhònghuì and Kǒng Xún.
From Huá Wēnqí onwards, it speaks of the origin of the discord between the ruler and his minister.
This is because Ān Zhònghuì relied on his old loyalties from the time of the emperor's ascension,
clinging to power and unwilling to retire,
while Míngzōng accumulated many slanders and insinuations,
wishing to distance him but unable to do so,
until the final rupture,
which became irreversible.
Hóngzhāo said:
"Your Majesty has always treated Ān Zhònghuì as your right-hand man.
How can you abandon him for a minor grievance!
I beg you to reconsider."
Zhū Hóngzhāo's words today
indicate that Ān Zhònghuì's favor had not yet waned;
Fèngxiáng's memorial
indicates that Ān Zhònghuì's power had already departed.
The wisdom of small men,
changing with the times,
is indeed fearsome!
The next day,
Wáng Jiànlì took leave to return to his commandery,
and the Emperor said:
"You previously memorialized your wish to come and share my worries;
now, where are you going again!"
At this time, Zhèng Yù, the Menxià Shìláng concurrently Xíngbù Shàngshū and Grand Councilor (*Tóng Píngzhāngshì*), requested to retire.
On the day of Jǐwèi,
Zhèng Yù was made Left Grand Master (*Zuǒ Púyè*) and retired;
on the day of Guǐhài,
Wáng Jiànlì was made Right Grand Master (*Yòu Púyè*) concurrently Zhongshu Shìláng and Grand Councilor (*Tóng Píngzhāngshì*), and Administrator of the Three Bureaus (*Pàn Sānsī*).
10. Mèng Zhīxiáng repeatedly competed with Dǒng Zhāng over salt profits.
In Shǔ, well salt
was found in all areas under the jurisdiction of the Eastern and Western Chuān,
and each wanted to secure it to monopolize the profit,
hence the dispute.
According to the Tang dynasty's prosperous period,
Qióng, Jiā, and Méi had thirteen wells,
administered by the Jiànnán Xīchuān Bureau;
Zǐ, Suí, Mián, Hé, Chāng, Yú, Lú, Zī, Róng, Líng, and Jiǎn had four hundred and sixty wells,
administered by the Jiànnán Dōngchuān Bureau.
The salt profits of Dōngchuān were greater than those of Xīchuān.
Mèng Zhīxiáng was troubled by this,
so he established three salt fields in Hànzhōu and heavily taxed them.
Hànzhōu is located southeast, bordering Dōngchuān,
so three fields were set up to tax salt merchants.
Merchants no longer traveled to Dōngchuān.
*Zhī*,
means "to go".
11. Chǔ Wáng Yīn went to Yuèzhōu
and dispatched the Commander of the Six Armies Yuán Quán,
Deputy Commander Wáng Huán, and Supervisor Mǎ Xīzhān to lead a naval force to attack Jīngnán.
Gāo Jìxīng met them with his own naval force.
Upon reaching Liúlángfú,
there is Liúlángpǔ, a sandy ford in Shíshǒu County, Jiānglíng Prefecture,
where Shǔ Xiānzhǔ married a Wu princess.
*Fú*,
read *fáng lù*.
A swirling current is called *fú*.
At dawn the next day,
the two armies clashed.
Mǎ Xīzhān brought his warships to outflank and strike them,
and Gāo Jìxīng was utterly defeated,
with thousands captured and beheaded.
They advanced and pressed towards Jiānglíng.
Gāo Jìxīng requested peace
and returned Shǐ Guāngxiàn to Chǔ.
Gāo Jìxīng had seized Shǐ Guāngxiàn, as seen in the previous volume's previous year.
Chǔ Wáng Yīn regretted that Wáng Huán did not continue to take Jīngnán.
Wáng Huán said:
"Jiānglíng is situated between the Central Court, Wú, and Shǔ.
The Central Court (*Zhōngcháo*)
refers to the Táng dynasty,
being both in the Central Plains
and the Celestial Court.
It is vulnerable to enemies on four sides,
a 'four-sided battleground'.
During the Sòng dynasty, Zhào Hánwáng advised Emperor Tàizǔ to take Tàiyuán slowly;
his intention was similar.
In every battle, Wáng Huán
personally led his troops,
sharing their hardships;
he always kept needles and medicine at his side.
After battle,
he would summon the wounded before his tent
and personally apply treatment.
The soldiers under Wáng Huán's command congratulated each other, saying:
"We have found a place to die!"
Therefore, wherever they advanced, they achieved success.
History shows that generals who can win the utmost loyalty of their soldiers are victorious.
12 Chǔ [楚] mobilized a large naval force to attack Hàn [漢],
besieging Fēngzhōu [封州].
Sòng Bái [宋白] said: Fēngzhōu [封州] was Guǎngxìn [廣信] County in Cāngwú [蒼梧] Commandery during the Hàn [漢] dynasty.
Liáng [梁] established Liángxìn [梁信] Commandery.
Suí [隋] established Fēngzhōu [封州],
located north of the Fēngshuǐ [豐水] River.
Meeting Dàyǒu [大有],
a turtle plastron for divination,
milfoil stalks for sortilege.
Forty-nine stalks are randomly divided,
their oddness or evenness observed,
three changes complete a yáo [爻],
eighteen changes complete a guà [卦].
The era name was changed to Dàyǒu [大有];
Sū Zhāng [蘇章], the Zǒuyòujiēshǐ [左右街使] (Left and Right Street Commissioner), was ordered to lead three thousand divine crossbows and one hundred warships to relieve Fēngzhōu [封州].
Hàn [漢] capital was Pānyú [番禺],
modeled after Táng [唐] Shàngjīng [上京],
establishing Zǒujiēshǐ [左街使] (Left Street Commissioner) and Yòujiēshǐ [右街使] (Right Street Commissioner).
Jiǔyùzhì [九域志] (Records of the Nine Regions): Guǎngzhōu [廣州] to Fēngzhōu [封州] in the west is six hundred and ten *lǐ*.
Iron cables were sunk into the water,
giant wheels were built on both banks to pull the cables,
a long dike was constructed to conceal them,
and brave warriors were ambushed within the dike.
Zhāng [章] engaged in battle with light boats,
feigning defeat.
The Chǔ [楚] people pursued him,
entering the dike.
The wheels were pulled to raise the cables,
preventing the Chǔ [楚] ships from advancing or retreating.
Powerful crossbows were used to shoot at them from both sides of the water.
The Chǔ [楚] army was utterly defeated,
lifted the siege, and fled.
The Hàn [漢] ruler appointed Zhāng [章] as the Fēngzhōu Tuánliànshǐ [封州團練使] (Military Commissioner of Fēngzhōu).
13 In summer,
in the fourth month,

Cóng Róng [從榮], the Yèdū Liúshǒu [鄴都留守] (Resident Agent of Yèdū), was appointed Hédōng Jiédùshǐ [河東節度使] (Military Commissioner of Hédōng) and Běidū Liúshǒu [北都留守] (Resident Agent of the Northern Capital).
Fēng Yūn [馮贇] of Tàiyuán [太原], the Kèshǐngshǐ [客省使] (Reception Bureau Commissioner), was appointed Deputy Resident Agent.
Yáng Sīquán [楊思權] of Xīnpíng [新平], the Jiāmǎ Zhǐhuīshǐ [夾馬指揮使] (Commander of Cavalry Guards), was appointed Bùjūn Dūzhǐhuīshǐ [步軍都指揮使] (Grand Commander of Infantry) to assist him.
On the *wùyín* [戊寅] day,

Shí Jìngtáng [石敬瑭], the Xuānwǔ Jiédùshǐ [宣武節度使] (Military Commissioner of Xuānwǔ), was appointed Yèdū Liúshǒu [鄴都留守] (Resident Agent of Yèdū) and Tiānxíong Jiédùshǐ [天雄節度使] (Military Commissioner of Tiānxíong),
and given the additional title of Tóng Píngzhāngshì [同平章事] (Chancellor).
Fàn Yánguāng [范延光], the Shūmìshǐ [樞密使] (Commissioner of Military Affairs), was appointed Chéngdé Jiédùshǐ [成德節度使] (Military Commissioner of Chéngdé).
On the *bǐngxū* [丙戌] day,
Ān Chónghuǐ [安重誨], the Shūmìshǐ [樞密使] (Commissioner of Military Affairs), was concurrently appointed Hénán Yǐn [河南尹] (Prefect of Hénán).
Cóng Hòu [從厚], the Hénán Yǐn [河南尹] (Prefect of Hénán), was appointed Xuānwǔ Jiédùshǐ [宣武節度使] (Military Commissioner of Xuānwǔ),
and retained the concurrent post of Pàn Liùjūn Zhūwèishì [判六軍諸衞事] (Supervisor of the Six Armies and Various Guards).
Cóng Hòu [從厚] originally served as Hénán Yǐn [河南尹] with the concurrent post of Pàn Liùjūn Zhūwèishì [判六軍諸衞事].
Now he was transferred to the garrison of Biànzhōu [汴州], but his role as Supervisor of the Six Armies and Various Guards remained as before.

14 Miáo Lín [苗璘], the Yòuxíongwǔjūnshǐ [右雄武軍使] (Right Commander of the Valiant and Martial Army) of Wú [吳], and Wáng Yànzhāng [王彥章], the Jìngjiāng Tǒngjūn [靜江統軍] (Commander of Jìngjiāng), led a naval force of ten thousand men to attack Chǔ [楚]'s Yuèzhōu [岳州].
They reached Jūnshān [君山].
Yuèzhōu [岳州] was governed from Bālíng [巴陵].
Dòngtíng Hú [洞庭湖] is west of Bālíng [巴陵].
Jūnshān [君山] is in Dòngtíng Hú [洞庭湖],
sixty *lǐ* in circumference.
Déxūn [德勳] said:
"The Wú [吳] people are catching us unprepared.
Upon seeing a large army,
they will surely be afraid and flee."
So he secretly deployed troops to Jiǎozǐ Hú [角子湖],
and sent Wáng Huán [王環] to lead three hundred warships by night,
to cut off
the Wú [吳] retreat route.
At dawn,
the Wú [吳] people advanced to Jīngjiāngkǒu [荊江口],
intending to rendezvous with Jīngnán [荊南] troops to attack Yuèzhōu [岳州].
On the *dīnghài* [丁亥] day,
they reached Dàorénjī [道人磯].
Déxūn [德勳] ordered Zhān Xìn [詹信], the Zhànzhào Dūyúhòu [戰棹都虞候] (Grand Commander of Warships), to take three hundred light boats out behind the Wú [吳] army.
Déxūn [德勳] faced them with his main army in front,
attacking from both sides.
The Wú [吳] army was utterly defeated,
and Lín [璘] and Yànzhāng [彥章] were captured and brought back.
15 Initially,
Wáng Dū [王都], the Yìwǔ Jiédùshǐ [義武節度使] (Military Commissioner of Yìwǔ) and concurrent Zhōngshūlìng [中書令] (Director of the Secretariat), had been garrisoned in Yìdìng [易定] for over ten years.
In the first year of Liáng Jūnwáng [梁均王] Lóngdé [龍德],
Wáng Dū [王都] took Dìngzhōu [定州].
By this time, it had been nine years.
All taxes and levies were used to support his own army.
When Ān Chónghuǐ [安重誨] came into power,
he gradually curtailed this practice through regulations.
The Emperor also disliked Dū [都] for usurping his father's position.
Wáng Dū [王都] imprisoned his father Chǔzhí [處直] and usurped his position,
as seen in volume 271, the first year of Later Liáng [後梁] Jūnwáng [均王] Lóngdé [龍德].
(*Note on pronunciation for* 惡: *wūlù fān* [烏路翻].)
The court stationed many troops in the Yōu-Yì [幽易] region,
with generals frequently traveling between Wǎqiáo [瓦橋] and Lú [蘆].
Dū [都] secretly prepared for this,
gradually growing suspicious and hostile.
Dū [都] feared the court would transfer him to another garrison,
and his confidant Hé Zhāoxùn [和昭訓] advised Dū [都] on a strategy for self-preservation.
Dū [都] then sought a marriage alliance with Zhào Déjūn [趙德鈞], the Lúlóng Jiédùshǐ [盧龍節度使] (Military Commissioner of Lúlóng).
He also knew that Wáng Jiànlì [王建立], the Chéngdé Jiédùshǐ [成德節度使] (Military Commissioner of Chéngdé), had a rift with Ān Chónghuǐ [安重誨],
so he sent envoys to establish a brotherhood,
secretly conspiring with him to restore the old system of Hébĕi [河北],
wishing to return to the hereditary rule of the Hébĕi [河北] garrisons of the Táng [唐] dynasty,
not submitting tribute or taxes to the court,
and not accepting conscription from the court.
Dū [都] also sent wax letters to the five commanders of Qīng [青], Xú [徐], Lù [潞], Yì [益], and Zǐ [梓],
to sow discord.
At this time, Huò Yànwēi [霍彥威] of Qīng [青], Fáng Zhīwēn [房知溫] of Xú [徐], Máo Zhāng [毛璋] of Lù [潞], Mèng Zhīxiáng [孟知祥] of Yì [益], and Dǒng Zhāng [董璋] of Zǐ [梓],
were all defiant and difficult to control.
(*Note on pronunciation for* 遺: *wéijì fān* [唯季翻]; *xiàjīn yíd tóng* [下金遺同]. *Note on pronunciation for* 間: *gǔxiàn fān* [古莧翻].)
Yàn Qiú [晏球] did not comply;
so [Dū] sent gold to Yàn Qiú [晏球]'s subordinates,
asking them to plot against him,
but it failed.
On the *guǐsì* [癸巳] day,
Yàn Qiú [晏球] reported Dū [都]'s rebellion,
and an imperial edict ordered Zhāng Yánlǎng [張延朗], the Xuānhuīshǐ [宣徽使] (Commissioner of the Palace Secretariat), to discuss suppressing him with the northern generals.

The northern generals refer to Zhāo Tǎo [招討] (Pacification Commissioner) Wáng Yànqiú [王晏球] and his subordinates garrisoned between Yōu [幽] and Yì [易], and Zhào Déjūn [趙德鈞], the Yōuzhōushuài [幽州帥] (Commander of Yōuzhōu).
16 On the *wùxū* [戊戌] day,
Wú [吳] moved Chángshān Wáng Méng [常山王濛] to Línchuān Wáng [臨川王].
17 On the *gēngzǐ* [庚子] day,
an imperial edict ordered the deprivation of Wáng Dū [王都]'s official titles and ranks.
On the *rényín* [壬寅] day,
Wáng Yànqiú [王晏球] was appointed Běimiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ [北面招討使] (Northern Pacification Commissioner) and acting Governor of Dìngzhōu [定州] (Quánzhī Dìngzhōu Xíngzhōushì [權知定州行州事]).
Ān Shěntōng [安審通], the Hénghǎi Jiédùshǐ [橫海節度使] (Military Commissioner of Hénghǎi), was appointed Deputy Pacification Commissioner.
Zhāng Qiánzhāo [張虔釗], the Zhèngzhōu Fángyùshǐ [鄭州防禦使] (Defense Commissioner of Zhèngzhōu), was appointed Dūjiān [都監] (Supervisor-in-chief).
Troops from various circuits were dispatched to rendezvous and suppress Dìngzhōu [定州].
On the same day,
Yàn Qiú [晏球] attacked Dìngzhōu [定州],
capturing its northern gate city.
"Acting Governor of Dìngzhōu [定州]" means that since Dìngzhōu [定州] city had not yet been taken,
Wáng Yànqiú [王晏球] was to provisionally manage administrative affairs outside the city,
to pacify the people of Dìngzhōu [定州].
This order had not yet been issued,
but Yàn Qiú [晏球]'s troops had already reached the city walls of Dìngzhōu [定州].
Tūnèi [禿餒] was the one who besieged Zhuāngzōng [莊宗], a chieftain among the captives.
(*Note on pronunciation for* 酋: *cíqiū fān* [慈秋翻].)
Tūnèi [禿餒] broke into Dìngzhōu [定州] with ten thousand cavalry.
Yàn Qiú [晏球] retreated to Qǔyáng [曲陽].
Qǔyáng [曲陽] was Hàn [漢]'s Shàngqǔyáng [上曲陽] County.
Suí [隋] renamed it Héngyáng [恆陽].
Táng [唐] in the fifteenth year of Yuánhé [元和] changed its name back to Qǔyáng [曲陽],
to avoid the name of Mùzōng [穆宗].
It belonged to Dìngzhōu [定州].
Jiǔyùzhì [九域志]: The county is sixty *lǐ* west of the prefecture.
Yàn Qiú [晏球] fought him at the foot of Jiāshān [嘉山],
decisively defeating him.
Tūnèi [禿餒] fled back to Dìngzhōu [定州] with two thousand cavalry.
Yàn Qiú [晏球] pursued him to the city gate,
then launched an attack,
capturing its western gate city.
Dìngzhōu [定州] city was strong and could not be taken by assault.
Yàn Qiú [晏球] reinforced and repaired the western gate city to serve as his provisional headquarters.
The provisional headquarters of the Pacification Commissioner and the provisional administration of Dìngzhōu [定州] were established in the western gate city.
The three prefectures were Dìng [定], Qí [祁], and Yì [易].
Wáng Yànqiú [王晏球]'s attack on Dìngzhōu [定州] aimed to wear it down through a prolonged siege.
This was his predetermined strategy.
18 On the *xīnyǒu* [辛酉] day,
Zhào Jìngyí [趙敬怡], the Tiānxíong Jiédù Fùshǐ [天雄節度副使] (Deputy Military Commissioner of Tiānxíong), was appointed Shūmìshǐ [樞密使] (Commissioner of Military Affairs).
19 Wáng Yànqiú heard that the Qìdān had dispatched troops to rescue Dìngzhōu,
and led his grand army towards Wàngdū.
He sent Zhāng Yánlǎng to divide his forces and retreat to defend Xīnlè.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Wàngdū County is sixty lǐ northeast of Dìngzhōu;
Xīnlè County is fifty lǐ southwest of the prefecture.
Zhī,
means to go.
In the early Tóngguāng reign,
the Northern Capital was established in Zhènzhōu.
Zhènzhōu was designated as Zhēndìng Fǔ.
Soon after, the Northern Capital was abolished, but Zhēndìng Fǔ remained.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: From Xīnlè County southwest to Zhēndìng is seventy lǐ.
The Qìdān had already entered Dìngzhōu by another route,
and with Wáng Dū, launched a night attack on Xīnlè,
defeating it
and killing Jiànfēng.
On the day yǐchǒu,
Wáng Yànqiú and Zhāng Yánlǎng met at Xíngtáng.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Xíngtáng County is fifty-five lǐ north of Zhēndìng Fǔ.
On the day bǐngyín,
they reached Qǔyáng.
From Xíngtáng northwest to Qǔyáng is about thirty lǐ.
Wáng Dū gathered all his forces, and with five thousand Qìdān cavalry, totaling over ten thousand men,
ambushed Yànqiú and others at Qǔyáng.
On the day dīngmǎo,
they fought south of the city.
Yànqiú assembled his generals and officers and commanded them, saying:
"Wáng Dū is careless and arrogant,
he can be captured in a single battle.
Today,
gentlemen, is the time to repay the nation.
Put away all bows and arrows,
attack them with short weapons.
Those who look back shall be beheaded!"
Thereupon, the cavalry advanced first,
brandishing clubs and waving swords,
directly charging their formation,
utterly routing them.
Corpses covered the field.
By using short weapons, the officers and soldiers were united in their determination to fight to the death.
By directly charging their formation, the enemy had no time to resist.
The northerners relied on bows and arrows,
but once their formation was breached,
they could not use them.
And where clubs and swords reached,
those not killed were wounded,
which led to their severe defeat.
Chuāi,
is pronounced like "guā fān".
Jiāng,
is pronounced like "jū liáng fān".
Chén,
is read as zhèn.
The remaining forces fled north.
Dū and Tūnèi escaped with only a few cavalry,
barely avoiding capture.
Zhào Déjūn, the Jìedùshǐ of Lúlóng, ambushed the fleeing Qìdān;
hardly any of those who fled north were left.
20 Wú sent envoys to seek peace with Chǔ,
requesting Miáo Lín and Wáng Yànzhāng.
King Yīn of Chǔ returned them,
and sent Xǔ Déxūn to bid them farewell.
Déxūn said to the two men:
"Although the state of Chǔ is small,
old ministers and veteran generals are still present.
I hope the Wú court will not concern itself.
You must wait until the many colts爭皁棧,
and then it can be planned."
At that time, Yīn had many concubines,
there was no distinction between the legitimate and illegitimate,
and his sons were arrogant and extravagant,
hence Déxūn alluded to this.
21 In the sixth month,
on the day xīnsì,
Gāo Jìxīng again requested to submit as a vassal to Wú.
Xú Wēn of Wú debated against accepting Gāo Jìxīng's submission;
refer to the previous year's fifth month in the upper volume.
The emperor ordered King Yīn of Chǔ to attack him.
Yīn sent Xǔ Déxūn to lead troops to attack Jīngnán,
making his son Xīfàn the Supervisor of the Army.
They halted at Shātóu;
halting at Shātóu
meant they were already close to Jiānglíng.
Jìxīng asked to challenge Xīfàn to a decisive battle.
The Deputy Commander Liáo Kuāngqí came out to fight him
and killed him by tearing him apart.
Jìxīng was afraid.
The next day,
he requested peace,
and Déxūn returned.
Kuāngqí was
a native of Gàn.
22 Wáng Yànqiú knew that Dìngzhōu was well-prepared
and not easy to attack quickly.
Zhū Hóngzhāo and Zhāng Qiánzhāo declared that the general was timid and afraid.
There was an imperial edict urging him to attack the city.
Yànqiú had no choice.
On the day yǐwèi,
he attacked it,
killing and wounding three thousand officers and soldiers.
Zhāng Qiánzhāo did not learn from the incident at Dìngzhōu.
Later, he hastily attacked Fèngxiáng,
leading to the ruin of the state
and his own capture as a prisoner.
He greatly erred the altars of Míngzōng.
23 Previously,
an edict had ordered troops from Xīchuān to garrison Kuízhōu
to guard against Gāo Jìxīng.
Xiān,
pronounced like "xī jiàn fān".
After a while,
Zhīxiáng reported:
"The three prefectures of Kuí, Zhōng, and Wàn are pacified.
I request to recall the garrison troops
to save on provisions and transport."
Mèng Zhīxiáng feared that the garrison troops would be retained by Táng,
thereby weakening himself,
so he requested their recall.
Zhīxiáng secretly sent people to entice them.
Zhòngwēi led his troops, beating drums and shouting, to flee back.
The emperor ordered an investigation into their crime,
but Zhīxiáng interceded for them and they were pardoned.
Historians say that Táng's authority and commands were ineffective in Shǔzhōng.
24 Wáng Zōngshòu, the Xíngjūn Sīmǎ of Shǎnzhōu, requested to bury the former ruler of Shǔ, Wáng Yǎn.
Wáng Yǎn died in Cháng'ān;
refer to the first year in volume 274.
Shǎn,
pronounced like "shī rǎn fān".
In the seventh month,
Yǎn was posthumously granted the title of Shùnzhèng Gōng,
and buried with the rites of a feudal lord.
Wáng Zōngshòu was
a commoner from Xǔzhōu.
Wáng Jiàn, seeing he shared the same surname,
adopted him as a son.
He served Wáng Yǎn
and repeatedly offered frank remonstrances,
but Yǎn did not listen,
leading to the fall of the state.
After Yǎn died,
Zōngshòu moved east.
Upon reaching Miǎnchí,
he heard that Zhuāngzōng had been assassinated,
and fled into Xióng'ěr Shān.
At this time, he reappeared,
went to the capital,
and requested to bury Yǎn's relatives.
The emperor praised his loyalty
and appointed him Bǎoyì Xíngjūn Sīmǎ.
He recovered eighteen coffins, including Yǎn's,
and buried them in Sānzhào Village south of Cháng'ān.
25 Ān Shěntōng, the Běimiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ, died.
After "Zhāotǎo"
there should be
the character "Fù"
(Deputy).
26 There was a commoner in Dōngdū who violated the private yeast prohibition.
Kǒng Xún, the Liúshǒu, punished his entire clan.
Someone requested to allow commoners to make yeast
and collect five cash per mu in the autumn tax.
On the day jǐwèi,
an imperial edict approved it.
According to records, in the early Táng dynasty, there was no salt and iron monopoly.
In the third year of Dézōng's Jiànzhōng reign, a monopoly on all wine in the empire was first established.
All brewing was to be done by officials,
with three thousand cash collected per hù (measure),
and even if rice was cheap, it could not be reduced below two thousand.
It was entrusted to prefectures and counties to manage,
and there were varying punishments for diluted or privately brewed wine.
The capital was specifically exempt from the monopoly.
In the sixth year of Yuánhé, the Jīngzhàofǔ reported that the monopoly wine tax, excluding official wine households,
would be uniformly distributed according to the land deeds based on the Two-Tax and Green Sprout systems.
In the sixth year of Huìchāng, an edict stated:
"In the eight circuits of Yángzhōu, a yeast monopoly and official wine shops are to be established
to collect the monopoly wine tax on behalf of the common people,
and also to serve as military funding.
If anyone privately sells wine or establishes private yeast,
the punishment is limited to the individual."
By this time,
because Kǒng Xún had excessively implemented harsh laws,
an edict was issued:
"All households in villages and towns across the Three Capitals, Yèdū, and various circuits, prefectures, and counties,
shall pay five full wén of yeast money per mu on their summer and autumn crops.
The common people are free to make yeast and brew wine for family consumption.
This money shall be collected with the summer and autumn taxes and not converted to other forms.
In the capital and in the wards and markets of various circuit counties and towns, and within the grass markets of customs passes and cities,
all households that annually sell official yeast wine
are now permitted to make their own yeast and brew wine for sale.
All yeast bureaus in various places
are ordered to sell at an eight-tenths price reduction
and are not allowed to request official capital for production."
Qū,
pronounced like "qǔ".
On the 27th, *rénxū*,
the Qìdān again dispatched their chieftain, Tìyǐn, leading seven thousand cavalry to relieve Dìngzhōu.
Wáng Yànqiú met them in battle north of the Táng River
and thoroughly defeated them.
On *jiǎzǐ*,
he pursued them to Yìzhōu.
At that time, continuous rain had caused the waters to swell.
The Qìdān who were captured, beheaded, or drowned by Táng forces
were innumerable.
On the 28th, *wùchén*,
Wáng Yánjūn, the Jìedùshǐ of Wēiwǔ, was made King of Mǐn.
On the 29th, the Qìdān retreated northward.
The roads were muddy,
their men and horses were hungry and exhausted,
and they entered Yōuzhōu territory.
In the eighth month,
on *rén*
*xū*,
Zhào Déjūn dispatched his *Yájiàng*, Wǔ Cóngjiàn, leading elite cavalry to intercept them.
He divided his troops to guard strategic passes,
capturing Tìyǐn and several hundred others alive.
The remaining troops scattered into villages,
where the villagers attacked them with white staves.
Those who managed to escape back to their country numbered no more than a few dozen.
From then on, the Qìdān lost their morale
and dared not lightly invade the frontier.
Initially,
Zhuāngzōng had been campaigning in Héběi
when he obtained a small child.
He kept him in the palace.
When the child grew up,
he was granted the name Lǐ Jìtáo.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
he released him.
Wáng Dū obtained him
and made him wear a yellow robe and sit on the battlements.
(Ōu Shǐ says: When the Emperor ascended the throne,
Ān Zhònghuì sent Jìtáo to Duàn Huái,
but Huái also disliked and expelled him,
so Dū sent men to find him.)
Yī (衣),
is *yú* *jì* *fān*.
Dié (堞),
is *dá* *xié* *fān*.
"This is the son of Emperor Zhuāngzōng.
He has already ascended the imperial throne.
Your Excellency received great favor from the previous dynasty;
do you not remember it?"
Wáng Yànqiú was Dù Yànqiú.
When Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng,
Yànqiú surrendered with his army.
Zhuāngzōng granted him a new name and employed him.
Wáng Dū intended to use this to sway Yànqiú.
"What good will this small trick do, Your Excellency?
I will now teach Your Excellency two strategies:
either gather all your troops for a decisive battle,
or surrender with your hands tied.
Besides these, there is no way to survive."
Wáng Jiànlì pleaded to be relieved of his duties as *Pàn Sānsī* because he was illiterate,
but his request was not granted.
On the 32nd, *yǐwèi*,
Wú declared a general amnesty.
On the 33rd, Wúyuè Wáng Qián Liú wished to establish his second son, Chuán Guàn, as heir.
He said to his sons,
"Each of you state your achievements,
and I will choose the one with the most to establish."
(He meant he wished to choose the one with the most achievements to establish as heir.)
He then memorialized, requesting to bestow two garrisons upon Chuán Guàn.
In the intercalary month,
on *dīngwèi*,
an imperial edict appointed Chuán Guàn as Jìedùshǐ of Zhènhǎi and Zhèndōng.
On the 34th, *wùshēn*,
Zhào Déjūn presented the captured Qìdān chieftain Tìyǐn and others.
All the generals requested their execution,
but the Emperor said,
"These individuals are all valiant generals among the barbarians.
Killing them would cause the barbarians to lose all hope.
It is better to spare them to alleviate border troubles."
He then pardoned Tìyǐn and fifty other chieftains,
assigning them to the Imperial Guards.
(The Later Táng evidently emulated the system of the Prosperous Táng, where court assemblies featured three guards: Qīn, Xūn, and Yì.)
(This laid the groundwork for the Qìdān repeatedly requesting Tìyǐn and others.)
The 35th, Qìdān dispatched Méi Lǎojìsù and others to offer tribute.
Initially,
Lú Wénjìn had come to surrender (details are in the first year of the previous volume).
He guarded Píngzhōu,
with a trusted general overseeing him with three hundred cavalry.
Xī Chóng was originally a scholar
who became a *Yájiàng* in Yōuzhōu and was captured by the Qìdān.
(Ōu Shǐ says: Liú Shǒuguāng sent Zhāng Xīchóng to guard Píngzhōu,
and the Qìdān captured him when they took Píngzhōu.)
The Qìdān general gradually trusted him.
He then conspired with his subordinates to return south.
His subordinates wept, saying,
"Returning is indeed what we never forget, whether awake or asleep.
However, the barbarians are numerous and we are few;
what can we do?"
Xī Chóng said,
"I will lure their general and kill him.
Their army will surely collapse and flee.
Their camp is over a thousand *lǐ* from here.
By the time they know and dispatch troops,
we will be far away."
The multitude said,
"Excellent!"
They first dug a pit
and filled it with quicklime.
The next day,
they invited the barbarian general to drink.
When he was drunk,
they killed him and his attendants
and threw them into the pit.
Their camp was north of the city.
They immediately dispatched troops to attack it.
(These troops were Hàn soldiers.)
Xī Chóng brought his entire department of over twenty thousand people to surrender.
An imperial edict appointed him as the Cìshǐ of Rǔzhōu.
(Ōu Shǐ says: He was appointed as the Fángyùshǐ of Rǔzhōu.)
The 37th, the Empress Dowager of Wú died.
(She was Lady Wáng, the mother of the Wú ruler.)
In the ninth month,
on *xīnsì*,
Jīngnán defeated the Chǔ army at Báitián,
captured Lǐ Tíngguī, the Cìshǐ of Yuèzhōu for Chǔ,
and sent him to Wú.
(The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Yuèzhōu's Bālíng County has Báitián Town.)
(At that time, Jīngnán was a vassal of Wú.)
Bài (敗),
is *bǔ* *mài* *fān*.
On the 39th, *yǐwèi*,
an imperial edict ordered Wēn Táo, for excavating imperial tombs,
and Duàn Níng, for treachery,
to be granted death wherever they were located.
Last year,
Wēn Táo was exiled to Dézhōu,
and Duàn Níng was exiled to Liáozhōu.
On the 40th, *jǐhài*,
Fáng Zhīwēn, the Jìedùshǐ of Wǔníng, was concurrently appointed *Jīngnán Xíngyíng Zhāotǎoshǐ*
and *Zhī Jīngnán Xíngfǔ Shì*.
Eunuchs were separately dispatched to mobilize troops from various circuits to Xiāngyáng
to suppress Gāo Jìxīng.
(Two years ago, Liú Xùn's campaign against Jīngnán failed,
and now they are again campaigning against it.)
On the 41st, *xīnchǒu*,
Dòu Tíngwǎn, the Fángyùshǐ of Qìngzhōu, was transferred to be the Cìshǐ of Jīnzhōu.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Tíngwǎn occupied Qìngzhōu and defied orders.
On the 42nd, *bǐngwǔ*,
Lǐ Cóngmǐn, the Jìedùshǐ of Hénghǎi, was concurrently appointed *Běimiàn Xíngyíng Fùzhāotǎoshǐ*.
(He replaced Ān Shěntōng.)
(He was a nephew of the Emperor.)
On the 43rd, *wùshēn*,
an imperial edict ordered Lǐ Jìngtōng,
the Jìedùshǐ of Jìngnàn, to dispatch troops to suppress Dòu Tíngwǎn.
(Qìngzhōu was under the jurisdiction of Jìngnàn Commandery,
hence he was ordered to suppress him.)
Nàn (難),
is *nǎi* *dàn* *fān*.
Wáng Dū occupied Dìngzhōu,
with strong defenses
and strict surveillance.
Several generals had repeatedly planned to turn over the city and respond to the imperial army,
but none succeeded.
The Emperor sent an envoy to urge Wáng Yànqiú to attack the city.
Yànqiú rode alongside the envoy to inspect the city.
Qí (騎),
is *qí* *jì* *fǎn*.
"The city walls are so high and steep.
Even if the occupants allowed external forces to ascend the walls,
it is beyond the reach of scaling ladders and battering rams.
(Tī (梯) refers to cloud ladders.)
(Chōng (衝) refers to battering rams.)
It would not harm the rebels,
so what is the point of this?
It is better to collect taxes from the three prefectures,
cherish the people, and maintain the army to await them.
They will surely collapse from within."
The Emperor agreed.
(In the art of warfare, attacking a city is the most difficult.
However, there are two methods for attacking a city: If the city has external reinforcements,
then one must exert full effort to quickly attack,
aiming for certain victory.
If the city has no external reinforcements,
then one should prolong the siege to exhaust them.
In this way, our forces are not diminished, and we secure a complete victory.
Ancient masters of warfare all knew this technique.)
In the eleventh month,
the relevant authorities requested to establish a temple for Emperor Ài.
An imperial edict ordered a temple to be established in Cáozhōu.
The 46th, Huò Yànwēi, Duke Zhōngwǔ of Jìn and Jìedùshǐ of Pínglú, passed away.
47 Wáng Yǎ, the Cìshǐ of Zhōngzhōu, captured Guīzhōu.
Zhōngzhōu at this time belonged to the Níngjiāng Army of Kuízhōu,
which was under the command of Xīfāng Yè.
Guīzhōu at this time belonged to the Jīngnán Army,
which was under the command of Gāo Jìxīng.
48 On the day of Gēngyín,
the Imperial Son Cónghòu took Kǒng Xún’s daughter as his wife.
Xún thus gained access to Dàliáng.
At this time, Kǒng Xún concurrently held the post of Liúshǒu of Dōngdū,
while the Emperor was in Dàliáng.
"Gained access" (得之)
means "gained passage to" (得往).
Those with official duties were not allowed to arbitrarily leave their posts.
Now, Xún was able to reach the temporary imperial residence due to the auspicious ceremony.
"Gained access" (得之)
was originally sometimes written as
"gained arrival" (得至).
According to the records, the Táng capital was Luòyáng,
and Dàliáng was designated as Dōngdū.
Kǒng Xún’s official post was in Dōngdū,
yet it is said that he gained access to Dàliáng.
This is because Ān Chónghuǐ was angry with Kǒng Xún,
and had him removed from the Púmì (Bureau) to become the Shuài of Zhōngwǔ, concurrently serving as Dōngdū Liúshǒu.
At this time, the Emperor was in Dàliáng,
and Xún had not yet been able to assume the post of Liúshǒu.
Now, by marrying his daughter, he was able to reach Dōngdū.
The following text, which states that he was promptly ordered to return to his garrison, clarifies this,
and thus it can be understood.
(Kǒng Xún) begged to stay.
Ān Chónghuǐ fully reported the matter,
and strongly opposed it.
After the ceremony concluded—
the auspicious ceremony concluded—
he returned to the garrison of the Zhōngwǔ Army.
49 On the day of Jiǎwǔ,
Wáng Jiànlì, who was Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì
and concurrently Jìedùshǐ of Pínglú.
50 On the day of Bǐngshēn,
the Emperor asked Zhào Fèng:
"Why do emperors bestow iron warrants upon people?"
He replied:
"It is to make a vow with them,
ensuring that their descendants will long enjoy their titles and emoluments."
The Emperor said:
"Only three individuals from the previous dynasty received this grant."
Xuē Jūzhèng’s Wǔdài Shǐ (History of the Five Dynasties) states: "In the first month of the Jiǎyín day of the second year of Tóngguāng of Zhuāngzōng,
the Emperor presided over the Zhōngxīng Hall
and personally bestowed an iron warrant upon Guō Chóngtāo.
In the second month, on the Dīnghài day,
an iron warrant was bestowed upon Lǐ Sìyuán.
In the second year,
Zhū Yǒuqīan, whose name was Lǐ Jìlín,
was registered in the imperial clan
and received an iron warrant."
The extermination of the two individuals' families is recorded in volume 274, first year.
"Cháo" (朝),
is pronounced "zhāo" (直遙翻).
The Emperor was suspected and resented by Zhuāngzōng,
and also suffered from slanders.
This began in volume 273, the third year of Tóngguāng, at the time of taking the fine armor from Yèdū,
and concluded in volume 274, the first year, on the day of leaving Yèdū at Wèixiàn.
Zhào Fèng said:
"When emperors hold great faith in their hearts,
there is certainly no need to carve it in metal or stone."
51 In the twelfth month,
on the day of Jiǎchén,
Lǐ Jìngzhōu reported the capture of Qìngzhōu
and the extermination of Dòu Tíngwǎn's clan.
52 Gāo Jìxīng, the Jìedùshǐ of Jīngnán, became critically ill.
He ordered his son, Xíngjūn Sīmǎ, Zhōngyì Jìedùshǐ, and Tóng Píngzhāngshì Cónghuǐ, to temporarily oversee the affairs of the military administration.
On the day of Bǐngchén,
Jìxīng died.
The Kǎoyì (Critical Examination of Differences) states: "Táng Míngzōng Shílù (Veritable Records of Emperor Míngzōng of Táng) says:
'On the Rénwǔ day of the eleventh month of the third year of Tiānchéng,
Fáng Zhīwēn reported Gāo Jìxīng's death.'
The Lièzǔ Shílù (Veritable Records of Emperor Lièzǔ) also states,
'In the eleventh month of the second year of Qiánzhēn,
Jìxīng died.'
This is likely a mistake due to傳聞 (hearsay).
However, Táo Gǔ’s Jìxīng Shéndàobēi (Spirit Way Stele for Jìxīng) and Bóhǎi Xíngniánjì (Chronicle of Bóhǎi)
all state
'died on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month.'
We now follow this.
Gāo Cónghuǐ,
courtesy name Zūnshèng,
was Jìxīng’s eldest son.
53 Zhāng Zhāoyuǎn, the Xiūzhuàn of the Shǐguǎn (Historiography Institute), submitted a memorial, saying:
"I humbly observe that in the time of the previous dynasty,
the imperial younger brothers and sons all enjoyed entertainers.
When at home, they adorned concubines;
when out, they flaunted their servants and horses.
With such customs,
how can they become worthy?
This means, how can they become worthy individuals?
It is fitting for the Imperial Sons to humble themselves and serve as disciples,
studying the classics of rites and righteousness,
and discussing the principles of safety and danger.
In ancient times, when a ruler ascended the throne, a crown prince was established,
in order to clarify the distinction between the嫡 (di) and庶 (shu) and
to block the sources of disaster and chaos.
As for selecting an heir and establishing a crown prince now,
I dare not lightly discuss it.
However, regarding the distribution of favors and gifts,
and during marriages and visits,
there should be distinctions made between the嫡 (di) and庶 (shu), and between elder and younger,
to demonstrate hierarchy and authority,
and to cut off any hopes of unwarranted gain."
The Emperor praised and admired his words but could not act upon them.
From the Kāngpíng era of Liáng
until Tiānchéng,
only Zhāng Zhāoyuǎn’s single memorial was able to discuss current affairs with his scholarship.
If there were no scholars,
how could the state be governed?
It is a pity that his words were not put into use.
The history states that he praised and admired but could not use them.
Alas!
The Emperor’s praise and admiration
were also because people at the time praised and admired Zhāng Zhāoyuǎn for his scholarship,
how could they know that what he said was deeply beneficial to the state of man!
54 Mǐn King Yánjūn permitted twenty thousand commoners to become monks,
and thus Mǐnzhōng had many monks.
55 Cóngróng, the Jìedùshǐ of Hédōng and Liúshǒu of Běidū,
was young and arrogant,
and did not involve himself in government affairs.
The Emperor sent trusted associates who were friendly with Cóngróng to stay with him,
to gently admonish and guide him.
These individuals privately said to Cóngróng:
"The Prime Minister of Hénán is respectful and prudent, fond of goodness,
and treats upright scholars with courtesy,
possessing the demeanor of an elder statesman.
Cónghòu was then the Yǐn of Hénán,
hence he was called the Prime Minister of Hénán.
"Duānshì" (端士)
means "upright scholar."
"Hǎo" (好)
is pronounced "hào" (呼到翻).
You should strive and exert yourself,
so that your reputation does not fall below that of Hénán."
Cóngróng was displeased.
He withdrew
and told Yáng Sīquán, the Bùjūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ (Commander of the Infantry):
"The people of the court all promote Cónghòu and disparage me.
Will I be deposed?"
Sīquán said:
"My Lord holds strong troops in your hands,
and moreover, Sīquán is here.
What is there to worry about?"
He then persuaded Cóngróng to recruit more personal troops,
repair his armor and weapons,
and secretly prepare for self-defense.
Observing Cóngróng's question and Yáng Sīquán's reply,
the very means by which they sought security was what endangered themselves.
"You always praise the younger brother and suppress the elder.
How can we not assist him?"
The person was afraid
and reported it to Fēng Yūn, the Fù Liúshǒu.
Yūn secretly submitted a memorial about it.
The Emperor sent trusted associates to admonish and guide Cóngróng.
This implies that he was secretly given very direct imperial instructions.
Cóngróng's displeasure and Yáng Sīquán's threat
and coercion —
all these circumstances
should have been secretly reported to the Emperor by the individual.
How could he report it to Fēng Yūn and wait for Yūn to memorialize it?
There must be some twists and turns here.
Due to Cóngróng’s position,
he was not punished for it either.
The Emperor did not punish Yáng Sīquán,
and later this led to Cónghòu's disaster.
However, the animosity between the two sons had already been formed;
even if Sīquán had been punished,
it would have made no difference.
1 In Spring,
the first month,
Fēng Yūn entered as Xuānhuīshǐ
and said to the ruling officials:
"Cóngróng is headstrong and conceited, yet fickle.
It is fitting to select someone of weighty virtue to assist him."
2 Wáng Dū and Tūněi tried to break out of the encirclement and flee,
but could not get out.
In the second month,
on the day of Guǐchǒu,
Mǎ Ràngnéng, the Dūzhīhuīshǐ of Dìngzhōu, opened the gate and admitted the imperial army.
Wáng Dū and his entire clan committed self-immolation.
Tūněi and two thousand Khitan people were captured.
Wáng Yànqiú had been attacking Wáng Dū since the fourth month of last year,
and now conquered him.
On the day of Xīnhài,
Wáng Yànqiú was appointed Tiānpíng Jìedùshǐ,
and he and Zhào Déjūn were both additionally granted the title of concurrently serving as Shìzhōng.
Wáng Yànqiú was rewarded
for his achievement in pacifying Wáng Dū;
Zhào Déjūn was rewarded
for his achievement in capturing Tìyǐn.
They were executed in the marketplace.
3 Zhào Jìngyí, the Púmìshǐ, died.
4 On the day of Jiǎzǐ,
the Emperor departed from Dàliáng.
5 On the *dīngmǎo* day,
Cuī Xié, *ménxià shìláng* and *tóng píngzhāngshì*, died at Xūshuǐ.
In the early Táng dynasty, Xūshuǐ county was established.
During the Zhēnguān period, it was merged into Guǎnchéng county of Zhèngzhōu.
*Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Yíngyáng county in Zhèngzhōu has Xūshuǐ Town.
卒 (died),
pronounced *zǐxù* (翻).
6 On the *gēngwǔ* day,
the Emperor arrived at Luòyáng.
In the tenth month of the second year (of Tóngguāng),
the Emperor went to Dàliáng,
and now returned to Luòyáng.
7 Wáng Yànqiú was beneath the walls of Dìngzhōu,
daily feasting his soldiers with his private wealth.
From the start of the assault until the capture of the city, not a single soldier was ever executed.
In the third month,
on the *xīnsì* day,
Yànqiú came to court.
The Emperor praised his achievements;
Yànqiú merely apologized for having troubled the provisions and transport for so long.
Historians say that Wáng Yànqiú was meritorious but not boastful.
8 Imperial Prince Cóngcàn, *yòuwèi dàjiāngjūn*, was by nature unyielding.
Ān Zhònghuǐ was in power,
and Cóngcàn would not bend to him.
The Emperor's eastern tour
refers to the time he went to Dàliáng.
Cóngcàn feasted with guests in Huìjié Yuán.
Huìjié Yuán was within the city of Luòyáng.
Zhāng Quányì had governed Luòyáng for many years.
His private residence was in Huìjié Fāng.
Its buildings, gardens, and ponds were of immense beauty for their time,
and he surrendered them to the government to be made into Huìjié Yuán.
He playfully ascended the imperial couch.
Imperial gardens were always equipped with an imperial couch
for the Emperor's visits and excursions.
On the *bǐngxū* day,
Cóngcàn was granted death.
9 The Héngshān barbarians raided Shàozhōu.
Shàozhōu,
in the Hàn dynasty, was Zhāolíng county,
subordinate to Chángshā Commandery.
In the Eastern Hàn, it belonged to Chángshā and Línglíng commanderies.
Later, Zhāolíng was changed to Zhāoyáng county.
The Wú established Shàolíng Commandery.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn changed Zhāoyáng to Shàoyáng county.
The Suí abolished the commandery.
The Táng established Nánliángzhōu,
which was changed to Shàozhōu.
At this time, it belonged to the territory of Chǔ.
10 Chǔ King Yīn ordered his second son, Xīshēng, *Wǔ'ān jiédù fùshǐ* and *pàn Chángshā fǔ*, to oversee political affairs,
supervising all military matters both internal and external.
From then on, state affairs first passed through Xīshēng
before being reported to Yīn.
Xīshēng,
courtesy name Ruònè,
was Yīn's second son.
This laid the groundwork for the killing of Gāo Yù.
11 Summer,
fourth month.
On the first day of the month, *gēngzǐ*,
iron and tin coins were prohibited.
At that time, Húnán exclusively used tin coins.
One copper coin was worth one hundred tin coins.
They flowed into the Central Plains,
and the law could not prohibit them.
Mǎ Yīn, having secured Húnán,
minted tin into coins,
originally for use within his territory.
Later, they flowed into the Central Plains.
*Wǔdài Huìyào* states: An imperial edict of the third month of the second year of Tóngguāng:
"Regarding the abuses of currency,
mixed with lead and tin,
outside of the Jiānghú region,
illicit minting is particularly rampant.
In markets and shops,
it is openly practiced without fear.
Because of this, merchants carry it,
boats transport it back and forth,
exchanging good money,
and wealthy families hoard it.
This is truly a harmful corruption and
requires regulations.
It should be ordered that in the capital and all circuits, inspections be made of the money in circulation in the markets,
and all mixed, inferior lead and tin coins should be prohibited.
In the counties along the river,
whenever boats arrive at the shore,
strict vigilance should be exercised.
If private transport occurs,
all goods should be confiscated."
An imperial edict of the twelfth month of the first year of Tiānchéng:
"Within the circulating copper coins,
it is heard that iron coins are mixed in.
If strict penalties are not enforced,
there is fear that illicit minting will increase.
All iron and tin coins within the copper coins used throughout the empire should be immediately destroyed,
and should not be allowed to circulate again.
If violated,
regardless of the quantity of money used,
all shall be confiscated by the government,
and severe penalties shall be imposed."
The prohibition on iron and tin coins was old.
Now it was re-enacted with stricter measures, but could not be enforced.
12 On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
Wáng Huán, *Chǔ liùjūn fùshǐ*, defeated the Jīngnán army at Shíshǒu.
13 Initially, an order was issued for border regions to establish markets for trading Dǎngxiàng horses,
prohibiting them from coming to the imperial court.
Previously,
all Dǎngxiàng came to the court,
under the guise of presenting tribute horses.
The state would agree on their value and pay them,
in addition to providing lodging, food, and gifts,
costing over 500,000 *mín* annually.
Officials suffered from this waste,
hence it was stopped.
*Wǔdài Huìyào* states: Since the Emperor ascended the throne,
crowds of Dǎngxiàng flocked to the capital to sell horses,
and were often given food in the imperial court.
When drunk, they would link arms and sing their native songs.
All horses brought,
whether good or poor,
were claimed to be tribute.
Although an agreed price was given,
the lodging, provisions, and gifts
caused much waste.
Although an imperial edict was issued to stop it,
it ultimately could not be implemented.
党 (Dǎng),
pronounced *dǐlǎng* (翻).
14 On the *rénzǐ* day,
Imperial Prince Cóngróng was appointed *Hénán Yǐn* and *pàn liùjūn zhūwèi shì*;
Cónghòu was appointed *Hédōng jiédùshǐ* and *Běidū liúshǒu*.
The positions of the two sons were changed twice.
15 The Qìdān raided Yúnzhōu.
16 On the *jiǎyín* day,
Zhào Fèng, *duānmíngdiàn xuéshì* and *bīngbù shìláng*, was appointed *ménxià shìláng* and *tóng píngzhāngshì*.
17 Fifth month.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
the Secretariat reported:
"The Grand Master of Ceremonies has posthumously honored Emperor Āi as Zhāoxuān Guāngliè Xiào Huángdì,
with the temple name Jǐngzōng.
If he is called Zōng, he should be enshrined in the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
If he is in a separate temple, he should not be called Zōng."
Emperor Āi's temple was in Cáozhōu.
18 The Emperor was about to perform the sacrifice at the Southern Suburb,
and sent Lǐ Rénjù, *kèshěngshǐ*, with an edict to the two Chuān regions,
ordering Xīchuān to contribute 1,000,000 *mín* and
Dōngchuān 500,000 *mín*.
Both excused themselves, citing insufficient military funds.
Xīchuān contributed 500,000 *mín*,
and Dōngchuān 100,000 *mín*.
Rénjù was
a guest general when the Emperor was a *fānzhèn*.
He was favored by Ān Zhònghuǐ
and, relying on this grace, became arrogant and insolent.
When he arrived at Zǐzhōu,
the *jiédù* of Dōngchuān governed from Zǐzhōu.
He did not go (to the office) by midday,
but instead embraced courtesans and drank heavily.
Zhāng (Yánzhāng) was enraged.
He entered the courier station with his retinue carrying weapons,
made Rénjù stand at the bottom of the steps, and reproached him, saying:
"You only heard that Xīchuān executed *kèshěng* Lǐ,
do you think I alone cannot do it?!"
Rénjù wept and prostrated himself, begging for mercy,
and barely escaped.
Afterwards, he generously bribed Rénjù to apologize.
(Zhāng) wanted to use bribes to silence him.
This implies that Zhāng was lawless.
Not long after,
the Emperor again sent Lǐ Yànxún, *tōngshì shèrén*, to Dōngchuān.
Upon entering the territory,
Yànxún committed a minor transgression.
Zhāng detained his attendants,
and Yànxún fled back.
19 When Gāo Jìxīng rebelled,
(see year two in the previous volume.)
he was not listened to.
After Cónghuǐ (Gāo Cónghuǐ) succeeded to his position,
he said to his subordinates:
"Táng is near, but Wú is far. This is not a good strategy."
He then used Chǔ King Yīn as an intermediary to apologize to Táng.
He also sent a letter to Ān Yuánxìn, *shānnán dōngdào jiédùshǐ*,
seeking his support for a plea,
and resumed tribute.
On the *bǐngshēn* day,
Yuánxìn reported Cónghuǐ's letter,
and the Emperor agreed.
20 The Qìdān raided Yúnzhōu.
The Qìdān raiding Yúnzhōu twice within a month means that Qìdān ruler Yēlǜ Déguāng was gradually moving westward.
On the 21st day of the sixth month,
on the *wùshēn* day,
Yèdū was once again made Wèizhōu.
Zhuāngzōng had ascended the throne in Wèizhōu in the first year of Tóngguāng,
making Wèizhōu into Xīngtángfǔ,
and established Dōngjīng.
After moving to Luò,
in the third year of Tóngguāng,
the old system of Táng was restored,
with Luòyáng as Dōngdū,
and Dōngjīng of Wèizhōu was renamed Yèdū.
Now it was again made Wèizhōu.
On the 22nd day, *gēngshēn*,
Gāo Cónghuì styled himself the former Jīngnán Xíngjūn Sīmǎ and Guīzhōu Cìshǐ,
and submitted a memorial requesting to submit himself to the court.
In Autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the *jiǎshēn* day,
Cónghuì was made Jīngnán Jiédùshǐ concurrently Shìzhōng.
On the *jǐchǒu* day,
the Jīngnán Zhāotǎoshǐ was abolished.
The campaign against Jīngnán began in the second year of the previous volume.
Now, with his submission, the military campaign was called off.
In the eighth month,
Lǐ Jiǎn, Wú's Wǔchāng Jiédùshǐ concurrently Shìzhōng, requested to return to Jiāngdū due to illness.
Yángzhōu's administrative seat was in Jiāngdū Xiàn,
the capital of Wú.
He died on the *guǐchǒu* day
at Cǎishí.
Xú Zhīxún,
Jiǎn's son-in-law,
detained two thousand of Jiǎn's personal guards at Jīnlíng.
Xú Zhīxún was at Jīnlíng, assisting his father Wēn in governing at the time.
The Wǔchāng Jiédùshǐ governed Èzhōu.
Zhīxún angrily said:
"Liú Chóngjùn,
a relative of my elder brother,
has been in Háozhōu for three generations;
Wú first appointed Liú Jīn as Háozhōu Cìshǐ;
when Jīn died,
his son Rén Guī succeeded him;
when Rén Guī died,
his son Chóngjùn succeeded him.
Why should I alone not get it!"
Initially,
Chǔ Wáng Yīn used Gāo Yù, the Commissioner of the Capital Army, as his chief strategist.
Mǎ Yīn, upon first acquiring Tánzhōu,
immediately appointed Gāo Yù as his chief strategist.
This included measures such as collecting tea taxes, ordering people to plant mulberries, and using silk floss to pay tribute, and similar policies.
When Zhuāngzōng entered Luò,
Yīn sent his son Xīfàn to present tribute.
This is mentioned in volume 272, in the first year of Zhuāngzōng's Tóngguāng era.
(Zhuāngzōng) said:
"I heard that the Mǎ clan would be seized by Gāo Yù.
Now that they have a son like this,
how can Yù succeed in seizing it!"
This remark was intended to sow discord with Gāo Yù.
Bǐ (比),
pronounced *pízhì*.
Yīn did not listen.
Then he sent an envoy with a letter to Jiédù Fùshǐ and Zhīzhèngshì Xīshēng,
highly praising Yù's achievements and fame,
wishing to be brothers.
The envoy said to Xīshēng:
"Gāo Gōng always says, 'The Mǎ clan's governance all comes from Gāo Yù.'
This is a concern for future generations."
Xīshēng believed him.
Yáng Zhāosuì, the Xíngjūn Sīmǎ,
was Xīshēng's wife's relative.
He plotted to replace Yù in his position,
and daily slandered him to Xīshēng.
Xīshēng repeatedly spoke to Yīn,
claiming that Yù was extravagant and presumptuous,
and also colluding with neighboring *fān* (vassals),
requesting his execution.
Yīn said:
"My achievements and enterprises
are all due to Yù's efforts;
do not speak of this again!"
Xīshēng persistently requested that his military authority be removed,
so Yù was demoted to Xíngjūn Sīmǎ.
Yù said to his intimates:
"Quickly prepare for Xīshān,
I will retire there.
Xīshān
refers to the various mountains of Yuèlù on the west bank of Chángshā.
It can bite people."
Xīshēng heard this,
and became even more enraged.
The next day,
he falsely issued Yīn's order and killed Yù in the governmental residence.
Fǔshè
refers to the administrative office of the Jīngnán military government.
He falsely accused Yù of plotting rebellion,
and also exterminated his clan and partisans.
By evening,
Yīn still did not know.
That day,
there was a great fog.
Yīn said to his attendants:
"When I followed Sūn Rú across the Huái River in the past,
in the third year of Guāngqǐ of Táng Zhāozōng,
Mǎ Yīn followed Sūn Rú across the Huái River,
this event is recorded in volume 257.
Such strange phenomena often occurred then.
Is there someone in the Mǎbùyuàn who has died unjustly?"
At that time, all *zhèn* (military regions) had Mǎbù Sī (departments of cavalry and infantry),
with prison courts established to interrogate prisoners.
Today, the great *fān* (vassals) also have Bīngmǎ Sī (military departments).
An official reported Yù's death,
and Yīn beat his chest and wailed loudly, saying:
"I am old and senile,
my governance is no longer my own,
causing my old meritorious retainers to suffer such cruel injustice!"
Héng (橫),
pronounced *hùměng*.
"How can I remain here much longer!"
At that time, Mǎ Yīn was merely a figurehead,
no longer able to control his son.
Chǔ (處),
pronounced *chānglǚ*.
In the ninth month,
the Emperor and Féng Dào conversed leisurely about the repeatedly abundant harvests
and the tranquility throughout the land.
Dào said:
"I often recall when I was in the previous Emperor's *mùfǔ* (staff headquarters),
referring to when he was Hédōng Zhǎngshūjì.
When passing through the perilous Jǐngxíng Pass,
when traveling from Tàiyuán to Zhōngshān via the Jǐngxíng route.
Xíng (陘),
pronounced *xíng*.
I held the reins very carefully,
and fortunately suffered no mishap;
but upon reaching flat ground,
I released the reins and became complacent,
and soon fell.
Governing the world is also like this."
The Emperor deeply agreed with this.
The Emperor then asked Dào:
"Although this year's harvest is abundant,
are the people well-fed and provided for?"
Dào said:
"When the harvest is bad, farmers die of starvation;
when the harvest is abundant, they suffer from cheap grain.
Farmers are the only ones who suffer in both good and bad years.
I remember the *jìnshì* Niè Yízhōng's poem says: 'In the second month, they sell new silk;
in the fifth month, they sell new grain;
curing a sore beneath the eye
by carving out a piece of flesh from the heart.'
Though the language is rustic,
it fully expresses the sentiments of farming families.
This means that before the silk and grain are ripe,
farming families struggle for food,
so they borrow to sustain themselves,
and by the time they sell silk and grain, it is barely enough to repay their debts.
Niè (聶),
pronounced *nízhé*.
Tiào (糶),
pronounced *tādiào*.
Wān (剜),
pronounced *wūwán*.
Scholars, farmers, artisans, merchants,
these are called the four classes of people.
The Táng dynasty avoided using the taboo character of Tàizōng,
and generally referred to people as 'rén' (人) instead of 'mín' (民).
The Emperor was pleased,
and ordered his attendants to record the poem,
and often recited it.
The Fūzhōu soldiers garrisoned in Dōngchuān returned to their home region.
Dǒng Zhāng detained the strong ones among them,
and sent back the weak and old,
and also confiscated their armor and weapons.
On the *guǐsì* day,
Mèng Róng, the Right Dūyāyá of Xīchuān, had a younger brother who was a tax official in Zīzhōu.
He was sentenced to death for embezzlement.
According to the law,
officials who commit embezzlement,
if the stolen amount is severe, can be sentenced to death.
Dǐ (抵)
means 'to reach'.
Mèng Zhīxiáng said:
"Even if my brother violates the law,
he cannot be pardoned,
much less others!"
28 Wúyuè Wáng Qián Liú (錢鏐) resided in his state and loved to be ostentatious.
If emissaries from the imperial court flattered him, he would bestow generous gifts;
otherwise, his treatment of them would be cold and neglectful.
He once sent a letter to Ān Zhònghuì (安重誨),
the tone of which was quite arrogant.
Xuē Shǐ (薛史) says: Qián Liú (錢鏐) sent a letter to Ān Zhònghuì (安重誨) saying:
"The King of Wúyuè (吳越) addresses this letter to the esteemed official."
He did not include any seasonal greetings.
Zhònghuì (重誨) was angered by his lack of courtesy.
Kǎoyì (考異) says: Both Wúyuè Bèi Shǐ (吳越備史) and Shíguó Jìnián (十國紀年) state
"Jiānmén Wèi Shàng Jiāngjūn (監門衞上將軍),"
which was likely a borrowed title.
Now we follow the Shílù (實錄) and other books.
Zhāoyù (昭遇) had a grudge against Méi (玫).
When the envoy returned,
Méi (玫) reported:
"Zhāoyù (昭遇) met Liú (鏐),
prostrated himself as a subject and danced,
addressed Liú (鏐) as 'Your Highness,'
and privately informed Liú (鏐) of state affairs."
Ān Zhònghuì (安重誨) memorialized for Zhāoyù (昭遇) to be granted death.
On Guǐsì (癸巳),
an imperial edict was issued to retire Liú (鏐) as Tàishī (太師);
all his other official titles and ranks were stripped.
All Wúyuè (吳越) presentation officials, envoys, and tax collectors
were ordered to be arrested and investigated in their respective localities.
Liú (鏐) ordered his sons Chuán'guàn (傳瓘) and others to submit memorials pleading their case,
but none were heeded.
29 Initially,
Shuòfāng Jiédùshǐ (朔方節度使) Hán Zhū (韓洙) passed away.
In the fourth year of Qiánhuà (乾化) of Liáng Jūn Wáng (梁均王),
Hán Zhū (韓洙) inherited the post of governor of Shuòfāng (朔方).
Not long after,
Dìngyuǎn Jūnshǐ (定遠軍使) Lǐ Kuāngbīn (李匡賓) gathered a party and occupied Bǎojìng Zhèn (保靜鎮) to rebel,
causing unrest in Shuòfāng (朔方).
In winter,
in the tenth month,
on Dīngyǒu (丁酉),
Hán Chéng (韓澄) dispatched an envoy with silk and a memorial, requesting the imperial court to appoint a commander.
Former Cízhōu Cìshǐ (磁州刺史) Kāng Fú (康福),
who was good at Hu (胡) language,
was often summoned by the emperor into the private audience hall after court was dismissed
to inquire about current affairs.
Fú (福) would reply in Hu (胡) language.
Ān Zhònghuì (安重誨) disliked him,
disliking that he reported on matters in Hu (胡) language,
which none of those around them understood.
È (惡),
read Wū Lù (烏路).
"Kāng Fú (康福),
if you merely make wild reports,
you will surely be beheaded!"
Fú (福) was afraid and
sought an external appointment.
Zhònghuì (重誨) considered Língzhōu (靈州) to be deep within Hu (胡) territory,
where many commanders were killed.
On Wùxū (戊戌),
Fú (福) was made Shuòfāng (朔方) and Héxī Jiédùshǐ (河西節度使).
During the prosperous times of the Táng (唐),
the Héxī Jiédùshǐ (河西節度使) governed Liángzhōu (涼州),
and together with Shuòfāng (朔方) and Lǒngxī (隴西), it was one of the great border garrisons.
After Sù (肅) and Dài (代) [periods], it fell.
It was recovered during the Dàzhōng (大中) era of Xuānzōng (宣宗),
but was separated by Tǔbō (吐蕃) and Dǎngxiàng (党項),
and the imperial court merely held a nominal claim.
By the end of the Táng (唐),
Shuòfāng (朔方) concurrently held the title of Héxī (河西) Jiédùshǐ,
but even then, its influence did not extend.
Zhào Xún's (趙珣) Jùmǐ Tújīng (聚米圖經) states: Língzhōu (靈州) is nine hundred *lǐ* west of Liángzhōu (涼州).
Fú (福) tearfully bid farewell.
The emperor ordered Zhònghuì (重誨) to find another post for Fú (福).
Zhònghuì (重誨) said:
"Fú (福) has achieved no merit since being Cìshǐ (刺史) to be appointed Jiédù (節度);
what more can he seek?
Moreover, the imperial edict has already been issued,
and it is difficult to change it again."
The emperor had no choice
and said to Fú (福):
"Zhònghuì (重誨) is unwilling;
this is not my intention."
As Fú (福) prepared to depart,
the emperor sent Jiāngjūn (將軍) Niú Zhīróu (牛知柔) and Hézhōng Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ (河中都指揮使) Wèi Shěn (衞審) and others, leading ten thousand soldiers, to escort him.
Shěn (審),
a native of Xúzhōu (徐州).
[The character is] the same as Dū (都).
30 On Xīnhài (辛亥),
Làng (閬) and Guǒ (果) two prefectures were partitioned to establish Bǎoníng Jūn (保寧軍).
On Rénzǐ (壬子),
Lǐ Rénjù (李仁矩), the Nèi Kèshěngshǐ (內客省使), was appointed Jiédùshǐ (節度使).
This was intended to control the two Chuān (川) regions.
This foreshadowed Lǐ Rénjù's (李仁矩) defeat and demise.
According to the Zhíguān Fēnjì (職官分紀),
during the Five Dynasties, there was one Nèi Kèshěngshǐ (內客省使), one Kèshěngshǐ (客省使), and one Fùshǐ (副使) each.
The Zīzhì Tōngjiàn (資治通鑑) records Kèshěngshǐ (客省使) Lǐ Rénjù (李仁矩) in the third month of the second year of Tiānchéng (天成).
Now it records Nèi Kèshěngshǐ (內客省使).
Could it be that he was promoted from Kèshěngshǐ (客省使) to Nèi Kèshěngshǐ (內客省使)?
Before this,
Xīchuān (西川) regularly supplied fodder and provisions to the Xiá (峽) route.
Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥) declined, citing that his own region had many soldiers
and it was difficult to serve other garrisons.
The Xiá (峽) route was then separately designated as Níngjiāng Jūn (寧江軍),
hence the statement.
He was repeatedly urged.
On Jiǎyín (甲寅),
Zhīxiáng (知祥) memorialized that he lacked financial resources
and would not comply with the edict.
31 Xú Zhīxún (徐知詢), the Wú (吳) Zhū Dào Fù Dūtǒng (諸道副都統), Zhènhǎi Níngguó Jiédùshǐ (鎮海寧國節度使) concurrently Shìzhōng (侍中), considered himself to hold military power and occupy the upper reaches.
Jīnlíng (金陵) is upstream from Guǎnglíng (廣陵).
He often competed with Zhīgào (知誥) for power,
and there was mutual suspicion between them.
Zhīgào (知誥) was troubled by this.
Nèi Shūmìshǐ (內樞密使) Wáng Lìngmóu (王令謀) said:
"You have assisted in governance for a long time,
holding the Son of Heaven to command within the borders.
Who would dare not obey?
Zhīxún (知詢) is young;
his benevolence and trust have not yet reached the people.
He can do nothing."
Zhīxún (知詢) treated his younger brothers poorly,
and they all resented him.
Xú Jiè (徐玠) knew that Zhīxún (知詢) could not be supported,
and instead seized upon his shortcomings to attach himself to Zhīgào (知誥).
Xú Jiè (徐玠) had originally advised Xú Wēn (徐溫) to replace Zhīgào (知誥) with Zhīxún (知詢).
This matter is found in the tenth month of the previous year in this volume.
All were adorned with dragons and phoenixes.
Zhīxún (知詢) did not consider it taboo
and used them.
Qián Liú (錢鏐) used this to sow discord with Xú Zhīxún (徐知詢).
Zhīxún (知詢) did not realize it;
such was his mediocrity and dullness.
Lù Zhèn (路振)'s Jiǔguó Zhì (九國志) considers it to have been given by Qián Hóngzuǒ (錢弘佐),
which is incorrect.
"If you can truly donate treasures to win over the meritorious old officials in the court,
so that they all turn their hearts to you,
then with whom will he side?"
Zhīxún (知詢) followed this advice and
sent Tíngwàng (廷望) to Jiāngdū (江都) to convey his intentions.
Tíngwàng (廷望) was close to Zhīgào's (知誥) trusted subordinate Zhōu Zōng (周宗),
and secretly expressed loyalty to Zhīgào (知誥).
Kuǎn (款) means sincerity.
Zhōu Tíngwàng (周廷望) placed himself between brothers,
and by being two-faced,
he was certainly inviting death.
Zhīgào (知誥) claimed that the Wú Zhǔ's (吳主) command did not allow it.
Zhōu Zōng (周宗) said to Tíngwàng (廷望):
"People say that the Shìzhōng (侍中) has seven acts of disloyalty."
When Xú Zhīxún (徐知詢) replaced his father to govern Jīnlíng (金陵),
he was granted the title of Shìzhōng (侍中),
hence he was referred to by this title.
"Luring him to court
is Xú Zhīgào's (徐知誥) plan."
He informed Zhīxún (知詢) of this.
In the eleventh month,
Zhīxún (知詢) came to court.
Zhīgào (知誥) kept Zhīxún (知詢) as Tǒngjūn (統軍)
and appointed him Zhènhǎi Jiédùshǐ (鎮海節度使).
He sent Yòu Xióngwǔ Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ (右雄武都指揮使) Kē Hòu (柯厚) to bring the Jīnlíng (金陵) troops back to Jiāngdū (江都).
Xìngpǔ (姓譜): The Kē (柯) surname
originated from Kē Lú (柯盧), a son of the Lord of Wú (吳).
Also, Tuòbá Xīng (拓跋興)
and other surnames of the Kēbá (柯拔) clan were changed to Kē (柯).
History states that Xú Zhīgào's (徐知誥) usurpation was only accomplished at this point.
"When the late king passed away,
'late king' refers to Xú Wēn (徐溫).
Would it be permissible not to attend the mourning at first?"
Zhīgào (知誥) said:
"You stand with a drawn sword awaiting me;
how dare I go?
As a subject,
is it also permissible for you to possess imperial carriages and attire?"
Zhīxún (知詢) further challenged Zhīgào (知誥) with what Tíngwàng (廷望) had said.
Zhīgào (知誥) said:
"The one who told me about your actions
was also Tíngwàng (廷望)."
Thereupon, he beheaded Tíngwàng (廷望).
32 On Rénchén (壬辰),
the Wú Zhǔ (吳主) was granted the exalted title Ruìshèng Wénmíng Guāngxiào Huángdì (睿聖文明光孝皇帝).
A general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed to Dàhé (大和).
33 Kāng Fú (康福) marched to Fāngqú (方渠),
where the Qiāng (羌) and Hú (胡) troops came out to intercept him.
Fú (福) repelled them.
Arriving at Qīnggāngxiá (青剛峽),
he exited Qīnggāngxiá (青剛峽) via the camel path from Fāngqú (方渠),
passed through the dry sea (hànhǎi 旱海) to Língzhōu (靈州).
Zhào Xún's (趙珣) Jùmǐ Tújīng (聚米圖經) states: Huánzhōu's (環州) Hóngdézhài (洪德寨) has Guīdé (歸德) and Qīnggāng (青剛) two streams.
Guīdé Chuān (歸德川) is to the east of Hóngdé (洪德) and penetrates into Yánzhōu (鹽州).
Qīnggāng Chuān (青剛川) is to the northwest of Hóngdé (洪德).
It is originally the main road to Língzhōu (靈州).
From here, one passes Měilìzhài (美利寨) into the Pǔluò Hé (浦洛河),
and reaches Língzhōu (靈州) via Yàodé Qīngbiānzhèn (耀德清邊鎮).
After passing Měilìzhài (美利寨), one gradually enters Píngxià (平夏),
passing through the dry sea (hànhǎi 旱海),
where water springs are scarce.
Not sensing the arrival of the Táng (唐) army,
Fú (福) dispatched Wèi Shěn (衞審) to launch a surprise attack,
thoroughly defeating them,
killing and capturing almost all.
Consequently, his prestige greatly increased,
and he advanced to Língzhōu (靈州).
From then on, Shuòfāng (朔方) began to be relieved.
34 In the twelfth month,
Wú (吳) promoted Xú Zhīgào (徐知誥) to concurrently serve as Grand Councilor (Zhōngshū Lìng 中書令)
and assume the title of Military Governor of Níngguó (Níngguó Jiédùshǐ 寧國節度使).
Xú Zhīgào (徐知誥) seized Zhīxún's (知詢) Níngguó (寧國) military commission and assumed it himself.
He poured wine into a golden cup and presented it to him,
saying:
"May my brother live for a thousand years."
Zhīxún (知詢) suspected it was poisoned,
and, taking another vessel, poured half of the wine into it,
then reverently presented it to Zhīgào (知誥), saying:
"May you and I each enjoy five hundred years."
Zhīgào's (知誥) expression changed.
He looked around,
unwilling to accept,
but Zhīxún (知詢) held the wine and did not retreat.
The attendants did not know what to do.
The entertainer Shēn Jiàngāo (申漸高) stepped forward and, making a jest,
snatched both cups and drank them.
To snatch (lüè 掠) means to take without ceremony.
Hé (合),
pronounced gé (閤).
Zhīgào (知誥) secretly sent someone with good medicine to counteract the poison,
but he died from a ruptured brain.
Kǎoyì (考異) states: Zhèng Wénbǎo's (鄭文寶) Nántáng Jìnshì (南唐近事):
"Lièzǔ (烈祖) held a private banquet in the side hall,
and offered a poisoned goblet to Zhōu Běn (周本).
Běn (本) was suspicious and did not drink.
Feigning drunkenness,
he took another cup,
poured half of the wine into it,
knelt and presented it, saying: 'May Your Majesty live for ten thousand years.
If Your Majesty does not drink this,
it would not be in accordance with the principle of ruler and minister being of one heart and one virtue.
Your servant dares not obey the decree.'
The emperor's expression changed, and he remained silent.
After a long time,
all the attendants looked at each other, sweating,
not knowing what to do.
The entertainer Shēn Jiàngāo (申漸高), who was resourceful,
secretly understood the situation.
Taking advantage of the humorous conversation,
he drank both cups,
hid the inner cup in his bosom,
and hastily exited.
The emperor secretly sent a trusted person with medicine to his private residence to counteract the poison,
but it was too late.
Jiàngāo (漸高) died from a ruptured brain."
Jiāngbiǎo Zhì (江表志) states:
"Lièzǔ (烈祖) held a private banquet,
and offered wine in a golden cup to Zhīxún (知詢),
saying: 'May my brother live for hundreds of thousands of years.'
Zhīxún (知詢) was suspicious and fearful,
and, taking another vessel, poured half of the wine into it,
