saying: 'May you and I each enjoy five hundred years.'
Zhīgào (知誥) did not drink.
After a long time,
the musician Shēn Jiàngāo (申漸高), seizing the opportunity of the humorous atmosphere, drank both,
and died from a ruptured brain upon reaching home."
Both books are by Wénbǎo (文寶),
yet they differ to such an extent.
It is noted that once Zhīgào (知誥) ascended the throne,
he wanted to eliminate Zhōu Běn (周本),
and would have had many ways to do so,
not needing to resort to this.
Saying that he poisoned Zhīxún (知詢) is closer to the truth,
and we follow that here.
35 Wáng Yánbǐng (王延稟), Military Governor of Fèngguó (Fèngguó Jiédùshǐ 奉國節度使) and Administrator of Jiànzhōu (Jiànzhōu Zhījiànzhōu 建州), claimed illness and retired to his private residence,
requesting that Jiànzhōu (建州) be conferred upon his son Jìxióng (繼雄).
On the day of Gēngzǐ (庚子),
an imperial edict appointed Jìxióng (繼雄) as the Prefect of Jiànzhōu (Jiànzhōu Cǐshǐ 建州刺史).
At that time, Wáng Yánbǐng (王延稟), having already assassinated his lord Yánhàn (延翰) with Wáng Yánjūn (王延鈞),
possessed strong military power and great authority.
Jiànzhōu (建州) was also located upstream from Fúzhōu (福州),
so his influence overshadowed Yánjūn (延鈞).
Therefore, he no longer obeyed Yánjūn's (延鈞) orders, but communicated directly with Luòyáng (洛陽).
36 Ān Chónghuì (安重誨) had already appointed Lǐ Rénjǔ (李仁矩) to govern Làngzhōu (閬州),
and sent him and Wǔ Qiányù (武虔裕), Prefect of Miánzhōu (Miánzhōu Cìshǐ 綿州刺史), to lead troops to the capital.
Fùzhì (赴治) means to proceed to the administrative seat.
Wǔ Qiányù (武虔裕) was an old official of the Emperor and Chónghuì's (重誨) maternal cousin.
Chónghuì (重誨) instructed Rénjǔ (仁矩) to investigate Dǒng Zhāng's (董璋) rebellious intentions,
and Rénjǔ (仁矩) exaggerated and embellished his report in the memorial.
The imperial court also ordered Xià Lǔqí (夏魯奇), Military Governor of Wǔxìn (Wǔxìn Jiédùshǐ 武信節度使), to repair the city walls and moats of Suìzhōu (遂州),
mend armor and weapons,
and reinforce its garrison.
Zhāng (璋) was greatly alarmed.
At that time, rumors spread along the roads
that Mián (綿) and Lóng (龍) would also be carved out to form a military command,
which also alarmed Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥).
Dividing Làng (閬) and Suì (遂) into military commands was intended to control Dōngchuān (東川),
hence Dǒng Zhāng (董璋) was alarmed.
Miánzhōu (綿州) was close to Chéngdū (成都),
and Lóngzhōu (龍州) was the route that Dèng Ài (鄧艾) took to enter Shǔ (蜀).
Since Wǔ Qiányù (武虔裕) was already appointed Prefect of Miánzhōu (綿州),
this was already a gradual step towards a separate military command.
Coupled with the rumors,
Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥) was also alarmed.
Though they had never communicated,
at this point,
Zhāng (璋) sent an envoy to Chéngdū (成都),
requesting to marry his son to Zhīxiáng's (知祥) daughter.
Zhīxiáng (知祥) agreed,
planning to combine forces to resist the imperial court.
This laid the groundwork for the two Chuān (川) regions to combine their armies and attack and capture Suì (遂) and Làng (閬).
Punctuation by Dèng Guǎngmíng (鄧廣銘), proofread by Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐).
Compiled by royal decree by Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光).
Hòu (後) Xué (學) Tiāntái (天台)
Chángxīng (長興) First Year
(Gēngyín 庚寅, 930) The reign title was changed in the second month of this year.
1 Spring,
First month.
Dǒng Zhāng (董璋) dispatched troops to build seven forts at Jiànmén (劍門).
On the day of Xīnsì (辛巳),
Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥) sent Zhào Jìliáng (趙季良) to Zǐzhōu (梓州) to improve relations.
Previously, Dǒng Zhāng (董璋) in Dōngchuān (東川) and Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥) were neighboring military governors but had never communicated.
In Tiānchéng (天成) third year (928),
the two territories had a dispute over salt profits, leading to discord.
Last year, Zhāng (璋) sent an envoy to seek a marriage alliance with Zhīxiáng (知祥).
Now Zhīxiáng (知祥) sent a return envoy to improve relations,
both releasing their grudges to reach an understanding,
fearing that the imperial court would deploy troops.
When sharing a boat in a storm, people from Hú (胡) and Yuè (越) respond to each other like left and right hands;
this is what is meant.
Ān Chónghuì (安重誨) was troubled by the difficulty of controlling the two Chuān (川) regions;
instead of exploiting their rift to make them fight,
he instead caused them to unite.
Can this be considered a good strategy for governing the state?
The Art of War says: Unite them, then you can divide them.
Ān Chónghuì (安重誨) did the opposite.
Hǎo (好),
pronounced hū dào fān (呼到翻);
similarly below.

2 Guō Zàihuī (郭在徽), Assistant Minister of the Court of State Ceremonials (Hónglú Shàōqīng 鴻臚少卿), memorialized to request the minting of large coins worth five thousand, three thousand, and one thousand.
The imperial court, considering his proposals to be baseless and his words reckless,
demoted him to Assistant Minister of the Court of the Imperial Insignia (Wèiwèi Shàōqīng 衞尉少卿), with the status of a regular official (tóng zhèng 同正).
This refers to what Táng (唐) officials called yuánwài zhì (員外置),
meaning "placed outside the quota," but having the same status as a regular official (tóng zhèngyuán 同正員).
3 Wú (吳) transferred Prince of Píngyuán (Píngyuán Wáng 平原王) Chè (澈) to be Prince of Déhuà (Déhuà Wáng 德化王).
Déhuà (德化) County in Jiāngzhōu (江州)
was originally Xúnyáng (尋陽) County of the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: It was changed by Nántáng (南唐).
4 In the second month,
on the first day of Ỳwèi (乙未),
Zhào Jìliáng (趙季良) returned to Chéngdū (成都) and told Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥):
"Dǒng Gōng (董公) is greedy, cruel, and fond of victory;
his ambitions are great, but his plans are short-sighted.
He will eventually become a problem for Xīchuān (西川)."
The historical record notes Zhào Jìliáng's (趙季良) words
as foreshadowing Dǒng Zhāng's (董璋) attack on Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥).
The General Commanders (Dōūzhīhuīshǐ 都指揮使) Lǐ Rénhǎn (李仁罕) and Zhāng Yè (張業) wanted to host a banquet and invite Zhīxiáng (知祥).
Two days prior,
a nun reported that the two generals planned to harm Zhīxiáng (知祥) on the day of the banquet.
Zhīxiáng (知祥) questioned her,
but found no evidence of it.
There was no sign of a plot to harm him.
Qí (詰),
pronounced qù jí fān (去吉翻).
On the day of Dīngyǒu (丁酉),
the military officers Dū Yánchāng (都延昌) and Wáng Xíngběn (王行本), who were the first to speak of the plot,
were cut in half at the waist.
On the day of Wùxū (戊戌),
Zhīxiáng (知祥) attended the banquet,
dismissing all his attendants,
and went alone to Rénhǎn's (仁罕) residence.
Rénhǎn (仁罕) kowtowed and wept, saying:
"This old soldier will only dedicate his life to repay your kindness."
From then on, all the generals became devoted to him and submitted to him.
The history states that Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥) was able to win the loyalty of others by showing his sincerity.
5 On the Rénzǐ day,
Mèng Zhīxiáng and Dǒng Zhāng jointly submitted a memorial saying:
“The two Shuǎn regions, upon hearing that the court has established a military command at Lángzhōng,
and that Mián and Suì have reinforced their troops,
are filled with anxiety and fear.”
“Establishing a military command at Lángzhōng”
refers to establishing the Bǎoníng Army at Lángzhōu;
“Mián and Suì reinforcing their troops”
refers to Wǔ Qiányù being appointed governor of Miánzhōu
and Xià Lǔqí being made commander of Suìzhōu,
both of whom reinforced their garrisons there.
These matters are all mentioned in the previous volume, last year.
6 On the Yǐmǎo day,
the Emperor performed a sacrifice at the Yuánqiú (Altar of Heaven),
granted a great amnesty,
and changed the reign title.
The reign title was changed to Chángxīng.
In the third month,
on the Rénshēn day,
an edict was issued transferring Lǐ Cóngyǎn to be the Military Governor of Xuānwǔ.
In the first year of Tiānchéng,
Lǐ Cóngyǎn was again stationed at Fèngxiáng;
at this time, he was transferred.
7 On the Guǐyǒu day,
the Wú ruler made Lián, Prince of Jiāngdū, the Crown Prince.
8 On the Bǐngzǐ day,
Zhū Hóngzhāo, the Commissioner of Xuanhui, was appointed Military Governor of Fèngxiáng.
9 Kāng Fú reported a victory at Bǎojìng Town,
where he beheaded Lǐ Kuāngbīn.
Lǐ Kuāngbīn's occupation of Bǎojìng Town is mentioned in the previous volume, last year.
10 The Ānyì Army was again renamed the Zhāoyì Army.
In the second year of Lóngdé of Liáng Jùn Wáng,
Jìn Wáng changed the Zhāoyì Army to the Ānyì Army,
as mentioned in volume 271.
11 The Emperor intended to enthrone Cáo Shú as Empress.
Shú said to Wáng Dé:
“I have always suffered from 'internal vexation' (zhōngfán).”
“Zhōngfán”
refers to a sensation of heat and vexation in the chest.
“Let my sister take my place.”
Dé replied:
“The Central Palace (Empress) is the peer of the Supreme One (Emperor);
who would dare to interfere with that!”
On the Gēngyín day,
Shú was enthroned as Empress.
Dé served the Empress with respect and diligence,
and the Empress also showed her affection.
Initially,
Wáng Dé gained advancement through Ān Zhònghuǐ,
and always held him in esteem.
Ōu Shǐ says: Dé, of the Wáng clan,
was the daughter of a pastry seller in Bīnzhōu;
she was very beautiful,
and known as Huā Jiànxiū (Shame-to-Flowers).
When young, she was sold to be the maid of Liú Xún, a general of Liáng.
When Xún died,
Lady Wáng had nowhere to go.
At that time, the Emperor's legitimate wife, Lady Xià, had already died,
and he was looking for another consort.
Someone mentioned Lady Wáng to Ān Zhònghuǐ,
who reported it to the Emperor, and she was taken in.
After he had been on the throne for a long time,
expenditures in the palace became somewhat extravagant,
and Zhònghuǐ often remonstrated.
When silk brocade was taken from the outer treasury to make floor coverings,
Zhònghuǐ strongly remonstrated,
citing Empress Liú as a warning;
this refers to Empress Liú of Zhuāngzōng.
12 Gāo Cónghuǐ sent an envoy with a memorial to Wú,
stating that his ancestral tombs were in Zhōngguó (the Central Plains).
Gāo Jìxīng was from Xiáshí in Shǎnzhōu,
hence the statement.
The Wú troops failed to provide aid,
and he was rejected.
Gāo Jìxīng's request to attach himself to Wú is mentioned in volume 275, Tiānchéng second year.
He was unsuccessful.
13 Dǒng Zhāng feared that Wǔ Qiányù, the governor of Miánzhōu, was spying on his activities.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì,
Miánzhōu is 137 lǐ southeast of Zǐzhōu.
Because of its proximity,
he feared being spied upon.
In the fourth month,
on the jiǎwǔ day, the first day of the month,
he submitted a memorial concurrently appointing Wǔ Qiányù as Xíngjūn Sīmǎ (Acting Military Commander),
and then imprisoned him in the prefectural courtyard.
He lured him with the concurrent appointment of Xíngjūn Sīmǎ,
and imprisoned him upon his arrival in Zǐzhōu.
“Fǔtíng”
refers to the prefectural courtyard of Dōngchuān.
14 Fú Xí, the Military Governor of Xuānwǔ,
prided himself on being a veteran general.
Fú Xí was originally a general of Chéngdé,
and fought with Zhuāngzōng at the river,
hence he considered himself an old veteran.
Zhònghuǐ sought out his faults
and reported them;
on the Dīngyǒu day,
an imperial edict ordered Xí to retire as Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince.
15 On the Wùxū day,
Mèng Zhīxiáng was additionally made concurrent Zhōngshū Lìng (Chancellor),
and Xià Lǔqí was made concurrent Píngzhāngshì (Grand Councilor).
16 Initially,
when the Emperor was in Zhēndìng,
in the second year of Tóngguāng of Zhuāngzōng, the Emperor was stationed at Zhēndìng.
Cóng Kē beat Zhònghuǐ,
who fled and escaped;
when he sobered up,
he repented and apologized,
but Zhònghuǐ held a grudge ever since.
By this time,
Zhònghuǐ was wielding power,
and even the imperial princes Cóngróng and Cónghòu were busy showing him respect.
“Bùxiá”
means they dared not be leisurely.
Zhònghuǐ repeatedly spoke ill of him to the Emperor,
but the Emperor did not listen.
Zhònghuǐ then falsely used an imperial command to instruct Yáng Yànwēn, the Commander of the Guards within the Headquarters of Hédōng, to drive him away.
“Hédōng”
should be
“Hézhōng.”
Following the Wùxū day above,
it is stated as "on this day."
Yànwēn led his troops to close the gates and resist him.
Cóng Kē sent someone to knock on the gate and question him, saying:
“I treated you well;
why are you doing this?”
He replied:
“Yànwēn dares not betray your grace,
but I received a decree from the Púmì Yuàn (Privy Council).”
The Púmì Yuàn used “xuān” (decree),
while the Three Departments (Sānshěng) used “tángtiě” (court dispatch).
Today, “tángtiě” is called “shěnzá” (departmental dispatch),
and “xuān” is called “mìzá” (privy dispatch).
Cóng Kē stopped at Yúxiāng.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Yúxiāng County is 60 lǐ east of Hézhōng Prefecture.
When the envoy arrived,
on the Rénzǐ day,
the Emperor asked Zhònghuǐ:
“How did Yànwēn get these words?”
This refers to his statement of having received a decree from the Púmì Yuàn.
“This scoundrel is speaking nonsense;
he should be quickly punished.”
The Emperor was suspicious,
and wanted to lure Yànwēn to interrogate him about the matter.
“Xùn”
means to question.
“Yòu”
is pronounced yòu.
Zhònghuǐ firmly requested to dispatch troops to attack him,
so the Emperor ordered Suǒ Zìtōng, the Resident Overseer of Xīdū,
and Yào Yànchóu, the Commander of the Infantry, to lead troops to suppress him.
Yào
is a surname;
there was Yào Sōng in the Hàn dynasty.
According to Xuē Shǐ: Yào Yànchóu was
a person of the Shatuo Three Tribes;
he must not have been a descendant of Sōng.
“I want to interrogate him face-to-face.”
Cóng Kē was summoned to Luòyáng.
Cóng Kē knew he was being framed by Zhònghuǐ,
and rushed in to clear his name.
17 Ān Zhònghuǐ was additionally made concurrent Zhōngshū Lìng (Chancellor).
18 Lǐ Cóngkē arrived in Luòyáng.
The Emperor rebuked him and ordered him to return to his residence,
and cut off his court attendance.
Xuē Shǐ says: He returned to his residence in Qīnghuà Lǐ.
On the Xīnhài day,
Suǒ Zìtōng and others captured Hézhōng
and beheaded Yáng Yànwēn,
following Ān Zhònghuǐ's instructions
to behead Yáng Yànwēn to silence him.
This serves as a prelude to Lù Wáng killing Yào Yànchóu and Suǒ Zìtōng throwing themselves into the water.
On the Guǐchǒu day,
his head was sent as an offering.
The Emperor was angry that Yào Yànchóu did not bring him alive.
Ān Zhònghuǐ insinuated to Fēng Dào and Zhào Fèng that they should memorialize regarding Cóng Kē's failure to hold his post,
suggesting he deserved punishment.
The Emperor said:
"My son was overthrown by a treacherous faction;
the right and wrong are not yet clear.
Why do you, gentlemen, utter such words?
Is it your intention not to let him live among men?
These are certainly not your true intentions."
He meant that the two men were instigated by Ān Zhònghuǐ.
Another day,
Zhào Fèng spoke of it again,
but the Emperor did not respond.
The next day,

Yēlǜ Túyù, the King of Dōngdān of the Qìdān, was granted the surname Dōngdān
and the personal name Mùhuá.
He was appointed Jiedushi of Huáihuà and Surveillance Commissioner of Ruì, Shèn, and other prefectures.
At that time, Huáihuà Jūn was established in Shènzhōu.
Ruìzhōu administered one county, Yuǎnlai,
and Shènzhōu administered one county, Fénglóng.
These were presumably established by the Later Táng.
Xuē Shǐ states: The two prefectures of Ruì and Shèn were originally lands of Liáodōng,
and at the end of the Táng, they were part of the Huáihuà Jiedu.
I note that in the tenth year of Zhēngguān of Táng,
Wēizhōu was established within the territory of Yíngzhōu for the Wūtúhàn Dádá tribe.
Later, it was renamed Ruìzhōu,
temporarily governed from Guǎngyáng Chéng in Liángxiāng.
In the early years of Wǔdé,
Shènzhōu was established for the Sùmò Wūsùgù tribe,
temporarily governed from the old Dūxiāng Chéng in Liángxiāng.
(Both) were granted surnames and personal names.
Tìyǐn was surnamed Dí
and named Huáizhōng.
15Lǐ Rénhǎn reached Kuízhōu.
Ān Chóngruǎn, the Jiedushi of Níngjiāng, abandoned his post
and fled back with Yáng Hànbīn from Jūn and Fáng.
On the day Rénxū,
Rénhǎn captured Kuízhōu.
Mèng Zhīxiáng thus came to possess the three prefectures of Kuí, Zhōng, and Wàn.
16After the Emperor relieved Ān Chónghuì of his Púmì duties,
he summoned Lǐ Cóngkē,
and weeping, said:
"If it were according to Chónghuì's wishes,
how could you ever see me again!"
The incident of Ān Chónghuì wanting to kill Cóngkē is recorded in the first year.
On the day Bǐngyín,
Cóngkē was appointed Great General of the Left Guard.
17On the day Rénshēn,
Kǒng Xún, the Jiedushi of Hénghǎi and Tongpíngzhāngshì, passed away.
18th, *yǐyǒu* day.
Again, Qián Liú was appointed Commander-in-Chief of all military forces under Heaven, Shàngfù, and King of Wúyuè.
Zhāng Jiān, the Commander-in-Chief of the Palace Gates, was dispatched to convey the imperial decree,
stating that his earlier resignation from office
was due to Ān Chónghuì’s forging of a decree.
19th, *dīnghài* day.
Lǐ Yú, the Táicháng Qīng, was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
20th, Summer.
Fourth month.
*Xīnmǎo* day.
Wáng Dé was appointed Shú.
The Táng system followed the old Suí system,
where one Guì, one Shú, and one Xián were each assigned,
all of the first rank.
At this time, Empress Cáo had already taken the position of Shú in the Central Palace,
hence Dé was promoted to Shú.
Wáng Yánbǐng, the Fèngguó Jiédùshǐ and concurrent Zhōngshū Lìng of Mǐn, heard that Wáng Yánjūn, the King of Mǐn, was ill,
so he made his second son Jìshēng the acting Jiànzhōu Liúhòu,
and led Jìxióng, the Cǐshǐ of Jiànzhōu, with a naval force to attack Fúzhōu.
*Guǐmǎo* day.
Yánbǐng attacked the west gate,
and Jìxióng attacked the east gate.
Yánjūn dispatched Wáng Rénádá, the Louquán Zhǐhuīshǐ, to lead a naval force to resist them.
Rénádá hid armored soldiers in the boats,
and pretended to raise a white banner to surrender.
Jìxióng was pleased,
dismissed his attendants,
and boarded Rénádá’s boat to offer comfort and assurance.
Rénádá decapitated Jìxióng
and displayed his head at the west gate.
Yánbǐng was then setting fire to attack the city.
Seeing this,
he wailed loudly.
Rénádá then unleashed his troops to attack him.
His forces crumbled,
and his attendants carried Yánbǐng away on a *hú* (bushel) and fled.
*Hú*
is a measuring vessel,
ten *dǒu* make one *hú*.
*Yú*,
pronounced *yú*,
also *yángrǔ* reversed.
*Jiǎchén* day,
he was pursued and captured.
Yánjūn, upon seeing him, said:
"It really troubled my elder brother to come down again!"
This quote from Wáng Yánbǐng can be found in Volume 275, Tiānchéng second year.
Yánjūn imprisoned him in a separate room,
and dispatched envoys to Jiànzhōu to pacify his partisans.
His partisans killed the envoys,
and escorted Jìshēng and his younger brother Jìlún to flee to Wúyuè.
Rénádá was
Yánjūn’s cousin.
This sets the stage for Yánjūn's jealousy of Rénádá and his eventual killing of him.
Cóng,
pronounced *cáiyòng* reversed.
22nd. Zhào Yánshòu, the Xuānhuī Běiyuànshǐ, was appointed Shūmìshǐ.
23rd, *jǐyǒu* day.
Shí Jìngtáng, the Tiānxíong Jiédùshǐ and concurrent Tóng Píngzhāng Shì, also served as Deputy Commander of the Six Armies and various Guards.
24th, *xīnhài* day.
Zhū Hóngzhāo was appointed Xuānhuī Nányuànshǐ.
25th, Fifth month.
Wáng Yánjūn, the King of Mǐn, executed Wáng Yánbǐng in the marketplace,
and restored his original name, Zhōu Yànchēn.
He then dispatched his younger brother Yánzhèng, the Dū Jiàoliànshǐ, to Jiànzhōu to pacify the officials and common people.
This sets the stage for Wáng Yánzhèng's conflict with Fúzhōu over Jiànzhōu.
26th, *dīngmǎo* day.
The land tax on麴 (brewer's yeast) was abolished.
The land tax on麴 (brewer's yeast) is mentioned in the previous volume, Tiānchéng third year.
Villagers were allowed to brew it themselves;
the people found this very convenient.
27th, *jǐmǎo* day.
Mèng Hànqióng was appointed Director of the Nèishìshěng Affairs,
and concurrent Xuānhuī Běiyuànshǐ.
Hànqióng
was originally a slave of Zhào Wáng Róng.
At this time, although Fàn Yánguāng and Zhào Yánshòu were Shūmìshǐ,
they, having learned from Ān Chónghuì's downfall due to his arrogance,
dared not express approval or disapproval in political matters.
Only Hànqióng and Wáng Shú held power in the court,
and everyone feared them.
Previously,
if palace demands slightly exceeded normal limits,
Chónghuì would immediately admonish against them,
which effectively curbed illicit requests.
However, at this point,
Hànqióng directly took goods from the treasury under the Empress's orders,
without consulting the Shūmìyuàn or the Sānsī,
and without any written records.
The amount taken was innumerable.
28th, *xīnsì* day.
Mèng Hú, the Cǐshǐ of Xiāngzhōu, was appointed Zúoxiāowèi Dàjiāngjūn,
and concurrent Sānsīshǐ.
29th. Zhào Tíngyǐn, the Zhāowǔ Liúhòu, went from Chéngdū to Lìzhōu.
After more than a month,
he requested troops to advance and conquer Xīngyuán, as well as Qín and Fèng.
Mèng Zhīxiáng, however, refused,
citing the fatigue of the troops and the hardship of the people.
Mèng Zhīxiáng acted only after assessing his capabilities,
which is why he was able to rule over the Three Shǔ.
30th. Ān Chónghuì, the Hùguó Jiédùshǐ and concurrent Zhōngshū Lìng, felt uneasy and
submitted a memorial requesting to resign from office.
Intercalary month.
*Gēngyín* day.
An imperial decree appointed him Tàizǐ Tàishī in retirement.
On this day,
his sons Chóngzàn and Chóngxù fled to Hézhōng.
On *rénchén* day,
Lǐ Cóngzhāng, the Bǎoyì Jiédùshǐ, was appointed Hùguó Jiédùshǐ.
On *jiǎwǔ* day,
Yào Yànchóu, the Bùjūn Zhǐhuīshǐ, was dispatched to lead troops to Hézhōng.
Swayed by slanderous words,
he dispatched Yào Yànchóu with troops to suppress Ān Chónghuì.
Ān Chóngzàn and others arrived in Hézhōng.
Chónghuì was shocked and said:
"How did you manage to come?"
Then he said:
"I understand now.
This is not his intention;
he is being used by others.
Qú
is like saying *tā* (he/him).
What more can be said!"
Thereupon, he seized his two sons and sent a memorial presenting them to the court.
The next day,
a palace envoy arrived,
met Chónghuì,
and wept for a long time.
Chónghuì asked him why.
The palace envoy said:
"People say that Your Excellency has rebellious intentions,
and the court has already dispatched Yào Yànchóu with troops."
Chónghuì said:
"I have received the nation's grace,
and death is not enough to repay it. How dare I have rebellious intentions!
To trouble the state further by deploying troops,
and to cause worry to the Emperor,
my crime would be even greater."
Chóngzàn and others arrived in Shǎn,
and an imperial decree ordered them imprisoned.
Zhái Guāngyè, the Huángchéng Shǐ, had long disliked Chónghuì.
The Emperor dispatched him to Hézhōng to investigate,
saying:
"If Chónghuì indeed has rebellious intentions, then execute him."
Historians say that the Emperor did not have a firm intention to kill Chónghuì.
The death of Guō Chóngtāo was also similar.
With no moral principles at the top
and no legal adherence below,
it is no wonder this happened.
Lǐ Cóngzhāng surrounded his residence with armored soldiers,
and entered alone to see Chónghuì,
bowing in the courtyard.
Chónghuì was surprised,
descended the steps, and returned the bow. Cóngzhāng then wielded a club and struck him on the head.
His wife, Lady Zhāng, cried out to save him
and was also beaten to death.
The *Kǎoyì* (Textual Variations) states: The Wǔdài Shǐ (History of the Five Dynasties) has a missing passage:
"Lǐ Cóngzhāng wielded a club and struck Chónghuì to the ground.
Chónghuì said:
'I have no regrets about my death,
but I regret not being able to execute Lù Wáng with the Emperor.
He will surely become a future threat to the court.'
He died as he finished speaking."
However, Chónghuì wanted to kill Cóngkē out of personal grudge.
At that time, Cóngkē had not yet shown any signs of arrogance,
so how could Chónghuì have known he would become a threat to the court?
This is likely a statement invented by those who praised Chónghuì after the usurpation of Qīngtài,
and it is not credible.
The memorial arrived.
*Jǐhài* day.
An imperial decree was issued,
accusing Chónghuì of the crime of alienating Mèng Zhīxiáng, Dǒng Zhāng, and Qián Liú,
and also falsely accusing him of wanting to personally attack Huáinán to seize military power,
based on Biān Yànwēn's accusations.
He and his two sons were executed.
31st, *bǐngwǔ* day.
The Emperor dispatched Sū Yuàn, the Xīchuān Jìnzòuguān, and Liú Chéng, a military commander from Dōngchuān,
each back to their respective prefectures,
informing them that Ān Chónghuì had acted arbitrarily
and raised troops to attack, but had now been punished for his crime.
32nd, Sixth month.
*Yǐchǒu* day.
Lǐ Cóngkē was again appointed Tóng Píngzhāng Shì,
and concurrent Xīdū Liúshǒu.
After Chónghuì's death,
Lǐ Cóngkē was again appointed to guard Cháng'ān.
33rd, *bǐngzǐ* day.
It was decreed that land taxes for common people be equalized across all circuits.
34 Mǐn Wáng Yánjūn (閩王延鈞) was fond of the arts of immortals.
The Daoist Chén Shǒuyuán (陳守元) and the shaman Xú Yànlín (徐彥林), together with
Shèng Tāo (盛韜), jointly lured him into building the Bǎohuáng Gōng (寶皇宮),
which was extremely grand in construction.
Xuē Shǐ (薛史) records: In Fúzhōu (福州) city, there were the Wáng Bà Tán (王霸壇) and the Liàndān Jǐng (鍊丹井).
Next to the altar was a honeylocust tree,
which had been long withered,
but suddenly sprouted branches and leaves one day.
A white turtle emerged from the well,
and digging into the ground, a stone inscription was found,
bearing the text
"Descendant of Wáng Bà (王霸)".
Chǎng (昶) believed it referred to himself,
and built the Bǎohuáng Gōng (寶皇宮) beside the altar.
Hǎo (好), hū dào fān (呼到翻).
Chén Shǒuyuán (陳守元) and Shèng Tāo (盛韜) and others were believed,
and Xuē Wénjié (薛文傑) was able to carry out his deceit and madness.
The history states that Mǐn's (閩) government became even more chaotic from then on.
35 In autumn,
the ninth month,
on the day Jǐhài (己亥),
Dōngdān Mùhuá (東丹慕華) was again granted the Han surname and given name Lǐ Zànhuá (李贊華).
In the third month of this year, Mùhuá (慕華) was given a name;
now he was again granted a surname.
36 Xú Zhījiàn (徐知諫), the Military Commissioner of Zhènnán (鎮南) and Concurrently Grand Councillor, passed away.
Xú Zhīxún (徐知詢), Vice Supreme Commander of All Circuits, Military Commissioner of Zhènhǎi (鎮海), and acting Grand Secretary, replaced him,
and was enfeoffed as Dōnghǎi Jùnwáng (東海郡王).
When Xú Zhīgào (徐知誥) summoned Zhīxún (知詢) to the court,
the event can be found in the previous scroll, Tiānchéng (天成) four years.
Zhīxún (知詢) encountered his funeral procession on the road.
Zhījiàn's (知諫) funeral procession was returning from Hóngzhōu (洪州),
while Zhīxún (知詢) was going to Hóngzhōu (洪州),
hence they met on the road.
"Brother, your intentions are thus,
I have no regrets either,
but how can I face the late king underground!"
The late king refers to Xú Wēn (徐溫).
37 On the day Xīnchǒu (辛丑),
Fàn Yánguāng (范延光), Commissioner of Military Affairs, was promoted to Concurrently Grand Councillor.
38 On the day Xīnhài (辛亥),
an imperial edict ordered the release of falcons and eagles from the Five Hunting Parks,
and no one, internal or external, was allowed to present them again.
Féng Dào (馮道) said:
"Your Majesty can be said to extend benevolence to birds and beasts."
The Emperor said:
"Not so.
I once followed Wǔ Huáng (武皇) on a hunt;
Wǔ Huáng (武皇) is the posthumous title of Jìn Wáng Kèyòng (晉王克用).
A beast escaped into the fields,
and cavalry were sent to retrieve it.
By the time the beast was caught,
little of the remaining crops was left.
Thinking of this,
hunting does harm but no good,
so I do not do it."
39 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Dīngmǎo (丁卯),
Lǐ Jìntáng (李進唐), Commander of Yángzhōu (洋州), attacked and
captured Tōngzhōu (通州).
Yángzhōu (洋州) is seven hundred thirty-nine li southeast of Tōngzhōu (通州).
Earlier,
the people of Shǔ (蜀) had once taken Tōngzhōu (通州),
so they attacked and captured it again.
In the second year of Gāndé (乾德) of the Sòng (宋) dynasty, Tōngzhōu (通州) was renamed Dázhōu (達州),
because Huáinán (淮南) also had a Tōngzhōu (通州).
40 On the day Rénwǔ (壬午),
Wáng Yánzhèng (王延政) was appointed Governor of Jiànzhōu (建州).
41 In the eleventh month,
on the first day Jiǎshēn (甲申),
there was a solar eclipse.
42 On the day Guǐsì (癸巳),
Sū Yuàn (蘇愿) arrived in Chéngdū (成都).
Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥), hearing that his nephews and nieces at the court were all safe,
sent an envoy to inform Dǒng Zhāng (董璋),
wishing to jointly submit a memorial to apologize.
Zhāng (璋) angrily said:
"Mèng Gōng's (孟公) relatives are all intact,
so it is natural for him to return to allegiance;
Zhāng (璋) has already suffered clan extermination,"
referring to the court's execution of his son Dǒng Guāngyè (董光業) and his clan.
"The imperial edicts are all in Sū Yuàn's (蘇愿) belly;
how could Liú Chéng'ān (劉澄安) have known in advance?
Does Zhāng (璋) not know this?!"
From then on, they became enemies again.
This laid the groundwork for Dǒng Zhāng's (董璋) defeat and death in the attack on Xīchuān (西川).
Fù (復), fú yòu fān (扶又翻).
43 On the day Yǐwèi (乙未),
Lǐ Rénhǎn (李仁罕) led his troops back to Chéngdū (成都) from Kuízhōu (夔州).
Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥), having completely gained the territories of Kuí (夔) and Qián (黔) from former Shǔ (蜀),
did not advance further east.
44 Xú Zhīgào (徐知誥), Grand Secretary of Wú (吳), submitted a memorial stating that he had assisted in government for many years
and requested to retire to Jīnlíng (金陵).
Thereupon, Zhīgào (知誥) was appointed Military Commissioner of Zhènhǎi (鎮海) and Níngguó (寧國),
stationed in Jīnlíng (金陵),
with his other offices remaining as before,
overseeing all court affairs as in the precedent of Xú Wēn (徐溫).
Xú Wēn (徐溫) was first stationed in Jīngkǒu (京口),
overseeing the government of the Wú (吳) court,
then moved to Jīnlíng (金陵).
Cháo (朝), zhí yáo fān (直遙翻).
Jing (景通) was appointed Chief of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside, Left and Right,
remaining in Jiāngdū (江都) to assist in government.
Xú Zhīgào (徐知誥) followed the footsteps of Xú Wēn (徐溫),
and Jǐngtōng (景通) followed the footsteps of Zhīgào (知誥),
and thus the Wú (吳) dynasty's mandate shifted to the Lǐ (李) clan.
Sòng Qíqiū (宋齊丘) was appointed concurrently Minister of the Palace Secretariat and Right Grand Master of Remonstrance,
and concurrently Minister of the Central Secretariat,
both with the title Concurrently Grand Councillor,
and concurrently Commissioner of Internal Military Affairs,
to assist Jǐngtōng (景通).
Zhāng Chóng (張崇), Military Commissioner of Déshèng (德勝), was granted the title Qīnghé Wáng (清河王).
Wú (吳) established the Déshèng (德勝) army in Lúzhōu (廬州).
The people of the prefecture suffered from him,
and he often visited the court,
lavishly bribing influential figures,
thus he was always able to return to his post,
causing trouble for Lúzhōu (廬州) for more than twenty years.
45 In the twelfth month,
on the first day Jiǎyín (甲寅),
common people were first allowed to cast their own farm tools and other iron implements.
According to Wǔdài Huìyào (五代會要), "other iron implements" refer to cooking utensils and various movable items.
Wrought iron was also permitted for common people to refine themselves.
Xú Wúdǎng (徐無黨) said: The tax on farm tools,
continues to this day.
Three cash for farm tools are paid in summer and autumn.
46 Mǎ Xīshēng (馬希聲), Military Commissioner of Wǔ'ān (武安) and Jìngjiāng (靜江), heard that Liáng Tàizǔ (梁太祖) loved eating chicken,
and emulated him.
After succeeding to his position,
he slaughtered fifty chickens daily for his meals;
during mourning, he showed no signs of grief.
On the day Gēngshēn (庚申),
Wǔmù Wáng (武穆王) was buried in Héngyáng (衡陽).
Mǎ Yīn (馬殷) was given the posthumous title Wǔmù Wáng (武穆王).
Héngyáng (衡陽) was originally Hàn (漢) Zhēngyáng (蒸陽) county;
Wú (吳) established Línzhēng (臨蒸) county from it;
Suí (隋) renamed Línzhēng (臨蒸) county to Héngyáng (衡陽) county;
Táng (唐) belonged to Héngzhōu (衡州)
and was its administrative seat.
He ate several plates of chicken at once.
Pān Qǐ (潘起), former Assistant Minister of Personnel, satirized him, saying:
"In the past, Ruǎn Jí (阮籍) ate steamed pork during mourning;
Ruǎn Jí (阮籍) of Jìn (晉) acted according to his feelings, unrestrained, yet was extremely filial.
When his mother died,
on the verge of burial,
he ate one steamed pork,
drank two dou of wine,
and then, at the moment of parting,
directly said,
'It's over!'
He let out a cry,
vomited several sheng of blood,
and became so emaciated that only bones remained,
almost to the point of losing his life.
However, this cannot be taught as a model."
47 On the day Guǐhài (癸亥),
Xú Zhīgào (徐知誥) arrived in Jīnlíng (金陵).
48 Zhào Tíngyǐn (趙廷隱), Acting Military Commissioner of Zhāowǔ (昭武), informed Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥) that the city walls and moats of Lìzhōu (利州) were complete.
Previously, in Jiànzhōu (劍州), he shared merits with Lǐ Zhào (李肇), Assistant Commander of the Imperial Army.
The event is found in the eleventh month of the previous year.
Zhīxiáng (知祥) praised and consoled him, but did not allow it.
Tíngyǐn (廷隱) declined three times.
On the day Guǐyǒu (癸酉),
Zhīxiáng (知祥) summoned Tíngyǐn (廷隱) back to Chéngdū (成都),
and appointed Zhào (肇) to replace him.
49 Chén Shǒuyuán (陳守元) and others of Mǐn (閩), claiming to be under the mandate of Bǎohuáng (寶皇),
told Mǐn Wáng Yánjūn (閩王延鈞):
"If you can relinquish your position and accept the Dao,
you will be emperor for sixty years."
Yánjūn (延鈞) believed them.
On the day Bǐngzǐ (丙子),
he ordered his son, the Deputy Military Commissioner Jìpéng (繼鵬), to take charge of the military government affairs.
Yánjūn (延鈞) relinquished his position and accepted the Daoist ordination,
taking the Daoist name Xuánxī (玄錫).
The Aìzhōu general, Yáng Tíngyì (楊廷藝), adopted three thousand foster sons,
plotting to retake Jiāozhōu (交州).
Lǐ Jìn (李進), the Hàn (漢) governor of Jiāozhōu, knew of this,
accepted his bribes,
and did not report it.
In this year,
Tíngyì raised an army and besieged Jiāozhōu.
According to the Geography Monograph of the Old Book of Táng (舊唐書地理志), Jiāozhōu extended west to the Xiǎohuángjiāng (小黃江) estuary on the Aìzhōu (愛州) border,
a water journey of 416 lǐ (里).
When [Tíngyì's army]
had not yet arrived,
the city fell.
Lǐ Jìn fled back,
and the Hàn ruler executed him.
[The Hàn general, Zhǎolín] Bǎo (寶), besieged Jiāozhōu.
Tíngyì came out to fight,
and Bǎo was defeated and killed.
Last year, Hàn took Jiāozhōu,
but now lost it again.
In spring,
the first month,
the Grand Councilor, Fàn Yánguāng (范延光), said:
"From Língzhōu (靈州) to Fāngqúzhèn (方渠鎮) in Bīnzhōu (邠州) —
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Tōngyuǎnjūn (通遠軍) was originally Fāngqúzhèn in Língzhōu.
In the fourth year of Tiānfú (天福) of Jìn (晉), it was changed to Wēizhōu (威州),
and the two garrisons of Mùbō (木波) and Mǎlíng (馬嶺) were then assigned to it.
In the second year of Guǎngshùn (廣順) of Zhōu (周), it was renamed Huánzhōu (環州) to avoid a taboo.

Mèng Zhīxiáng, considering the court's generous favor,

Sāi (塞) is pronounced Sè (悉則).
wished to send an envoy to submit a memorial via the Xiágōng (峽江) waterway.

In the second month,
Zhào Jìliáng (趙季良) and the generals discussed sending the Zhaōwǔ (昭武) Dūjiān (都監) from Tàiyuán (太原), Gāo Yànchóu (高彥儔), to lead troops to attack Bìzhōu (壁州).
The Geography Monograph of the Old Book of Táng states: Bìzhōu's Nuòshuǐ (諾水) County

During the Liáng (梁) dynasty, Xuānhàn was divided to establish Shǐníng (始寧) County.
During the Yuán Wèi (元魏) dynasty, Shǐníng was divided to establish Nuòshuǐ County.
In the early Wǔdé (武德) era of Táng,
Bìzhōu was established by dividing Shǐníng of Bādōng (巴東),
with its seat in Nuòshuǐ.
During the Sòng (宋) dynasty, Bìzhōu was abolished,
and its territory was incorporated into Zēngkǒu (曾口) and Tōngjiāng (通江) Counties of Bāzhōu (巴州).
"The various prefectures behind the mountains"
refers to Bā (巴), Péng (蓬), Guǒ (果), and other prefectures.
Lǐ Hào said:

Mèng Zhīxiáng's ancestral tombs were in Lónggāng (龍岡) County, Xíngzhōu (邢州),
and his nephews and nieces were all serving in the court at that time.
—what use is Bìzhōu?"
Zhīxiáng then desisted.
Jìliáng henceforth disliked Hào.
On the day Xīnwèi (辛未),
it was first ordered that the Guózǐjiān (國子監) (Directorate of Education) proofread the Nine Classics
and engrave them for printing and sale.
The printing and sale of the Nine Classics began here.
Yào Yànchóu and others reported defeating nineteen Dǎngxiàng tribes

Gāo Cónghuì (高從誨) was granted the title Bóhǎiwáng (勃海王).
Xú Zhīgào (徐知誥) of Wú (吳) built the Lǐxiányuàn (禮賢院) in his official residence,

He invited scholars and officials,

Mèng Zhīxiáng sent envoys three times to persuade Dǒng Zhāng,

Zhāng did not comply.
In the third month,
on the day Xīnchǒu (辛丑),

When Zhāng saw Hào,

Hào returned

"Zhāng is not open to discussion—

You should be prepared for him."
On the day Jiǎchén (甲辰),
Mǐnwáng (閩王) Yánjūn (延鈞) was restored to his position.
Wáng Yánjūn had abdicated his position and undergone Taoist rituals,
as mentioned in the previous year.
Wúyuè (吳越) Wǔsùwáng (武肅王) Qián Liú (錢鏐) fell ill

"My illness will surely be fatal.
All my sons are foolish and weak.
Who can be the commander?"
The crowd wept and said:
"The commander of the two garrisons is benevolent, filial, and meritorious;

In the third year of Tiānchéng (天成), Qián Liú conferred the two garrisons upon Chuán Guàn (傳瓘),
as mentioned in the previous volume.
According to this, in the autumn of this year,
the court first added the title Zhōngshūlìng (中書令) to Chuán Guàn.
His subordinates merely called him that [prematurely].
The seal
refers to the seal of Wúyuè Kingdom and the seals of Zhènhǎi (鎮海) and Zhèndōng (鎮東).
The keys
refer to the keys for all gates of the inner and outer cities and the palace gates.
"The generals and officials promote you;

At that time, the Middle Kingdom often changed dynasties every few years.
Qián Liú's intention
was probably that, being based in a corner,
he understood the importance of serving the great power.
If the Middle Kingdom had a ruler,
then one should serve him as a subject.
As for its rise and fall,
"I do not inquire."
He was 81 years old
on the day Gēngxū (庚戌).
Chuán Guàn mourned with his brothers under the same tent.
The commander of the Inner Guards, Lù Rénzhāng (陸仁章), said:

Although Lù Rénzhāng was unlearned,
his actions tacitly coincided with those of Zhào Xī (趙熹).
Only Rénzhāng had repeatedly offended him with affairs.
At this point,
Chuán Guàn praised him.
Rénzhāng said:

Wúyuè was founded

He exempted rent and taxes for abandoned and unowned farmland.
"Abandoned" refers to land that has an owner but is not cultivated;

with Shěn Sōng (沈崧), the Deputy Commissioner of Agrarian Affairs for western Zhè (浙), in charge.
The 內牙指揮使 (Commander of the Palace Guards), 劉仁章 (Liú Rénzhāng) of 富陽 (Fùyáng),
富陽縣 (Fùyáng Xiàn) was originally 漢 (Hàn)'s 富春縣 (Fùchūn Xiàn).
During the 晉 (Jìn) dynasty, to avoid the taboo name of Empress Dowager 鄭 (Zhèng), it was renamed 富陽 (Fùyáng).
Later generations continued this name.
The 九域志 (Jiǔyù Zhì) states: 富陽縣 (Fùyáng Xiàn) belongs to 杭州 (Hángzhōu),
73 *lǐ* southwest of the prefecture.
仁章 (Rénzhāng)'s nature was unyielding,

One day,

saying:

The 錢 (Qián) family originally resided in 臨安 (Lín'ān).

Summer,
4th month,
on the day *guǐhài* (癸亥),

hundreds of Emperor Zhuangzong's (莊宗) palace women were all ordered to return to their families.

Emperor Mingzong (明宗), considering 夏魯奇 (Xià Lǔqí) to be of the same clan,
ordered her to return to him.
Now she is married to 贊華 (Zànhuá).
妻 (qī),

Lady 夏 (Xià) could not bear his cruelty,
and requested a divorce to become a nun.

宋王 (Sòng Wáng) 從厚 (Cónghòu) was additionally given the concurrent title of 中書令 (Zhōngshūlìng) (Grand Chancellor).
14 董璋 (Dǒng Zhāng), the 東川節度使 (Dōngchuān Jiédùshǐ) (Military Commissioner of Dōngchuān), gathered his generals to plot an attack on Chéngdū (成都).
They all said it would surely be victorious.
However, 王暉 (Wáng Huī), the former 陵州刺史 (Língzhōu Cìshǐ) (Prefect of Língzhōu), said:
"Jiànnán (劍南) spans thousands of *lǐ*, and Chéngdū (成都) is vast.
It is now the height of summer,
and the army is without a just cause.
There will certainly be no success."
孟知祥 (Mèng Zhīxiáng), hearing this,
dispatched 馬軍都指揮使 (Mǎjūn Dūzhīhuǐshǐ) (Commander of the Cavalry) 潘仁嗣 (Pān Rénsì) with three thousand men to 漢州 (Hànzhōu) to scout the situation.
董璋 (Dǒng Zhāng)'s army entered the territory,
captured 白楊林鎮 (Báiyánglín Zhèn).
白楊林鎮 (Báiyánglín Zhèn) should be on the border of 漢州 (Hànzhōu).
His momentum was very strong.
孟知祥 (Mèng Zhīxiáng) was worried.
趙季良 (Zhào Jìliáng) said:

Now that he does not defend his home base,
it is to your advantage.
璋 (Zhāng)'s elite forces are all in his vanguard.
You should use weak troops to lure them,
and strong troops to await them.
Although there may be a small setback at first,
there will surely be a great victory later.
This is Sun Bin's (孫臏) strategy of 'three chariots.'
From ancient times, many have achieved victory with this.
Chǔ (楚) used it to defeat the Wú (吳) army and destroy Shūjiū (舒鳩).
Zhōu Fǎng (周訪) used it to defeat Dù Zēng (杜曾) and pacify Xiāng (襄) and Miǎn (沔).
Wáng Màozhāng (王 Màozhāng) used it to slay Zhū Yǒuníng (Zhū Yǒuníng).
Their strategies all stem from this.
羸 (léi),
pronounced like 倫為 (lún wéi).
衄 (nǜ),
pronounced like 女六 (nǚ liù).
Now that the army has arrived suddenly,
people's hearts are fearful.
You should personally go out to resist them,

saying:
"璋 (Zhāng) is rash and lacks strategy;
his army will surely be defeated.
I will capture him for you."
On the day *xīnsì* (辛巳),

5th month,
on the day *rénwǔ shuò* (壬午朔),
廷隱 (Tíngyǐn) entered to take his leave.
董璋 (Dǒng Zhāng)'s official summons arrived,

Therefore, he first tried to entice them with letters.
李仁罕 (Lǐ Rénhǎn) had never worked with him,

遺 (wèi),
pronounced like 唯季 (wéi jì).

"Why are these men exposing themselves in the midday sun!"

Hóng Mài said: Táng Jìedù would hold concurrent inspectorate titles.

From Xī and Zhāo onwards,
the regional warlords became powerful,
and military men gained influence.
As soon as they established their authority,
their ranks were already high,
and thus they were further promoted to Tàibǎo, Tàifù, Tàiwèi.
Above that, there was only Tàishī,
which is why commanders were all called Tàiwèi.
I observe that according to Táng regulations,
Tàishī, Tàifù, Tàibǎo were the Three Masters,
and Tàiwèi, Sītú, Sīkōng were the Three Dukes.
Tàiwèi historically commanded troops,
so generals were called Tàiwèi.
In the late Táng,
regional warlords also sometimes received the title of Tàishī.
From the end of Ruìzōng's reign in Táng,
Jìedùshǐ were established in frontier garrisons,
such as Xuē Nà, who already held the later positions of Shǐxiàng;
those holding concurrent titles of Yùshǐ Dàfū, Zhōngchéng, the Six Cáo Shàngshū,
Púyè, Shìzhōng, Zhōngshū Lìng
were frequently seen.
Lǐ Sù, as commander of Táng, Dèng, Suí,
held the concurrent title of Sànqí Chángshì due to his junior seniority.
Hóng's explanation is not entirely accurate.
What happened?"
Wáng Zhāng wept and could not answer.
When he reached his residence
and was about to eat,
Wáng Huī, along with Wáng Zhāng's nephew, Yán Hào, the Yánèi Dūyúhòu, led three hundred soldiers in with a great clamor.
Wáng Zhāng took his wife and children and ascended the city wall.
His son, Guāngsì, committed suicide.
Wáng Zhāng reached the North Gate tower
and called out to Pān Chóu, the Zhīhuīshǐ, to suppress the mutinous soldiers.
Pān Chóu led ten soldiers up the wall,
beheaded Wáng Zhāng,
and also took Guāngsì's head to Wáng Huī.
Wáng Huī opened the city gates to welcome the surrender.
Zhào Tíngyǐn entered Zīzhōu
and sealed the government storehouses to await Mèng Zhīxiáng.
Upon hearing of Wáng Zhāng's defeat,
Lǐ Zhào then beheaded Wáng Zhāng's envoy to report the news.
Lǐ Zhào played both sides;
only upon hearing of Wáng Zhāng's defeat did he behead his envoy.
On the Bǐngxū day,
Mèng Zhīxiáng entered Chéngdū.
On the Dīnghài day,
he again led eight thousand troops to Zīzhōu.
When he reached Xīndū,
the Jiǔyù Zhì states: Xīndū Xiàn is forty-five lǐ north of Chéngdū Fǔ.
Fù,
pronounced Fúyòu.

he departed from Xuánwǔ.
The Jiù Tángshū Dìlǐ Zhì states: Xuánwǔ was Hàn Dīdào Xiàn,

The Jiǔyù Zhì states: In the fifth year of Dàzhōng Xiángfú of the Sòng dynasty, it was renamed Zhōngjiāng Xiàn,
ninety lǐ west of Zīzhōu.

16 on *rénchén* (壬辰) day,
Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥) became ill.
On *guǐsì* (癸巳) day,
his illness worsened.
Wáng Chǔhuí (王處回), the deputy commander of the central gate, attended to him.
When the chef brought in food,
the utensils would always be empty when taken out,

Lǐ Rénhǎn (李仁罕) came from Suìzhōu (遂州),

Bǎnqiáo (板橋) is southeast of Zǐzhōu (梓州).
He insulted and humiliated Tíngyǐn (廷隱),

On *yǐwèi* (乙未) day,
Zhīxiáng (知祥)'s illness subsided;
on *dīngyǒu* (丁酉) day,
he entered Zǐzhōu (梓州).
On *wùxū* (戊戌) day,
he rewarded the officers and soldiers.
After they had dispersed,
Zhīxiáng (知祥) said to Lǐ Rénhǎn (李仁罕) and Zhào Tíngyǐn (趙廷隱):
"Which of you two generals should garrison this place?"
Rénhǎn (仁罕) replied:
"If the *Lìnggōng* (令公) gives me Shǔzhōu (蜀州) again,
I will go."
Earlier,
the imperial court had appointed Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥) as *Zhōngshū Lìng* (中書令),
hence Lǐ Rénhǎn (李仁罕)'s address.
Rénhǎn (仁罕) had previously held Shǔzhōu (蜀州).
Zhīxiáng (知祥) was astonished.
He withdrew
and ordered Lǐ Hào (李昊) to draft a document,
stating that if the two generals recommended someone, one person would be appointed *Liúhòu* (留後).
Hào (昊) said:
"In the past, Liángzǔ (梁祖) and Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) both concurrently held four garrisons.
Grand Ancestor of Liáng (梁太祖) held the four garrisons of Xuānwǔ (宣武), Xuānyì (宣義), Tiānpíng (天平), and Hùguó (護國).
Zhuāngzōng (莊zōng) held the four garrisons of Hédōng (河東), Wèibó (魏博), Lúlóng (盧龍), and Chéngdé (成德).
It would be more convenient for you to take charge yourself.
You should return to the prefectural seat quickly."
The prefectural seat
refers to Chéngdū (成都),
where the headquarters of Xīchuān (西川) were located.
Zhào Púshè (趙僕射)
refers to Zhào Jìliáng (趙季良).
17 On *jǐhài* (己亥) day,
Dieluó Qīng (迭羅卿), an envoy from Qìdān (契丹), took leave to return to his country.
The emperor said:
"My ambition is to secure the border,
so I cannot but somewhat fulfill their request."
He then sent Cè Gǔshèlì (萴骨舍利) to return with him.
As Qìdān (契丹) did not get Cè Lá (萴剌),
from then on they frequently raided Yúnzhōu (雲州) and Zhènwǔ (振武).
18 Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥) ordered Lǐ Rénhǎn (李仁罕) to return to Suìzhōu (遂州),
and kept Zhào Tíngyǐn (趙廷隱) as the patrol inspector of Dōngchuān (東川),
appointing Lǐ Hào (李昊) to manage the affairs of Zǐzhōu (梓州) military prefecture.
Hào (昊) said:
"The two tigers are fighting;
I dare not accept the order.
I wish to return with you."
So Wáng Yànzhū (王彥銖), the Chief Officer of the Army Headquarters, was appointed as the supervisor of Dōngchuān (東川).
On *guǐmǎo* (癸卯) day,
Zhīxiáng (知祥) arrived in Chéngdū (成都).
Zhào Tíngyǐn (趙廷隱) soon also led his troops back west.
Zhīxiáng (知祥) said to Lǐ Hào (李昊):
"My acquisition of Dōngchuān (東川) has deepened my troubles."
Hào (昊) asked for the reason.
Zhīxiáng (知祥) said:
"Since I left Zǐzhōu (梓州),
I have received seven memorials from Rénhǎn (仁罕),
all stating, 'You should personally take charge of Dōngchuān (東川);
otherwise, the generals will not submit.'
Tíngyǐn (廷隱) said, 'I originally did not dare to take Dōngchuān (東川),
but because Rénhǎn (仁罕) was unyielding,
I developed a desire to contend.'
Please explain to Tíngyǐn (廷隱) for me,
and restore Lángzhōu (閬州) as Bǎoníng Jūn (保寧軍).
Dǒng Zhāng (董璋) had taken Lángzhōu (閬州) and abolished Bǎoníng Jūn (保寧軍).
Now Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥) reinstated it as a *jiézhèn* (節鎮)
to reward Zhào Tíngyǐn (趙廷隱).
Go and garrison it.
I will personally take charge of Dōngchuān (東川)
to end Rénhǎn (仁罕)'s hopes."
Tíngyǐn (廷隱) was still not content,
and requested to fight Rénhǎn (仁罕),
with the winner taking Dōngchuān (東川).
Hào (昊) deeply persuaded him,
and only then did he accept the order.
In the sixth month,
Tíngyǐn (廷隱) was made *Bǎoníng Liúhòu* (保寧留後).
On *wùwǔ* (戊午) day,
Zhào Jìliáng (趙季良), leading the generals and officials, requested Zhīxiáng (知祥) to concurrently govern Dōngchuān (東川).
He agreed.
Jìliáng (季良) and others also requested Zhīxiáng (知祥) to assume the title of King
and to provisionally issue imperial edicts
to reward meritorious officials.
He refused.
When Dǒng Zhāng (董璋)
attacked Zhīxiáng (知祥),
Wáng Sītóng (王思同), the *Jiédùshǐ* (節度使) of Shānnán Xīdào (山南西道), reported it to the throne.
Fàn Yánguāng (范延光) said to the emperor:
"If the two Chuans unite under one rebel,
consolidating forces and holding strongholds,
it will be even more difficult to take them.
It is advisable to act quickly while they are contending."
The emperor ordered Sītóng (思同) to secretly plan an advance with the troops from Xīngyuán (興元).
The troops from Xīngyuán (興元) were not sufficient for an advance,
nor was Wáng Sītóng (王思同)'s talent sufficient for an advance.
Liú Yè (劉曄) had calculated that no Wei (魏) minister could contend with Liú Bèi (劉備) and Sūn Quán (孫權),
which is why he was cautious about using troops.
Hearing of Zhāng (璋)'s defeat and death,
Yánguāng (延光) said:

If Your Majesty does not condescend to pacify him,

The emperor said:
"Zhīxiáng (知祥) is my old friend.
He has been alienated to this extent.
How can I not condescend?"
"Alienated"
probably refers to Ān Zhònghuǐ (安重誨).
Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥) originally had the ambition to seize Shu (蜀).
Even if Zhònghuǐ (重誨) had not fostered suspicion,

Míngzōng (明宗) probably did not fully perceive Zhīxiáng (知祥)'s intentions.
*Jiàn* (間) is pronounced *gǔ xiàn* (古莧).
Wáng Huái (王褱),

"Dǒng Zhāng (董璋) is a fox and a wolf."

"Maintain the great principle of ruler and minister."
Wáng Huái (王褱) was saved.

11 Xú Zhīgào (徐知誥) of Wú (吳) expanded the city of Jīnlíng (金陵) to a circumference of twenty *lǐ*.
Xú Wēn (徐溫) had already built Jīnlíng (金陵),

12 Initially,
after the Qìdān (契丹) grew strong,
they repeatedly plundered all prefectures of Lúlóng (盧龍),
and outside the gates of Yōuzhōu (幽州) city, barbarian cavalry were abundant.
Whenever grain was transported from Zhuōzhōu (涿州) into Yōuzhōu (幽州),

and plundered it.
According to the *Shuǐjīng* (水經),
in the former Āngù (故安) county of Zhuō (涿) Commandery of the Hàn (漢) dynasty, there was Yán (閻) Township,
and the Yìshuǐ (易水) originated from the mountains to its west.
Ōu (歐) History writes it as
"Yángōu" (鹽溝).
A city was built at Yángōu (閻溝) and garrisoned,
becoming Liángxiāng (良鄉) county.
Liángxiāng (良鄉) was
an ancient county of the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
Zhào Déjūn (趙德鈞) merely moved it to Yángōu (閻溝).
It should be known that Yángōu (閻溝) county is sixty *lǐ* north of Yān (燕),
and the old empty city of Liángxiāng (良鄉) is forty *lǐ* south of Zhuōzhōu (涿州).
It seems that after the Qìdān (契丹) took Yān (燕), they changed Liángxiāng (良鄉) county to Yángōu (閻溝) county,
and the so-called old empty city of Liángxiāng (良鄉) was the ancient city before Zhào Déjūn (趙德鈞) moved the county seat.
East of Yōuzhōu (幽州), beyond ten *lǐ*,
people dared not cut firewood or herd;
Zhào Déjūn (趙德鈞) built a city at Lù (潞) county, fifty *lǐ* east of the prefecture, and garrisoned it.
Lù (潞)
was an ancient county of the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
and belonged to Yōuzhōu (幽州) during the Táng (唐).
It should be known that two *lǐ* east of Lù (潞) county is the Lùhé (潞河) River,
and from Lù (潞) county west to Yān (燕) is sixty *lǐ*.
At this time,
he also built the city of Sānhé (三河) county over a hundred *lǐ* northeast of the prefecture to facilitate the transport route to Jìzhōu (薊州).
In the 4th year of Kāiyuán (開元) of Táng (唐),
Sānhé (三河) county was established by separating it from Lù (潞) county,
and belonged to Jìzhōu (薊zhou).
It should be known that Sānhé (三河) county is one hundred seventy *lǐ* west of Yān (燕),
and Jìzhōu (薊zhou) is seventy *lǐ* west of Sānhé (三河) county.
Zhào Déjūn (趙德鈞) repelled them.
In the ninth month,
on the first day of the Gēngchén (庚辰) moon,
a memorial reported the completion of the Sānhé (三河) city.
The border people relied on it.

Mǎ Xīfàn (馬希範) entered to succeed from Lǎngzhōu (朗州) as Military Governor of Zhènnán (鎮南).
Now he is made Military Governor of Wǔ'ān (武安),
which is a step towards his enfeoffment as King of Chǔ (楚).
14 Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥) ordered his son Mèng Rénzàn (孟仁贊) to serve as Acting Military Sīmǎ (司馬),
concurrently Commander-in-Chief of all cavalry and infantry within the two Chuan (川) garrisons.
15 In winter,
tenth month,
on the first day of the Jǐyǒu (己酉) moon,
the Emperor again sent Lǐ Cúnkuí (李存𫓧) to Chéngdū (成都).
In the seventh month of that year, Lǐ Cúnkuí (李存𫓧) had returned from Chéngdū (成都),
and now he was sent again.
"復" (fù)
is pronounced *fú yòu fān*;
it will not be the same below.
Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知xiáng) was allowed to appoint officials and then report to the throne.
The imperial court would no longer appoint anyone else.
Only the wives and children of the garrison troops were not sent away,
but the troops were not recalled either.
16 Qín (秦) King Lǐ Cóngróng (李從榮) enjoyed writing poetry,
gathering frivolous scholars like Gāo Niǎn (高輦) and others in his staff,
and composing poems with them,
often boasting about himself.
Whenever he held a banquet,
he would order his subordinates to compose poems.
If someone's poem was not to his liking, he would openly tear it up and discard it.
On the Rénzǐ (壬子) day,
Lǐ Cóngróng (李從榮) entered for an audience.
The Emperor said to him:
"Although I am not well-read,
I enjoy listening to scholars explain the meaning of the classics,
which broadens one's wisdom and thought.
I saw that Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) was fond of writing poetry;
as a general's son, literature was not his original habit,
he merely invited ridicule from others.
You should not imitate him."
The advice of Míngzōng (明宗) to his son
can be called famous words.
"好" (hào)
is pronounced *hū dào fān*.
"將" (jiàng)
is pronounced *jí liàng fān*.
17 On the Bǐngchén (丙辰) day,
Yōuzhōu (幽zhou) reported that the Qìdān (契丹) were camped at Nàlā Pō (捺剌泊).
At that time, Yōuzhōu (幽zhou) was prepared,
so the Qìdān (契丹) raids did not achieve their objective.
The Qìdān (契丹) ruler moved his nomadic camp westward,
dwelling at Nàlā Pō (捺剌泊),
and raided between Yún (雲) and Shuò (朔).
In Xuē (薛) History's Basic Annals,
in the eleventh month of this year,
Yúnzhōu (雲州) reported that the Qìdān (契丹) ruler was at Nàlā Pō (捺剌泊) south of Hēiyúlín (黑榆林), manufacturing siege equipment.
Thereafter, Shí Jìngtáng (石敬瑭) was stationed in Hédōng (河東),
and because the Qìdān (契丹) tribes were close to Yún (雲) and Yìng (應),
he used their military strength to seize the Central Plains,
and the sixteen prefectures of Yān (燕) and Yún (雲) all fell to the bow-wielding people of the north.
"捺" (nà)
is pronounced *nú gé fān*.
"剌" (là)
is pronounced *lái dá fān*.
18 The former Military Governor of Zhāngyì (彰義), Lǐ Jīnquán (李金全), repeatedly presented horses.
Lǐ Jīnquán (李金quán) had previously been stationed in Jīngzhōu (涇州).
The Emperor said:
"How was your governance when you were stationed there?
Do not just focus on presenting horses!"
Although Emperor Míngzōng (明宗) of Táng (唐) was of Hu (胡) origin,
these words
are indeed the words of a ruler.
"治" (zhì)
is pronounced *zhí lì fān*.
He was a Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) person.
19th year, Rénshēn
day, Kāng Chéng, Deputy Minister of Dá Lǐ Sì, submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard that children's rhymes are not the basis of good or ill fortune,
nor are omens of prosperity or decline the source!
Thus, when a hen pheasant crowed from a tripod and mulberries and grains grew in the court,
it could not stop the prosperity of the Yīn dynasty;
when a divine horse neighed loudly and a jade turtle announced a prognostication,
it could not prolong the duration of the Jìn dynasty.
In the second month of the 6th year of Yǒngjiā, during the reign of Jìn Huái Dì,
a divine horse neighed at the South City Gate.
During the reign of Wèi Míng Dì,
water surged from the Liǔgǔ River in Zhāngyè,
with omens of stone horses, stone oxen, and stone turtles,
which people took as a sign of the Jìn dynasty's rise.
There are six deeply fearful things: disharmony of Yīn and Yáng is not to be feared;
misalignment of the three luminaries is not to be feared;
the false rumors of petty men are not to be feared;
collapsing mountains and dried-up rivers are not to be feared;
insect pests harming the crops are not to be feared;
but worthy men hiding away is deeply fearful;
the common people changing occupations is deeply fearful;
superiors and subordinates mutually flattering each other is deeply fearful;
the disappearance of integrity and shame is deeply fearful;
praise and blame confusing the truth is deeply fearful;
and straightforward speech being ignored is deeply fearful.
As for what is not to be feared,
I wish Your Majesty would tolerate it and not discuss it;
as for what is deeply fearful,
I wish Your Majesty would rectify it without fault."
What Kāng Chéng called "not to be feared"
was not truly "not to be feared,"
but rather a direct statement that when human affairs are not handled properly,
the things to be feared are far worse than those merely causing apprehension.
However, his tone and manner were excessively dramatic,
which might lead the ruler to overlook unusual changes and disasters and fail to be vigilant,
so it was not a profound discourse.
20 Qín Wáng Cóngróng was a hawk-eyed person,
frivolous and impetuous;
"hawk-eyed" means
like a soaring hawk about to seize prey,
looking down with a sidelong glance at objects.
"Tiāo"
is pronounced tǔ diāo.
He again participated in court affairs,
and often acted arrogantly and lawlessly.
Originally,
when Ān Chónghuì was Commissioner of Military Affairs,
the Emperor solely entrusted him with responsibilities.
Cóngróng and Sòng Wáng Cónghòu had been intimate with him since infancy,
and although they commanded troops,
they were always controlled by Chónghuì,
and feared him.
After Chónghuì's death,
Ān Chónghuì was executed,
as seen in the second year of the previous volume.
Fàn Yánguāng and Zhào Yánshòu became Commissioners of Military Affairs,
but Cóngróng treated them with contempt.
Shí Jìngtáng, Military Governor of Héyáng and concurrently Administrator of the Affairs of the Secretariat-Chancellery, also served as Deputy Commander of the Six Armies and Various Guards.
His wife, Princess Yǒngníng, was Cóngróng's half-sister,
and they had always hated each other.
The histories do not record the mothers of Míng Zōng's other sons;
only Xǔ Wáng Cóngyì was born to Wáng Shú,
who was still young at the time.
All other children of age were born during his humble times.
(Cóngróng) particularly resented him;
the matter first appears in volume 276, Tiānchéng 3rd year.
Therefore, the rift was not outwardly visible.
Shí Jìngtáng did not wish to serve with Cóngróng;
Cóngróng managed the affairs of the Six Armies and Various Guards,
and Shí Jìngtáng was his deputy,
meaning they served together.
Fàn Yánguāng and Zhào Yánshòu also feared disaster,
repeatedly declined crucial positions,
and requested to alternate with veteran officials,
but the Emperor did not permit it.
Coincidentally, the Qìdān desired to invade,
and the Emperor ordered a military commander to be chosen to guard Hédōng.
Yánguāng and Yánshòu both said:
"Currently, the only commanders who can go are Shí Jìngtáng and Kāng Yìchéng."
Kāng Yìchéng rose from Dàiběi,
serving Jìn Wáng, Zhuāng Zōng, and the Emperor;
three generations were in the military,
but no merit was heard of,
except for assisting the Emperor in raising troops to march south during the Yèdū military chaos.
"Shuài"
is pronounced suǒ lèi;
same below.
The Emperor immediately ordered him appointed.
After receiving the edict,
(Shí Jìngtáng) did not lose his position as Deputy Commander of the Six Armies,
so Jìngtáng again declined.
The Emperor then appointed Zhū Hóngzhāo, the Commissioner of the Xuanhui Academy, to govern Shānnán Dōngdào,
replacing Yìchéng at the capital.
Kāng Yìchéng was then the Military Governor of Shānnán Dōngdào;
now he was summoned to the capital,
and Zhū Hóngzhāo was ordered to govern the military governorship in his place,
but not yet formally invested with the ceremonial staff.
21 In the eleventh month,
on the Xīnsì
day, Mèng Hú, Commissioner of the Three Bureaus, was appointed Military Governor of Zhōngwǔ;
Fēng Yūn, Military Governor of Zhōngwǔ, was appointed Commissioner of the Southern Branch of the Xuanhui Academy,
and concurrently managed the Three Bureaus.
Hú was originally a scribe,
and was very close with Fàn Yánguāng,
who was from Línzhāng, Xiāngzhōu.
Mèng Hú was from Wèizhōu.
Xiāng and Wèi were adjacent,
indicating the two were close when living in their hometowns.
Although the Emperor knew this was too quick,
he could not refuse.
22 On the Yǐyǒu
day, the Emperor, seeing the Hu barbarians pressing close to the northern frontier,
ordered immediate deliberation on a commander for Hédōng.
Shí Jìngtáng desired the post,
but Fàn Yánguāng and Zhào Yánshòu wanted to use Kāng Yìchéng,
and the discussion remained unresolved for a long time.
Lǐ Sōng, acting Scholar of the Bureau of Military Affairs, believed that none but Grand Commandant Shí would do.
Yánguāng said:
"I too have repeatedly memorialized for him to be used,
but the Emperor wishes to keep him as a palace guard."
Coincidentally, the Emperor sent an imperial envoy to hasten the decision,
and the assembly then followed Sōng's suggestion.
On the Dīnghài
day, Shí Jìngtáng was appointed Defender of Běijīng and Military Governor of Hédōng,
concurrently General Commander of Fān and Hàn cavalry and infantry of Dàtóng, Zhènwǔ, Zhāngguó, Wēisài, and other armies.
At the end of the Táng dynasty, the Dàtóng army was moved to Yúnzhōu, and the Zhènwǔ army to Shuòzhōu.
The Emperor was from Yìngzhōu,
so he established the Zhāngguó army in Yìngzhōu,
and subordinated the Xīngtáng army to Huánzhōu.
During Zhuāng Zōng's Tóngguāng 1st year, the Wēisài army was established in Xīnzhōu,
with the three prefectures of Guī, Rú, and Wǔ subordinated to it.
All four armies were military regions.
This laid the groundwork for Shí Jìngtáng to rely on Qìdān's support for Hédōng to obtain control of the Central Plains.
23 On the Jǐchǒu
day, Zhào Yánshòu, Commissioner of Military Affairs, was granted the concurrent title of Administrator of the Affairs of the Secretariat-Chancellery.
24 The Wú state appointed Xú Zhīgào, Grand Commander of all circuits, as Grand Chancellor and Grand Tutor,
additionally granting him the command of the Déshèng Military Governorship.
"Déshèng"
should be written as "Déshèng."
[Note: In the 11-line edition, it is indeed written as "Déshèng."]
The former King of Wú, Yáng Xíngmì, arose from Lúzhōu,
hence the Déshèng Military Governorship was established in Lúzhōu,
meaning to triumph through virtue.
25 Zhāng Jìngdá, Military Governor of Dàtóng, gathered troops at strategic points,
and the Qìdān ultimately dared not advance south and returned.
According to Xuē Shǐ, at that time the Qìdān tribal camps stretched from Hēiyúlín Nàlà Pò to Méiyuè Pò,
claiming to borrow water and grass from the Hàn border;
Zhāng Jìngdá gathered troops to block their vital passage,
and the barbarians ultimately dared not graze south.
"Huán"
is pronounced cóng xuān,
or as written.
He was from Dàizhōu.
26 Zhāng Yànchāo, Prefect of Yùzhōu, was originally a Shātuó man,
and had once been an adopted son of the Emperor,
having a rift with Shí Jìngtáng.
Hearing that Jìngtáng was appointed General Commander,
he offered his entire city to the Qìdān,
and the Qìdān appointed him Military Governor of Dàtóng.
27 When Shí Jìngtáng arrived in Jìnyáng,
he appointed his generals Liú Zhīyuǎn and Zhōu Huái as chief commanders of the guards,
entrusting them with his confidence;
military affairs were entrusted to Zhīyuǎn.
This laid the groundwork for Liú Zhīyuǎn to assist Shí Jìngtáng, and subsequently to establish the Hàn dynasty.
Zhōu Huái
was from Jìnyáng.
28 In the twelfth month,
on the Wùwǔ
day, Kāng Yìchéng was appointed Military Governor of Héyáng,
concurrently Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Guards (cavalry and infantry).
Yè Mèngdé's Shílín Yànyǔ states: From the Liáng dynasty, the position of Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Guards (cavalry and infantry) was established in the capital;
the Later Táng then established the position of Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Guards.
Zhū Hóngzhāo was then formally invested with the ceremonial staff of Xiāngyáng.
29 That year,
the Hàn Lord appointed his son Yào-Shū (耀樞) as Yōng-wáng (雍王),
Guī-Tú (龜圖) as Kāng-wáng (康王),
Hóng-Dù (弘度) as Bīn-wáng (賓王),
Hóng-Xī (弘熙)
as Jìn-wáng (晉王),
Hóng-Chāng (弘昌) as Yuè-wáng (越王),
Hóng-Bì (弘弼) as Qí-wáng (齊王),
Hóng-Yǎ (弘雅) as Sháo-wáng (韶王),
Hóng-Zé (弘澤) as Zhèn-wáng (鎮王),
Hóng-Cāo (弘操) as Wàn-wáng (萬王),
Hóng-Gǎo (弘杲) as Xún-wáng (循王),
Hóng-Wěi (弘暐) as Sī-wáng (思王),
Hóng-Miǎo (弘邈) as Gāo-wáng (高王),
Hóng-Jiǎn (弘簡) as Tóng-wáng (同王),
Hóng-Jiàn (弘建) as Yì-wáng (益王),
Hóng-Jì (弘濟) as Biàn-wáng (辯王),
Hóng-Dào (弘道) as Guì-wáng (貴王),
Hóng-Zhāo (弘昭) as Yí-wáng (宜王),
Hóng-Zhèng (弘政) as Tōng-wáng (通王),
Hóng-Yì (弘益) as Dìng-wáng (定王);
not long after,
Hóng-Dù (弘度) was transferred to be Qín-wáng (秦王).
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Wù-Zǐ (戊子),
Qín-wáng (秦王) Cóng-Róng (從榮) was given the additional titles of Shàng-Shū-Lìng (尚書令)
and concurrently Shì-Zhōng (侍中).
On the day Gēng-Yín (庚寅),
Liú Xù (劉昫), a scholar of the Duān-Míng-Diàn (端明殿) from Guī-Yì (歸義), was appointed Zhōng-Shū-Shì-Láng (中書侍郎) and Tóng-Píng-Zhāng-Shì (同平章事).
Guī-Yì (歸義) County was subordinate to Zhuō-Zhōu (涿州).
Xù (昫)
is pronounced xū-jù (吁句)
and also xǔ-yǔ (許羽).
2 There was a person from Mǐn (閩) who reported seeing a dragon at the True-Sealing (真封) Residence.
The True-Sealing (真封) Residence
was where Wáng Yán-Jūn (王延鈞) had resided before he obtained the state.
Jiàn (見)
is pronounced xián-biàn (賢遍).
He named the residence the Dragon Leap Palace (龍躍宮).
Thereupon, he proceeded to the Treasure Emperor Palace (寶皇宮) to receive the imperial rescript,
with full ceremonial guards,
entered the government office,
and ascended the throne as emperor.
He named his state Dà-Mǐn (大閩),
granted a general amnesty,
and changed the era name to Lóng-Qǐ (龍啟);
he also changed his name to Lín (璘).
He posthumously honored his father and grandfather
and established five ancestral temples.
He appointed his aide Lǐ Mǐn (李敏) as Zuǒ-Pú-Shè (左僕射) and Mén-Xià-Shì-Láng (門下侍郎),
and his son, the Jíe-Dù-Fù-Shǐ (節度副使) Jì-Péng (繼鵬), as Yòu-Pú-Shè (右僕射) and Zhōng-Shū-Shì-Láng (中書侍郎),
both concurrently holding the title of Tóng-Píng-Zhāng-Shì (同平章事);
he appointed his close attendant Wú Xù (吳勗) as Shū-Mì-Shǐ (樞密使).
The Táng (唐) envoys for the enfeoffment ceremony, Péi Jié (裴傑) and Chéng Kǎn (程侃), happened to arrive at Hǎi-Mén (海門).
Hǎi-Mén (海門)
is the Hǎi-Mén (海門) Town of the present-day Fú-Qīng (福清) County.
Kǎn (侃) earnestly requested to return north,
but was not permitted.
The Mǐn (閩) Lord considered his state small and its territory remote,
and always carefully served his four neighbors,
thus the territory within his borders was relatively peaceful.
The historian says that although the Mǐn (閩) Lord was deluded by divine immortals and absurdities,
he was able to maintain relative peace
because of his good neighborly relations.
3 In the second month,
on the day Wù-Shēn (戊申),
Mèng Zhī-Xiáng (孟知祥) issued a verbal edict appointing Zhào Jì-Liáng (趙季良) and others as Jíe-Dù-Shǐ (節度使) of five garrisons.
Mèng Zhī-Xiáng (孟知祥) requested imperial seals and axes for the five commanders,
but the imperial court equivocated and did not reply,
only allowing him to issue verbal edicts of appointment.
Thus, Zhī-Xiáng (知祥) proceeded to appoint the five commanders.
In the late Táng (唐) dynasty,
the powerful regional governors and fierce generals still knew the intrinsic value of the imperial court;
but as for Zhào Jì-Liáng (趙季良) and others,
they only knew to obey Mèng Zhī-Xiáng (孟知祥)'s orders.
How could they still value the imperial court's commands!
4 The commander of Liáng-Zhōu (涼州), Tuò-Bá Chéng-Qiān (拓跋承謙), and the elders submitted a memorial,
requesting that the acting commander Sūn Chāo (孫超) be appointed Jíe-Dù-Shǐ (節度使).
The emperor asked the envoy,
"Who is Chāo (超)?"
He replied,
"When Zhāng Yì-Cháo (張義潮) was in Hé-Xī (河西),
Zhāng Yì-Cháo (張義潮) brought Hé-Xī (河西) to allegiance; this event began in volume 249, Dà-Zhōng (大中) 5th year of Emperor Xuān-Zōng (宣宗) of Táng (唐).
Since the chaos of Huáng Cháo (黃巢),
Liáng-Zhōu (涼州) was cut off by the Dǎng-Xiàng (党項).
The people of Yún (鄆) gradually died out.
Chāo (超) and the people in the city are all their descendants."
5 On the day Yǐ-Mǎo (乙卯),
Mǎ Xī-Fàn (馬希範) was appointed Jíe-Dù-Shǐ (節度使) of Wǔ-Ān (武安) and Wǔ-Píng (武平).
Mǎ Xī-Fàn (馬希範) inherited the achievements of his father and brothers,
so the imperial court still appointed him to the two garrisons of Tán (潭) and Lǎng (朗).
6 On the day Wù-Wǔ (戊午),
the Jíe-Dù-Shǐ (節度使) of Dìng-Nán (定難), Lǐ Rén-Fú (李仁福), died;
on the day Gēng-Shēn (庚申),
the army installed his son Yí-Chāo (彞超) as Liú-Hòu (留後).
7 On the day Guǐ-Hài (癸亥),
Mèng Zhī-Xiáng (孟知祥) was appointed Jíe-Dù-Shǐ (節度使) of Dōng-Xī-Chuān (東西川) and King of Shǔ (蜀).
8 Previously,
all the garrisons west of the river (Hé-Xī, 河西) said that Lǐ Rén-Fú (李仁福) was secretly communicating with the Qì-Dān (契丹).
At this time, there were only two garrisons in Hé-Xī (河西): Liáng-Zhōu (涼州) and Shā-Zhōu (沙州);
however, communications were not always open.
I suspect
that "Hé-Xī" (河西)
should be
"Guān-Xī" (關西).
Ōu (歐) History simply states,
"Many border generals said Rén-Fú (仁福) communicated with the Qì-Dān (契丹),"
which is even more concise.
Xiān (先)
is pronounced xī-jiàn (悉薦).
He planned to annex the region west of the river (Hé-Yòu, 河右)
and invade Guān-Zhōng (關中) from the south.
Coincidentally, Rén-Fú (仁福) died.
In the third month,
on the day Guǐ-Wèi (癸未),
his son Yí-Chāo (彞超) was appointed Zhāng-Wǔ (彰武) Liú-Hòu (留後).
In the late Táng (唐), Bǎo-Sāi Army (保塞軍) was established in Yán-Zhōu (延州);
Qí (岐) was changed to Zhōng-Yì Army (忠義軍);
later Táng (唐) changed it to Zhāng-Wǔ Army (彰武軍).
Still, the Jíe-Dù-Shǐ (節度使) of Jìng-Sāi (靜塞), Yào Yàn-Chóu (藥彥稠), was ordered to lead an army of fifty thousand,
with the Gōng-Yuàn-Shǐ (宮苑使) Ān Zhòng-Yì (安重益) as supervisor,
to escort Cóng-Jìn (從進) to his post.
Cóng-Jìn (從進)
was from Suǒ-Gě (索葛).
9 On the day Yǐ-Yǒu (乙酉),
an edict was finally issued appointing Zhào Jì-Liáng (趙季良) and others as Jíe-Dù-Shǐ (節度使) of the five garrisons.
Since Mèng Zhī-Xiáng (孟知祥) had appointed them by verbal edict,
the imperial court could not contravene it,
and so issued an official edict.
10 On the day Dīng-Hài (丁亥),
an imperial edict was issued to the officers, soldiers, officials, and people of Xià (夏), Yín (銀), Suí (綏), and Yòu (宥),
stating that
"Xià-Zhōu (夏州) is a remote frontier,
and Lǐ Yí-Chāo (李彞超) is young
and unable to defend it,
therefore he is sent
to Yán-Ān (延安)."
Yán-Zhōu (延州)
was Yán-Ān (延安) Commandery.
The matter of Lǐ Cóng-Yǎn (李從曮) is found in the previous volume, Cháng-Xīng (長興) first year;
also, in this year, Gāo Yǔn-Tāo (高允韜) was transferred from Fū (鄜) and Yán (延) to Ān-Guó (安國).
The matter of Wáng Dū (王都) is found in volume 276, Tiān-Chéng (天成) fourth year;
the matter of Lǐ Kuāng-Bīn (李匡賓) is found in the previous volume, first year.
In the fourth month,
Yí-Chāo (彞超) reported that
he was detained by the soldiers and common people
and unable to proceed to his post.
An imperial edict was issued to send an envoy to urge him.
11 Those who spoke on affairs of state requested that tutors be appointed for the imperial princes.
The prime ministers feared Qín-wáng (秦王) Cóng-Róng (從榮)
and dared not appoint anyone,
requesting instead that the king choose himself.
The Registrar of the Qín-wáng (秦王) Mansion and Crown Prince's Junior Supervisor, Wáng Jū-Mǐn (王居敏), recommended the Bīng-Bù-Shì-Láng (兵部侍郎) Liú Zàn (劉瓚) to Cóng-Róng (從榮).
Cóng-Róng (從榮) memorialized to request him.
