it implies the establishment of the Shùnhuà Jìedù in Míngzhōu.
Also, according to Xuē Shǐ,
in the third year of Chángxīng, Chǔzhōu was elevated to Shùnhuà Jūn,
and Qián Yuánxiǎng, the Administrator of Míngzhōu, was made the Jìedùshǐ of this prefecture.
Chǔzhōu at that time belonged to the Yáng clan.
Yuánxiǎng likely garrisoned Míngzhōu while holding the Jìedù seal of Chǔzhōu.)
'Xiǎng'
is pronounced Xǔ-liàng fān.
The Royal Residence
refers to the residence of the King of Wúyuè.
He once became angry at an official
and placed him on an iron bed to brand him,
the stench filling the city.
Wúwáng Yuánguàn sent his general Yǎng Rénquán to Míngzhōu to summon him.
Rénquán's attendants worried that Yuánxiǎng would be difficult to control
and advised him to prepare.
Rénquán refused,
and in ordinary clothes, went directly to the administrative hall.
(The Xìngyuàn contains the surname Yǎng.)
'Quán'
is pronounced Qiě-yuán fān.
'Zào'
is pronounced Qī-dào fān.
'Tīng'
is read as 'tīng.'
trembled, and
consequently returned to Qiántáng,
where he was confined in a separate residence.
(Rénquán was from Húzhōu.)
Qīn Cóng Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ Wáng Réndá had the merit of capturing Wáng Yánbǐng.
He was generous and outspoken,
unafraid to speak his mind on matters.
The Mǐn ruler disliked him,
and once privately said to his attendants:
“Réndá has excessive wisdom,
and while I can still control him,
he is not a minister for the young ruler.”
Now,
he was eventually falsely accused of rebellion
and executed along with his family.
51 Initially,
Mǎ Xīshēng and Xīfàn were born on the same day.
Xīshēng’s mother was Yuán Dé,
and Xīfàn’s mother was Lady Chén.
Xīfàn resented Xīshēng for being established first without yielding,
and upon succeeding to the throne,
he was disrespectful towards Yuán Dé.
According to Ouyáng Xiū’s history,
Chǔ Wáng Yīn had more than ten sons.
His eldest legitimate son Xīzhèn was old and virtuous;
his next sons, Xīshēng and Xīfàn, were born on the same day.
Xīshēng was established because his mother, Lady Yuán, was beautiful and highly favored,
while Xīzhèn abandoned his office to become a Daoist priest.
Xīshēng, by order of seniority, should have yielded to Xīzhèn,
not necessarily to Xīfàn.
Xīfàn often reproached her;
Yuán Dé requested to surrender Xīwàng’s official position so he could become a Daoist priest,
but this was not permitted.
His military post was removed,
and he was made to live in a bamboo hut with a thatched door,
not allowed to participate in his brothers’ banquets.
When Dé died,
Xīwàng died of grief and indignation.
Qīngtài first year
(Jiǎwǔ, 934)
He ascended the throne in the fourth month of this year,
and the era name was changed to Qīngtài.
1 In spring,
first month,
on the day Wùyín,
Emperor Mǐn granted a general amnesty
and changed the era name to Yìngshùn.
It was named with the meaning of "responding to Heaven and conforming to the people,"
which is not how a ruler who inherits the throne should mark his reign.
On the day Rénwǔ,
Kāng Yìchéng, Jìedùshǐ of Héyáng and concurrently Shìwèi Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ, was additionally appointed concurrently Shìzhōng
and Pàn Liùjūn Zhūwèi Shì.
2 Zhū Hóngzhāo and
Féng Yūn were jealous of Shìwèi Mǎjūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ Ān
Yànwēi and Shìwèi Bùjūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ and Zhōngzhèng Jìedùshǐ Zhāng Cóngbīn.
(Wǔdài Huìyào: In the tenth month of Tiānchéng second year,
Shòuzhōu was promoted to Zhōngzhèng Jìedù.
At that time, Shòuzhōu belonged to Wú.
The Later Táng probably promoted it to a military region to bestow it upon their officials as a distant appointment.)
On the day Jiǎshēn,
Yànwēi was sent out as Hùguó Jìedùshǐ,
and Běngshèng Mǎjūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ Zhū Hóngshí replaced him.
Cóngbīn was sent out as Zhāngyì Jìedùshǐ,
and Yánwèi Bùjūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ Huángfǔ Yù replaced him.
The excessive jealousy of Zhū and Féng
was the cause of their swift misfortune.
(Xuē’s History: In the third year of Míngzōng’s Chángxīng reign,
the Shenjié, Shénwēi, Xióngwēi, and Guǎngjié commands, and others, were reorganized into the Left and Right Yǔlín Armies.
Upon Emperor Mǐn’s ascension,
the Left and Right Yǔlín Armies were renamed Yánwèi,
and the Left and Right Lóngwǔ and Shénwǔ Armies were renamed Běngshèng.
Note: Xuē’s History contains the same error as the Huìyào.)
Yànwēi was from Guō;
Yù
was from Zhēndìng.
3 On the day Wùzǐ,
Zhū Hóngzhāo, Shūmìshǐ and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, Féng Yūn, Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Èrpǐn, and Shí Jìngtáng, Hédōng Jìedùshǐ and concurrently Shìzhōng, were all concurrently appointed Zhōngshūlìng.
Yūn, deeming his promotion too rapid,
firmly declined;
on the day Jǐchǒu,
he was changed to concurrently Shìzhōng.
4 On the day Rénchén,
Gāo Cónghuì, Jìedùshǐ of Jīngnán, was enfeoffed as Nánpíng Wáng,
and Mǎ Xīfàn, Jìedùshǐ of Wǔ’ān and Wǔpíng, was enfeoffed as Chǔ Wáng.
5 On the day Jiǎwǔ,
Wú Wáng Yuán Guàn, Jìedùshǐ of Zhènhǎi and Zhèndōng, was enfeoffed as Wúyuè Wáng.
6 Xú Zhīgào of Wú built a private residence in Jīnlíng.
On the day Yǐwèi,
he moved into his private residence,
vacating his official residence to await the Wú ruler.
This Wú ruler was
Yáng Pǔ.
7 Lù Wáng Cóngkē, Jìedùshǐ of Fèngxiáng and concurrently Shìzhōng,
and Shí Jìngtáng had followed Emperor Míng in campaigns since their youth,
gaining renown and achievements
and winning the hearts of the people.
Zhū Hóngzhāo and Féng Yūn, whose positions and prestige were far beneath these two,
suddenly took control of the court
and were jealous of both.
(They were jealous of Cóngkē and Jìngtáng.)
read zhāo.)
Lù Wáng repeatedly sent his wife to visit and serve in the palace;
when Emperor Míng died,
Lù Wáng declined to come, feigning illness,
because the ruler was young and the state was in doubt,
and signs of their mutual suspicion and obstruction were evident.
(This refers to the struggle of petty individuals who tried to conform to the intentions of those in power.)
read shǐ.)
read sì.)
Zhū and Féng did not want him to command the imperial guard.
On the day Jǐhài,
he was sent out as Bózhōu Tuánliànshǐ.
Lù Wáng had a daughter, Huìmíng, who was a nun
in Luòyáng;
she was also summoned into the forbidden palace.
Lù Wáng was thus suspicious and fearful.
(This laid the groundwork for Lù Wáng to raise an army.)
8 Jiǎng Yánhuī of Wú defeated the Mǐn troops at Pǔchéng.
(At the end of the Hàn dynasty, Hànxīng County was established in the southern part of Kuàijī;
Wú renamed it Wúxīng,
making it the seat of Jiàn’ān Commandery.
Suí abolished the commandery and made it a county.
In the first year of Táng Zàichū, Tángxīng County was established by dividing Jiàn’ān County.
In the second year of Tiānshòu, it was renamed Wǔníng.
In the first year of Shénlóng, it was restored to Tángxīng.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo, it was renamed Pǔchéng
and belonged to Jiànzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Pǔchéng was originally the northern village of Dōnghòuguān.
At the end of the Hàn, Hànxīng County was established.
Wú called it Wúxīng.
Táng called it Tángxīng.
Tiānbǎo changed it to Pǔchéng.
There are two ‘pǔ’ (rivers),
and the city is beside a ‘pǔ’,
hence the name Pǔchéng.
Jiǔyù Zhì: It is three hundred thirty *lǐ* northeast of the prefecture.)
read bài.)
Mǐn ruler Lín sent Shàngjūnshǐ Zhāng Yánróu
(Mǐn established Shàngjūnshǐ, Zhōngjūnshǐ, and Xiàjūnshǐ.)
and Yánzōng’s army. On the way,
the soldiers refused to advance,
saying:
“Without Xuē Wénjié,
we cannot defeat the rebels.”
Yánzōng quickly sent a messenger to report this,
and the people of the state were terrified.
The Empress Dowager and Fú Wáng Jìpéng
(Jìpéng was
the eldest son of the Mǐn ruler.)
said, “Wénjié has usurped state power,
unjustly harming the innocent.
Resentment and anger have long festered among all levels of society.
Now that Wú forces are deep within our territory,
and the soldiers refuse to advance,
if the state is overthrown overnight,
what good will keeping Wénjié do!”
Wénjié was also present,
and they argued the pros and cons.
Lín said,
“I can do nothing to you,
you must make your own plans.”
As Wénjié exited,
Jìpéng waited for him outside Qǐshèng Gate,
struck him to the ground with his *hù*,
and sent him to the front in a caged cart.
The townspeople vied to throw bricks and tiles at him.
Wénjié was skilled in prognostication
and claimed that after three days he would be out of danger.
Those escorting him heard this
and doubled their pace, traveling day and night,
arriving in two days.
The soldiers rejoiced upon seeing him,
and tore him to pieces and ate him.
The Mǐn ruler hastily dispatched an amnesty,
but it was too late.
Originally,
Wénjié thought the ancient caged carts were too open and loose,
so he redesigned one,
shaped like a wooden box,
studded with iron spikes
pointing inwards,
which would pierce anyone who moved.
When the cart was finished,
Wénjié himself was the first to enter it.
Shèng Tāo was also executed.
(Shèng Tāo
was a conniver who used matters of ghosts and spirits to ally with Xuē Wénjié.)
Jiǎng Yánhuī attacked Jiànzhōu and was on the verge of success.
Xú Zhīgào considered Yánhuī to be the son-in-law of Wú Tàizǔ (Wú
honored Yáng Xíngmì with the temple name Tàizǔ).
He feared that if Yánhuī captured Jiànzhōu, he would support Méng to attempt a restoration.
Méng was disliked by Xú’s father and son.
This matter began in volume 271, Liáng Jūnwáng Zhēnmíng’s 5th year.
Yánhuī also heard that Mǐn and Wúyuè troops were approaching,
so he withdrew his forces;
the Mǐn people pursued and attacked him,
defeating him.
Many soldiers died.
He blamed Dū Yúhòu Zhāng Chóngjìn
and executed him.
Zhīgào demoted Yánhuī to Yòu Wēiwèi Jiāngjūn
and sent an envoy to seek good relations with Mǐn.
9 In the intercalary month,
Táng Ruì, former Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū, and Chén Yì, Shànbù Lángzhōng and Zhī Zhìgào, were both made Gěishìzhōng
and appointed Shūmì Zhí Xuéshì.
Ruì, with his literary talent, followed the emperor,
serving in three prefectures in the mùmén.
The emperor, in Kāichéng’s 3rd year, garrisoned Xuānwǔ.
The next year, he moved to garrison Hédōng.
In Chángxīng’s 1st year, he moved to garrison Tiānxíong.
Among the generals and aides who possessed talent,
Zhū and Féng dismissed and expelled them all.
Ruì was simple and straightforward by nature.
Zhū and Féng feared that the emperor harbored resentment that might erupt at some point,
so they brought Ruì into their close circle,
and had Chén Yì, their partisan, supervise him.
10 On bǐngwǔ,
the empress was honored as the empress dowager.
The empress
was Míngzōng’s Empress Cáo.
11 Wáng Xīquán and Rèn Hè'ér, slaves of Ānyuǎn Jiédùshǐ Fú Yànchāo,
seeing that the court was embroiled in many affairs,
conspired to kill Yànchāo
and seize Ānzhōu to join Wú.
At night,
they knocked on the door, claiming an urgent dispatch.
Military deadlines were urgent.
Documents that needed to be delivered without delay of even a moment
were called urgent dispatches.
“Dì”
refers to postal transmission.
The "dì" here
means that postal stations transmit in succession to reach their destination.
The two slaves killed him,
then, using Yànchāo’s name, summoned the generals,
and killed anyone who did not comply with them.
On jǐyǒu dawn,
Fùshǐ Lǐ Duān led the provincial troops to attack and execute them,
along with their partisans.
“Fùshǐ”
refers to Jiédù Fùshǐ.
“Shuài”
is pronounced “lǜ.”
12 On jiǎyín,
Wáng Shú was made Tàihòu.
The text does not say
“zūn” (honored)
but says
“yǐ” (made),
which the historian uses to indicate Mǐndì’s slight regard for Wáng Shú.
13 The Shǔ generals and officials urged Shǔwáng Zhīxiáng to claim emperorship.
On jǐsì,
Zhīxiáng ascended to the imperial throne in Chéngdū.
Mèng Zhīxiáng,
courtesy name Bǎoyìn,
was a native of Xíngzhōu Lónggāng.

Hòu Táng Tàizǔ
Qīngtài 1st year
(jiǎwǔ, 934)
1 In the second month,
on guǐyǒu,
the Shǔ ruler appointed Wǔtài Jiédùshǐ Zhào Jìliáng as Sīkōng concurrently Ménxià Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
retaining his position as Jiédùshǐ.
Zhào Jìliáng thus became a founding minister who helped Mèng Shǔ establish its rule.
2 Many Wú people were unwilling to relocate the capital.
The discussion of Wú relocating its capital
began in the previous volume, Míngzōng Chángxīng’s 4th year.
“If the sovereign moves west,
you must again go east.
‘Dū Yāyá’
refers to Dū Yāyá of the Zhènhǎi and Níngguó two prefectures.
Shēngzhōu is west of Yángzhōu,
and Yángzhōu is east of Shēngzhōu.
This means that if the Wú ruler moves west to Jīnlíng,
Xú Zhīgào must garrison Dū Jiāngdū in the east.
‘Fù’
is pronounced ‘fú yòu.’
Moreover, this goes against the will of the multitude.”
On bǐngzǐ,
the Wú ruler sent Sòng Qíqiū to Jīnlíng
to instruct Zhīgào to abandon the plan to relocate the capital.
Previously,
Zhīgào had long harbored the ambition of receiving the imperial abdication.
However, as the Wú ruler had committed no moral faults,
he feared that the hearts of the people would be displeased,
and wished to wait for the heir-apparent.
Sòng Qíqiū also agreed with this.
One day,
Zhīgào looked in the mirror and plucked a white hair,
sighing,
“The state is at peace, but I am old,
what can be done?”
Zhōu Zōng understood his intention
and requested to go to Jiāngdū to subtly suggest the abdication to the Wú ruler
and also to inform Qíqiū.
Qíqiū, seeing Zōng had preempted him,
resented him.
He sent an envoy to rush to Jīnlíng,
hand-writing a strong remonstrance,
arguing that the time and circumstances were not yet right.
Zhīgào was astonished.
Xú Zhīgào did not expect Sòng Qíqiū to hold a differing view,
and was suddenly confronted with his differing opinion,
hence his astonishment.
“Shǐ”
is pronounced “shū lì.”
When Qíqiū arrived,
he requested to execute Zōng to apologize to the Wú ruler,
whereupon Zōng was demoted to Chízhōu Fùshǐ.
“Chízhōu Fùshǐ”
refers to Chízhōu Tuánliàn Fùshǐ.
Jiédù Fùshǐ Lǐ Jiànxūn and Xíngjūn Sīmǎ Xú Jiè and others repeatedly presented Zhīgào’s achievements,
arguing that he should fulfill the popular wish early.
Zōng was recalled and reinstated as Dū Yāyá.
Zhīgào thenceforth distanced himself from Qíqiū.
This laid the groundwork for Sòng Qíqiū to suffer misfortune by obstructing the ruler’s intentions.
Alas!
As a minister,
at the juncture of a dynastic change,
one must be careful not to claim credit for one’s achievements.
Xún Wénruò died by poison because of this.
Liú Mùzhī fell ill and died because of this.
Fàn Yún feared being too late and sought quick recovery from illness,
even at the cost of shortening his life, without a moment’s hesitation.
Sòng Qíqiū’s resentment of Zhōu Zōng
is merely a minor and superficial example.
3 Zhū Hóngzhāo and Féng Yūn did not want Shí Jìngtáng to remain in Tàiyuán for long.
They also wanted to summon Mèng Hànqióng,
who temporarily administered the Tiānxíong military headquarters, as seen in the previous volume from last year.
On jǐmǎo,
Fàn Yánguāng, the Chéngdé Jiédùshǐ, was transferred to be Tiānxíong Jiédùshǐ,
replacing Hànqióng.
Lùwáng Cóngkē was transferred to be Hédōng Jiédùshǐ,
concurrently Běidū Liúshǒu.
Shí Jìngtáng was transferred to be Chéngdé Jiédùshǐ.
None of these appointments were made by issuing imperial edicts;
instead, each was sent with an envoy carrying a xuān to supervise their departure to the garrisons.
“Xuān”
refers to documents issued by the Shūmìyuàn.
Later, during the reign of Hàn Yǐndì, Guō Wēi, as head of the Shūmìyuàn, replaced the Xījīng Liúshǒu.
Was this not due to familiarity with such practices that it was not considered unusual?
Among the Xībān, there were Dà Shǐchén and Xiǎo Shǐchén.
“Jiān”
is pronounced “gǔ xián.”
4 The Wú ruler issued an edict for Xú Zhīgào to return to his official residence.
Xú Zhīgào had vacated his official residence to await the Wú ruler, as seen in the previous volume for this year.
On jiǎshēn,
a large fire broke out in Jīnlíng.
On yǐyǒu,
another fire occurred.
Zhīgào suspected an uprising
and mustered his troops for self-defense.
5 Lù Wáng 既與朝廷猜阻，
朝廷又命 Yáng Wáng Cóngzhāng 權知 Fèngxiáng。
Cóngzhāng 性粗率樂禍，
前代 Ān Chónghuì 鎮 Hézhōng，
手殺之；
見二百七十七卷 Míngzōng Chángxīng 二年。
尤惡之，
欲拒命則兵弱糧少，
不知所為，
謀於將佐，
皆曰：
「主上富於春秋，
政事出於 Zhū、Féng，
大王功名震主，
離鎮必無全理，
不可受也。 」
言不可受代。
Suí Kāihuáng 十六年置 Dīhé Xiàn，
屬 Bóhǎi Jùn，
Táng 屬 Dìzhōu。
Jiǔyù Zhì: Dīhé Xiàn 在 Dìzhōu 西南八十里。
註云：漢都尉 Xǔ Shāng 鑿此河近海，
故以 Shāng 為名，
後人加
焉。
「今道過京師，
當何向為便？ 」
發此問以觀衆意。
「君命召，
不俟駕。
引 Lúnyǔ Kǒngzǐ 之言。
又何疑焉！
諸人凶謀，
不可從也。 」
衆哂之。
言當過京師臨大行之喪，
然後赴 Tàiyuán 也。
Mǎ Yìnsūn 之言，
儒生守經學之言也。
是時勸 Lù Wáng 拒命者以其言為不達時變，
故相與哂之。
哂，
矢忍翻。
笑不壞顏為哂。
言
「Zhū Hóngzhāo 等乘先帝疾亟，
殺長立少，
謂殺 Cóngróng 而立帝也。
長，
知兩翻。
少，
詩照翻。
別疏骨肉，
動搖藩垣，
謂易置 Shí Jìngtáng 及己也。
朝，
直遙翻；
下同。
別，
彼列翻。
今 Cóngkē 將入朝以清君側之惡，
而力不能獨辦，
願乞靈鄰藩以濟之。 」
Lù Wáng 以西都留守 Wáng Sītóng 當東出之道，
自 Fèngxiáng 趣 Luòyáng，
道出 Cháng'ān。
遣推官 Hǎo Xǔ、押牙 Zhū Tíngyì 等相繼詣 Cháng'ān，
說以利害，
餌以美妓，
不從則令就圖之。
Sītóng 謂將吏曰：
「吾受 Míngzōng 大恩，
Wáng Sītóng 自 Yān 降 Jìn，
Liáng、Jìn 相距，
Sītóng 未嘗有戰功，
Míngzōng 時以久次為節度使，
故自言受大恩。
借使事成而榮，
猶為一時之叛臣，
況事敗而辱，
流千古之醜跡乎！ 」
遂執 Xǔ 等，
以狀聞。
時 Lù Wáng 使者多為鄰道所執，
不則依阿操兩端，
惟 Lǒngzhōu 防禦使 Xiānglǐ Jīn 傾心附之，
Lǒngzhōu 東至 Fèngxiáng 一百五十里。
Xuē Wényù 由此為 Lù Wáng 所信用。
Bìngzhōu 人也。
朝廷議討 Fèngxiáng。
Kāng Yìchéng 不欲出外，
恐失軍權，
Míngzōng 以 Kāng Yìchéng 為朴忠，
豈知其陰狡乃爾邪！
以羽林都指揮使 Hóu Yì 為行營馬步軍都虞候。
Sòng Bái 曰：Chángxīng 二年二月，
敕衞軍神捷、神威、雄武及魏府廣捷已下指揮改為左、右羽林，
置四十指揮，
每十指揮立為一軍，
每一軍置都指揮使一人，
兼分為左、右廂。
辭
不行；
Hóu Yì 曾經 Yèdū 之變，
故爾。
出為 Shāngzhōu 刺史。
Luòyáng 至 Shāngzhōu 八百八十六里。
Xīnmǎo
以 Wáng Sītóng 為西面行營馬步軍都部署，
前此用兵置帥，
率以都招討使命之。
Zhuāngzōng 時，
Míngzōng 為北面招討使以禦 Qìdān，
Fáng Zhīwēn 為副都部署，
當時為都部署者必有其人。
又 Mèng Zhīxiáng 拒 Dǒng Zhāng，
以 Zhào Tíngyǐn 為行營都部署，
後遂以為元帥之任，
Sòng Shì 建國之初猶因而用之。

Zhāowǔ Army's Lìzhōu

Xú Zhīgào manufactured weapons.
On the day *bǐngzǐ*,

After Dào had taken up a regional post,

When there were matters that needed to be changed,

The *Classic of Rites* says: The father of one's wife is called *hūn* (昏),

Marriage takes place at dusk (*hūn* 昏)

The son-in-law's family
is that on which the daughter relies;
hence it is called *yīn*.
When the two fathers address each other,

"更" (gēng),

From this, disputes often arose,

the seventh month,

Ráo's son.

[Someone said:] "Your Majesty is the father of all under Heaven;

"元" (yuán),

However, he was not involved in any affairs.

Zhīgào gave him the Southern Garden.
Yuáng Wáng Cóngzhāng, Jìedùshǐ of Hùguó,
and Jīng Wáng Cóngmǐn, Jìedùshǐ of Guīdé,
were both dismissed from their posts and resided in private mansions in Luòyáng.

Guīdé Jūn was
Sòngzhōu.

"È" [detest],
is pronounced wū lù fān.
In the midst of wine,
the Emperor looked at the two princes and said:

Shǔ established the Yǒngpíng Army in Yǎzhōu,
appointing Sūn Hànsháo as Jìedùshǐ.
Zhāng Qiánzhāo was again appointed Shānnán Xīdào Jìedùshǐ and Tóng Píngzhāngshì;

Sūn Hànsháo went to Yǎzhōu,

At the end of the Táng dynasty, the Yǒngpíng Army was established in Qióngzhōu,
later moving to Yǎzhōu.
It was abolished by Zhuāngzōng when he extinguished Shǔ,
and now Hòu Shǔ re-established it.
The Shǔ ruler had been suffering from a stroke for over a year,
and by this time it worsened.
On the jiǎzǐ day,
he established his son Rénzàn, Jìedùshǐ of Dōngchuān, Tóng Píngzhāngshì, and Commander of the Imperial Guards (Ma and Foot), as Crown Prince,
and he also supervised the state.

He summoned Sīkōng Tóng Píngzhāngshì Zhào Jìliáng, Wǔxìn Jìedùshǐ Lǐ Rénhǎn, Bǎoníng Jìedùshǐ Zhào Tíngyǐn, Shūmìshǐ Wáng Chǔhuí, Běngshèng Kònghè Dūzhīhuīshǐ Zhāng Gōngduó, and Fèngluán Sùwèi Zhīhuī Fùshǐ Hóu Hóngshí, to receive his last will and assist in governance.
He passed away that evening,
but the news of his death was kept secret.
Wáng Chǔhuí secretly opened the Yìxīng Gate at night to inform Zhào Jìliáng.
Chǔhuí wept incessantly,
but Jìliáng sternly said:
"Now, powerful generals hold military power
and are intently watching for changes in the situation.
We should quickly establish the heir to cut off their ambitions.
'Powerful generals'
refers to Lǐ Hǎnzī, Lǐ Zhào, and others.
'Jī' [ambition]
is pronounced yì.
'Yú' [covet]
is pronounced yú."
Chǔhuí wiped away his tears and thanked him.
Jìliáng instructed Chǔhuí to see Lǐ Rénhǎn,
to first ascertain his intentions before informing him.
When Chǔhuí arrived at Rénhǎn's residence,
Rénhǎn came out prepared for defense,
so Chǔhuí did not tell him the truth.
History states that Lǐ Rénhǎn was already among those like Zhào Jìliáng.
On the bǐngyín day,
the imperial will was proclaimed,
ordering Crown Prince Rénzàn to change his name to Chǎng.
On the dīngmǎo day,
he ascended the imperial throne.
Chǎng was
the third son of the Shǔ ruler.
"Gēng" [change]
is pronounced gōng héng fān.
Initially, the Emperor, noting Wáng Méi's inaccurate reporting of funds in the Zǔocáng treasury,
an event seen in the fourth month above,

is pronounced xián biàn fān.
ordered auditor Gāo Yánshǎng to thoroughly examine and scrutinize the accounts.
These were all long-standing arrears and debts,
which corrupt officials kept so they could profit from demanding and extorting payments.

Xù fully reported the situation,
and requested that those that could be collected be promptly urged,
and those that certainly could not be repaid be all exempted.
Hán Zhāoyìn strongly argued for the convenience of this.

on the gēngwǔ day,
an edict was issued to remit 3.38 million in overdue taxes from the Hùbù and various circuits from before Chángxīng,
which only cluttered the account books,
all were exempted and not to be collected.
The poor people greatly rejoiced,

On the xīnwèi day,
Yáo Yǐ was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Suǒ Zìtōng, Commander of the Right Lóngwǔ Army, regarding the dispute over Hézhōng,
seen in volume 277, Míngzōng Chángxīng First Year,
on the wùzǐ day, after returning from court and passing through Luòyáng,
threw himself into the water and died.
The Luò River flowed through the imperial city,
so Zìtōng, passing it after court,
threw himself into the water.
This caused great shock;
he was posthumously granted Tàiwèi.
On the bǐngshēn day,
Zhào Fèng, former An'guó Jìedùshǐ and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was appointed Crown Prince's Tàibǎo.
In the ninth month, on the guǐmǎo day,
an edict ordered Fèngxiáng to send additional troops to garrison Dōng'ān Zhèn to guard against Shǔ.
Dōng'ān Zhèn should be on the western border of Fèngxiáng;
since Shǔ had left the pass and recaptured the lands of Jiē and Chéng,
additional troops were sent to guard against it.
Lǐ Rénhǎn, Shǔ's Wèishèng Zhūjūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ and Wǔxìn Jìedùshǐ, relying on his status as an old general with meritorious service
and having received a dying entrustment,
sought to take charge of the Six Armies.
He sent the advanced memorial clerk Sòng Cónghuì to convey his intentions to the Shūmìyuàn,
and also went to the Xuéshìyuàn to spy on the drafting of edicts.
The Shǔ ruler, left with no choice,
on the jiǎyín day, added the title of Jiān Zhōngshūlìng to Rénhǎn,
and put him in charge of the Six Armies;
he appointed Zhào Tíngyǐn, Zǔokuāngshèng Dūzhīhuīshǐ and Bǎoníng Jìedùshǐ, as Jiān Shìzhōng
and his deputy.
On the jǐwèi day,
Yúnzhōu reported a Khitan invasion.

Jìngtáng reported that Yáng Tán, Jìedùshǐ of Zhènwǔ, had engaged the Khitan on the border
and repelled them.
Lǐ Zhào, Shǔ's Fèngluán Sùwèi Dūzhīhuīshǐ and Zhāowǔ Jìedùshǐ Jiān Shìzhōng, upon hearing of the Shǔ ruler's ascension,
hesitated
and did not promptly come to court.
He stayed in Hánzhōu, feasting and drinking with relatives for over ten days.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the gēngwǔ day,
he finally arrived in Chéngdū.
Claiming a leg ailment,
he used a cane to enter court and meet the Shǔ ruler,
but did not bow.
Lǐ Zhào's arrogance towards the young ruler
also stemmed from a strong-willed, stubborn military man,
unlearned and ignorant,
thereby bringing disaster upon himself.
On the wùyín day,
Lǐ Yú, Zuǒ Púyè, Ménxià Shìláng, and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was dismissed from his concurrent posts;

Upon hearing of Xù's dismissal as prime minister, the Sānsī officials
all congratulated each other,
not a single one accompanied him home.
This was because Xù had memorialized to exempt overdue taxes from various circuits,
depriving officials of means to profit from collecting them.
Zhāng Gōngduó, Shǔ's Běngshèng Kònghè Dūzhīhuīshǐ, along with medical official Hán Jìxūn, Fēngdé Kùshǐ Hán Bǎozhēn, and Chájǐu Kùshǐ Ān Sīqiān, had all served the Shǔ ruler in his princely residence,
and had long resented Lǐ Rénhǎn.
They jointly slandered him,
claiming Rénhǎn harbored ulterior motives.
The Shǔ ruler ordered Jìxūn and others to conspire with Zhào Jìliáng and Zhào Tíngyǐn,
and when Rénhǎn came to court, he commanded warriors to seize and kill him.
Zhào Tíngyǐn and Lǐ Rénhǎn had a deep-seated grievance and animosity dating back to their quarrel over merit after conquering Dōngchuān.
When Rénhǎn sought to take charge of the Six Armies,
the Shǔ ruler appointed Tíngyǐn as his deputy,
precisely to guard against Rénhǎn.
Rénhǎn's failure to realize this,
his obstinacy and perversity,
made his death deserved.
However, Zhào Tíngyǐn ultimately also could not escape the slanders of the close attendants;
his good fortune was to die in his bed.
On the guǐwèi day,
an edict was issued proclaiming his crimes,
and he, his son Jìhóng, and several others including Sòng Cónghuì, were all executed.
On that day,
Lǐ Zhào put down his cane and bowed.
Lǐ Zhào served Mèng Zhīxiáng,
and during the rebellion of Dǒng Zhāng,
he stood idly by, observing who would win.
After Dǒng Zhāng's death,
Zhào should have been executed,
but Mèng Zhīxiáng, recalling his service in Jiànzhōu,
did not hold it against him.
However, when he served the young ruler,
he relinquished his post and came to court,
arrogant and refusing to bow—
who could tolerate such behavior!
The moment he saw Lǐ Rénhǎn's execution,
he immediately put down his cane and bowed.
Such initial arrogance followed by later deference—
was it not difficult to seek forgiveness in this way!
Zīzhì Tōngjiàn records this
as a warning to military men who rely on their achievements to become arrogant and perverse.

Having exhaustively examined the Xīn Táng Zhì (新唐志) and Jiù Táng Zhì (舊唐志), as well as the Jiǔyù Túzhì (九域圖志) and Huányǔ Jì (寰宇記),
none of them record the reason for Yuánzhōu’s (源州) establishment or its location.
Ōu Shǐ Zhífāng Kǎo (歐史職方考) says: Regarding prefectures and counties,
all those that were established during the Táng (唐) and abolished during the Five Dynasties,
or those established during the Five Dynasties and still exist today, and those counties whose jurisdiction was transferred and remains so today,
should all be listed to serve as a reference for official gazetteers;
as for the rest that were once established and then abolished,
or once had their jurisdiction changed and then reverted,
they are not worth recording.
From this, we know that Yuánzhōu (源州) was likely established by Shǔ (蜀) and soon abolished,
which is why there is no record of it.
When Tóngguāng (同光) conquered Shǔ (蜀),
sixty-four prefectures were obtained,
but only fifty-three prefectures are mentioned in the Zhífāng Kǎo (職方考).
Prefectures like Yuánzhōu (源州) were likely among those sixty-four prefectures.
According to Xuē Shǐ (薛史),
Hòu Shǔ’s (後蜀) Pān Rénsì (潘仁嗣) was appointed Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Wǔdìng (武定), and also Observer and Commissioner of Agricultural Colonies for Yuán (源) and Bì (壁) prefectures;
when the Zhōu (周) army attacked Qín (秦) and Fèng (鳳),
Mèng Yíyè (孟貽業) garrisoned Pínglì (平利) to reinforce Bāo (褒) and Yuán (源),
indicating that the Shǔ (蜀) established Yuánzhōu (源州) under the Wǔdìng Jūnjìedù (武定軍節度).

Faced with Your Majesty's era of reform,

while those in higher positions lacking strategic ability should be demoted to lower ranks.
For civil officials,
Your servant requests that topics for policy questions be issued from the palace, and the Chūngshū Lìng and prime ministers conduct face-to-face interviews.

On *wùyín* 戊寅,
an edict ordered Zhīyǐn Zhīyǐn to be executed.
the Mǐn Mǐn ruler had a favorite eunuch named Guī Shǒumíng Guī Shǒumíng,
who had access to his sleeping quarters.
In his later years, the Mǐn Mǐn ruler suffered from a stroke.
Empress Chén Chén had a private affair with Shǒumíng Shǒumíng and Lǐ Kěyīn Lǐ Kěyīn, Commissioner of the Bureau of Craftsmen.
Everyone in the country detested them,
but no one dared to speak.
Kě Yīn had once slandered the Imperial City Commissioner, Lǐ Fǎng, to the Ruler of Mǐn.
The empress's relative, Chén Kuāngshèng, was rude to Fúwáng Jìpéng.
Fǎng and Jìpéng both resented him.
The Ruler of Mǐn was gravely ill,
and Jìpéng showed signs of pleasure.
Fǎng believed the Ruler of Mǐn would surely not recover.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day of Jǐmǎo,
he ordered several strong men to strike Lǐ Kěyīn with white cudgels,
killing him.
Both the court and the populace were shocked.
On Gēngchén,
the Ruler of Mǐn's illness slightly abated.
(The character "間" is to be read as written.)
The Ruler of Mǐn, despite his illness, attended court
and questioned the circumstances of Kěyīn's death.
Fǎng, in fear, withdrew.
A moment later,
he led his troops, beating drums and shouting, into the palace.
The Ruler of Mǐn heard of the rebellion
and hid under the Jiǔlóng canopy.
(The Ruler of Mǐn had ordered a craftsman to make a Jiǔlóng canopy.)
The people sang about it, saying:
"Who says the Jiǔlóng canopy
only shelters one Guīláng?"
(Guīláng
refers to Shǒumíng.)
The Ruler of Mǐn was still twisting and not yet dead.
The palace attendants, unable to bear his suffering,
finished him off.
(They ended his life.)
(The character "為"
is pronounced yú wěi fān.)
Jìtāo had always been hostile towards Jìpéng.
On Xīnsì,
Jìpéng claimed to act as regent by order of the Empress Dowager.
On that very day,
he ascended the imperial throne.
(The Empress Dowager
was Lín's mother, Lady Huáng.)
(Jìpéng
was Lín's eldest son.)
He posthumously named his father Qí Sù Míng Xiào Huángdì,
with the temple name Huìzōng.
After this, he styled himself Provisional Commissioner of Fújiàn,
dispatched envoys to present a memorial to Táng,
and granted a general amnesty throughout his territory.
He appointed Lǐ Chūnyàn as Xian.
At first,
Mǐn Huìzōng married Qīngyuǎn Gōngzhǔ, daughter of the Ruler of Hàn.
(Guǎngzhōu has Qīngyuǎn Xiàn.)
(The Táng Zhì does not mention Mǐnqīng Xiàn,
so it was probably first established by the Wáng family.)
(The Jiǔyù Zhì says Mǐnqīng Xiàn belongs to Fúzhōu,
150 *lǐ* northwest of the prefecture.)
(Sòng Bái said: In the first year of Táng Zhēnyuán (785), ten townships of Hòuguān Xiàn were carved out to form Méixī Chǎng.
In the first year of Liáng Qiánhuà (911), it was changed to Mǐnqīng Xiàn.)
(The character "番"
is pronounced Pān.)
The Ruler of Hàn bestowed upon him a grand residence,
and his allowances were very generous.
He frequently questioned him about Mǐn affairs.
Yányù did not answer.
Upon retiring,
he said to others:
"To leave Mǐn and speak of Mǐn,
to leave Yuè and speak of Yuè—
if one lives in another's palace,
how can one do that?!"
The Ruler of Hàn heard of this and considered him worthy,
appointing him as Internal Regular Attendant,
and ordering him to investigate affairs of various departments.
Yányù, hearing that Huìzōng had been assassinated,
sought to return,
but was not permitted.
He wore plain mourning clothes and wept facing his homeland for three days.
(History states that Lín Yányù did not forget his former lord.)
31 Gāo Cónghuì, Jīngnán Military Commissioner,
was discerning and understanding,
treated worthy scholars with respect,
and entrusted authority to Liáng Zhèn,
treating him like an elder brother.
Zhèn often addressed Cónghuì as "Lángjūn."
(Disciples and former officials refer to their lord's son as "Lángjūn.")
(Liáng Zhèn served Gāo Jìxīng,
Cónghuì's father,
therefore he called Cónghuì "Lángjūn.")
Chǔwáng Xīfàn was fond of extravagance and luxury,
and conversationalists vied in praising his grandeur.
Cónghuì said to his subordinates:
"Someone like King Mǎ can truly be called a great man."
Sūn Guāngxiàn replied:
"Between the Son of Heaven and feudal lords,
there are differences in rites.
That immature boy's arrogance, extravagance, and usurpation of authority
satisfy him for a moment,
but he does not plan for the long term.
His ruin and demise are imminent.
Is he really worth admiring?"
Cónghuì pondered for a long time and then understood,
saying:
"Your words are right."
Another day,
he said to Liáng Zhèn:
"I reflect that the provisions I have enjoyed throughout my life
have indeed been excessive."
Thereupon, he discarded his luxuries
and found joy in classics and history.
He reduced punishments and lightened taxes,
and his territory became peaceful.
Liáng Zhèn said:
"The late king treated me like a commoner friend
and entrusted his heir to me.
(The 'late king'
refers to Gāo Jìxīng.)
(The 'heir'
refers to Cónghuì.)
(The character "屬"
is pronounced zhī yù fān.)
I have not allowed his enterprise to fall.
I am old now,
and I will no longer serve anyone."
So he firmly requested to retire.
Cónghuì could not keep him,
so he built a house for him on Tǔzhōu.
Zhèn wore a crane-feather cloak,
styled himself the Hermit of Jīngtái,
and whenever he visited the government office,
he rode a yellow ox to the administrative hall.
Cónghuì occasionally visited his home
and gave him very generous gifts throughout the seasons.
From then on, he entrusted all political affairs to Sūn Guāngxiàn.
Your servant Guāng says: Sūn Guāngxiàn saw the subtle beginnings and was able to admonish,
and Gāo Cónghuì heard good advice and was able to change.
Gāo Cónghuì's admiration for Mǎ Xīfàn
was the sprouting of a luxurious inclination,
but Sūn Guāngxiàn spoke strongly to prevent it in its infancy.
Gāo Cónghuì, acting on Guāngxiàn's words,
discarded his luxuries and delighted in classics and history,
pondering how to enrich the people and secure the territory.
This is changing for the better.
Liáng Zhèn assisted Gāo's father and son,
and was able to preserve their state.
This is his achievement.
How could there be the ruin of a state, the downfall of a family, or the loss of one's person?
32 Wú granted Xú Zhīgào the titles of Grand Chancellor, Shàngfù, Grand Tutor, Grand Prime Minister, and Grand Marshal.
He was advanced to the title of Qíwáng and accorded special rites.
Shēng, Rùn, Xuān, Chí, Shè, Cháng, Jiāng, Ráo, Xìn, and Hǎi—these ten prefectures—were designated as the State of Qí.
(Upon examining the ten prefectures conferred upon Xú Zhīgào,
from Rùn, following the Jiāng River upstream to Jiāng, it would sever the waist and backbone of the Wú kingdom.
Jiāngdū, along with Hóng and È,
would no longer be organically connected.)
(From Cháng and Rùn, sweeping along the sea boundary to Huái, to include Hǎizhōu,
there would be a tendency to encompass the entire Wú kingdom.)
(His strategic plan was considered clever by himself.
At that time, if the people of the whole Wú had given their allegiance to Zhīgào,
why would he have needed to do this before usurping the throne?)
(The character "歙"
is pronounced shū shè fān.)
Zhīgào declined the special rites.
33 Lǐ Fǎng, Imperial City Commissioner and Judicial Officer of the Six Armies and various Guards of Mǐn,
monopolized court governance.
He secretly maintained a retinue of sworn followers.
Mǐnzhǔ Chǎng, along with Gǒngchén Commander Lín Yánhào and others, plotted against him.
Yánhào and others feigned allegiance to Fǎng,
and Fǎng trusted them without suspicion.
In the eleventh month,
on Rénzǐ,
Fǎng entered the court.
Yánhào and others had hundreds of guards lying in wait in the inner hall.
They seized and beheaded him,
displaying his head at the court gate.
Over a thousand of Fǎng's troops attacked the Yìngtiān Gate with white cudgels,
but failed to breach it.
They burned the Qǐshèng Gate,
seized Fǎng's head, and fled to Wúyuè.
An imperial edict was issued, exposing Fǎng's crimes of regicide and killing Jìtāo, etc.,
and making it known to the court and the populace.
(This was an edict by the Ruler of Mǐn.)
Yè Qiáo of Yǒngtài, the judicial officer of the Six Armies, was appointed Internal Palace Grandee and Participant in Government Affairs.
(In the second year of Táng Yìzōng's Xiántōng reign (861), Yǒngtài Xiàn was established by dividing Liánjiāng and Mǐn,
and it belonged to Fúzhōu.)
(The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is 350 *lǐ* southwest of the prefecture.)
(The Fúzhōu Tújīng says: Yǒngtài Xiàn was established in the second year of Táng Yǒngtài (766),
named after the reign title.)
(The character "翹"
is pronounced qí xiāo fān.)
Qiáo was erudite and straightforward.
Mǐn Huìzōng promoted him to be Advisor to the Prince of Fú.
Mǐn Zhǔ Chǎng was initially enfeoffed as the Prince of Fú.
He was of great help.
In the palace, he was called
"Guówēng".
After Chǎng inherited the throne,
he became arrogant and indulgent,
and no longer discussed state affairs with Qiáo.
One day,
as Chǎng was attending to matters,
Qiáo, dressed in a Taoist robe, passed through the courtyard and was about to leave.
Chǎng called him back,
bowed to him,
and said,
"Military and state affairs are pressing,
and I have not seen you for a long time.
This is my fault."
Qiáo kowtowed and said,
"This old official's guidance has been ineffective,
leading to Your Majesty having no commendable good deeds since ascending the throne.
I request to retire."
Chǎng said,
"The late emperor entrusted me to you.
If policies are not good,
you should speak your mind fully.
Why would you abandon me and leave!"
He generously bestowed gold and silk,
comforted him, and ordered him to resume his post.
Chǎng's primary wife was Lady Lǐ of Liángguó,
daughter of Tóng Píngzhāngshì Mǐn.
Chǎng favored Lǐ Chūnyàn.
Chǎng asked for Chūnyàn from Empress Chén.
(See above, June.)
The character 嬖 (bì) is pronounced
'bēi yì' in fanqie,
and also 'bó jì' in fanqie.
Qiáo remonstrated, saying,
"The Lady is the late emperor's nephew by marriage,
formally betrothed with propriety.
How can you abandon her for a new favorite!"
Chǎng was displeased
and thenceforth distanced himself from Qiáo.
Not long after,
Qiáo again submitted a memorial regarding state affairs.
Chǎng wrote on the bottom of the paper, saying,
"A single leaf drifts with the wind into the imperial canal."
He then dismissed him to Yǒngtài.
Lù Zhèn's Jiǔguó Zhì states: Yè Qiáo was dismissed and returned to Yǒngchūn.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì,
Quánzhōu has Yǒngchūn County,
and Fúzhōu has Yǒngtài County.
It is unknown which is correct.
The Emperor praised Mǎ Quánjié's achievements.
These were the achievements of repelling the Shu army and saving Jīnzhōu.
Liú Yánlǎng sought bribes,
but Quánjié had nothing to give him.
Yánlǎng wanted to remove Quánjié as the Prefect of Jiàngzhōu,
and the public outcry was immense.
The Emperor heard of this.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
he appointed Quánjié as the Acting Military Governor of Hénghǎi.
The Emperor had heard of it,
but did not punish Liú Yánlǎng.
Rewarding the good and punishing the evil,
this is why Guō perished.
In the twelfth month,
on the day Rénshēn,
Hán Zhāoyìn, who was Zhōngshū Shìláng, Tóng Píngzhāngshì, and concurrently Shūmìshǐ, was appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì
and concurrently Jìedùshǐ of Hùguó.
On the day Yǐyǒu,
Fēng Dào, formerly Jìedùshǐ of Kuāngguó and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, was appointed Sīkōng.
At that time, there had been no regular appointment to the Three Dukes for a long time.
Since the period of chaos and disorder, there were those who concurrently held or nominally held the Three Dukes positions with other offices,
but none were regularly appointed.
Lú Wénjì wanted to make him responsible for sacrifices and sweeping.
According to the Suí system: the Three Dukes participated in deliberating major state affairs.
In sacrifices, the Tàiwèi offered the second libation,
the Sītú presented the sacrificial meats,
and the Sīkōng performed sweeping.
Lú Wénjì did not investigate deeply
and thus believed sweeping to be the Sīkōng's specific duty.
The character 朝 (cháo) is pronounced
'zhí yáo' in fanqie.
"The Sīkōng
is responsible for sweeping.
What do I fear?"
Afterward, Wénjì realized he was wrong
and stopped.
Historians say that although the Later Táng claimed to inherit the old institutions of the Táng,
its literary documents were all deficient.
The Mǐn Zhǔ bestowed the title Tiānshī upon the Dòngzhēn Xiānshēng Chén Shǒuyuán.
He trusted and valued him greatly,
even to the extent that changes in generals and prime ministers,
punishments,
and selections for office
were all discussed with him.
Shǒuyuán accepted bribes and made requests,
and his words were always followed.
His gate was like a marketplace.
Punctuation by Dèng Guǎngmíng, reviewed by Niè Chóngqí
